title: The IP map for software
oneLiner: Software is protected by four overlapping rights and by contract, and each one attaches to a different layer of the product.
keyPoints: Software is protected by four overlapping rights (copyright, patent, trade secret and trademark) and by contract. Each attaches to a different part of a product, lasts for a different time and fails in a different way.

**Copyright:** Under the Copyright Act (17 U.S.C.), code and documentation are protected once [[fixed|fixation]] in a tangible medium, but not the ideas, methods or functions behind them (17 U.S.C. § 102(a), (b)).

**Patent:** The Patent Act (35 U.S.C.) covers a new and useful process, machine, manufacture or composition of matter, for a term ending 20 years from filing (35 U.S.C. §§ 101, 154(a)(2)). Software claims face eligibility challenges first.

**Trade secret:** The Defend Trade Secrets Act (DTSA) protects information that the owner keeps secret and that has economic value from not being generally known (18 U.S.C. § 1839(3)). California's version works the same way (Cal. Civ. Code § 3426.1(d)).

**Trademark:** The Lanham Act (15 U.S.C.) protects names and logos used in commerce to identify a source. It does not protect the code behind them, because the Act covers marks that identify a source (15 U.S.C. §§ 1125(a), 1127; drafting inference).

**Contract:** Licences, NDAs and terms of use decide who may copy, change or disclose the code and data. Open source licences are copyright licences with terms attached, and some, such as Apache-2.0, add a patent licence (Apache-2.0 s.2, s.3).

deepDive.heading: Four rights, four different triggers
deepDive.lede: Each right arises in its own way and fails in its own way, so one right rarely covers a product on its own.

visual.caption: How each right arises, what it lasts for and what it does not reach.

items.label: Copyright
items.note: Arises on fixation; suit on a U.S. work needs registration (17 U.S.C. § 411(a))

items.label: Patent
items.note: Examined and granted; a right to exclude for 20 years from filing (35 U.S.C. § 154(a))

items.label: Trade secret
items.note: No registration; the owner must take reasonable measures to keep it secret (18 U.S.C. § 1839(3)(A))

items.label: Trademark
items.note: Rights follow bona fide use in trade; they end on abandonment (15 U.S.C. § 1127)

items.label: Contract
items.note: Binds the parties who sign or accept it, and no one else

points: **Copyright:** Protects the expression in code, not the function it performs. Copying or adapting that expression infringes (17 U.S.C. §§ 102(b), 106(1), (2)).
**Patent:** Stops anyone from making, using, offering to sell, selling or importing the patented invention without authority (35 U.S.C. § 271(a)).
**Trade secret:** Stops misappropriation, not independent discovery. Reverse engineering is not an improper means (18 U.S.C. § 1839(6)(B)).
**Trademark:** Protects the mark's role in identifying source. It stops uses likely to confuse, and false designations of origin (15 U.S.C. §§ 1114(1), 1125(a)).

deepDive.heading: Layers of a software product
deepDive.lede: A product has several layers, and each layer usually needs a different right.

visual.caption: The usual lead right for each layer. Contract overlays all of them.

items.label: Source and object code
items.note: Trade secret for unreleased source

items.label: Architecture and algorithms
items.note: A patent needs eligibility and novelty; publication destroys secrecy

items.label: Interface and documentation
items.note: Visible to users once released, so exposed at launch

items.label: Data and databases
items.note: Copyright protects little raw data

items.label: Names and logos
items.note: Rights follow use in commerce

points: **Code:** Programs are sets of statements or instructions (17 U.S.C. § 101). Courts have held object code protected too (Apple Computer, Inc. v. Franklin Computer Corp., 714 F.2d 1240 (3d Cir. 1983)).
**Ideas and methods:** Architecture, algorithms and methods of operation are outside copyright (17 U.S.C. § 102(b)). Those layers need a patent, a trade secret or a contract.
**Data:** Copyright does little for raw data, so the contract and the bank's secrecy measures do most of the work (drafting inference).

**Names:** A product name can earn trademark rights through [[use in commerce]], meaning bona fide use in the ordinary course of trade (15 U.S.C. § 1127), but a merely descriptive name may need proof that it identifies the source (drafting inference). Clear the name before launch (good practice).

deepDive.heading: Where open source fits
deepDive.lede: An [[open source licence]] is a licence of rights, not a transfer of them.
points: **Copyright and patent:** Apache-2.0 grants a copyright licence to reproduce, adapt and distribute the work, and a patent licence from each contributor (Apache-2.0 s.2, s.3).
**Trademark:** The same licence grants no right to use the licensor's trade names or marks, beyond reasonable and customary use to describe the origin of the work (Apache-2.0 s.6).
**Conditions:** The grant is subject to the licence's terms and conditions, so the licensee must meet them to rely on it (Apache-2.0 s.2).
**Permission, not title:** The bank as licensee receives permission on stated terms. It does not become the owner of the code (drafting inference).

deepDive.heading: How long each right lasts, and what ends it
deepDive.lede: Terms differ widely, and some rights end through conduct rather than time.

visual.caption: Duration as the statutes set it. Trade secret and trademark rights have no fixed term.

items.label: Copyright, work made for hire
items.note: Whichever ends first, from publication or creation (§ 302(c))

items.label: Trade secret
items.note: Lost once the information is generally known (18 U.S.C. § 1839(3)(B))

items.label: Trademark
items.note: Lost on abandonment (15 U.S.C. § 1127)

points: **Copyright:** For an individual author, protection lasts for life plus 70 years (17 U.S.C. § 302(a)). A work made for hire lasts 95 years from publication or 120 from creation, whichever ends first (§ 302(c)).
**Patent:** The term ends 20 years from the US filing date, subject to fees and adjustments (35 U.S.C. § 154(a)(2)). Years left at grant depend on how long examination takes.
**Trade secret:** There is no fixed term. Protection lasts only while the information is not generally known and is kept secret (18 U.S.C. § 1839(3)).
**Trademark:** Rights last while the mark is used in commerce and is not abandoned (15 U.S.C. § 1127).

deepDive.heading: Federal law, state law and the courts
deepDive.lede: Federal law sets most of the rules. State law still governs contracts, employment and much of trade secret practice.
points: **Federal claims:** No state court may hear a claim under the patent or copyright Acts; trademark claims can be heard in federal courts under 28 U.S.C. § 1338(a), and state courts may hear them too (drafting inference).

**Patent appeals:** The [[Federal Circuit]] has exclusive jurisdiction over appeals in patent cases from district courts (28 U.S.C. § 1295(a)(1)). Copyright and trademark appeals go to the regional circuit, unless the action also arises under the patent laws or has a compulsory patent counterclaim (drafting inference).
**Trade secrets:** The DTSA gives the owner a federal civil action (18 U.S.C. § 1836(b)(1)). State claims under California's version run alongside it (Cal. Civ. Code § 3426.1).

**Employment:** State law can limit what staff must assign. California voids an assignment clause for an invention made entirely on the employee's own time without the employer's equipment, supplies, facilities or trade secret information, with exceptions (Cal. Lab. Code § 2870(a), (b)).

deepDive.heading: The bank's IP estate
deepDive.lede: A bank's software estate has three parts: what it owns, what it licenses in and what it licenses out.

visual.caption: Each part needs a register entry with its right and its governing contract.

items.label: Owned
items.note: In-house code, models, rules and names, once staff and contractor terms are right

items.label: Licensed in
items.note: Commercial software, open source, SaaS and data feeds

items.label: Licensed out
items.note: SDKs, sample code, APIs and fintech partner access

points: **Owned:** The bank owns code its employees wrote within the scope of employment, because it is treated as the author (17 U.S.C. § 201(b)). Contractor code is usually outside that rule, so the bank needs a written assignment (drafting inference).
**Licensed in:** The bank holds permission, not title. The licence sets the scope and conditions of use (Apache-2.0 s.2).
**Licensed out:** Each SDK or API the bank publishes needs a licence that states what others may do with it. Any open source code it releases carries its own licence terms.
**Register:** Keep one register of owned, in-licensed and out-licensed assets, with the right, the owner and the governing contract for each (good practice).

deepDive.heading: How this volume is organised
deepDive.lede: The volume runs from the rights in code, through open source licences, to day-to-day practice.

visual.caption: Three phases. The rest of the volume follows this order.

items.label: Foundations
items.note: Copyright, ownership, patents, trade secrets and trademarks

items.label: Open source licences
items.note: How licences work, then permissive, copyleft and network licences

items.label: In practice
items.note: Policy and SBOMs, releases, deals, AI-generated code, disputes and product counsel

points: **Scope:** The volume covers US law in full, and each stage has a Hong Kong law tab. EU, UK and Canadian points appear as short notes, so the rules below are US rules unless stated.
**Reading order:** Start with the rights in code and ownership, because most open source and deal questions depend on who owns the code first.
**Practice:** The later stages turn these rules into intake, release and diligence steps that the bank's teams can run.

provisions.title: Computer program (definition)
provisions.summary: Defines a computer program as a set of statements or instructions used directly or indirectly in a computer to bring about a certain result. The definition is broad and does not refer to any particular language or form of code. Programs are protected as literary works (§ 102(a)(1)).
provisions.counselNote: Treat source and object code as copyright assets in every licence and vendor contract, since both fall within the definition.

provisions.title: Subject matter of copyright: In general
provisions.summary: Protects original works of authorship fixed in a tangible medium, including literary works. Section 102(b) excludes any idea, procedure, process, system, method of operation or concept, however it is described or embodied.
provisions.counselNote: The exclusion explains why software needs patents, trade secrets or contracts as well as copyright, since methods and functions are not copyright subject matter.

provisions.title: Exclusive rights in copyrighted works
provisions.summary: Gives the copyright owner the exclusive rights to reproduce the work, prepare derivative works and distribute copies, and to perform or display certain works publicly. Sections 107 to 122 limit those rights. The owner may allow others to exercise them.
provisions.counselNote: Copying code to a server, a repository or a device is a reproduction, so each licence must cover every step the bank takes with the code.

provisions.title: Inventions patentable
provisions.summary: Allows a patent for any new and useful process, machine, manufacture or composition of matter, or an improvement to one, subject to the conditions of the Act. Courts have added judicial exceptions, such as abstract ideas, which software claims commonly have to clear.
provisions.counselNote: Before the bank patents a software method, counsel should test the claim for eligibility as well as novelty, because eligibility is often the first hurdle.

provisions.title: Contents and term of patent; provisional rights
provisions.summary: Grants the right to exclude others from making, using, offering for sale, selling or importing the invention in the United States. The term ends 20 years from the US filing date, subject to fees and to adjustments for certain delays.
provisions.counselNote: The term runs from filing, not grant, so the protection left when a patent issues depends on how long examination takes.

provisions.title: Civil proceedings
provisions.summary: Lets the owner of a misappropriated trade secret bring a civil action where the secret relates to a product or service used, or intended for use, in interstate or foreign commerce. Ex parte seizure is available only in extraordinary circumstances.
provisions.counselNote: The federal claim covers code and models that serve the bank's products, but the bank must prove the secret was protected and taken, so access logs and secrecy measures are key evidence.

provisions.title: Definitions
provisions.summary: Defines a trade secret as information, including programs and codes, that the owner protects by reasonable measures and that derives independent economic value from not being generally known. Reverse engineering and independent derivation are not improper means.
provisions.counselNote: Source code and models qualify only while the bank keeps them secret, so publishing them, including by an open source release, ends that protection.

provisions.title: Uniform Trade Secrets Act: definitions
provisions.summary: Defines improper means and misappropriation. A trade secret is information that derives independent economic value from not being generally known and is subject to reasonable efforts to keep it secret. Reverse engineering or independent derivation alone is not improper means.
provisions.counselNote: The California definitions track the federal ones, so one set of secrecy measures and contract terms can support both claims.

provisions.title: False designations of origin, false descriptions, and dilution forbidden
provisions.summary: Makes liable any person who uses in commerce a word, name, symbol or device, or a false designation of origin, that is likely to cause confusion about the origin, sponsorship or approval of goods or services. The remedy is a civil action by anyone likely to be damaged.
provisions.counselNote: This covers unregistered product and project names as well as registered marks, so a launch name needs clearance even before it is registered.

provisions.title: Construction and definitions; intent of chapter
provisions.summary: Defines use in commerce as the bona fide use of a mark in the ordinary course of trade, not made merely to reserve a right in it. It also says when a mark is deemed abandoned, on one of two grounds.
provisions.counselNote: Trademark rights follow real use in trade, so a name reserved for a future launch but not used earns little protection (drafting inference).

provisions.title: Patents, plant variety protection, copyrights, mask works, designs, trademarks, and unfair competition
provisions.summary: Gives the district courts original jurisdiction over civil actions under the patent, copyright and trademark Acts. No state court may hear a claim for relief under the patent or copyright Acts. Unfair competition claims joined to a related claim under those Acts can also be heard in federal court.
provisions.counselNote: Patent and copyright suits against the bank go to federal court, so federal litigation counsel and state contract counsel need to coordinate from the start.

provisions.title: Jurisdiction of the United States Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit
provisions.summary: Gives the Federal Circuit exclusive jurisdiction over appeals from district courts in civil actions arising under Acts of Congress relating to patents. Section 1295(a)(4)(A) also gives it appeals from the Patent Trial and Appeal Board in patent proceedings.
provisions.counselNote: Federal Circuit precedent on eligibility and damages governs the bank's patent disputes in every district, so track it when assessing patent risk.

provisions.title: Employee inventions: employment agreements
provisions.summary: Makes an assignment clause unenforceable for an invention the employee made entirely on their own time, without the employer's equipment, supplies, facilities or trade secret information. Exceptions cover inventions related to the employer's business or research, or resulting from work for the employer. Clauses reaching further are void.
provisions.counselNote: Invention assignment terms for California staff need to follow these carve-outs, and the notice duty in the same chapter applies to each agreement.

provisions.title: Grant of Copyright License
provisions.summary: Gives each user a perpetual, worldwide, non-exclusive, royalty-free and irrevocable licence to reproduce, adapt, display, perform, sublicense and distribute the work and its derivative works, in source or object form. The grant is subject to the licence's terms and conditions.
provisions.counselNote: This is the permission the bank relies on when it uses or redistributes Apache-2.0 code, and it applies only as far as the licence's conditions are met.

checklist: **Inventory the software estate:** List owned, in-licensed and out-licensed code, models, names and data, with the governing right and contract for each.
**Record who owns each code base:** Confirm which employer, contractor or vendor holds title, and keep the signed assignment or licence on file.
**Classify each asset by its main protection:** Say whether copyright, trade secret, patent, trademark or contract does most of the protecting, so controls match the right.
**Rely on trade secrets only where secrecy holds:** Check access controls, publication and open source release plans before treating code or models as secret.
**Clear product and project names:** Run a clearance search and confirm the planned use in commerce before a launch or an open source release.
**Keep one licence register:** Track every open source and third-party licence against the product that uses it, with its version and conditions.
**Confirm the governing law and contract:** Check which law governs each licence, NDA and terms of use, and whether state law limits it.
**Name an escalation owner:** Appoint the person who decides on IP disputes, takedown requests and licence breaches.
**Refresh the map when products change:** Update the asset register and the rights it relies on whenever products, vendors or policies change.
itAngle: **Repositories hold every right:** Source code carries copyright, trade secret status and licence notices, so access control, branch protection and secret scanning are IP controls too.
**Build pipelines create the record:** Build logs, dependency manifests and generated SBOM files show which code, third-party components and licences went into each release.
**Object code is protected too:** Compiled apps, libraries and container images still carry copyright and any licence conditions, so compilation does not separate the bank from the licence.
**Names reach the stores:** App names, package names, bundle identifiers and domain names are trademark risks, and they should be cleared before release, not after it.

**Models and datasets need secrecy controls:** Trained models, prompts and training data need access controls and contract terms, because trade secret protection depends on reasonable secrecy measures (18 U.S.C. § 1839(3)(A)).
virtualBankNotes: **Third-party oversight:** The interagency guidance on third-party relationships (88 Fed. Reg. 37920, 9 June 2023) covers the vendors who supply or support software across the relationship's life cycle. It does not single out open source as such.

**Cybersecurity rules:** New York's Part 500 requires written procedures for secure development of in-house applications and for assessing externally developed ones (23 NYCRR 500.8), and a policy for third-party service providers (23 NYCRR 500.11).
**Models in model risk:** Models licensed in or built in house belong in the model inventory, with their licence terms and training-data sources recorded (good practice).
**Secrecy as a regulatory asset:** The bank's models, rules and fraud logic are protected as trade secrets only while access is controlled, so access reviews serve both security and IP purposes.
**Examiner requests:** Examiners may ask for code inventories, licence records and vendor evidence, so keep them retrievable without a special project (good practice).
productNotes: **Describe each feature by its parts at the idea stage:** Tell counsel what the feature is made of, including its code, screens, data, name, any new method and any partner or open source code. Each part usually needs a different right, and a method or idea falls outside copyright, so it needs a patent, a trade secret or a contract (17 U.S.C. § 102(b)). Counsel can then say early which parts need protection and which need only a licence (good practice).

**Clear the name before marketing announces it:** A product name earns trademark rights through use in commerce, and an uncleared name can infringe a registered mark or an unregistered one (15 U.S.C. §§ 1114(1), 1125(a)). Marketing should bring the name, any tagline and any partner logo to counsel before the first public use (good practice).

**Treat a licensed-in SDK or library as permission, not ownership:** Before engineering adopts a vendor SDK, a data feed or an open source library, ask counsel to review its licence, because the bank holds permission on stated terms and does not own the code (Apache-2.0 s.2). Record each one in the licence register (good practice).

**Set the terms before partners or customers get code or data:** Product and partnership teams should not promise a partner rights in the bank's SDK, API or sample code until counsel has written the licence, because that licence decides what others may do with it. Any open source code the bank releases carries its own terms (good practice).
pitfalls: **Copyright covers everything:** It protects expression only. Ideas, methods and functions need a patent, a trade secret or a contract (17 U.S.C. § 102(b)).
**Publishing a secret:** Open sourcing or publishing code ends its trade secret status, and a licence cannot restore it (drafting inference).
**Treating an in-licence as ownership:** An in-licence gives permission on stated terms, not title. Treat licensed code as a dependency to be managed, not as an asset the bank owns (Apache-2.0 s.2).
**Launching an uncleared name:** A project name used in commerce without clearance can infringe a registered mark (15 U.S.C. § 1114(1)) and an unregistered one (15 U.S.C. § 1125(a)).
**Ignoring state law:** Employment and contract terms follow state law, and California can void an invention assignment clause that goes further than § 2870 allows (Cal. Lab. Code § 2870(b)).

points: **Copyright is the main right:** programs are literary works, but ideas and principles are not protected (Directive 2009/24/EC, Art. 1(2)), and programs 'as such' are excluded from patents (EPC Art. 52(2)(c), (3)).
**Functionality is unprotected:** functionality, programming language and data file formats are not protected by copyright (SAS Institute v World Programming, C-406/10, 2 May 2012).
**Same starting point:** programs are literary works (CDPA 1988 s.3(1)(b)), so the copyright map is close to the US one, and patents exclude programs 'as such' (Patents Act 1977 s.1(2)(c)).
**Software patents are moving:** Emotional Perception AI Ltd v Comptroller-General of Patents [2026] UKSC 3 (11 February 2026) moved away from Aerotel towards the EPO approach (reported; check).
**Moral rights cannot be assigned:** moral rights may be waived but not assigned (Copyright Act s.14.1(2)), so an assignment clause alone will not deal with them.

**Patents need more than a principle:** Patent Act s.27(8) bars a mere scientific principle or abstract theorem, and no separate test applies to computer-implemented inventions (Canada (AG) v Benjamin Moore, 2023 FCA 168).

hongKong.summary: Hong Kong protects software through copyright, which arises on recording with no registration, through patents, designs and trade marks that each need a filing, and through confidence and contract. There is no trade secrets statute (reported; check). The biggest differences from the US are that there is no copyright register at all, so nothing is filed even before suing (Cap. 528 s.4(2); drafting inference), and that a computer program cannot be registered as a design (Cap. 522 s.8(1)).
keyPoints: **Copyright arises on recording:** A computer program is a literary work, and copyright subsists once it is recorded in writing or otherwise (Cap. 528 s.4(1)(b), s.4(2)-(3)). The only register under the Ordinance is of copyright licensing bodies (Cap. 528 s.147(1)).

**Three patent routes:** A standard patent (R) registers a patent granted by a designated patent office outside Hong Kong (Cap. 514 s.3(b), s.8). A standard patent (O) is granted after substantive examination (Cap. 514 s.37U). A short-term patent is granted after formality examination only (Cap. 514 s.117).
**Designs do not cover programs:** A computer program cannot be registered as a design (Cap. 522 s.8(1)). Whether a screen display or icon can be registered is a separate question (reported; check).

**Trade marks need registration for statutory rights:** A registered trade mark is a property right (Cap. 559 s.10(1)). No proceedings lie for an unregistered mark, but passing off is preserved (Cap. 559 s.10(3)).
**No trade secrets statute:** Confidential information is protected by the equitable action for breach of confidence and by contract, not by a trade secrets statute (reported; check).

sections.heading: Four rights, four different doors
sections.lede: Each right attaches to a different layer of a Hong Kong software product, so a single right rarely covers the whole product.
points: **Code and written material:** Copyright protects a program, its preparatory design material and other original written work once it is recorded (Cap. 528 s.2(1)(a), s.4(1)(b)-(c)).

**Ideas and methods:** The Ordinance has no section that separates idea from expression (Cap. 528 s.2(1)(a); drafting inference). Courts are reported to treat English decisions as persuasive on what software protects (reported; check).

**Look and feel:** A registered design protects the features of shape, configuration, pattern or ornament applied to an article and judged by the eye (Cap. 522 s.2(1)). Software cannot be registered, so a design filing must claim a feature applied to an article (Cap. 522 s.8(1); drafting inference).
**Brand:** A registered trade mark is a property right (Cap. 559 s.10(1)). Passing off preserves protection for unregistered marks (Cap. 559 s.10(3)).
**Moral rights:** The right to be identified as author and the right to object to derogatory treatment do not apply to a computer program (Cap. 528 s.91(2)(a), s.93(2)).
sections.takeaway: Map each layer of the product to a right before choosing how to protect it, and record which rights need a filing (good practice).

sections.heading: Terms, offences and what ends a right
sections.lede: Each right runs on its own clock, and some offences attach to marking a product or using a registration claim falsely.
points: **Copyright term:** A literary work, including a program, is protected for the author's life plus 50 years. A computer-generated work is protected for 50 years from the end of the year it was made (Cap. 528 s.17(2), s.17(6)).

**Patent term:** A standard patent runs for 20 years from filing. A short-term patent runs for up to 8 years from filing, but lapses after the 4th year unless the renewal fee is paid (Cap. 514 s.39(1)(b), s.126(1)(b), (2)).
**Design term:** A registered design runs for 5 years from filing, renewable in 5-year steps to 25 years in total (Cap. 522 s.28(1)-(2)).

**False marking:** Representing that a patent has been applied for in respect of an article disposed of for value, when no application has been made or it has been refused, withdrawn or deemed withdrawn, is an offence, unless the accused used due diligence to prevent it (Cap. 514 s.143(1), (2), (4)). Falsely representing a sign as a registered trade mark is an offence where the person knows or has reason to believe the representation is false (Cap. 559 s.94(1)).
**Prosecution time limit:** No prosecution under the Copyright Ordinance may start more than 3 years after the offence was committed (Cap. 528 s.120A).
sections.takeaway: Record each right's expiry or renewal date in the bank's IP register, and check every product marking before launch (good practice).

provisions.title: Original works that attract copyright
provisions.summary: Copyright is a property right in original literary, dramatic, musical and artistic works, and in some other works such as sound recordings. Copyright subsists in a work only if the qualification rules in the Part are met.
provisions.counselNote: This sets the starting point for protection of the bank's code, documents and data compilations, and no registration step is needed.

provisions.title: Computer programs not registrable
provisions.summary: Computer programs and protected layout-designs cannot be registered as designs. The rules may also exclude designs for articles of a primarily literary or artistic character.
provisions.counselNote: A user interface cannot be registered as software, so any design filing must claim an article. Whether a screen display is an article is reported to be open (reported; check).

provisions.title: Term of a standard patent
provisions.summary: A standard patent stays in force for 20 years, counted from the deemed filing date for a standard patent (R) and from the filing date for a standard patent (O), subject to renewal fees.
provisions.counselNote: The bank's patent expiry dates run from filing, not from grant, so the patent docket should track both dates.

provisions.title: Short-term patent: formality examination and term
provisions.summary: A short-term patent is granted after formality examination only, and the Registrar does not consider patentability. It can last up to 8 years from filing, but lapses at the end of the 4th year unless the renewal fee is paid.
provisions.counselNote: Because patentability is not examined at grant, the bank should expect the validity of a short-term patent to be tested in court rather than at the Registry, and the proprietor cannot start enforcement proceedings until it holds a certificate or request for substantive examination or a court certificate of validity (Cap. 514 s.129(1); drafting inference).

provisions.title: Registered trade mark as property; passing off
provisions.summary: A registered trade mark is a property right, and its owner has the remedies the Ordinance gives. No proceedings lie to prevent infringement of an unregistered mark, but the Ordinance leaves the law of passing off unchanged.
provisions.counselNote: A product name without a Hong Kong registration relies on passing off, a common law action, rather than on statutory remedies.

provisions.title: Identification and integrity rights do not reach programs
provisions.summary: The right to be identified as author does not apply to a computer program or a computer-generated work. The integrity right, which covers derogatory treatment, is also excluded for a program or computer-generated work (s.93(2)).
provisions.counselNote: Developers cannot rely on moral rights to stop the bank changing or retiring their code, so the commercial terms carry that risk.

provisions.title: Time limit for prosecutions
provisions.summary: No prosecution for an offence under the Copyright Ordinance may begin more than 3 years after the offence was committed.
provisions.counselNote: The criminal route for copyright offences is short-term compared with civil claims, so the bank's exposure timeline is different for each route.

provisions.title: General Principles for Technology Risk Management
provisions.summary: Non-statutory guidance note (V.1, 24 June 2003) setting baseline expectations for technology risk governance, information security, system development and change management, IT operations and management of technology service providers.
provisions.counselNote: The HKMA uses this as its baseline for whether IT controls are adequate. It is old, so read it with later HKMA modules and circulars.

bankNotes: **Technology risk baseline:** The HKMA's technology risk guidance (TM-G-1) sets baseline expectations for governance, information security, change management and technology service providers.

**Marking control:** Product and marketing teams should check each 'patent pending' and registered-trade-mark marking before release, since some false markings are offences (Cap. 514 s.143(1); Cap. 559 s.94(1)). (good practice).
**Confidentiality:** Hong Kong has no trade secrets statute, so the bank's NDAs and code-access terms carry more of the load (reported; check).
**Register of rights:** Because Hong Kong has no copyright register of works, the bank's own IP register should record each program's author, licence and each filing and renewal date (good practice).

glossary.definition: A work is fixed when its embodiment in a copy, by or under the author's authority, is stable enough to be perceived, reproduced or communicated for more than a transitory period. Copyright protects original works once they are fixed (17 U.S.C. § 102(a)).

Program instructions written in a human-readable programming language. The statutory definition of a computer program, a set of statements or instructions, is broad enough to cover it (17 U.S.C. § 101).
The machine-readable form of a program, produced from source code by compilation. Courts have held object code protected by copyright (Apple v. Franklin).
Information, including programs and codes, that the owner keeps secret by reasonable measures and that has independent economic value from not being generally known (18 U.S.C. § 1839(3)).
The bona fide use of a mark in the ordinary course of trade, not made merely to reserve a right in it. Trademark rights depend on it (15 U.S.C. § 1127).

The loss of trademark rights when use stops with intent not to resume (three years of non-use is prima facie evidence), or when the owner's conduct lets the mark become generic or lose its significance as a mark (15 U.S.C. § 1127).
A licence that meets the Open Source Definition of the Open Source Initiative. It grants copyright permission subject to its terms, as Apache-2.0 does in section 2.
The US Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit, which has exclusive jurisdiction over appeals in patent cases from district courts (28 U.S.C. § 1295(a)(1)).
A standard patent registered in Hong Kong from a patent granted by a designated patent office outside Hong Kong (Cap. 514 s.3(b), s.8).
A standard patent granted after substantive examination by the Registrar (Cap. 514 s.37U(2)-(3)).
A patent granted after formality examination only, lasting up to 8 years from filing if renewed after the 4th year (Cap. 514 s.117, s.126(1)(b), (2)).

title: Copyright in code
oneLiner: Code is protected as a literary work, but copyright stops at expression, so the real disputes are about where expression ends.
keyPoints: Programs are literary works under the Copyright Act (17 U.S.C.), so source code and object code are both protected (§ 101; § 102(a)(1)).
**Idea limit:** Copyright never reaches an idea, procedure, process, system, method of operation or concept, however it is written down (§ 102(b)).
**Exclusive rights:** The owner controls copying, adapting and distributing the program (§ 106). Sections 109 and 117 then carve out rights that software users need.
**Owner or licensee:** Whether a user owns its copy or only licenses it decides whether the owner's rights under § 117(a) and § 109(a) apply. The contract matters.
**Registration:** No infringement suit can be brought on a U.S. work until registration has been made or refused (§ 411(a)). Late registration can cost statutory damages and fees (§ 412).

**DMCA:** Stripping licence terms from code can breach § 1202(b) if done knowing it will enable infringement. Circumventing a technological measure that effectively controls access to a work, without authority, breaches § 1201(a)(1), subject to the exemptions the Librarian of Congress sets (§ 1201(a)(1)(B) to (D)).

conceptMap.caption: Protection attaches to the expression in a program. Ideas and functions stay outside copyright, and software-specific rules shape what owners and users may do.

items.label: Literary work
items.note: Literal code and original structure

items.label: Ideas, methods and functions
items.note: Outside copyright altogether

items.label: Exclusive rights
items.note: Copy, adapt, distribute, display

items.label: Owner and licensee rights
items.note: Turn on whether the user owns the copy

items.label: Registration
items.note: Needed before suit on a U.S. work

items.label: Access controls and licence terms
items.note: Anti-circumvention and copyright management information

deepDive.heading: What copyright protects in a program
deepDive.lede: Code is a literary work, and the protection reaches object code too.

visual.caption: Copyright reaches literal code. Ideas and filtered-out elements fall away before any comparison.

items.label: Literal source and object code
items.note: Copying it is reproduction (§ 106(1))

items.label: Structure, sequence and organisation
items.note: Protected only if original expression survives filtering

items.label: Efficiency-driven or external elements
items.note: Dictated by efficiency or outside factors

items.label: Ideas, methods and functions
items.note: Excluded by § 102(b)

points: **Literary work:** A computer program is a set of statements or instructions used directly or indirectly in a computer to bring about a result (§ 101 “computer program”). Programs are protected as literary works (§ 101 “literary works”; § 102(a)(1)).

**Object code:** In Apple Computer, Inc. v. Franklin Computer Corp., 714 F.2d 1240 (3d Cir. 1983), the court held that object code and operating system programs are protected, so compiled code is not outside copyright.
**Idea and expression:** Copyright protects how a program is expressed, not what it does (§ 102(b)). Two products can perform the same function with different code, and both can be lawful.
**Non-literal copying:** Copying can infringe without identical text, but only protected expression counts, so the claimant has to identify what was taken.

deepDive.heading: Filtering before comparison
deepDive.lede: Courts strip out unprotectable material before asking whether a copy took protected expression.

visual.caption: The three steps of the abstraction-filtration-comparison test for non-literal copying.

items.label: Abstract
items.note: Break the program into levels of structure, from its overall function down to the code

items.label: Filter
items.note: Remove ideas, efficiency-driven elements, outside factors and public domain material

items.label: Compare
items.note: Compare what remains with the allegedly copied work

points: **AFC test:** Computer Associates Int'l, Inc. v. Altai, Inc., 982 F.2d 693 (2d Cir. 1992), set out the [[AFC test|abstraction-filtration-comparison]] for non-literal copying: abstract the program into levels, filter out unprotectable elements, then compare what remains.

**Filtration failures:** In SAS Institute Inc. v. World Programming Ltd., 64 F.4th 1319 (Fed. Cir. 2023), the Federal Circuit affirmed dismissal because SAS did not show what protectable expression remained after filtering.

**Practical effect:** A claimant that cannot isolate its protectable core may lose early. A defendant can use the same filtering to show that what was kept is ideas or public domain code (drafting inference).
**Records:** Keep records that separate original expression from third-party and standard elements, so the bank can show what it protects (good practice).

deepDive.heading: Menus, methods and APIs
deepDive.lede: The hard cases are the interfaces a program exposes to users and to other programs.
points: **Menus:** Lotus Development Corp. v. Borland Int'l, Inc., 49 F.3d 807 (1st Cir. 1995), held that the Lotus 1-2-3 menu command hierarchy was an uncopyrightable method of operation under § 102(b).
**No Supreme Court ruling:** The Supreme Court affirmed by an equally divided court, 516 U.S. 233 (1996), so the affirmance sets no Supreme Court precedent.

**APIs:** Google LLC v. Oracle America, Inc., 593 U.S. 1 (2021), decided 5 April 2021 by six votes to two, assumed without deciding that the Java SE declaring code was copyrightable. Copying about 11,500 lines to build Android was fair use (§ 107).

**Fair use:** Section 107 weighs the purpose and character of the use, the nature of the work, the amount used and the effect on the market. The answer depended on those facts, so it is not a general licence to copy interfaces.
deepDive.takeaway: Reuse of an interface is a licence question first and a fair use question second.

deepDive.heading: Owner, licensee and the rights that follow
deepDive.lede: Whether the bank owns a copy decides which software-specific rights apply.

visual.caption: The owner of a copy gets statutory rights. A licensee gets what the licence grants.

items.label: Owner of a copy
items.note: May make essential copies and resell the copy

items.label: Licensee
items.note: No § 109(a) privilege without ownership (§ 109(d))

items.label: Rental or lending
items.note: Barred for commercial advantage without the owner's authority

points: **Exclusive rights:** The owner controls copies, adaptations and distribution (§ 106(1)-(3)). MAI Systems Corp. v. Peak Computer, Inc., 991 F.2d 511 (9th Cir. 1993), held that loading software into RAM makes a copy. Congress later added § 117(c) for maintenance and repair copies (1998).

**Owner's copies:** The owner of a copy may make another copy or adaptation as an essential step in running the program on a machine, or for archive use only, and must destroy archive copies if rightful possession ends (§ 117(a)(1)-(2)).

**Owner tests:** Vernor v. Autodesk, Inc., 621 F.3d 1102 (9th Cir. 2010), treats a user as a licensee where the owner says so, restricts transfer and imposes notable use limits. Krause v. Titleserv, Inc., 402 F.3d 119 (2d Cir. 2005), asks about incidents of ownership, not formal title.
**Different tests:** The Ninth and Second Circuits frame the question differently, so draft the licence to hold the bank's intended result under either test (good practice).
deepDive.takeaway: Draft the grant of rights, not just the label.

deepDive.heading: Reverse engineering and contract bans
deepDive.lede: Courts protect reverse engineering that has a legitimate aim, but licence bans can still bind.
points: **Lawful disassembly:** Sega Enterprises Ltd. v. Accolade, Inc., 977 F.2d 1510 (9th Cir. 1992), held that disassembly to reach unprotected functional elements can be fair use where it is the only way and the aim is interoperability.
**Ban enforced:** Bowers v. Baystate Technologies, Inc., 320 F.3d 1317 (Fed. Cir. 2003), held 2-1 that a shrink-wrap ban on reverse engineering was enforceable and not preempted.

**Shrink-wrap terms:** ProCD, Inc. v. Zeidenberg, 86 F.3d 1447 (7th Cir. 1996), held that a [[shrink-wrap licences|shrink-wrap licence]] is enforceable unless it is objectionable on general contract grounds.
**Two directions:** Read reverse engineering clauses both as licensor, which wants a ban, and as licensee, which may need one lifted for interoperability (good practice).

deepDive.heading: Registration, damages and remedies
deepDive.lede: Registration decides when a U.S. suit can start and which remedies are open.

visual.caption: Registration timing under § 412. These are the usual outcomes, not every case.

items.label: Registered before infringement began
items.note: Statutory damages and fees available

items.label: Published work, registered within three months
items.note: Statutory damages and fees available

items.label: Registered later
items.note: No statutory damages or fees for earlier infringement

points: **Suit:** No infringement suit on a U.S. work until registration has been made or refused (§ 411(a)). Fourth Estate Public Benefit Corp. v. Wall-Street.com, LLC, 586 U.S. 296 (2019), held that registration has been made when the Copyright Office registers the work, not when the application is filed.

**Late registration:** No award of [[statutory damages]] or attorney's fees is made for infringement of an unpublished work that began before registration, or for infringement that began after first publication and before registration, unless registration came within three months of first publication (§ 412).
**Amounts:** The owner may elect $750 to $30,000 per work instead of actual damages and profits, rising to $150,000 for wilful infringement and falling to $200 for innocent infringement (§ 504(c)).

**Deposits:** Applicants can deposit redacted source code to protect trade secrets, using page options set by the Copyright Office (37 C.F.R. § 202.20(c)(2)(vii)) (reported; check the current options).
deepDive.takeaway: Register code on release, not when a dispute starts.

deepDive.heading: The DMCA: licence terms and access controls
deepDive.lede: The Digital Millennium Copyright Act (DMCA) adds two rules that reach code directly.
points: **Licence headers:** Copyright management information (CMI) includes terms and conditions for use (§ 1202(c)(6)), so a licence header can be [[copyright management information|copyright management information]]. Removing it, knowing it will facilitate infringement, breaches § 1202(b). Courts have accepted this for licence headers in some cases (reported; check).

**Access controls:** No one may circumvent a technological measure that effectively controls access to a copyrighted work (§ 1201(a)(1)). Such a measure requires information or a process, applied with the owner's authority, to gain access (§ 1201(a)(3)(B)).
**Trafficking:** Making, importing or offering devices or products primarily designed to circumvent such a measure is also barred (§ 1201(a)(2)).

**Interoperability:** Section 1201(f) gives a limited exception for achieving interoperability of an independently created program. Check its limits before any project that touches a licence check (good practice).
deepDive.takeaway: Licence terms in code and licence checks are legal controls, not only engineering details.

provisions.title: Definitions: computer program, literary works, derivative work
provisions.summary: Defines a computer program as a set of statements or instructions used directly or indirectly in a computer to bring about a certain result. Literary works are works expressed in words, numbers or other symbols, whatever the material object. A derivative work is a work based on one or more preexisting works, such as a translation, adaptation or abridgment.
provisions.counselNote: These definitions decide whether code is protected at all and whether a modified version is a derivative work that needs permission.

provisions.title: Subject matter of copyright
provisions.summary: Protects original works of authorship fixed in a tangible medium, and lists literary works as a category (§ 102(a)(1)). Subsection (b) excludes any idea, procedure, process, system, method of operation, concept or principle, however it is described or embodied.
provisions.counselNote: Subsection (b) is where most disputes about software functions begin. Copyright does not stop others using the functional logic, although patents and trade secrets may (drafting inference).

provisions.title: Exclusive rights in copyrighted works
provisions.summary: Gives the copyright owner the exclusive rights to reproduce the work, prepare derivative works, distribute copies by sale, rental, lease or lending, and perform or display the work publicly. These rights are subject to the limits in §§ 107 to 122.
provisions.counselNote: Copying code into a repository, a container image or an app is reproduction. Each internal copy of third-party code is an exercise of these rights, so the licence must cover it (good practice).

provisions.title: Limitations on exclusive rights: fair use
provisions.summary: Makes fair use of a copyrighted work for purposes such as criticism, teaching, scholarship or research not an infringement. Courts weigh four factors: the purpose and character of the use, including whether it is commercial; the nature of the work; the amount used; and the effect on the market.
provisions.counselNote: Fair use is decided case by case on the facts. Treat it as a defence to budget for, not a planning assumption for reusing a third party's interface (good practice).

provisions.title: Effect of transfer of particular copy: first sale and computer program rental
provisions.summary: Lets the owner of a lawfully made copy sell or dispose of it (§ 109(a)). Renting, leasing or lending a copy of a program for commercial advantage is barred without the copyright owner's authority, with exceptions (§ 109(b)(1)(A)). The § 109(a) and (c) privileges do not extend to a person who got possession by rental, lease or loan without acquiring ownership (§ 109(d)).
provisions.counselNote: The first-sale right for software depends on owning the copy. A licence that grants only possession does not carry it, so the contract must say which the bank is getting.

provisions.title: Limitations on exclusive rights: computer programs
provisions.summary: Lets the owner of a copy of a program make another copy or adaptation as an essential step in using it with a machine, or for archive purposes only, with archive copies destroyed if rightful possession ends (§ 117(a)). Exact copies move only with the whole program (§ 117(b)). Maintenance and repair copies are covered by § 117(c).
provisions.counselNote: This is the statutory safe harbour for owners. Any licence term that restricts these copies should be checked against it, since the owner's position here is set by statute (good practice).

provisions.title: Registration and civil infringement actions
provisions.summary: Bars a civil infringement action on a U.S. work until registration or preregistration has been made, or the application has been refused and notice given (§ 411(a)). The bar does not apply to claims under § 106A(a).
provisions.counselNote: Unregistered code that is a U.S. work cannot be sued on in U.S. courts. A bank that relies on its code for competitive advantage should register it so that it can enforce (good practice).

provisions.title: Registration as prerequisite to certain remedies
provisions.summary: Denies statutory damages and attorney's fees for infringement of an unpublished work that began before the registration's effective date. It also denies them for infringement that began after first publication and before registration, unless registration came within three months of first publication.
provisions.counselNote: Late registration can remove the damages and fee-shifting that would otherwise deter a copier. Register promptly on release (good practice).

provisions.instrument: Digital Millennium Copyright Act (17 U.S.C. Chapter 12)
provisions.title: Circumvention of copyright protection systems
provisions.summary: Bars circumventing a technological measure that effectively controls access to a copyrighted work (§ 1201(a)(1)), and bars making or offering devices primarily designed for that purpose (§ 1201(a)(2)). Fair use and other defences to infringement are not affected (§ 1201(c)(1)), but the Second Circuit held that this does not make fair use a defence to a § 1201 claim (Universal City Studios, Inc. v. Corley, 273 F.3d 429 (2d Cir. 2001)).
provisions.counselNote: Licence keys, signing checks and obfuscation in an app may be access controls. Testing that defeats them needs legal review first, because the exceptions are narrow.

provisions.instrument: Digital Millennium Copyright Act (17 U.S.C. Chapter 12)
provisions.title: Integrity of copyright management information
provisions.summary: Bars knowingly supplying false copyright management information (CMI) to induce or conceal infringement (§ 1202(a)). Bars intentionally removing or altering CMI, knowing it will induce, enable, facilitate or conceal infringement (§ 1202(b)). CMI includes terms and conditions for use of the work (§ 1202(c)(6)).
provisions.counselNote: A licence header in code can be CMI, so removing it during refactoring, minification or reuse of vendor code is a DMCA risk. The case law on licence headers is limited (reported; check).

provisions.instrument: Apple Computer, Inc. v. Franklin Computer Corp.
provisions.title: Object code and operating system programs protected
provisions.summary: The Third Circuit held that object code and operating system programs are protected by copyright, not only source code. The decision settled that the protected form of a program is not limited to human-readable text.
provisions.counselNote: Shipping only compiled code does not take the program outside copyright, so the bank still needs a clear licence or assignment chain for binaries.

provisions.instrument: Computer Associates Int'l, Inc. v. Altai, Inc.
provisions.title: Abstraction-filtration-comparison test
provisions.summary: The Second Circuit set out the test for non-literal copying: abstract the program into levels, filter out ideas, elements dictated by efficiency or external factors, and public domain material, then compare what remains.
provisions.counselNote: Expect a defendant to run this test on the bank's code, so keep records that show which parts are original and what they do (good practice).

provisions.instrument: Google LLC v. Oracle America, Inc.
provisions.title: Copying of Java SE declaring code held fair use
provisions.summary: The Supreme Court, by six votes to two, assumed that the Java SE declaring code was copyrightable and held that Google's copying of about 11,500 lines to build Android was fair use under § 107. The Court did not decide copyrightability.
provisions.counselNote: The decision lowers the risk of reusing a published interface, but it turned on its facts and does not make APIs free to copy. Treat API reuse as a licence question first (good practice).

checklist: **Map the protected layers:** Split each product into literal code, structure and ideas or functions before deciding what copyright covers (§ 102(b)).
**Confirm who owns each copy:** Check whether the bank owns or only licenses each program, because § 117(a) and § 109(a) depend on ownership (§ 109(d)).
**Register code the bank may need to enforce:** File registration on release, ideally within three months of first publication, to keep statutory damages and fees available (§ 411(a); § 412).
**Deposit redacted source code for trade-secret programs:** Use the Copyright Office's redacted deposit options, so trade secrets stay out of the public record (reported; check the rules).
**Keep licence headers in place:** Preserve copyright notices and licence terms through builds, minification and refactoring, since removing them can breach § 1202(b).
**Check reverse engineering bans in licences:** Confirm that each ban is enforceable under the Bowers and ProCD line of cases, and that it leaves room for the bank's interoperability needs.
**Record independent development:** Keep design records for code written without copying third-party code, so the bank can show its expression is independent (good practice).
**Limit copying of interfaces:** Treat reuse of a third party's code or published interface as needing a licence, because fair use is decided case by case (good practice).
**Review testing that touches access controls:** Get legal sign-off before any testing that defeats licence checks, signing or access keys, given the narrow exceptions in § 1201.
itAngle: **Repository copies:** Each clone, fork, vendored directory and container layer is a reproduction under § 106(1). Keep a record of which third-party code sits where, and under which licence, so the bank can show what it has copied.
**Header hygiene:** Minifiers, bundlers and code generators can strip comments, including licence banners. That can engage § 1202(b). Configure the build to keep licence banners (good practice).
**Access controls in code:** Licence checks, signature verification and obfuscation can be access controls under § 1201(a)(3)(B). Security tests that defeat them need legal review first.
**Binary-only releases:** Compiled apps and firmware are protected object code (Franklin). Distributing binaries does not end the bank's copyright position, so the licence still has to be right.
**Deposit steps in release pipelines:** A release job can produce the redacted copy needed for a Copyright Office deposit. Add that step to the release checklist so it is not missed (good practice).
virtualBankNotes: **Vendor code:** Vendors that write the bank's code often keep copyright unless the contract assigns it, so without an assignment the bank's use rests on a licence. The interagency guidance on third-party relationships covers risk across the life of the relationship, so ownership and licence terms belong in vendor risk management (drafting inference).
**Escrow and continuity:** Source code escrow needs a licence that survives vendor failure. Who owns the copy decides what the bank can use after that event (good practice).
**Internal sharing:** Copying third-party code into internal systems is reproduction. Each licence must allow the bank's internal use and any sharing with affiliates or contractors (good practice).

**Published SDKs and sample code:** Code the bank distributes to customers is a distribution under § 106(3). Fix the copyright notices and licence before release, not after a customer finds a problem (good practice).

**Secure development records:** Under the NYDFS Cybersecurity Regulation (23 NYCRR 500.8), entities must maintain written procedures for in-house applications. Code ownership and licence records support that duty (drafting inference).
productNotes: **Build the feature from its own specification:** Designers and engineers should not copy a competitor's screens, flows, code or documentation, even where the function is the same. Copyright protects expression, not the function a feature performs, so the bank can match a function with its own design and code (17 U.S.C. § 102(b)).

**Keep a record of reference material:** When the team uses a third-party document, sample app or open source snippet as a model, tell counsel and note what was taken and where it sits. In a dispute a court filters out ideas and standard elements before comparing what is left, so a clear record separates the bank's expression from the rest (Computer Associates Int'l, Inc. v. Altai, Inc., 982 F.2d 693 (2d Cir. 1992); good practice).

**Do not strip notices from third-party code during a rewrite:** When product asks for a redesign or rebrand of a vendor-supplied component, engineering should keep its licence text in place. Removing copyright management information, knowing it will enable infringement, breaches 17 U.S.C. § 1202(b).

**Tell counsel each release date so registration can follow:** A U.S. suit needs registration first, and statutory damages and fees are lost if registration comes late (17 U.S.C. §§ 411(a), 412). If a team used generative AI to make code or images, tell counsel too, because the Copyright Office expects applicants to disclose AI-generated content that is more than de minimis (88 Fed. Reg. 16190 (16 Mar. 2023); reported; check).
pitfalls: **Relying on a label:** Calling a user a licensee or an owner does not settle the question. Courts weigh the substance of the deal, and a label is only one factor (Vernor; Krause).
**Assuming the API case clears reuse:** Google v. Oracle assumed copyrightability and turned on its facts. Treat API reuse as a licence question, not a free pass.
**Stripping headers in a build step:** A minifier or repackaging script that removes licence text can breach § 1202(b) when it is done knowing it will enable infringement.
**Registering late:** Waiting until a dispute to register can remove statutory damages and fees (§ 412). Register on release instead.
**Assuming binaries are safe:** Distributing object code without source does not take the program outside copyright. The licence still has to be right (Franklin).

points: **Functionality stays free:** functionality, programming language and data file formats are not protected (SAS Institute v World Programming, C-406/10, 2 May 2012).

**Lawful users have fixed rights:** a lawful user may observe, study or test a program (Directive 2009/24/EC, Art. 5(3)) and decompile for interoperability (Art. 6); contract terms that override these are void (Art. 8).
**Resale of downloaded software:** the distribution right is exhausted when downloaded software is sold under a perpetual licence (UsedSoft v Oracle, C-128/11, 3 July 2012).
**Statutory user rights:** lawful users have back-up copy, decompilation and observe-study-test rights (CDPA 1988 ss.50A-50C), so the bank's licence terms should be checked against them.
**Same core position:** programs are literary works (CDPA 1988 s.3(1)(b)), and the idea-expression line is drawn much as in the US.

**Owner and licensee exceptions:** an owner or licensee of a program may adapt it, where essential for compatibility with a particular computer, and make a back-up copy, provided the person proves the copy is solely for its own use and is destroyed when it stops owning or licensing the program (Copyright Act s.30.6); it may reproduce a program to obtain interoperability information, without using or disclosing that information beyond that purpose (s.30.61).
**Anti-circumvention carve-out:** s.41.12 gives an interoperability exception to the anti-circumvention rules for a lawfully obtained program.

hongKong.summary: Hong Kong protects code as a literary work under the Copyright Ordinance (Cap. 528 s.4(1)(b)), with no registration step and no general fair use, only listed fair dealing purposes (Cap. 528 ss.38-39A). The biggest differences from the US are the statutory lawful-user rules for back-up, copying and adaptation (Cap. 528 s.60, s.61) and a criminal offence for business possession of infringing programs (Cap. 528 s.118(2A)).
keyPoints: **Programs are literary works:** A computer program, its preparatory design material and a data compilation with an original selection or arrangement are literary works (Cap. 528 s.4(1)(a)-(c)).
**Protection starts on recording:** A program is protected once it is recorded in writing or otherwise, and nothing needs to be filed (Cap. 528 s.4(2)-(3)).

**Restricted acts:** Copying, which includes storing the program electronically, issuing copies, communicating to the public and adapting, which includes translating code, need the owner's licence (Cap. 528 s.22(1), s.23(2), s.29(4)).

**Lawful users:** A person with a contractual right to use a program may back it up, and may copy or adapt it where necessary for that use. A contract can exclude the back-up right (Cap. 528 s.60(1)-(3)), but s.61 has no equivalent words, so whether a contract can exclude the copy-or-adapt right is a question of construction.

**Business possession offence:** Possessing an infringing copy of a program for a trade or business, with a view to its use in that business, is a criminal offence (Cap. 528 s.118(2A), s.119(1)). The accused has a defence if they prove they did not know and had no reason to believe the copy was infringing (Cap. 528 s.118(3)).

sections.heading: What the Ordinance protects in code
sections.lede: The Ordinance protects a program once it is recorded, and it has no statutory rule that separates idea from expression.
points: **Program as literary work:** A program is protected as a literary work once it is recorded (Cap. 528 s.4(1)(b), s.4(2)).

**No idea and expression rule:** The Ordinance has no section that separates idea from expression (Cap. 528 s.2(1)(a); drafting inference). Courts are reported to treat English decisions as persuasive on what software protects (reported; check).

**Selection and arrangement:** A compilation of data, including a table, is protected where its selection or arrangement is an intellectual creation, even if the data is not original (Cap. 528 s.4(1)(a)).
**No separate database right:** The Ordinance has no separate database right, so a data set is protected only through its selection or arrangement (Cap. 528 s.4(1)(a); drafting inference).

**Owner's rights in code:** The owner has the exclusive right to copy, issue copies, communicate and adapt the work in Hong Kong, and infringement covers anyone who does one of those acts without licence (Cap. 528 s.22(1), s.22(2)).
sections.takeaway: Before reusing or reimplementing an interface, identify which parts are protected expression under s.4(1)(a) and the restricted acts, rather than assuming the functional elements are free (good practice).

sections.heading: Copying, adapting and using licensed code
sections.lede: The restricted acts reach storage and translation, and the lawful-user rules set a baseline that a licence can cut back.
points: **Storage counts as copying:** Storing a work in any medium by electronic means is copying (Cap. 528 s.23(2)), so loading or hosting code in the bank's systems is restricted unless a licence or lawful-user right covers it (drafting inference).

**Translation and adaptation:** For a program, an adaptation is an altered version or a translation, and a translation includes conversion into, out of or between computer languages or codes (Cap. 528 s.29(3)(b), s.29(4)).
**Back-up by a lawful user:** A lawful user may make a back-up copy where necessary for lawful use, but the agreement can exclude this right (Cap. 528 s.60(1)-(3)).

**Copying and adapting by a lawful user:** A lawful user may copy or adapt a program where necessary for lawful use, including to correct errors (Cap. 528 s.61(1)-(2)). The Ordinance gives no express contractual override for this right (drafting inference).

**Reverse engineering:** The Ordinance has no decompilation exception and no general interoperability exception for copying, so reverse engineering that copies or adapts a program infringes unless the licence allows it or it falls within the lawful-user rule or another exception, such as fair dealing for research (s.38); circumventing a technological measure for interoperability is separately excused where s.273D(1) is met (Cap. 528 s.61(1)-(2); drafting inference).
sections.takeaway: Before engineers decompile, translate or copy third-party code, confirm that the licence or a lawful-user right covers the act, and do not rely on a general exception (good practice).

sections.heading: Remedies, offences and who is exposed
sections.lede: Civil remedies are broad, and the business possession offence reaches the bank's own staff and contractors, not only pirates.
points: **Civil remedies:** The owner may claim damages, injunctions and accounts (Cap. 528 s.107(2)). The court may award additional damages having regard to flagrancy, benefit to the defendant and its conduct (Cap. 528 s.108(2)).

**Innocent infringer:** Damages are barred only where the defendant did not know, and had no reason to believe, that copyright subsisted in the work. Other remedies remain available (Cap. 528 s.108(1)).

**Knowledge for secondary acts:** Importing, dealing in or possessing an infringing copy needs knowledge or reason to believe that the copy is infringing (Cap. 528 s.30, s.31(1)). Primary infringement under s.22 does not need that knowledge.

**Business possession offence:** On indictment the penalty is a level 5 fine for each infringing copy and 4 years' imprisonment (Cap. 528 s.119(1)). The offence does not cover printed copies or programs technically required to view a work (Cap. 528 s.118(2C)-(2D)). Directors and managers commit the offence where it is done with their consent or connivance, or is attributable to them (Cap. 528 s.125(1)).

**Circumvention:** Circumventing an effective technological measure is actionable where the person knows or has reason to believe the act circumvents it (Cap. 528 s.273A(1)). The Secretary for Commerce and Economic Development may exclude classes of works or devices from these rules by Gazette notice (Cap. 528 s.273H).
sections.takeaway: Before raising an infringement claim, establish knowledge or reason to believe for the secondary acts, and check the business-use element before treating conduct as an offence (good practice).

provisions.title: Literary works, including programs
provisions.summary: A literary work includes a compilation of data protected by its selection or arrangement, a computer program and preparatory design material for a program. Copyright does not subsist until the work is recorded in writing or otherwise, and the qualification rules apply.
provisions.counselNote: The bank's code is protected without any filing, so the record of who wrote the code and when matters in a dispute.

provisions.title: Acts restricted by copyright
provisions.summary: The owner has the exclusive right to copy the work, issue copies to the public, communicate it to the public and make an adaptation, in Hong Kong. Infringement is committed by a person who does, or authorises another to do, a restricted act without the owner's licence.
provisions.counselNote: Each internal copy, hosted copy and customer download is a restricted act, so each needs a licence that covers it.

provisions.title: Adaptation of a program, including translation
provisions.summary: For a computer program, an adaptation is an arrangement or altered version of the program, or a translation of it. A translation includes conversion into, out of or between computer languages or codes.
provisions.counselNote: Porting code to another language or platform is a translation, so a migration or rewrite of licensed code needs a licence that allows it.

provisions.title: Copies lawfully made abroad
provisions.summary: A copy of a program that was lawfully made in the place where it was made is not an infringing copy for the purposes of the importation rule in s.35(3).
provisions.counselNote: This protects copies lawfully made abroad from the importation rule in s.35(3), including its breach-of-exclusive-licence limb in s.35(3)(b), but the bank's licence terms still bind it in contract, so check them before copies made outside Hong Kong are brought in (drafting inference).

provisions.title: Back-up copies by lawful users
provisions.summary: A lawful user, meaning a person with a contractual right to use the program, may make a back-up copy where it is necessary for that lawful use. The section has effect subject to any agreement to the contrary.
provisions.counselNote: The bank can contract out of this right, so the licence terms decide whether its own back-up copies are lawful.

provisions.title: Copying and adapting by lawful users
provisions.summary: A lawful user may copy or adapt a program without infringement where that is necessary for lawful use, including to correct errors. The section does not apply to copying permitted under section 60.
provisions.counselNote: The Ordinance has no separate interoperability exception, so this section is the route engineers will ask about first.

provisions.title: Damages and innocent infringers
provisions.summary: Damages are barred only where the defendant did not know, and had no reason to believe, that copyright subsisted, and other remedies remain available. The court may award additional damages having regard to the flagrancy of the infringement, any benefit to the defendant and its conduct.
provisions.counselNote: The bank's copyright notices and licence terms affect how far a defendant can rely on ignorance of the copyright.

provisions.title: Business possession offence for programs
provisions.summary: It is an offence to possess an infringing copy of a program without licence for a trade or business, with a view to its use in that business. Printed copies, and programs technically required to view or listen to a work, are excluded.
provisions.counselNote: This offence reaches the bank's own staff and contractors, so licence compliance for internal use is a criminal-law issue as well as a civil one.

provisions.title: Circumventing technological measures
provisions.summary: Circumventing an effective technological measure applied to a copyright work is actionable where the person knows, or has reason to believe, that the act circumvents the measure. The owner and certain licensees have the same remedies as for copyright infringement.
provisions.counselNote: Licence keys and access controls in the bank's products are protected, so a vendor or staff member who breaks them may face a claim even without copying, if the person knew or had reason to believe the act circumvents the measure and no s.273D or s.273H exception applies.

provisions.title: Outsourcing
provisions.summary: Non-statutory HKMA guidance (V.1, dated 28 December 2001). It expects board accountability, due diligence, written agreements, confidentiality of customer data, monitoring, contingency planning and HKMA access. An authorised institution planning to outsource a banking-related business area should discuss it with the HKMA in advance.
provisions.counselNote: This is the main source of the clauses the HKMA expects in vendor contracts, in particular supervisory inspection and access rights. Build the HKMA discussion into procurement timelines.

bankNotes: **Commissioned code:** Unless the contract expressly says who owns the copyright, the author (usually the developer) keeps it under s.13, and the bank gets an exclusive licence for all purposes both sides could reasonably have contemplated when the work was commissioned, with a power to restrain uses it could reasonably object to (Cap. 528 s.13, s.15(2)(a)-(b)).

**Vendor agreements:** The HKMA expects written agreements with outsourcing vendors, covering confidentiality of customer data, monitoring and access rights (SA-2). Code ownership and licence terms belong in those agreements (drafting inference).

**Escrow and continuity:** Escrow needs a licence that survives vendor failure, because the bank's rights after a vendor failure depend on the licence rather than on the copy held in escrow (good practice).

**Published SDKs and sample code:** Code the bank distributes to customers is issued and communicated to the public, which are restricted acts (Cap. 528 s.22(1)(b), (fa)). Check copyright notices and licence terms before release, not after a customer finds a problem (good practice).

glossary.definition: The Second Circuit's test for non-literal copying: abstract a program into levels, filter out unprotectable elements, then compare what remains (Altai).
The way a user operates a program, such as its commands and menus. Copyright does not protect it under § 102(b), as the Lotus decision held.
A work expressed in words, numbers or other symbols, whatever the material object. Computer programs are protected as literary works (§ 101; § 102(a)(1)).
A work based on one or more preexisting works, such as a translation or adaptation. Preparing one is an exclusive right of the copyright owner (§ 101; § 106(2)).
The person who holds title to a lawfully made copy of a program, as distinct from a licensee. Ownership is the trigger for the rights in § 117(a) and § 109(a).
A user who holds a licence to a program rather than owning the copy, so it cannot rely on the owner's privileges in § 117(a) or § 109(a) (Vernor).
A copy or adaptation needed to use a program with a machine. Section 117(a)(1) lets the owner of a copy make one.
Terms printed on or inside software packaging that bind the user by opening the package or using the software. ProCD held these enforceable unless objectionable on general contract grounds.
Analysing a program to learn how it works. It can be fair use where it is the only way to reach functional elements (Sega), but an enforceable contract ban can still apply (Bowers).
Damages the court sets per work, from $750 to $30,000, which the owner can elect instead of actual damages and profits (§ 504(c)). They are unavailable where registration comes too late (§ 412).
Information conveyed with a work, such as its title, author, owner and terms of use. Removing it knowing it will facilitate infringement breaches § 1202(b).
A person with a contractual right to use a program, who may back it up and copy or adapt it where necessary for that use (Cap. 528 s.60(2), s.61(1)).
The offence in s.118(2A) of possessing an infringing copy of a program for a trade or business (Cap. 528 s.118(2A)).
For a program, an altered version of the program or a translation of it, including conversion into or between computer languages or codes (Cap. 528 s.29(3)(b), s.29(4)).

title: Who owns the code
oneLiner: Authors own code first, so the bank gets staff code through work made for hire and contractor or vendor code only through a signed assignment.
keyPoints: Under the Copyright Act (17 U.S.C.), copyright in code vests first in its author, so the bank owns code if it is the author, or if it takes a transfer that is in writing unless it passes by operation of law (§ 201(a); § 204(a)).
**Employees:** Code an employee writes within the scope of employment is a work made for hire, so the bank is treated as the author (§ 101; § 201(b)).
**Contractors and vendors:** Their code is usually not a work made for hire, so the bank needs a transfer signed by the author (§ 101; § 204(a)).
**Termination:** An author's grant of rights, other than in a work made for hire, can be terminated decades later despite any contrary agreement (§ 203(a)(5)).
**Patents:** Under the Patent Act (35 U.S.C.), inventors own their inventions until they assign them in writing, and an unrecorded assignment can lose out to a later buyer (§ 261).

**State law and counsel:** California limits invention assignment for an employee's own-time inventions and requires written notice of that limit (Cal. Lab. Code §§ 2870-2872). Check each template against it (good practice).

conceptMap.caption: How the bank comes to own code. Copyright and patent title pass by different routes, and each route needs its own paperwork.

deepDive.heading: Authors start with the code
deepDive.lede: Ownership begins with whoever creates the code. The bank gets it through the work made for hire rules or a signed transfer.
points: **Initial owner:** Copyright in a protected work vests first in its author or authors (§ 201(a)). Writing the code makes the writer the author, and the bank must then show how the rights reached it.

**Joint works:** A [[joint work]] needs contributions meant to merge into one unitary whole (§ 101). Its authors are co-owners (§ 201(a)). A valuable contribution alone does not make someone a joint author: Aalmuhammed v. Lee, 202 F.3d 1227 (9th Cir. 2000), looked at control, shared intent and audience appeal.

**Co-owners:** Each co-owner may license non-exclusively without the others' consent but must account for profits. An exclusive licence needs all co-owners (Davis v. Blige, 505 F.3d 90 (2d Cir. 2007); reported; check).

**Written agreement:** For a work made for hire, the employer or commissioning party owns all the rights unless the parties agree otherwise in a signed writing (§ 201(b)). A contract cannot make most commissioned software a work made for hire, but it can assign the copyright in writing (drafting inference; § 101(2); § 204(a)).
