deepDive.heading: Employees and the scope of employment
deepDive.lede: Staff code is a work made for hire only when the author is an employee writing within the job.

visual.caption: Who owns the code, and what the bank must do to hold it.

items.label: Employee
items.note: Bank is the author, if the code is within the scope of employment (§ 201(b))

items.label: Independent contractor
items.note: Not a work made for hire by default; needs a transfer in writing (§ 204(a))

items.label: Vendor
items.note: Read the deliverable terms; a work made for hire label does not fit most software

items.label: Co-developer
items.note: Co-owners where contributions were meant to merge (§ 201(a))

points: **Employee test:** A work prepared by an employee within the [[scope of employment]] is a work made for hire (§ 101(1)). 'Employee' follows common-law agency principles, not payroll status (Community for Creative Non-Violence v. Reid, 490 U.S. 730 (1989)).

**Agency factors:** Courts weigh the hiring party's control over the manner and means of work, the skill required, who supplies the tools, the location and duration of the work, the method of payment, and benefits and tax treatment (Reid).
**Outside the job:** Code written for a side project, or outside the employee's job duties, may fall outside the scope of employment, so the bank cannot assume it owns that code (drafting inference).

**Contractors:** Code from an independent contractor is not a work made for hire under § 101(1). Even with a signed clause, § 101(2) covers only nine categories, and software usually does not fit one of them.

deepDive.heading: Transfers need a signed writing
deepDive.lede: A transfer of ownership is valid only if it is in writing, unless it passes by operation of law. A non-exclusive licence needs no writing.
points: **Writing:** A transfer of copyright ownership is not valid unless the owner of the rights conveyed, or its agent, signs a writing that records it (§ 204(a)).

**What counts:** A transfer covers assignments and exclusive licences, but not a [[non-exclusive licence]] (§ 101). A non-exclusive licence therefore needs no signed writing under § 204(a), although signing one is still sensible (good practice).
**Recording:** Recording with the Copyright Office gives [[constructive notice]] only if the document identifies the work and the work is registered (§ 205(c)).

**Priority:** Between two conflicting transfers, the earlier one prevails if it is recorded within one month after signing in the United States (two months if signed abroad), or before the later one is recorded. Otherwise the later transfer prevails only if it was recorded first, taken in good faith, for valuable consideration or on a binding promise to pay royalties, and without notice of the earlier transfer (§ 205(d)).

deepDive.heading: Contractor code and the termination right
deepDive.lede: An author's grant can be taken back decades later, whatever the contract says.

visual.caption: Timing for an author's grant that is not a work made for hire. Dates depend on the grant and on any publication.

items.label: Grant executed
items.note: Assignment or licence signed by the author

items.label: Notice served
items.note: Served on the grantee, and recorded in the Copyright Office before termination takes effect

items.label: Window opens
items.note: Year 35 if the grant does not cover publication; otherwise the earlier of 35 years from publication or 40 from the grant

items.label: Window closes
items.note: Termination must take effect within this window

points: **Scope:** The right covers exclusive and non-exclusive grants that an author executed on or after 1 January 1978. It does not apply to a work made for hire (§ 203(a)).

**Window:** Termination takes effect in a five-year period that starts 35 years after the grant. For a grant that covers publication, the period starts at the earlier of 35 years from publication or 40 years from the grant (§ 203(a)(3)).
**Notice:** The author, or the heirs who hold the termination interest, serve written notice two to ten years before the effective date, and record it before that date (§ 203(a)(4)).
**Override:** Termination applies notwithstanding any agreement to the contrary (§ 203(a)(5)), so the [[termination window]] cannot be contracted away.

**What survives:** A derivative work prepared under the grant before termination may keep being used on the old terms. The privilege does not extend to preparing other derivative works after termination (§ 203(b)(1)).
deepDive.takeaway: Treat a contractor's assignment of core code as a long-term exposure that the bank can plan for but cannot contract out of.

deepDive.heading: Patents: inventors own until they assign
deepDive.lede: Patent rights start with the inventor, so the bank needs a written, present assignment and should record it.

visual.caption: Steps that help a patent assignment hold against a later buyer.

items.label: Use present wording
items.note: Passes title to the invention when it is made

items.label: Sign in writing
items.note: Required for any assignment of a patent or application

items.label: Record in time
items.note: Or before a later purchase or mortgage

points: **Inventor ownership:** Inventors own their inventions until they assign them. In Board of Trustees of Leland Stanford Junior University v. Roche Molecular Systems, Inc., 563 U.S. 776 (2011), the Supreme Court held that the Bayh-Dole Act does not itself vest title in federal contractors.

**Wording:** The Federal Circuit read 'agree to assign' as a promise to assign in future. It read 'do hereby assign' as a [[present assignment]] of future inventions that transfers title when the invention is made (Stanford v. Roche, 583 F.3d 832 (Fed. Cir. 2009); FilmTec Corp. v. Allied-Signal, Inc., 939 F.2d 1568 (Fed. Cir. 1991)).

**Formalities:** An assignment of a patent or application must be in writing (35 U.S.C. § 261). It is void against a later purchaser or mortgagee for value without notice, unless it is recorded within three months of its date or before that later purchase.

**Shop right:** An employer may hold a [[shop right]], a non-exclusive, royalty-free right to use an invention an employee made with its time, materials or equipment. It depends on the facts and on state law (reported; check).
**Practice:** Put present-tense assignment wording in staff and contractor agreements, and record each patent assignment in the USPTO when the bank's title matters (good practice).

deepDive.heading: State limits on invention assignment
deepDive.lede: California and several other states limit how far an employer's invention clause can reach.
points: **Own-time inventions:** An [[invention assignment clause]] does not reach an invention made entirely on the employee's own time, without the employer's equipment, supplies, facilities or trade secrets. Exceptions cover inventions related to the employer's business or research, or resulting from work for it (Cal. Lab. Code § 2870).

**Conditions:** The employer may require confidential disclosure of inventions and a review process. It cannot require a clause that § 2870 makes void as a condition of employment (Cal. Lab. Code § 2871).

**Notice:** For an agreement entered into after 1 January 1980 that requires assignment, the employer must give written notice, when the agreement is made, that § 2870 inventions are excluded. The employee who claims that protection bears the burden of proof (Cal. Lab. Code § 2872).

**Other states:** Several states have similar statutes with their own wording, including Illinois, Minnesota and Washington, which also require written notice. Nevada works differently, reaching employer-related inventions unless agreed otherwise (reported; check each statute).
**Software and visual art:** The Visual Artists Rights Act covers only works of visual art, so it does not reach software. Code ownership turns on the authorship and transfer rules above.

deepDive.heading: Vendors, side projects and open source
deepDive.lede: Ownership is most often lost at the edges: vendor deliverables, side projects and staff contributions to public projects.
points: **Deliverables:** Decide in the contract which deliverables the bank owns by assignment, which it licenses, and which stay with the vendor. A work made for hire label does not turn most software into a work made for hire (§ 101(2); good practice).

**Customisations:** A vendor's changes to the bank's code are usually a derivative work of it (§ 101). The contract should say who owns the changes and whether the bank can keep using them after the engagement ends (good practice).

**Licence-backs:** If the bank assigns its own improvements back to a vendor, it may lose title to code it wrote. A licence back is the safer route if it covers the bank's affiliates and future use (good practice).

**Side projects:** Code an employee writes on their own time, outside the job, may not be a work made for hire (§ 101(1)). For inventions, California's own-time rule may still protect the employee (§ 2870), so check the agreement.

**Open source contributions:** Code a staff member writes within the job is usually the bank's work made for hire. Contributing it to a public project is then the bank's grant under that project's licence, so approve such contributions in advance (good practice).

provisions.title: Initial ownership, joint authors and works made for hire
provisions.summary: Copyright vests initially in the author or authors of a work, and the authors of a joint work are co-owners (§ 201(a)). For a work made for hire, the employer or other person for whom the work was prepared is the author and owns all the rights, unless the parties agree otherwise in a signed writing (§ 201(b)).
provisions.counselNote: This is the starting point for every ownership question. Staff code reaches the bank by operation of law, while contractor and vendor code reaches it only through the paperwork.

provisions.title: Definitions: work made for hire, joint work and transfer of copyright ownership
provisions.summary: A work made for hire is a work prepared by an employee within the scope of employment, or a specially commissioned work in one of nine listed categories where both parties expressly agree in a signed writing. A joint work is one prepared by two or more authors who intend their contributions to merge into a unitary whole. A transfer of ownership includes an assignment or exclusive licence, but not a non-exclusive licence.
provisions.counselNote: The definitions decide whether staff code belongs to the bank automatically, and whether a vendor's work made for hire clause does anything. For most software from a vendor or contractor, it does not.

provisions.title: Termination of transfers and licences granted by the author
provisions.summary: Lets an author terminate an exclusive or non-exclusive grant executed on or after 1 January 1978, other than a work made for hire, in a five-year window that opens 35 years after the grant (for a grant covering publication, the earlier of 35 years from publication or 40 years from the grant). Notice must be served two to ten years ahead and recorded, and termination applies notwithstanding any contrary agreement (§ 203(a)).
provisions.counselNote: Long-lived code built on contractor assignments needs a termination plan. The right cannot be contracted out of, so the bank should track its older grants and rely on work made for hire status only where the statute gives it.

provisions.title: Execution of transfers of copyright ownership
provisions.summary: A transfer of copyright ownership, other than by operation of law, is not valid unless an instrument of conveyance, or a note or memorandum of the transfer, is in writing and signed by the owner of the rights conveyed or its duly authorised agent (§ 204(a)). A certificate of acknowledgement is prima facie evidence of execution but is not required for validity (§ 204(b)).
provisions.counselNote: The signature requirement is the bank's main answer to an undocumented claim to code. Check that the person who signs for a vendor or contractor holds the rights and has authority to sign.

provisions.title: Recordation of transfers and other documents
provisions.summary: A transfer of copyright ownership may be recorded in the Copyright Office. Recording gives constructive notice only if the document identifies the work and the work is registered (§ 205(c)). Between conflicting transfers, the first prevails if recorded within one month after signing in the United States (two months if signed abroad), or before the later transfer is recorded (§ 205(d)).
provisions.counselNote: Recording is how the bank protects a contested title. A bank that signs first and records promptly is better placed against a later, conflicting transfer.

provisions.title: Ownership; assignment
provisions.summary: Patent applications and patents, and any interest in them, are assignable only by an instrument in writing. An interest that is an assignment is void against a later purchaser or mortgagee for value without notice, unless it is recorded in the Patent and Trademark Office within three months of its date or before that later purchase.
provisions.counselNote: Record bank-owned patent assignments at once. The three-month rule is short, and a missed deadline can cost the bank title against a later buyer.

provisions.title: Employee inventions: employment agreements
provisions.summary: An employment-agreement clause requiring assignment does not reach an invention the employee developed entirely on their own time, without the employer's equipment, supplies, facilities or trade secret information. The exceptions are inventions related to the employer's business or actual or demonstrably anticipated research, and inventions that result from work for the employer. A clause that goes further is unenforceable.
provisions.counselNote: The § 2870 carve-out applies by statute, so a clause that reaches side inventions is void to that extent, and the bank cannot make a void clause a condition of employment (§ 2871).

provisions.title: Employee inventions: written notification
provisions.summary: For an employment agreement entered into after 1 January 1980 that requires assignment of inventions, the employer must give the employee written notice, when the agreement is made, that the agreement does not apply to an invention that qualifies fully under § 2870. The employee who claims that protection bears the burden of proof.
provisions.counselNote: Keep a signed copy of the § 2870 notice with each California employee agreement. A missing notice is an easy point for an employee to take in a dispute (good practice).

provisions.instrument: Community for Creative Non-Violence v. Reid
provisions.title: 'Employee' follows common-law agency principles
provisions.summary: The Supreme Court held that 'employee' in the work made for hire definition takes its common-law agency meaning. Courts weigh the hiring party's control over the manner and means of work, skill, tools, location, duration, method of payment, benefits and tax treatment, among other factors.
provisions.counselNote: A contractor label does not settle employee status, and neither does a payroll record. Courts look at the facts of the working relationship, so the bank should document them (good practice).

provisions.instrument: Board of Trustees of Leland Stanford Junior University v. Roche Molecular Systems, Inc.
provisions.title: Inventors own their inventions until they assign them
provisions.summary: The Supreme Court held that the Bayh-Dole Act does not itself vest title to federally funded inventions in the federal contractor. The inventor keeps the rights until the inventor assigns them.
provisions.counselNote: A general 'we own the IP' clause may not transfer patent rights. The bank should check that each inventor has signed a present assignment of the invention.

provisions.title: 'Agree to assign' differs from 'do hereby assign'
provisions.summary: The Federal Circuit held that 'agree to assign' is a promise to assign in future, while 'do hereby assign' is a present assignment of future inventions that transfers title when the invention is made.
provisions.counselNote: Wording decides title. Replace 'agree to assign' with present-assignment language in staff and vendor templates, and check existing agreements for it (good practice).

provisions.title: Present assignment of future inventions
provisions.summary: The Federal Circuit held that wording by which an inventor presently assigns future inventions transfers title to each invention as it is made, without a further act.
provisions.counselNote: Present-tense wording in staff and vendor agreements is the practical route to title over inventions that do not yet exist (good practice).

provisions.title: Joint authorship needs more than a valuable contribution
provisions.summary: The Ninth Circuit held that joint authorship needs more than a valuable contribution. Courts look at control, objective manifestations of shared intent and audience appeal.
provisions.counselNote: Engineers who contribute to a shared project may claim co-authorship. A written allocation of roles and an agreed owner for the combined code reduce that risk.

checklist: **Map each code base to its route:** For every repository, record whether the code came from employees, contractors, vendors or open source, and which signed paper covers it.

**Use present-tense invention wording:** Put 'hereby assign' language for inventions and work within the job into staff agreements, with the § 2870 carve-out and the § 2872 notice for California staff.
**Get a signed transfer from each contractor:** Obtain a written, signed assignment before contractor code is merged, and do not rely on a work made for hire label alone (§ 101(2); § 204(a)).
**Settle vendor deliverables in the contract:** Say which deliverables the bank owns by assignment, which it licenses, and which stay with the vendor, with schedules for any background code.
**Track older grants for termination windows:** Diarise the § 203 windows for contractor and vendor grants, and plan a renegotiation before an author serves notice.

**Record material transfers:** Record assignments of code and patent filings with the Copyright Office or the USPTO (§ 205; 35 U.S.C. § 261), and keep the recordation receipts with the signed originals.
**Set a policy for side projects and contributions:** Require pre-approval for staff contributions to public projects that use bank code, and say how own-time inventions are handled.

**Check state invention law for each staff location:** Review invention clauses against the statute of each state where staff work, starting with California, and confirm the notice requirements (reported; check each statute).
itAngle: **Commit authorship:** Version control records who committed each change, but a commit author is not the legal owner. Tie commit identities to employment and contractor records, so the bank can show who wrote what (good practice).

**Contributor agreements:** Require a signed contributor licence or assignment before outside code is merged, and check that the signer is the author or has authority to sign. Automate the check in the pull-request flow (good practice).

**Joint code:** Code several people write in one repository may be a joint work if each contribution was meant to merge into one whole (§ 101). Where modules are separable, keep their ownership and licence notices in each module.
**Vendor code drops:** Vendor deliverables often arrive as archives without history. Ask for commit history and author identities, so the bank can trace which code came from which contractor.

**Invention disclosures:** Design documents and invention disclosures often come before any filing. Route them through an invention process so that present assignments attach before the patent application is filed (good practice).
virtualBankNotes: **Third-party guidance:** The interagency third-party guidance (88 Fed. Reg. 37920 (2023)) is technology-neutral and does not deal with open source as such. Vendors that supply or support open source still fall within it, so put ownership and continuity terms into due diligence (drafting inference).

**Continuity and escrow:** No US bank regulation mandates source code escrow. The interagency guidance treats exit as a contract point, so check that a deposit includes the environment, data and credentials needed to run the code (drafting inference; market practice).

**NYDFS:** Covered entities under 23 NYCRR Part 500 must have written procedures for secure development of in-house applications and for assessing externally developed applications (23 NYCRR 500.8). Knowing what the bank wrote and what it received makes that assessment possible (drafting inference).

**Proof of title:** Examiners and diligence teams ask for signed assignments and invention records. Keep them in a searchable register that is owned by legal, not in individual inboxes (good practice).
**Acquisitions:** Known title gaps are usually excluded from representations and warranties insurance, so buyers ask for special indemnities (reported; market practice).
productNotes: **Settle ownership in the contract before work starts:** Tell counsel before a vendor, agency or contractor starts a feature. Code belongs to its author, and the bank is treated as the author only for code an employee writes within the scope of employment. Otherwise the bank needs a transfer signed by the author (17 U.S.C. §§ 101, 201(a)-(b), 204(a)).

**Do not accept a deliverable without the signed paper:** Product managers should not take vendor or contractor code into a release until the signed assignment or licence is on file. Calling software a work made for hire does not make it one, because most software falls outside the nine categories in § 101(2) (17 U.S.C. §§ 101, 204(a)).

**Route side projects and public contributions through approval:** Staff should not contribute bank code to a public project, or build a personal product on it, without approval. Code written within the job is usually the bank's, so a contribution is the bank's grant under that project's licence (17 U.S.C. § 101; good practice).

**Tell HR and counsel when staff in California join product teams:** California limits an employer's invention clause, which cannot reach an own-time invention that does not use the employer's resources, unless the invention relates to the employer's business or actual or demonstrably anticipated research or development, or results from work done for the employer (Cal. Lab. Code § 2870(a)). The employer must also give written notice of that limit (Cal. Lab. Code §§ 2870, 2872).
pitfalls: **Relying on a work made for hire label for vendors:** Assuming that a vendor's clause makes its software the bank's, when most software does not fit the nine categories in § 101(2).
**Unsigned contractor code:** Merging contractor code without a signed transfer, so the bank may hold no title to code it ships (§ 204(a)).
**Missing California carve-out:** Using one invention clause for all staff that reaches inventions § 2870 excludes, or leaving out the § 2872 notice for California employees.
**Agree-to-assign wording:** Using 'agrees to assign' where the bank needs title now, so that ownership waits for a further signed document (Stanford v. Roche, 583 F.3d 832 (Fed. Cir. 2009)).
**Unrecorded patent assignments:** Leaving a patent assignment unrecorded beyond three months, which risks losing it to a later purchaser or mortgagee without notice (35 U.S.C. § 261).
**Assuming open source contributions carry no ownership consequences:** The bank's position in staff contributions still follows the employment and assignment rules (good practice).

points: **Employer exercises economic rights:** for a program made by an employee in the execution of duties or following instructions, the employer exercises the economic rights unless agreed otherwise (Directive 2009/24/EC, Art. 2(3)).
**Contractors are outside that rule:** the statutory employer rule covers employees only, so contractor and vendor code still needs a written assignment or licence.
**Employer first owner:** the employer owns works made by an employee in the course of employment, subject to agreement (CDPA 1988 s.11(2)).
**Computer-generated works:** the author is the person who made the arrangements necessary for creation (s.9(3)), with a 50-year term (s.12(7)).
**Employer owns by default:** where a work is made in the course of employment, the employer is the first owner absent agreement to the contrary (Copyright Act s.13(3)).
**Moral rights need waivers:** moral rights cannot be assigned (s.14.1(2)), so employee and contractor agreements should take waivers in addition to the assignment.
**Software the employee was not asked or expected to write:** the employer did not own it, as reported in Nexus Solutions Inc. v. Krougly, 2026 ONCA 199 (reported; check).

hongKong.summary: Hong Kong starts from the author or the inventor and gives an employer or a commissioner ownership only in defined cases. Copyright in commissioned code belongs to the developer unless the contract names someone else, but the commissioner keeps a statutory exclusive licence. The two biggest differences from the US position are the award an employer must pay for unforeseen exploitation of staff work (Cap. 528 s.14(2)) and the commissioner's licence that applies whatever the contract says (Cap. 528 s.15(2)).
keyPoints: **Authors own first:** The author of a copyright work is its first owner, and the bank gets staff code through the employee rule or a written transfer (Cap. 528 s.13, s.14(1)).
**Employee award:** Where staff work is exploited in a way neither side could reasonably have contemplated, the employer must pay an award unless the parties agreed otherwise (Cap. 528 s.14(2)).

**Commissioned code:** Unless the contract expressly says who owns the copyright, the developer keeps it and the bank gets only an exclusive licence for the purposes both had in mind when the work was commissioned (Cap. 528 s.15(1)-(2)).
**Written transfers:** An assignment of copyright is not effective unless it is in writing and signed by or for the assignor (Cap. 528 s.101(3)).
**Inventions:** The inventor owns the right to a patent, but an employer owns an employee's invention in the defined cases of s.57 (Cap. 514 s.9E(1), s.57(1)).

sections.heading: Copyright in staff work: the employer owns, with an award
sections.lede: Hong Kong gives the employer first ownership of staff work made in the course of employment, but it also gives the employee a right to an award in some cases.
points: **The author owns first:** The author of a work is its first copyright owner, subject to the employee, commissioned and government rules (Cap. 528 s.13).

**Who the author is:** The author is the person who creates the work. For a computer-generated work, the author is the person who undertook the arrangements necessary for its creation (Cap. 528 s.11(1), (3)).

**Employee works:** A literary work, which includes a computer program, made by an employee in the course of employment belongs first to the employer, subject to any agreement to the contrary (Cap. 528 s.4(1)(b), s.14(1)).

**Unforeseen exploitation:** If the employer or someone with its permission exploits the work in a way neither side could reasonably have contemplated when it was made, the employer must pay an award, unless they agreed otherwise (Cap. 528 s.14(2)).
**Setting the award:** The parties agree the amount, or the Copyright Tribunal fixes it if they cannot agree (Cap. 528 s.14(2)).
sections.takeaway: Check each engineer's employment contract for an express ownership clause and an agreed position on awards, because the default rule applies only to work done in the course of employment (good practice).

sections.heading: Commissioned and contractor code: the contract decides, with a statutory licence
sections.lede: A developer keeps copyright in commissioned code unless the contract names someone else, but the commissioner always has a licence that is hard to take back.
points: **Ownership follows the contract:** Copyright in a commissioned work belongs to the person the agreement expressly entitles (Cap. 528 s.15(1)).

**Statutory exclusive licence:** Whatever the agreement says, the commissioner has an exclusive licence to exploit the work for all purposes both sides could reasonably have contemplated when it was commissioned (Cap. 528 s.15(2)(a)).
**Power to restrain:** The commissioner may restrain any exploitation for a purpose it could reasonably object to (Cap. 528 s.15(2)(b)).
**Silent contracts:** Without an express term, the author stays first owner under s.13, subject to that licence (Cap. 528 s.13, s.15(2)).
**Exclusivity needs writing:** An exclusive licence must be in writing and signed by or on behalf of the copyright owner (Cap. 528 s.103(1)).
sections.takeaway: Name the owner of each deliverable in the vendor contract, and write down the purposes the bank needs, so that the bank does not rely on the statutory licence to cover what it actually plans to do (good practice).

sections.heading: Formalities for transfers and signatures
sections.lede: A transfer of copyright needs a signature that the law recognises, and a click-through acceptance is not automatically one.
points: **Signed writing:** An assignment is effective only if it is in writing and signed by or for the assignor (Cap. 528 s.101(3)).

**Electronic signature test:** Where neither party acts for a government entity, an electronic signature satisfies a signature requirement only if the method identifies the signer and shows approval, is reliable and appropriate for the purpose, and the other party consents to the method (Cap. 553 s.6(1)(b)-(e)).

**Click-through terms:** Online acceptance can form a contract under the electronic records rule (Cap. 553 s.17(1)-(2)), but a bare click is not automatically an electronic signature (drafting inference).

**Excluded matters:** Schedule 1 to the Electronic Transactions Ordinance lists matters such as land dispositions and wills, but does not list copyright or patent assignments (Cap. 553 s.3 and Sch. 1).
sections.takeaway: Agree the signing method in the contract, and keep a signed assignment on file before the bank relies on the transfer (good practice).

sections.heading: Patents and registered designs: the inventor starts as owner
sections.lede: Patent ownership starts with the inventor, and an employer owns an employee's invention only in the cases the Ordinance defines.
points: **Inventor first:** The right to a patent belongs to the inventor or the inventor's successor in title (Cap. 514 s.9E(1)).

**Place of employment:** For an employee, the right is decided under the law of the place where the employee is wholly or mainly employed, or the place of the employer's business if that cannot be found (Cap. 514 s.9E(2)).

**Employer owns in defined cases:** An invention belongs to the employer if it was made in the course of normal duties or specifically assigned duties where an invention might reasonably be expected, or where the employee had a special obligation to further the employer's interests (Cap. 514 s.57(1)).
**Compensation:** An employee may seek compensation where a granted patent on an employer-owned invention is of outstanding benefit to the employer (Cap. 514 s.58(1)).

**Designs:** Where a design is commissioned for money or money's worth, the commissioner owns it, and an employer owns a design made by an employee in the course of employment, unless the parties agree otherwise (Cap. 522 s.3(2)-(3)).
sections.takeaway: Put an invention assignment in each employment and contractor agreement, and record each patent transfer promptly, because a late registration can cost the right to damages (good practice).

provisions.title: First ownership of copyright
provisions.summary: The author of a work is the first owner of any copyright in it, subject to the employee, commissioned and government rules in sections 14 to 16.
provisions.counselNote: This is the starting point for every staff and vendor code question, so the bank should not assume that the employer or the commissioner owns the work unless one of the exceptions applies.

provisions.title: Authorship
provisions.summary: The author is the person who creates the work. For a computer-generated literary, dramatic, musical or artistic work, the author is the person who undertook the arrangements necessary for its creation.
provisions.counselNote: Code produced with the help of tools is computer-generated only where there is no human author (s.198), and only then is the person who made the arrangements the author (s.11(3); drafting inference).

provisions.title: Employee works
provisions.summary: A literary, dramatic, musical or artistic work, or a film, made by an employee in the course of employment belongs first to the employer, subject to any agreement to the contrary. The employer must pay an award for exploitation neither side could reasonably have contemplated, unless the parties agreed otherwise.
provisions.counselNote: Engineers' code is covered only if written in the course of employment, so the job description and the employment contract both matter to the bank.

provisions.title: Commissioned works
provisions.summary: Ownership follows the agreement where it expressly provides for it. Whatever the agreement says, the commissioner has an exclusive licence for purposes both sides could reasonably have contemplated, and may restrain exploitation it could reasonably object to.
provisions.counselNote: Where a vendor contract is silent on ownership, the bank's rights are fixed by what was contemplated at commissioning, so the intended uses should be written into the contract.

provisions.title: Assignment must be in writing
provisions.summary: An assignment of copyright is not effective unless it is in writing and signed by or on behalf of the assignor. A licence binds successors in title, except a good-faith purchaser for value without notice.
provisions.counselNote: A signed instrument is needed for an assignment, so the bank should not accept an email exchange or an unsigned statement of transfer as proof of ownership.

provisions.title: Exclusive licences
provisions.summary: An exclusive licence must be in writing and signed by or on behalf of the copyright owner. The licensee has the same rights against a successor in title who is bound by the licence as against the grantor.
provisions.counselNote: The bank's exclusivity in vendor code depends on this formality, so an exclusivity term that is not signed is a gap in the bank's position.

provisions.title: Electronic signatures
provisions.summary: An electronic signature satisfies a signature requirement only if the method identifies the signer and shows approval, is reliable and appropriate for the purpose, and the other party consents to the method.
provisions.counselNote: Signing platforms used for vendor deals should be agreed in the contract, so that the signature formality for an assignment is met.

provisions.title: Ownership of designs
provisions.summary: The designer is the original owner of a design. A commissioner owns a commissioned design, and an employer owns a design made by an employee in the course of employment, in each case subject to any contrary agreement.
provisions.counselNote: This reverses the copyright default for commissioned designs, so design agency contracts should state who owns each design expressly (good practice).

provisions.title: Right to a patent
provisions.summary: The right to a patent belongs to the inventor or the inventor's successor in title. For an employee, the question is decided under the law where the employee is wholly or mainly employed.
provisions.counselNote: With staff in more than one place, the law of the place of employment decides who owns an invention, so the employment contract should say which law governs.

provisions.title: Employees' inventions
provisions.summary: An employee's invention belongs to the employer if made in the course of normal duties, or in specifically assigned duties, where an invention might reasonably be expected, or where the employee had a special obligation to further the employer's interests. Otherwise it belongs to the employee.
provisions.counselNote: Engineers working on the bank's payment or security systems may fall within the normal-duties limb, so the bank should record those duties in job descriptions.

bankNotes: **Vendor deliverables:** Name the owner of each deliverable in the contract, and state the purposes for which the bank will use it, because the statutory licence covers only what both sides contemplated (Cap. 528 s.15(2)) (good practice).

**Staff code:** Keep the ownership clause in the employment contract up to date for engineers who write code for the bank, and record any agreed position on awards for unforeseen exploitation (Cap. 528 s.14(2)) (good practice).

**Patent transfers:** Apply to record each patent transfer within 6 months, because an unregistered transfer cannot found a claim for damages or profits for infringement in the gap (Cap. 514 s.87) (good practice).

glossary.definition: A work prepared by an employee within the scope of employment, or a specially commissioned work in one of nine listed categories under a signed writing. The employer or commissioning party is treated as the author (17 U.S.C. § 101; § 201(b)).
The part of an employee's job that a work must fall within for it to be a work made for hire under 17 U.S.C. § 101(1). It turns on the facts of the job.
A work by two or more authors who intend their contributions to merge into inseparable or interdependent parts of a unitary whole (17 U.S.C. § 101). The authors are co-owners (§ 201(a)).
One of the joint authors of a joint work, each of whom co-owns the copyright in the whole work (17 U.S.C. § 201(a)).

Wording such as 'do hereby assign' that transfers title when the right arises, including to future inventions, rather than promising to transfer it later (Stanford v. Roche, 583 F.3d 832 (Fed. Cir. 2009)).

The five-year period in which an author may end an earlier grant, which opens 35 years after the grant or, for a grant covering publication, at the earlier of 35 years from publication or 40 years from the grant (17 U.S.C. § 203(a)(3)).
Notice the law treats as given to everyone once a document is recorded. Under 17 U.S.C. § 205(c), recording gives it only if the document identifies the work and the work is registered.
A non-exclusive, royalty-free right for an employer to use an employee's invention made with the employer's time, materials or equipment. It depends on the facts and state law (reported; check).

A clause in an employment agreement requiring the employee to assign inventions to the employer. California limits it for inventions made entirely on the employee's own time (Cal. Lab. Code §§ 2870-2872).
A licence that does not transfer ownership. It is not a transfer of copyright ownership under 17 U.S.C. § 101, so it needs no signed writing under § 204(a).
The body that fixes the amount of an employee's award for unforeseen exploitation if the employer and employee do not agree it (Cap. 528 s.14(2)).
A licence in writing, signed by the copyright owner, that excludes everyone else, including the owner, from exercising a right (Cap. 528 s.103(1)).

title: Patents for software
oneLiner: US patents protect how software works, but each claim must pass eligibility, novelty and clarity tests before it can be enforced.
keyPoints: Patents protect how software works, not its code. The Patent Act (35 U.S.C.) allows a new and useful process or machine to be patented, so a patent can stop an independent rewrite of the same method (35 U.S.C. §§ 101, 154(a)(1)).

**Four tests:** A claim must be eligible (§ 101), novel (§ 102), non-obvious (§ 103) and clearly drafted (§ 112). Eligibility and functional wording are where software claims are most often challenged (drafting inference).
**Timing:** Publishing code can destroy novelty. An inventor's own disclosure is excused only if the application is filed within one year (35 U.S.C. § 102(b)(1)).

**Infringement:** Software methods often run across the bank, a cloud host and customers. The bank can still be liable for steps that others perform if it directs or controls them (35 U.S.C. § 271(a); Akamai Technologies, Inc. v. Limelight Networks, Inc., 797 F.3d 1020 (Fed. Cir. 2015) (en banc)).
**Remedies:** Damages are at least a reasonable royalty (35 U.S.C. § 284), and marking and notice can limit how far back a patentee may recover (§ 287(a)).

**Counsel's role:** Screen features for eligibility and publication timing before release, keep dated development records, and plan the forum (district court, the Patent Trial and Appeal Board or the International Trade Commission) before any demand letter arrives.

conceptMap.caption: Each claim faces a separate statutory test, and each test can be fought in a different forum.

deepDive.heading: Eligibility: the abstract idea test
deepDive.lede: Section 101 is a threshold test, and courts apply a two-step test from case law to software claims.

visual.caption: The two steps come from Alice Corp. v. CLS Bank International, 573 U.S. 208 (2014).

items.label: Step one
items.note: Is the claim directed to an abstract idea or another judicial exception

items.label: Step two
items.note: Do the elements, alone or in order, add something more

items.label: Result
items.note: A claim directed to an abstract idea that adds nothing more is ineligible

points: **Statute:** A patent may be obtained for any new and useful process, machine, manufacture or composition of matter, or improvement of one (35 U.S.C. § 101).

**Two steps:** Alice asks first whether the claim is directed to an abstract idea, then whether its elements add an [[inventive concept]]. The Supreme Court unanimously held computerised intermediated settlement claims ineligible.
**Generic computers:** Implementing an abstract idea on a generic computer adds nothing (Alice). The claim must show something more than the idea performed on a computer.

**Specific improvements:** Enfish, LLC v. Microsoft Corp., 822 F.3d 1327 (Fed. Cir. 2016), held that a self-referential database table improving computer functionality was not abstract. McRO, Inc. v. Bandai Namco Games America Inc., 837 F.3d 1299 (Fed. Cir. 2016), held specific rules for automated lip-sync animation eligible.

**Facts:** Whether elements are well-understood, routine and conventional is a question of fact (Berkheimer v. HP Inc., 881 F.3d 1360 (Fed. Cir. 2018)), so an early win on eligibility is not assured (drafting inference).

**Machine learning:** Recentive Analytics, Inc. v. Fox Corp., 134 F.4th 1205 (Fed. Cir. 2025), held that claims applying established machine-learning methods to a new data environment are ineligible (decided 18 April 2025).
deepDive.takeaway: Draft each claim around a specific technical improvement, and describe that improvement in the specification (good practice).

deepDive.heading: Novelty, obviousness and the grace period
deepDive.lede: Timing decides whether the bank's own publication counts against its patent.

visual.caption: The one-year grace period runs from the bank's own public release.

items.label: Public release
items.note: Code, documentation or a demo goes public

items.label: Grace period ends
items.note: A filing by this date keeps the inventor's own release excused (§ 102(b)(1))

items.label: Later filing
items.note: The release is prior art and novelty is lost (§ 102(a)(1))

points: **Prior art:** A claim is not patentable if the invention was patented, described in a printed publication, in public use, on sale or otherwise available to the public before its [[effective filing date]] (35 U.S.C. § 102(a)(1)).

**Own disclosure:** A disclosure by the inventor, or by someone who got the subject matter from the inventor, is not prior art if made one year or less before the effective filing date (35 U.S.C. § 102(b)(1)(A)).

**Open source:** A public repository, package release or published API document can count as a printed publication or as public availability (drafting inference). Only the inventor's own disclosure is excused, and only inside the one-year window.
**Obviousness:** A claim is not patentable if the difference between it and the prior art would have been obvious to a person of ordinary skill before the effective filing date (35 U.S.C. § 103).
**Filing rule:** The first-inventor-to-file rules apply to claims with an effective filing date on or after 16 March 2013.
deepDive.takeaway: Set a rule that no candidate invention is published until counsel has decided whether to file (good practice).

deepDive.heading: Claim scope and § 112
deepDive.lede: Software claims are often written in functional terms, and § 112 decides how far those terms reach.
points: **Written description:** The specification must describe the invention and the manner of making and using it in terms that enable a skilled person to make and use it (35 U.S.C. § 112(a)).
**Clarity:** Claims must particularly point out and distinctly claim the subject matter that the inventor regards as the invention (35 U.S.C. § 112(b)).

**Means-plus-function:** An element written as a means or step for a function, without structure, covers the structure, material or acts in the specification and their equivalents (35 U.S.C. § 112(f)). Such an element is a [[means-plus-function]] element.

**Nonce words:** Williamson v. Citrix Online, LLC, 792 F.3d 1339 (Fed. Cir. 2015) (en banc in relevant part), held that there is no strong presumption against § 112(f) where 'means' is absent, and that 'module' can be a [[nonce word]].
**Drafting:** Describe in the specification how the code performs each function, so that a court construing a functional element has structure to match (good practice).
deepDive.takeaway: Treat 'module' and similar generic words as possible means-plus-function terms, and check each one against the code the specification describes.

deepDive.heading: Infringement: who performs the steps
deepDive.lede: A bank can infringe directly, by inducing others, or by supplying a component.

visual.caption: Three routes to liability under the Patent Act (35 U.S.C. § 271).

items.label: Direct infringement
items.note: Make, use, offer to sell, sell or import in the US

items.label: Induced infringement
items.note: Actively encourage others to infringe

items.label: Contributory infringement
items.note: Supply a component especially made for the infringing use

points: **Direct:** Making, using, offering to sell, selling or importing a patented invention within the US infringes (35 U.S.C. § 271(a)).
**Inducement:** Whoever actively induces infringement is liable as an infringer (35 U.S.C. § 271(b)). User guides that tell customers to run a claimed method are a typical risk (drafting inference).

**Contributory:** Supplying a component that is especially made for an infringing use, and is not a staple article suitable for substantial non-infringing use, is contributory infringement when sold knowing it (35 U.S.C. § 271(c)). An SDK that is sold, offered for sale or imported can fall within this; one given away free is mainly an inducement risk under § 271(b) (drafting inference).

**Split steps:** Akamai Technologies, Inc. v. Limelight Networks, Inc., 797 F.3d 1020 (Fed. Cir. 2015) (en banc), holds one party liable for a method performed by several actors if it directs or controls them, for example by conditioning participation or a benefit on performance of the steps and setting the manner or timing of that performance, or if they form a joint enterprise.
**Hosting:** A bank that runs a claimed method on its own systems in the US carries the direct risk. A vendor's hosting does not remove that risk if the bank directs the steps (drafting inference).
deepDive.takeaway: Map which party performs each claimed step, including customers, cloud providers and vendors, before launch.

deepDive.heading: Remedies, marking and fees
deepDive.lede: Damages start from a reasonable royalty, and marking and notice set how far back a claim can reach.
points: **Floor:** Damages must be adequate to compensate and in no event less than a reasonable royalty for the infringer's use (35 U.S.C. § 284).

**Enhancement:** The court may increase damages up to three times. Halo Electronics, Inc. v. Pulse Electronics, Inc., 579 U.S. 93 (2016), makes enhancement discretionary and reserves it for egregious cases, typified by wilful misconduct.

**Fees:** The court may award reasonable attorney fees to the prevailing party in exceptional cases (35 U.S.C. § 285). Octane Fitness, LLC v. ICON Health & Fitness, Inc., 572 U.S. 545 (2014), judges exceptional cases on the totality of the circumstances.
**Look-back:** No recovery is allowed for infringement committed more than six years before the complaint or counterclaim (35 U.S.C. § 286).

**Marking:** If a patentee does not mark its product, damages run only from actual notice, and filing suit counts as notice (35 U.S.C. § 287(a)). A web address that links the product to the patent number can serve as the marking.
deepDive.takeaway: Keep a public patent marking page for products that practise the bank's patents, and update it when each patent issues (good practice).

deepDive.heading: Forums and proceedings
deepDive.lede: A software patent dispute can run in district court, before the Patent Trial and Appeal Board (PTAB), and, for imported hardware, at the International Trade Commission (ITC).

visual.caption: Each forum decides different questions and offers different remedies.

items.label: District court
items.note: Damages and injunctions; venue by residence or a regular place of business

items.label: PTAB (IPR or PGR)
items.note: Cancels claims only, with no damages

items.label: ITC
items.note: Blocks infringing imports; needs a US industry

points: **District court:** A patent suit may be brought where the defendant resides, or where it has committed infringing acts and has a regular and established place of business (28 U.S.C. § 1400(b)). TC Heartland LLC v. Kraft Foods Group Brands LLC, 581 U.S. 258 (2017), limits a domestic corporation's residence to its state of incorporation.
**Appeals:** The Federal Circuit hears appeals from district courts in patent cases, from PTAB decisions and from final ITC determinations (28 U.S.C. § 1295(a)).

**Inter partes review:** A petition may raise only §§ 102 or 103 grounds, using patents or printed publications (35 U.S.C. § 311(b)). It may be filed after the later of nine months from grant or the end of any post-grant review (§ 311(c)).

**Timing bars:** An [[inter partes review]] cannot start if the petitioner has sued on validity. It must be filed within one year of service of an infringement complaint (35 U.S.C. § 315(a)(1), (b)). A final written decision bars later grounds the petitioner raised or could reasonably have raised (§ 315(e)).
**Post-grant review:** A petition filed within nine months of grant may raise any ground under § 282(b)(2) or (3), including §§ 101 and 112 (35 U.S.C. § 321(b)-(c)).

**ITC:** Importing articles that infringe a valid and enforceable US patent is unlawful where a US industry exists or is being established (19 U.S.C. § 1337(a)(1)(B), (a)(2)). The remedy includes an [[exclusion order]].
deepDive.takeaway: Calendar the one-year IPR deadline from service of any complaint, and treat the PTAB as an option from the start (good practice).

deepDive.heading: Prior use, assertions and defensive measures
deepDive.lede: The bank's own use, its licences and its patent commitments all shape the risk of being sued.
points: **Prior commercial use:** A good-faith US commercial use at least one year before the earlier of the effective filing date or public disclosure is a defence (35 U.S.C. § 273(a)). The defence must be proved by clear and convincing evidence (§ 273(b)).

**Limits:** The defence is personal. It can pass only with an enterprise or line of business, and only to sites where the use already occurred (35 U.S.C. § 273(e)(1)). It does not make the patent invalid (§ 273(g)).

**Assertions:** Banks are frequent patent defendants. As reported, the Federal Circuit held USAA's mobile remote deposit claims ineligible under § 101 on 12 June 2025, wiping out about $218 million in jury damages in the USAA v. PNC Bank litigation (reported; check).

**Licences:** Apache-2.0 grants each contributor's patent licence for claims its contribution necessarily infringes. That licence ends for the Work if the licensee sues alleging that the Work, or a contribution in it, directly or contributorily infringes a patent (Apache-2.0 s.3).
**Defensive pools:** Open Invention Network is a royalty-free patent non-aggression community covering a defined 'Linux System' (reported; check its current terms).
**Defensive publication:** Publishing an invention makes it prior art for later filers under 35 U.S.C. § 102(a)(1), which can block a rival's later patent on it (drafting inference).
deepDive.takeaway: Keep dated records of commercial use and of publication, because they decide both the § 273 defence and the grace period (good practice).

provisions.title: Inventions patentable
provisions.summary: Allows a patent for any new and useful process, machine, manufacture or composition of matter, or improvement of one. Courts have added judge-made limits for abstract ideas, natural phenomena and laws of nature.
provisions.counselNote: This is the first gate for every software claim. Expect an abstract idea argument in any dispute over a software patent.

provisions.title: Conditions for patentability; novelty
provisions.summary: Bars a patent if the invention was patented, described in a printed publication, in public use, on sale or otherwise available to the public before its effective filing date. An inventor's own disclosure made one year or less before filing is excused.
provisions.counselNote: Publishing code, documentation or demos before filing can destroy novelty. Set a release rule that protects filing dates.

provisions.title: Conditions for patentability; non-obvious subject matter
provisions.summary: Bars a patent where the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious, before its effective filing date, to a person of ordinary skill in the field.
provisions.counselNote: Public code and open source projects are part of the prior art that a challenger will search, so review them before a filing decision.

provisions.title: Specification
provisions.summary: Requires a written description that enables a skilled person to make and use the invention, and claims that particularly and distinctly point out the subject matter. An element written as a means or step for a function covers the disclosed structure and its equivalents (§ 112(f)).
provisions.counselNote: Only functional elements within § 112(f) are narrowed to the code the specification describes. Describe the implementation, not only the result.

provisions.title: Infringement of patent
provisions.summary: Makes it infringement to make, use, offer to sell, sell or import a patented invention in the US. Inducing infringement is also liable, and so is supplying a component especially made for an infringing use unless it is a staple article.
provisions.counselNote: Multi-party methods, SDKs and vendor-run systems can create liability for the bank even when others perform some steps.

provisions.title: Defense to infringement based on prior commercial use
provisions.summary: A personal defence for a good-faith US commercial use at least one year before the earlier of the effective filing date or public disclosure. It must be proved by clear and convincing evidence and does not make the patent invalid.
provisions.counselNote: Useful for in-house processes, but only with dated proof of use. The defence passes only in an enterprise transfer.

provisions.title: Damages
provisions.summary: Damages must be adequate to compensate and in no event less than a reasonable royalty. The court may increase them up to three times, and may use expert testimony on what royalty would be reasonable.
provisions.counselNote: A reasonable royalty is the baseline for any settlement model on a software claim, so get the royalty evidence early.

provisions.title: Limitation on damages and other remedies; marking and notice
provisions.summary: Without marking the patented article, by the patent number or by a public web address that links the article to it, damages run only from actual notice of infringement. Filing an infringement action counts as notice.
provisions.counselNote: A patentee's marking practice sets how much past use it can recover, which matters on both the assertion and the defence side.

provisions.title: Inter partes review
provisions.summary: Lets a person who does not own a patent petition to cancel claims on §§ 102 or 103 grounds, using only patents or printed publications as prior art. The petition is filed after the later of nine months from grant or the end of any post-grant review.
provisions.counselNote: A lower-cost route to challenge a software patent asserted against the bank, but the grounds are narrower than in court.

provisions.title: Relation to other proceedings or actions
provisions.summary: Bars an IPR if the petitioner has already sued on validity. Stays a later validity suit, bars an IPR filed more than one year after service of an infringement complaint, and estops later invalidity arguments after a final written decision.
provisions.counselNote: The one-year clock runs from service of the complaint, so calendar it on the day any complaint is served.

provisions.title: Post-grant review
provisions.summary: Lets a person who does not own a patent petition to cancel claims on any ground that could be raised under § 282(b)(2) or (3), including §§ 101 and 112. The petition must be filed within nine months of grant.
provisions.counselNote: The earliest challenge to a rival's new software patent can raise eligibility and clarity points that an IPR cannot.

provisions.title: Patents and copyrights, mask works, and designs
provisions.summary: Venue for a patent infringement suit lies where the defendant resides, or where it has committed infringing acts and has a regular and established place of business.
provisions.counselNote: Venue decides the forum for a suit against the bank. A domestic corporation resides only in its state of incorporation (TC Heartland).

provisions.title: Unfair practices in import trade
provisions.summary: Makes unlawful the importation of articles that infringe a valid and enforceable US patent, where a US industry exists or is being established. The ITC can exclude the articles.
provisions.counselNote: Relevant to terminals and devices with embedded software that the bank imports, not to software delivered within the US (drafting inference).

provisions.instrument: Alice Corp. v. CLS Bank International
provisions.title: Two-step test for abstract ideas in software claims
provisions.summary: A unanimous Supreme Court decision. Claims are first checked for an abstract idea, then for an inventive concept in their elements. Implementing an idea on a generic computer does not supply one.
provisions.counselNote: This is the test that governs every software eligibility challenge, so review claims against it before filing and before any dispute.

checklist: **Screen each feature for eligibility:** Ask whether the claim describes a specific technical improvement, not only a business process run on a computer, before deciding to file (good practice).

**Set a publication rule:** Clear every open source release, conference talk, blog post and API document with patent counsel before it goes public, because a public release can start the one-year clock (35 U.S.C. § 102(b)(1)).
**Keep dated development records:** Log authors, design decisions and commercial use dates, so that inventors and the § 273 defence can be proved.

**Map each claimed step to an actor:** For every method claim, record who performs each step (the bank, a customer, a cloud provider or a vendor) and whether the bank directs or controls them (Akamai).
**Require vendor indemnities for patents:** Ask vendors to warrant non-infringement and defend claims over the code they supply, and check the carve-outs (good practice).
**Calendar the patent deadlines:** Record the one-year IPR bar from service of a complaint (§ 315(b)) and the nine-month post-grant window for a rival's new patent (§ 321(c)).
**Read each licence for its patent terms:** Check the patent grant and termination clauses (for example Apache-2.0 s.3), and record any patents the bank contributes or licenses out.

**Mark patented products:** Post a patent marking page for patented articles the bank sells or offers, so that damages are not lost for lack of notice (35 U.S.C. § 287(a)); a method-only patent needs no marking (drafting inference).
**Document prior commercial use:** For in-house processes that may matter, keep dated evidence of good-faith US use, because § 273 requires clear and convincing proof.
**Screen imported hardware:** Where the bank imports terminals or devices with embedded software, check for ITC exposure under 19 U.S.C. § 1337 before purchase.
itAngle: **Claims follow the architecture:** Where a rule runs (device, bank server or vendor cloud) decides who performs each step, and so who may infringe (35 U.S.C. § 271(a); Akamai).
**Repositories as evidence:** Commit history, design documents and issue trackers give dated proof of conception and of commercial use. Keep them complete and retain them under the records policy.

**Publication gates:** Pipelines that publish packages, release tags, public repositories or API documentation should pass a patent check, because each public release is a disclosure (35 U.S.C. § 102(a)(1)).
**Marking in the product:** A product's public web page, app store description or documentation can carry the patent marking that § 287(a) allows, and the release build can insert it automatically.
**Claim-to-code map:** Keep a map from claim elements to modules. It shows where § 112(f) may apply and lets the infringement analysis run against the code the bank actually ships.
virtualBankNotes: **Vendor patent risk:** The Interagency Guidance on Third-Party Relationships (88 Fed. Reg. 37920) asks banks to manage risk across the life of a vendor relationship. A patent claim against a vendor's product is a third-party risk to assess (drafting inference).
**Assertions as operational risk:** A patent claim against a payment or app feature can force a product change, so product owners and risk staff should hear about assertions early (good practice).
**Fintech partnerships:** A bank-fintech arrangement should say who gives patent indemnities, who may change the product, and who pays for a design-around (good practice).
**Marketing claims:** Calling a product 'patented' when only an application is pending can mislead customers. Check every public claim against issued patents (good practice).
productNotes: **Hold publication until counsel has decided on filing:** Tell product and marketing teams that a demo, beta, talk, blog post or public release can start the patent clock. The inventor's own disclosure is excused only if the application is filed within one year (35 U.S.C. § 102(b)(1)(A)), and outside the US the grace period is narrower or absent (EPC Art. 54 and 55; reported; check).

**Describe the technical improvement in the spec:** Product managers and designers should describe what the feature changes in the system, not only the business result. A claim that is a business process run on a computer may be held ineligible (35 U.S.C. § 101; Alice Corp. v. CLS Bank International, 573 U.S. 208 (2014)). A specific technical improvement is easier to defend (good practice).

**Map who runs each step of a method:** When a flow runs partly on the bank's systems, partly on a cloud host and partly on a customer's device, product should tell counsel who performs each step. A bank that directs or controls others' steps can be liable for the whole method (35 U.S.C. § 271(a); Akamai Technologies, Inc. v. Limelight Networks, Inc., 797 F.3d 1020 (Fed. Cir. 2015) (en banc)).

**Tie product markings to issued patents:** Marketing and product teams should add a patent marking page or number to product pages once a patent issues. A patentee that does not mark can recover damages only from notice, and a web address that links the product to the patent number can serve as the marking (35 U.S.C. § 287(a)).
pitfalls: **Early release:** Publishing a method or code before filing and assuming the grace period covers it. Third-party disclosures, and the bank's own disclosures older than a year, are prior art (35 U.S.C. § 102).
**Functional claims:** Writing 'module for' or 'means for' language with no structure described, which § 112(f) narrows to the specification.
**Single-actor assumption:** Assuming the bank is not liable because a customer or a cloud provider runs the steps (Akamai).
**Late IPR:** Missing the one-year bar under § 315(b) by waiting until discovery or the expert phase.
**Defence without records:** Relying on the § 273 prior use defence without dated proof, which must be shown by clear and convincing evidence.

**Relying on IPR:** Treating IPR as a sure route, although institution practice has changed since 2025 and a proposed rule would limit IPR where litigation runs in parallel (reported; check current practice as at November 2026).

points: **Programs as such are excluded:** a program for a computer is excluded 'as such' (EPC Art. 52(2)(c), (3)), and the EPO requires a further technical effect before a claim is allowed.
**Simulations:** the Enlarged Board decided G 1/19 (March 2021) on simulations; check it for how the exclusion applies to models and simulated systems.
**Unified Patent Court:** it opened on 1 June 2023 and does not include the UK, so UK rights need separate treatment.
**Program exclusion:** a program for a computer is not patentable as such (Patents Act 1977 s.1(2)(c)).

**Neural networks on hardware:** an artificial neural network is a computer program but is not excluded merely as such when implemented on hardware (Emotional Perception [2026] UKSC 3, 11 February 2026; reported; check).

**Employee inventions:** an invention made in normal duties belongs to the employer, with compensation where the patent is of outstanding benefit (Patents Act 1977 ss.39-41; Shanks v Unilever [2019] UKSC 45).
**Abstract theory is excluded:** no patent is granted for a mere scientific principle or abstract theorem (Patent Act s.27(8)).

**No separate software test:** no separate test applies to computer-implemented inventions (Canada (AG) v Benjamin Moore & Co., 2023 FCA 168); CIPO practice guidance has been updated since (reported; check).

hongKong.summary: Hong Kong has three patent routes: a standard patent (R) registers a patent granted abroad, a standard patent (O) is examined on substance by the Registrar, and a short-term patent is granted on formalities only. Software is excluded from patentability only as such, so the claim wording decides the outcome. The biggest differences from the US position are the narrow six-month disclosure exceptions and the rule that a short-term patent cannot be enforced until a certificate of substantive examination has issued, a request for substantive examination has been made and not terminated by a court order, or a court has certified it.
keyPoints: **Program exclusion:** A program for a computer is not an invention, but only to the extent the patent relates to it as such (Cap. 514 s.9A(2)(c), (3)). The courts are reported to follow the English approach to 'as such' (reported; check).

**Three routes:** A standard patent (R) registers a designated foreign grant, a standard patent (O) is examined on substance, and a short-term patent is granted after formality examination only (Cap. 514 s.3, s.37U, s.117).

**Novelty and the grace period:** A disclosure before filing counts against novelty unless it falls within six months and is an evident abuse or a display at an official or officially recognised international exhibition (for a standard patent (R), a prescribed exhibition or meeting) (Cap. 514 ss.11A, 37B, 109).

**Own earlier applications:** An earlier application published after the new application's material date counts as state of the art for novelty, so the bank's own application can defeat its later one (Cap. 514 s.9B(3)).

**Enforcement:** A short-term patent can be enforced only after a certificate of substantive examination, an unterminated request for substantive examination, or a court certificate (Cap. 514 s.129(1)).

sections.heading: Patentability: the program exclusion and the three tests
sections.lede: An invention must be new, inventive and industrially applicable, and a program is excluded only as such, so claim wording matters most for software.
points: **Three tests:** An invention is patentable if it is new, involves an inventive step and is susceptible of industrial application (Cap. 514 s.9A(1)).
**Novelty:** An invention is new if it does not form part of the state of the art, which includes anything made available to the public anywhere before the material date (Cap. 514 s.9B(1)-(2)).
**Inventive step:** The invention must not be obvious to a person skilled in the art (Cap. 514 s.9C(1)).
**Industrial application:** The invention must be capable of being made or used in any kind of industry, including agriculture (Cap. 514 s.9D).
**Program exclusion:** A program for a computer, a scheme for doing business and a presentation of information are not inventions, but only as such (Cap. 514 s.9A(2)(c)-(d), (3)).
**Reported approach:** The Hong Kong courts are reported to apply the English approach to the 'as such' limit (reported; check).
sections.takeaway: Before filing, have counsel test each software claim against the 'as such' limit, and keep business-method wording out of the claim unless the technical content is clear (good practice).

sections.heading: Three routes to a Hong Kong patent
sections.lede: The route decides how much the Registrar checks before grant and when the proprietor can start enforcement.
points: **Standard patent (R):** A designated patent application published abroad is recorded, the designated patent is registered on a second request filed within 6 months after the designated office grants it or the request to record is published, whichever is later, and a standard patent (R) is granted for the invention in its published specification (Cap. 514 s.3, s.8, s.23(1)-(2)).
**Designated offices:** The Chief Executive in Council designates the foreign patent offices by Gazette notice (Cap. 514 s.8).
**Standard patent (O):** The applicant must request substantive examination, and the Registrar examines patentability, disclosure, claims and added matter before grant (Cap. 514 s.37T, s.37U(3)).
**Short-term patent:** The Registrar considers formalities only and has no duty to examine patentability, novelty, inventive step or disclosure (Cap. 514 s.117).

**Term:** A standard patent lasts 20 years from filing, and a short-term patent lasts up to 8 years from filing, but lapses after the 4th year unless the renewal fee is paid (Cap. 514 s.39(1)(b), s.126(1)(b), (2)).
sections.takeaway: Choose the route by how soon the bank needs to enforce and how much it wants examination first, since a short-term patent is quicker to obtain but harder to enforce (drafting inference).

sections.heading: Novelty and the bank's own disclosures
sections.lede: The bank's own publication can cost it a patent, and the Ordinance excuses only a narrow set of disclosures.
points: **Six-month window:** A disclosure is ignored for novelty only if it occurred no earlier than 6 months before filing (Cap. 514 ss.11A(2)(a), 37B(2)(a), 109).

**Excused causes:** The disclosure must be due to an evident abuse against the applicant, or a display at an official or officially recognised international exhibition, or, for a standard patent (R), a prescribed exhibition or meeting (Cap. 514 ss.11A(2)(b), 37B(2)(b), 109).
**Display evidence:** For a display, the filing must say so and include the prescribed evidence or statement (Cap. 514 s.11A(3), s.37B(3)).
**Earlier applications:** Earlier applications published after the material date count as state of the art for novelty, but not for inventive step (Cap. 514 s.9B(3), s.9C(2)).
**No general grace:** Other disclosures, such as a public code release or a product launch, are not excused by these sections (drafting inference).
sections.takeaway: Before any public code release, product launch or conference talk, decide whether a patent filing is needed, because the exceptions are narrow and the window is at most six months (good practice).

sections.heading: Infringement, threats and marking
sections.lede: A patent reaches making, importing and using in Hong Kong, while threats and false marking carry their own risks.
points: **Direct acts:** The proprietor may stop third parties without consent from making, putting on the market, using or importing a patented product, or using a patented process in Hong Kong (Cap. 514 s.73(a)-(b)).

**Indirect supply:** Supplying means for an essential element of the invention is also restricted where the supplier knows, or it is obvious, that the means are suitable and intended for use in Hong Kong, but not staple commercial products unless the supply is made to induce an infringing act (Cap. 514 s.74(1)-(2)).
**Exceptions:** Private non-commercial acts and experimental acts are excepted (Cap. 514 s.75(a)-(b)).

**Threats:** A person aggrieved by groundless threats of proceedings can seek a declaration, an injunction and damages, but a mere notice that a patent exists is not a threat, and for a standard patent the threatener escapes that relief if it proves infringement and the claimant fails to prove invalidity (Cap. 514 s.89(1)-(3), (5), s.89A(1)).

**Marking:** Falsely representing an item sold for value as patented is an offence, but it is a defence for the seller to prove that it used due diligence to prevent the offence (Cap. 514 s.142(1)-(2), (4)), and a bare 'patent' mark without a number does not by itself show awareness for damages (Cap. 514 s.81(2)).
sections.takeaway: Before writing to a vendor or competitor about a patent, have counsel check whether the letter could be a threat under s.89 and what it would expose the bank to (good practice).

provisions.title: Patentable inventions and the program exclusion
provisions.summary: An invention is patentable if it is new, involves an inventive step and is susceptible of industrial application. A program for a computer, a scheme for doing business and a presentation of information are not inventions, but only to the extent the patent relates to them as such.
provisions.counselNote: This is the first test for any software claim, so a claim that reads as the program or the business method itself is at risk of refusal.

provisions.title: Novelty and the state of the art
provisions.summary: An invention is new if it does not form part of the state of the art, which includes everything made available to the public before the material date. Earlier-filed applications published after that date also count.
provisions.counselNote: The bank's own earlier application can defeat a later one, so the bank should check its filing history before filing a related application.

provisions.title: Non-prejudicial disclosure for a standard patent (R)
provisions.summary: A disclosure within 6 months before filing is disregarded for novelty only if it was due to an evident abuse against the applicant or a display at a prescribed exhibition or meeting. A display needs a statement and evidence in the application.
provisions.counselNote: The exception is narrow, so a bank's own launch or code release will usually count against novelty (drafting inference).

provisions.title: Formality examination only
provisions.summary: For a short-term patent the Registrar has no obligation to consider patentability, priority, disclosure or the other listed matters during examination.
provisions.counselNote: A short-term patent is a registration of form, not a finding of validity, so the bank should not present it to a vendor or a court as proof that the invention is valid.

provisions.title: Enforcing a short-term patent
provisions.summary: The proprietor of a short-term patent can start enforcement proceedings only after a certificate of substantive examination has been issued, a request for substantive examination has been made and not terminated by a court order, or a court has certified the patent.
provisions.counselNote: The bank cannot sue on a short-term patent on the strength of the grant alone, so enforcement planning must include the examination step.

provisions.title: Direct use of a patented invention
provisions.summary: The proprietor may prevent third parties without consent from making, putting on the market, using, importing or stocking a patented product in Hong Kong, and from using a patented process, or offering it for use there where the third party knows or it is obvious to a reasonable person that the use is prohibited, and from putting on the market, using, importing or stocking products obtained directly by a patented process.
provisions.counselNote: Using a licensed third-party product in Hong Kong can infringe where the product embodies a patented process, so vendor warranties should cover patent non-infringement.

provisions.title: Indirect use: supplying means
provisions.summary: A third party may not supply or offer to supply means relating to an essential element of the invention, where it knows or it is obvious that the means are suitable and intended for putting the invention into effect in Hong Kong. Staple commercial products are excluded unless supplied to induce an infringing act.
provisions.counselNote: A bank that supplies components or APIs to a third party for a patented system may be caught, so product teams should check the purpose of what they supply.

provisions.title: Groundless threats of patent proceedings
provisions.summary: A person aggrieved by threats of patent infringement proceedings can seek a declaration that the threats are unjustifiable, an injunction and damages. Threats to sue over making a product for putting on the market, or over using a process, are excluded, and a mere notice that a patent exists is not a threat.
provisions.counselNote: A letter to a vendor or competitor about a patent can expose the bank to a claim, so the wording of any notice should be reviewed by counsel.

provisions.title: Falsely claiming a patent
provisions.summary: It is an offence, on summary conviction to a level 3 fine, to falsely represent that an item sold for value is a patented product, and marking an item with 'patent' or an equivalent counts as such a representation.
provisions.counselNote: Product labels and marketing material that mention patents must match the patents the bank actually holds.

bankNotes: **Claim review:** Involve counsel in drafting software claims, so that each claim is tested against the program exclusion in s.9A(2)(c) and (3) before filing (good practice).

**Filing before release:** Decide on any filing before a public code release, open source publication or conference talk, because the disclosure exceptions in s.11A and s.37B are narrow and limited to six months (good practice).
