**Short-term patents:** Do not present a short-term patent as enforceable until a certificate of substantive examination or a court certificate is in place (Cap. 514 s.129(1)) (good practice).
**Notices to third parties:** Route any patent notice to a vendor or competitor through legal review, since a notice can amount to a threat under s.89 (good practice).

glossary.definition: An element, alone or in combination, that adds something more than an abstract idea applied on a generic computer, tested at the second step of the Alice test (Alice Corp. v. CLS Bank International, 573 U.S. 208 (2014)).
A judicially recognised exception to patent eligibility under § 101. A claim directed to one must add an inventive concept to be patentable (Alice, 573 U.S. 208 (2014)).
The date that sets the prior art cut-off for a claim, and the start point for the one-year grace period for the inventor's own disclosures (35 U.S.C. § 102(b)(1)).
The one-year window in which an inventor's own disclosure is not prior art, if the application is filed within it (35 U.S.C. § 102(b)(1)).
A claim element written as a function without the structure that performs it. It covers only the structure in the specification, and its equivalents (35 U.S.C. § 112(f)).
A generic word, such as 'module', that a court may treat as a function rather than a structure, bringing § 112(f) into play (Williamson v. Citrix Online, LLC, 792 F.3d 1339 (Fed. Cir. 2015)).
A USPTO proceeding, brought by a person who does not own the patent, to cancel claims on §§ 102 or 103 grounds using patents or printed publications (35 U.S.C. § 311).
A USPTO proceeding filed within nine months of grant, which can raise any invalidity ground, including §§ 101 and 112 (35 U.S.C. § 321).
An International Trade Commission order that keeps infringing articles out of the US, the main remedy for unlawful import under 19 U.S.C. § 1337.
A personal defence for good-faith US commercial use at least one year before the effective filing date or public disclosure, proved by clear and convincing evidence (35 U.S.C. § 273).
A Hong Kong patent that registers and grants a patent already granted by a designated foreign patent office (Cap. 514 s.3, s.8).
A Hong Kong patent granted after formality examination only, which lasts up to 8 years from filing if renewed after the 4th year (Cap. 514 s.117, s.126(1)(b), (2)).

title: Trade secrets and source code
oneLiner: Code stays protected only while it stays secret, so the bank's access controls, contracts and release decisions form the legal case.
keyPoints: Trade secret protection lasts only while the information stays secret. It needs no registration, and publication ends it for whatever is made public (18 U.S.C. § 1839(3)).

**Two layers:** The Defend Trade Secrets Act (DTSA) gives a federal civil claim (18 U.S.C. § 1836(b)(1)). State law runs alongside it, mostly under the [[Uniform Trade Secrets Act (UTSA)]] (reported; check).

**Reasonable measures:** The owner must have taken [[reasonable measures]] to keep the code secret (18 U.S.C. § 1839(3)(A)). For source code, that means controlled access, binding contracts and records showing both work in practice.
**Reverse engineering:** Taking apart a lawfully obtained product is not improper means (18 U.S.C. § 1839(6)(B)). A contract is the usual way to restrict it (good practice).
**Publication:** Releasing code publicly, including as open source, ends its secrecy, so the right must be chosen before release (drafting inference).
**Employees and contractors:** Agreements must carry the [[whistleblower immunity notice]], or the bank may not recover exemplary damages or fees against that individual (18 U.S.C. § 1833(b)(3)).

conceptMap.caption: The DTSA sits alongside state law. Secrecy and reasonable measures are the test; publication ends the right.

deepDive.heading: What counts as a trade secret
deepDive.lede: Code is named in the definition, so the contest is over secrecy and value.

visual.caption: Three tests, applied to the code, decide whether it is a trade secret.

items.label: Subject matter
items.note: Programs and codes are expressly included

items.label: Reasonable measures
items.note: The owner's own conduct is tested

items.label: Value from secrecy
items.note: Not generally known or readily ascertainable

points: **Definition:** The DTSA covers information, including programs and codes, however it is stored (18 U.S.C. § 1839(3)).
**Two tests:** The owner must take reasonable measures to keep the information secret, and it must derive independent economic value from not being generally known (18 U.S.C. § 1839(3)(A)-(B)).
**Misappropriation:** Acquiring a secret by improper means, or using or disclosing it in breach of a duty of secrecy, is misappropriation (18 U.S.C. § 1839(5)).
**Improper means:** Theft, bribery, misrepresentation and breach of a secrecy duty are [[improper means]]. Reverse engineering and independent derivation are not (18 U.S.C. § 1839(6)(A)-(B)).
deepDive.takeaway: Record why the code is valuable and kept secret, because both tests are proved with evidence.

deepDive.heading: Reasonable measures for code
deepDive.lede: The measures are the proof, so they need to exist before a dispute starts.

visual.caption: A workable measures programme, in the order it is usually built (good practice).

items.label: Classify
items.note: Name the code, models and rules the bank treats as secret

items.label: Limit access
items.note: Role-based repository rights, logging and periodic review

items.label: Bind people
items.note: Confidentiality terms for staff, contractors and vendors

items.label: Mark and monitor
items.note: Confidentiality markings and scanning for leaked secrets

items.label: Exit
items.note: Revoke access, recover devices and restate duties in writing

points: **Conduct counts:** The statute asks what the owner has taken, so a policy on paper needs practice behind it (18 U.S.C. § 1839(3)(A)).
**Access:** Restrict repositories and build secrets by role, and log access, so the bank can show who could see the code (good practice).
**Binding terms:** Staff, contractor and vendor agreements should cover code and carry the [[whistleblower immunity notice]] (18 U.S.C. § 1833(b)(3)(A)).
**Keys and secrets:** Keep credentials out of repositories, because a leaked key can open code that is otherwise secret (good practice).
**Exit:** Revoke access, recover devices and restate confidentiality duties in writing when someone leaves (good practice).
deepDive.takeaway: A court tests the measures against practice, so keep dated evidence of access reviews and training (good practice).

deepDive.heading: What ends secrecy
deepDive.lede: Publication is the usual way secrecy is lost, and it is easy to do by accident.

visual.caption: Each disclosure route has a different effect on the trade secret.

items.label: Public release or open source
items.note: Generally known once published (§ 1839(3)(B))

items.label: Shared under a confidentiality agreement
items.note: Protection holds while the terms are kept

items.label: Patent filing
items.note: Describes the invention to the public

items.label: Reverse engineering of a shipped product
items.note: Not improper means (§ 1839(6)(B))

points: **Public release:** Posting code online, or open sourcing it, makes it generally known, so the trade secret in that code is lost (18 U.S.C. § 1839(3)(B)).
**Partial release:** A release of part of a code base ends secrecy only for what was released, so define the boundary of each release (drafting inference).

**Patents:** A patent describes the invention to the public, so the same material cannot stay secret once the application publishes, normally 18 months after the earliest filing date (35 U.S.C. § 122(b)) (drafting inference). Choose the right before filing.
**Leaks:** A mistaken public repository or a shared link can make code generally known, so check settings and monitor for copies (good practice).

deepDive.heading: Reverse engineering, independent creation and contract limits
deepDive.lede: The statute protects against improper means, and contract terms fill the rest.
points: **Contract bans:** In Bowers v. Baystate Technologies, Inc., 320 F.3d 1317 (Fed. Cir. 2003), the court held by two to one that a shrink-wrap ban on reverse engineering was enforceable and not preempted.
**Independent creation:** A competitor that builds the same function without the bank's secret is not misappropriating it (18 U.S.C. § 1839(6)(B)).

**Injunctions:** A court may not bar a person from taking a job, and any condition must rest on evidence of threatened misappropriation, not merely on what the person knows (18 U.S.C. § 1836(b)(3)(A)(i)(I)).
**State limits:** An injunction may not conflict with state law prohibiting restraints on a lawful profession, trade or business (18 U.S.C. § 1836(b)(3)(A)(i)(II)).
**Shipped product:** Reverse engineering a lawfully obtained binary is not improper means under the DTSA, so a licence term is often the only tool that forbids it (good practice).
deepDive.takeaway: Put reverse engineering bans in the licence, and support any employee injunction with evidence of threatened use.

deepDive.heading: Remedies and non-competes
deepDive.lede: Remedies are strong, but employment terms decide how far they reach.

visual.caption: Remedies available under the DTSA for a proven misappropriation.

items.label: Injunction
items.note: Limits on employment and state law apply

items.label: Damages
items.note: Actual loss, unjust enrichment or a reasonable royalty

items.label: Exemplary damages
items.note: Wilful and malicious misappropriation only (§ 1836(b)(3)(C))

items.label: Limitation period
items.note: From discovery (§ 1836(d))

points: **Fees:** The court may award fees to the prevailing party for a bad-faith claim or motion, or for wilful and malicious misappropriation (18 U.S.C. § 1836(b)(3)(D)).

**FTC rule:** The FTC's nationwide non-compete rule was set aside in Ryan LLC v. FTC (N.D. Tex., 20 August 2024) before it took effect. The FTC has reportedly dismissed its appeals and removed the rule (reported; check), so there is no federal ban on [[non-competes|non-compete]] as at November 2026.

**California:** Section 16600 voids employee non-competes however narrowly tailored, read broadly in accordance with Edwards v. Arthur Andersen LLP (2008) 44 Cal.4th 937 (Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 16600(b)(1)).
**Lookback:** The bar applies regardless of where and when a contract was signed (Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 16600.5; reported; check).
**Code protection:** Without a valid non-compete, protect code with confidentiality duties, access limits and exit steps, which a court can test (good practice).
deepDive.takeaway: Take California advice before any restrictive covenant, and do not treat a non-compete as a code control.

deepDive.heading: Criminal exposure and reach abroad
deepDive.lede: Theft is a federal crime, and the DTSA can follow conduct outside the United States.
points: **Crime:** Stealing or copying a trade secret, or possessing one known to be stolen, is a federal offence when done with intent to convert it to the economic benefit of someone other than the owner and intending or knowing that it will injure the owner, with up to ten years' imprisonment (18 U.S.C. § 1832(a)).
**Criminal secrecy:** The court must act to preserve the confidentiality of trade secrets in a prosecution, and the owner may file a sealed submission (18 U.S.C. § 1835(a)-(b)).

**Abroad:** In Motorola Solutions, Inc. v. Hytera Communications Corp., 108 F.4th 458 (7th Cir. 2024), the court held that the DTSA can reach misappropriation abroad where an act in furtherance occurred in the United States. Damages can then rest on foreign sales.
**Scale:** A 2020 Chicago jury award of about $764.6 million in that dispute was later reduced (reported; check), which shows what a foreign-sales claim can be worth.
**Acts in the US:** A download or transfer in the United States is the act that can bring foreign use of copied code within reach (drafting inference).

deepDive.heading: Registration and the bank's own assets
deepDive.lede: Some code is registered, models are assets, and AI tools are a new route out.

visual.caption: Where the bank's secrets can leave, and the point at which protection is lost.

items.label: Registered code
items.note: Trade-secret parts redacted (reported; check)

items.label: Models and rules
items.note: Fraud logic, pricing and scoring code

items.label: Pasted into an AI tool
items.note: Depends on the vendor's retention and training terms

items.label: Published or open sourced
items.note: Generally known once public

points: **Redacted deposits:** Registered code can be deposited with trade-secret parts redacted, which the Copyright Office allows (37 C.F.R. § 202.20(c)(2)(vii); reported; check the current options).

**Models and rules:** Fraud logic, pricing models and scoring code can be trade secrets if they meet the § 1839(3) tests (18 U.S.C. § 1839(3)). Ask counsel how regulator productions are marked and which terms protect them (drafting inference).
**AI tools:** Pasting code into a third-party AI tool discloses it to that vendor, so approved tools need terms that limit retention and training (good practice).
deepDive.takeaway: Treat a model or rule as a secret only if it meets the same measures test as the code.

provisions.title: Civil proceedings
provisions.summary: Gives the owner of a misappropriated trade secret a federal civil action where the secret relates to a product or service used in interstate or foreign commerce. Courts may grant injunctions, damages for actual loss and unjust enrichment (or a reasonable royalty), and exemplary damages of up to twice that award for wilful and malicious misappropriation. An injunction may not stop a person from taking a job, and the claim must be brought within three years of discovery.
provisions.counselNote: The DTSA claim sits beside state law rather than replacing it. Its employment limits matter when the bank acts against a departing engineer, so the injunction request needs evidence.

provisions.title: Definitions
provisions.summary: Defines a trade secret as information, including programs and codes, that the owner protects by reasonable measures and that derives independent economic value from not being generally known or readily ascertainable. Misappropriation covers improper acquisition, and use or disclosure in breach of a duty of secrecy. Reverse engineering and independent derivation are not improper means.
provisions.counselNote: These definitions decide every DTSA claim. Code is named expressly, so disputes usually turn on the measures and on secrecy.

provisions.title: Exceptions to prohibitions
provisions.summary: Protects individuals from liability under trade secret law for confidential disclosure to a government official or an attorney to report a suspected violation of law, and for filings made under seal. An employer must give notice of this immunity in any agreement with an employee that governs trade secrets or confidential information, and contractors count as employees. Without the notice, the employer may not recover exemplary damages or fees against that employee.
provisions.counselNote: Every employee and contractor template needs the notice or a cross-reference to a reporting policy. It is a cheap fix with an expensive omission.

provisions.title: Theft of trade secrets
provisions.summary: Makes it a federal crime to steal, copy, receive or possess a trade secret in the ways listed, with intent to benefit someone other than the owner and knowing or intending to injure the owner. An individual faces up to ten years' imprisonment. An organisation faces a fine of up to the greater of $5 million or three times the value of the secret.
provisions.counselNote: Criminal exposure arises when a departing employee takes code or a model. Refer suspected theft to counsel early, because the criminal case can affect the civil one.

provisions.instrument: Uniform Trade Secrets Act as enacted in California (Cal. Civ. Code)
provisions.title: Uniform Trade Secrets Act: definitions
provisions.summary: Defines improper means, misappropriation and trade secret for California claims. Reverse engineering or independent derivation alone is not improper means. A trade secret must derive value from not being generally known and must be the subject of efforts that are reasonable under the circumstances to keep it secret.
provisions.counselNote: The California definition is close to the DTSA, so one set of secrecy controls can support both claims (drafting inference).

provisions.title: Contracts in restraint of trade void
provisions.summary: Voids every contract that restrains anyone from a lawful profession, trade or business, to the extent of the restraint. Subdivision (b) directs that the section be read broadly, in accordance with Edwards, to void any employee non-compete, however narrowly tailored, unless a statutory exception applies.
provisions.counselNote: A non-compete will not protect code in California, so the protection has to come from confidentiality terms, access limits and evidence.

provisions.title: Order setting aside the FTC non-compete rule
provisions.summary: The court set aside the FTC's rule that would have banned most non-compete agreements, on a nationwide basis, before the rule took effect. Reported later events, including the FTC's dismissal of its appeals, are as at November 2026 (reported; check).
provisions.counselNote: Most non-compete questions now turn on state law and the DTSA, not a federal rule. Check the current position before relying on any federal view (drafting inference).

provisions.instrument: Motorola Solutions, Inc. v. Hytera Communications Corp.
provisions.title: Extraterritorial reach of the DTSA
provisions.summary: The Seventh Circuit held that the DTSA can reach misappropriation abroad where an act in furtherance of it occurred in the United States. Damages may therefore rest on sales made outside the United States.
provisions.counselNote: A US act in furtherance, such as a download or a server used to store the code, can bring foreign sales into the damages claim (drafting inference). Map where copied code was used, not just where it was taken.

provisions.title: California restraint-of-trade case on employee non-competes
provisions.summary: The California Supreme Court decision that section 16600(b)(1) directs courts to follow in reading the section broadly, so that employee non-competes are void. The statute describes that reading as declaratory of existing law.
provisions.counselNote: Any employee non-compete in a California contract is likely void, so the bank's protection of code must rest on other terms.

provisions.title: Shrink-wrap ban on reverse engineering enforced
provisions.summary: The Federal Circuit, by two to one, held that a shrink-wrap ban on reverse engineering was enforceable and not preempted by federal law. The decision lets a licence restrict reverse engineering even where the trade secret statute would not.
provisions.counselNote: Shipped products can carry contractual bans on reverse engineering. Put them in the licence itself, not only in marketing or policy documents.

provisions.instrument: Interagency Guidance on Third-Party Relationships: Risk Management (Federal Reserve, FDIC, OCC)
provisions.title: Third-party relationships: risk management
provisions.summary: The agencies say that banks should manage risk across the life cycle of third-party relationships. The guidance is technology-neutral and does not deal with open source as such.
provisions.counselNote: Vendors that see bank code, models or customer data sit inside this guidance, so confidentiality and termination terms are supervisory points as well as contract points.

checklist: **Register the secrets:** Keep a register of the code, models and rules the bank treats as trade secrets, with each owner and repository.
**Limit access:** Restrict secret repositories by role, log access, and review the list on a set cycle.
**Add the immunity notice:** Put the § 1833(b) notice, or a cross-reference to a reporting policy, in every employee and contractor agreement that covers confidential information.
**Gate publication:** Require legal sign-off before any code moves to a public repository, a release or a conference talk.
**Decide patent or secret:** Choose between a patent and secrecy for each invention before filing or publication.
**Control AI tools:** Block confidential code from approved-tool exceptions unless the vendor's terms limit retention and training.
**Set exit steps:** Revoke access, recover devices and restate confidentiality duties in writing when people leave.
**Document the measures:** Keep dated evidence of policies, training and access reviews, because the owner must show reasonable measures.
**Limit non-competes:** Take California advice before any restrictive covenant, and do not rely on one to protect code.
**Use redacted deposits:** Choose the redacted or partial deposit option for registered code that is also a trade secret (reported; check the current options).
itAngle: **Repository permissions:** Map access to source repositories, build pipelines and secrets stores by group, and export the map as evidence of reasonable measures.
**Secrets scanning:** Scan commits and pull requests for keys and tokens, because a leaked credential can expose code that is otherwise secret.
**Public mirrors:** Check that internal mirrors, forks and package feeds are not public. A repository exposed by mistake can end secrecy for what it held.
**Release gates:** Before code leaves the bank, scan for internal hostnames, customer data and proprietary modules, and record the result for legal.
**AI coding tools:** Configure tools so prompts and code context are not stored or used for training under the bank's contract, and log which tools staff use.
virtualBankNotes: **Vendor access:** The interagency guidance expects banks to manage risk from vendors that see bank code or models (88 Fed. Reg. 37920 (9 June 2023)).

**Cybersecurity rules:** The NYDFS Cybersecurity Regulation requires written procedures for secure development and for assessing externally developed applications (23 NYCRR 500.8), and a third-party service provider policy (23 NYCRR 500.11).

**Model risk:** Supervisory guidance on model risk has covered vendor models, and the agencies replaced it on 17 April 2026 (Federal Reserve SR 26-2; OCC Bulletin 2026-13). Models and rules are both trade secrets and governed assets.
**Examiner requests:** Mark code and model documents given to examiners as confidential, and record what was sent. Ask counsel whether the bank's production terms protect them (good practice).
**Customer data:** Code, test data and logs can carry customer information, so a trade secret review should also check privacy and security (good practice).
productNotes: **Decide secret or patent before the feature is shown:** For a scoring model, pricing logic or fraud rule, tell counsel early whether to protect it by secrecy or by a patent. Secrecy lasts only while the information stays secret (18 U.S.C. § 1839(3)), and a patent application is normally published 18 months after the earliest filing date (35 U.S.C. § 122(b); drafting inference).

**Clear each public release, demo and talk:** Open sourcing a repository, publishing a package or showing internals in a conference talk can make the code generally known. A partial release ends secrecy only for what was released, so ask counsel to review the release boundary before a date is set (18 U.S.C. § 1839(3)(B); drafting inference).

**Share secrets only under confidentiality terms:** Sales and partnership teams should show partners a feature's internal logic only under a written confidentiality agreement, and keep it out of decks and public posts. Reverse engineering a shipped app is not improper means, so the licence needs its own limit on reverse engineering (18 U.S.C. § 1839(6)(B); Bowers v. Baystate Technologies, Inc., 320 F.3d 1317 (Fed. Cir. 2003)).

**Use only approved AI tools with secret material:** Product, design and marketing staff should not paste a feature's code, rules or training data into an AI tool unless the bank has approved it and its terms limit retention and training. Pasting material into a vendor's tool discloses it to that vendor (18 U.S.C. § 1839(3)(A); good practice).
pitfalls: **Accidental publication:** Making a repository public, or releasing a package that contains proprietary code, which can end secrecy for that code.
**Paper controls:** Confidentiality policies that nobody enforces, which a court may not treat as reasonable measures.
**Overbroad restraints:** Restrictions on former staff that go beyond the DTSA injunction limits or California's bar, and may be void.
**Missing notice:** Leaving out the § 1833(b) notice, which removes exemplary damages and fees against the employee.

**Assuming shipped code is safe:** Reverse engineering is not improper means, so trade secret protection for a shipped app depends on the licence terms (Bowers v. Baystate Technologies, Inc., 320 F.3d 1317 (Fed. Cir. 2003)).

points: **Directive-based regime:** trade secrets are protected under the Trade Secrets Directive (EU) 2016/943 as implemented by member states, not by one federal statute as in the US.

**Reverse engineering is lawful within limits:** decompilation for interoperability is allowed (Directive 2009/24/EC, Art. 6), and a lawful acquirer may decompile to correct errors affecting operation (Top System, C-13/20, 6 October 2021).
**Statute beside confidence:** the Trade Secrets (Enforcement, etc.) Regulations 2018 (SI 2018/597) operate alongside the law of confidence.
**Contract still matters:** NDAs and confidentiality terms in employment and vendor contracts remain the main protection for code (good practice).
**No federal civil statute:** there is no federal civil trade secret statute, so protection rests on the common law and Quebec civil law.
**Criminal offences:** Criminal Code s.391 creates trade secret offences, in force 1 July 2020 (reported; check).

hongKong.summary: Hong Kong has no trade secrets statute, so confidential code and business information is protected mainly by the equitable action for breach of confidence and by contract (reported; check). The biggest difference from the US is that there is no statutory misappropriation claim to rely on, so the bank's NDAs, code-access terms and exit undertakings carry most of the weight (drafting inference). Criminal offences for dishonest computer access, and for damaging programs or data, add a further layer (Cap. 200 ss.59, 60, 161).
keyPoints: **No trade secrets statute:** Hong Kong has no statute that creates a trade secret right, so confidential code and business information rests on the common law of confidence and on contract (reported; check).

**Breach of confidence:** The equitable action needs information with the necessary quality of confidence, imparted in circumstances that import an obligation of confidence, and used without authority (reported; check).
**Employees and contractors:** An employee owes a duty of fidelity during employment, and without a restraint covenant only true trade secrets are protected after employment (reported; check).

**Computer access offence:** Obtaining access to a computer with intent to commit an offence, or with a dishonest intent, is an offence carrying up to 5 years' imprisonment on indictment, whether the intended offence, gain or loss is to happen on that occasion or a later one (Cap. 200 s.161(1)(a)-(d)).
**Practical consequence:** NDAs, code-access terms and exit undertakings carry the weight that the Defend Trade Secrets Act and state statutes carry in the US (drafting inference).

sections.heading: Confidence, contract and the employee
sections.lede: Protection for code and business information comes from the common law of confidence, from contract, and from the duties an employee owes while employed.
points: **Quality of confidence:** The information must have the necessary quality of confidence before the equitable action is available (reported; check).
**Circumstances of imparting:** The obligation arises from the circumstances in which the information was given (reported; check). A written term should name what is confidential (good practice).
**Use without authority:** The claim needs the information to have been used without authority (reported; check), so the bank should define the permitted use for each vendor and team (good practice).
**Duty of fidelity:** An employee owes the employer a duty of fidelity while employed (reported; check).
**After employment:** Without a restraint covenant, only true trade secrets are protected, not general skill and knowledge, and any restraint must be reasonable (reported; check).
sections.takeaway: Put confidentiality, return-of-code and post-exit undertakings in writing for every employee and contractor, and keep any restraint no wider than the bank needs (good practice).

sections.heading: Computer misuse and criminal exposure
sections.lede: Hong Kong makes dishonest or unauthorised access to programs and data a crime, which gives the bank a route beyond a civil claim.
points: **Dishonest access:** Obtaining access to a computer with intent to commit an offence, with a dishonest intent to deceive, with a view to dishonest gain, or with a dishonest intent to cause loss is an offence (Cap. 200 s.161(1)(a)-(d)).
**Gain and loss:** For that offence, gain includes keeping what one already has, and loss includes not getting what one might have got (Cap. 200 s.161(2)).
**Unauthorised access:** Knowingly causing a computer, by telecommunications, to obtain unauthorised access to a program or data is an offence with a fine at level 4 (Cap. 106 s.27A(1)).

**Who is unauthorised:** Access is unauthorised where the person is not entitled to control access of that kind, has no authority from someone who is, and does not believe they were or would have been authorised had they applied (Cap. 106 s.27A(2)(b)).
**Damage to programs and data:** A program or data held in a computer is property for the criminal damage offences, and altering, erasing or adding to it counts as damage (Cap. 200 s.59(1)(b), (1A)).

**Own devices:** The Court of Final Appeal held that s.161(1)(c) does not extend to a person's use of their own computer, such as their own phone, so sending or using information from a person's own device, without obtaining access to the bank's computer, may fall outside the offence (Secretary for Justice v Cheng Ka Yee [2019] HKCFA 9).
sections.takeaway: Map who may reach each system and record it, because the unauthorised-access offence turns on entitlement and the dishonest-access offence turns on intent, and a clear record helps prove both (good practice).

sections.heading: Personal data and time limits
sections.lede: Data security duties and limitation periods decide how the bank must protect its secrets and how long it has to act on a breach.
points: **Practicable security steps:** A data user must take all practicable steps to protect personal data it holds against unauthorised or accidental access, processing, erasure, loss or use (Cap. 486 Sch. 1, DPP 4(1)).
**Factors:** The steps depend on the kind of data and the harm that could result, and on where the data is stored (Cap. 486 Sch. 1, DPP 4(1)(a)-(b)).
**Six-year limit:** An action founded on simple contract or on tort must be brought within 6 years of the cause of action accruing (Cap. 347 s.4(1)(a)).

**Concealment and fraud:** Where the defendant's fraud or deliberate concealment is relevant, time does not start to run until the claimant discovers it or could with reasonable diligence have discovered it (Cap. 347 s.26(1)(a)-(b)), subject to s.26(4), which stops such an action to recover property or set aside a transaction against an innocent purchaser for value.

**Equitable relief:** The six-year limit does not apply to an injunction or other equitable relief, so a claim to stop use of confidential information may not be barred by it (Cap. 347 s.4(7); drafting inference).
sections.takeaway: Diarise the six-year limit from the date the cause of action accrued, which for breach of contract is usually the breach, and keep records of when the bank discovered it, because concealment can postpone the start of time (good practice).

provisions.title: Access to computer with criminal or dishonest intent
provisions.summary: A person who obtains access to a computer with intent to commit an offence, with a dishonest intent to deceive, with a view to dishonest gain, or with a dishonest intent to cause loss commits an offence. The intended offence, gain or loss may be on the same occasion as the access or a later one. On indictment the maximum is 5 years' imprisonment.
provisions.counselNote: This reaches an insider or contractor who uses system access dishonestly, which is relevant to the bank's own staff and vendors.

provisions.title: Unauthorised access to a computer by telecommunications
provisions.summary: Knowingly causing a computer, by telecommunications, to obtain unauthorised access to a program or data is an offence with a fine at level 4. Access is unauthorised where the person is not entitled to control access of that kind, has no authority from someone who is, and does not believe they were or would have been authorised had they applied.
provisions.counselNote: This can cover a former employee or contractor who reaches production code or data after access should have ended.

provisions.title: Programs and data as property for criminal damage
provisions.summary: For the criminal damage provisions, a program or data held in a computer or computer storage medium is property. Destroying or damaging it in relation to a computer includes misuse, such as altering or erasing a program or data or adding one to a computer. Property belongs to anyone with custody or control of it, a proprietary interest in it, or a charge over it.
provisions.counselNote: An employer holding code on its own systems can be treated as its owner for these offences, which can support a complaint to the police against a leaver who alters or deletes code.

provisions.title: Security of personal data
provisions.summary: A data user must take all practicable steps to protect personal data it holds against unauthorised or accidental access, processing, erasure, loss or use. The steps depend on the kind of data, the harm that could result, and where the data is stored.
provisions.counselNote: Customer records copied into test sets, logs or source repositories bring this duty into engineering work, not only into security work.

provisions.title: Six-year limit for contract and tort
provisions.summary: An action founded on simple contract or on tort must not be brought after 6 years from the date the cause of action accrued. The limit does not apply to an injunction or other equitable relief, although the court may apply it by analogy.
provisions.counselNote: A damages claim for breach of an NDA runs on this clock, while an injunction to stop use of code is usually sought in equity.

provisions.title: Fraud and deliberate concealment
provisions.summary: Time does not start to run on an action based on the defendant's fraud, or where a relevant fact was deliberately concealed from the plaintiff, until the plaintiff discovers it or could with reasonable diligence have discovered it.
provisions.counselNote: If code or data was taken in a way the bank could not discover, the start of time may be postponed, but counsel should not plan on that.

bankNotes: **Access rights:** Whether access is unauthorised turns on whether the person was entitled to control access of that kind, or was authorised by someone who is (Cap. 106 s.27A(2)(b)), so recorded role-based access is the bank's best evidence (good practice).

**Personal data in engineering:** Source code, logs and test sets that hold customer data fall under the security duty in DPP 4(1), so they need controls comparable to production data (Cap. 486 Sch. 1, DPP 4(1); drafting inference).

**Vendor and contractor terms:** Agreements should say what is confidential, who owns the code and what happens on exit, because the bank relies on contract where Hong Kong has no trade secrets statute (reported; check).

glossary.definition: Information, including programs and codes, that the owner protects by reasonable measures and that derives independent economic value from not being generally known (18 U.S.C. § 1839(3)).
Acquisition of a secret by improper means, or its use or disclosure without consent by a person who owed a duty of secrecy (18 U.S.C. § 1839(5)).
Theft, bribery, misrepresentation, breach of a secrecy duty and electronic espionage. Reverse engineering and independent derivation are not improper means (18 U.S.C. § 1839(6)).

The steps an owner takes to keep information secret, such as access limits, confidentiality terms and exit controls. The statute requires them, and courts look at what the owner actually did (18 U.S.C. § 1839(3)(A)).
Developing the same information without using the owner's secret. It is not improper means (18 U.S.C. § 1839(6)(B)).
Damages of up to twice the award for actual loss and unjust enrichment, available only for wilful and malicious misappropriation (18 U.S.C. § 1836(b)(3)(C)).
The notice an employer must give in an employee or contractor agreement about the immunity for confidential reports of suspected violations of law (18 U.S.C. § 1833(b)(3)).

A model state law defining trade secrets and misappropriation. California's version is Cal. Civ. Code § 3426.1. Reported to be adopted in every state except New York and North Carolina (reported; check).
An agreement that stops an employee from working for a competitor after leaving. California voids employee non-competes (Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 16600(b)(1)).
A copy of registered code with trade-secret portions redacted, which the Copyright Office accepts in place of a full deposit (37 C.F.R. § 202.20(c)(2)(vii); reported; check).

The equitable action that protects confidential information against use without authority, where the information was imparted in circumstances that import an obligation of confidence (reported; check).
The implied duty an employee owes the employer during employment, which limits conduct that works against the employer's interests (reported; check).

title: Trademarks and project names
oneLiner: A trademark guards the name customers use to tell who stands behind software, and an open source licence does not hand that name over.
keyPoints: Software is protected by copyright, patents and trade secrets, but the name and logo customers see belong to a separate right: the trademark.
**Two routes:** Rights arise from use in commerce, and the Lanham Act (15 U.S.C.) protects unregistered marks under § 1125(a) and registered marks under § 1114.
**Confusion:** Infringement turns on whether use is likely to confuse customers about source, sponsorship or affiliation (§ 1114(1)(a); § 1125(a)(1)(A)).

**Open source:** A code licence does not carry the project's name. Apache-2.0 (s.6) and MPL-2.0 (s.2.3) give no trademark permission beyond customary origin statements and notices, and GPL-3.0 (s.7(e)) lets a licensor add a term declining trademark rights.
**Renames:** Several forks have taken new names, such as OpenSearch, OpenTofu and Valkey (reported; check), so a fork should not assume it keeps the original name.
**Counsel's role:** Clear names before launch, write trademark terms into every licence and partner agreement, and keep a register of the bank's marks (good practice).

deepDive.heading: What a trademark protects
deepDive.lede: A trademark protects the identifier that tells customers who stands behind a product, not the code.
points: **Scope:** The right covers names, logos and other identifiers. It does not cover the code, the algorithms or the features, which copyright, patents and trade secrets address.
**Definition:** The Lanham Act (15 U.S.C.) defines a trademark as any word, name, symbol or device used to identify goods and indicate their source, even if that source is unknown (§ 1127).
**Other marks:** A service mark covers services, a certification mark certifies origin or quality for use by others, and a collective mark shows membership of a group (§ 1127).
**Bank use:** Product names, SDK names, API brands, app names and logos can each function as marks, so each needs its own clearance (good practice).

visual.caption: The four mark types defined in § 1127 and what each identifies.

items.label: Trademark
items.note: Identifies and distinguishes goods from those of others

items.label: Service mark
items.note: Identifies the services of one person

items.label: Certification mark
items.note: Used by someone other than the owner to certify origin, quality or other characteristics

items.label: Collective mark
items.note: Used by members of a cooperative, association or group

deepDive.takeaway: Protect the names you launch under, and treat the code as a separate asset with its own rights.

deepDive.heading: How rights arise and how far they reach
deepDive.lede: Rights come from use in US commerce, and registration adds a second route to court.
points: **Use in commerce:** Use must be bona fide, in the ordinary course of trade, and not made merely to reserve a right in the mark (§ 1127).
**Unregistered marks:** § 1125(a)(1) reaches use of a word, name, symbol or device in commerce that is likely to confuse customers about affiliation, origin, sponsorship or approval.

**Registered marks:** § 1114(1)(a) gives the registrant a claim against use in commerce of a reproduction or colorable imitation that is likely to cause confusion, in connection with goods or services.

**US reach:** Under Abitron Austria GmbH v. Hetronic International, Inc., 600 U.S. 412 (2023), these claims reach only infringing use in commerce in the United States, so use abroad alone does not infringe.

deepDive.heading: Confusion, dilution and fair use
deepDive.lede: The test is likely confusion, and some references to another company's name are protected.
points: **Confusion:** The core question is whether customers are [[likely to be confused|likelihood of confusion]] about source, sponsorship or affiliation (§ 1125(a)(1)(A)).
**Dilution:** § 1125(c)(1) gives the owner of a famous mark an injunction against blurring or tarnishment, without proof of confusion.
**Fair use:** Any fair use of a famous mark, including nominative or descriptive use, other than as a designation of source for one's own goods, is not actionable dilution (§ 1125(c)(3)(A)).
**Source identifiers:** Jack Daniel's Properties, Inc. v. VIP Products LLC, 599 U.S. 140 (2023), held that the Rogers test does not apply where the accused mark is used as a source identifier.
**Compatibility:** Say 'compatible with' and name the other product, with no logo, no stylised version and no suggestion of endorsement (good practice).
deepDive.takeaway: Use another company's name only to say what your product works with or replaces.

deepDive.heading: Open source licences and names
deepDive.lede: A licence to the code does not license the project's name or logo.
points: **Apache-2.0 (s.6):** The licence gives no permission to use the licensor's trade names or marks, except reasonable and customary use to describe the work's origin and to reproduce the NOTICE file.
**MPL-2.0 (s.2.3):** The licence grants no rights in any contributor's trademarks, service marks or logos, except as needed to meet its notice duties in s.3.4.
**GPL-3.0 (s.7(e)):** A licensor may add a term declining to grant trademark rights for some names or marks, so check each project's notices for one.
**Open source status:** 'Open source' is not a registered US trademark, and the OSI's 1999 application lapsed. The OSI uses its own marks, including for 'OSI Approved' (reported; check).

deepDive.takeaway: Treat the code licence and the name as separate questions, and say in each contract which name rights apply (drafting inference).

deepDive.heading: Forks and renames
deepDive.lede: A fork that keeps the upstream name takes on a trademark risk that the code licence does not cover.
points: **Renames:** Each of these [[forks|fork]] took a new name rather than keep the upstream mark (reported; check).
**Code and name:** Permission to copy code does not extend to the upstream name, and Apache-2.0 (s.6) and MPL-2.0 (s.2.3) say so in terms.
**Fork policy:** Before the bank uses an upstream name for a fork, package or product, decide whether the name is needed only to describe what the product does (good practice).
**Records:** A rename changes package names, binary names and provenance, so the SBOM and the licence inventory must record the new name and the upstream source (drafting inference).

deepDive.heading: Keeping a mark alive
deepDive.lede: Marks are lost through disuse, generic use and loose licensing.
points: **Nonuse:** A mark is abandoned when use stops with intent not to resume. Three consecutive years of nonuse is prima facie evidence of [[abandonment]] (§ 1127).
**Generic use:** Conduct that makes the mark the generic name for the goods or services, or otherwise removes its significance as a mark, also leads to abandonment (§ 1127).

**Naked licensing:** [[Licensing a mark without quality control|naked licensing]] can lead to abandonment. Barcamerica International USA Trust v. Tyfield Importers, Inc., 289 F.3d 589 (9th Cir. 2002), and FreecycleSunnyvale v. Freecycle Network, 626 F.3d 509 (9th Cir. 2010), are reported for that point (reported; check).
**Partner use:** Give licensees approved logo files, usage rules and a right to approve quality, and keep ownership of the mark with the bank (good practice).

visual.caption: A mark-keeping cycle for the bank's names.

items.label: Clear the name
items.note: Search registers, company names, domains and app stores

items.label: File and launch
items.note: Use the mark consistently, in commerce, on the product

items.label: Control partner use
items.note: Written brand rules, approval and quality control

items.note: Monitor look-alike names and act on infringers

deepDive.heading: Domain names and store listings
deepDive.lede: Domain names and app store listings often carry a bank's name into the open market.
points: **Cybersquatting:** Registering, trafficking in or using a domain name in bad faith to profit from another's mark is [[cybersquatting]] under § 1125(d)(1)(A).
**Who is liable:** Liability for using a domain name falls on its registrant or the registrant's authorised licensee (§ 1125(d)(1)(D)), so keep licence records for each domain that partners use.
**Action against the name:** Subject to statutory conditions, the owner may bring an in rem action against the domain name itself (§ 1125(d)(2)(A)).
**Store names:** App and SDK names raise the same confusion questions, and each store sets its own rules for names and listings, so check those before submission (good practice).
deepDive.takeaway: Register core names early in the bank's own name, and keep a list of every domain, store account and package owner (good practice).

provisions.title: Remedies for infringement of registered marks
provisions.summary: Gives the owner of a registered mark a civil action against anyone who uses, without consent, a reproduction, counterfeit or colorable imitation of the mark in commerce where the use is likely to cause confusion, mistake or deception. Subsection (2) limits remedies in some cases, such as for printers, publishers and domain name registrars.
provisions.counselNote: This is the registered-mark claim the bank would bring against a look-alike product or name. Registration is what brings a name within this claim, so the filing decision also shapes enforcement.

provisions.title: False designations of origin and false descriptions
provisions.summary: Makes liable anyone who uses in commerce a word, name, symbol or device, or a false designation of origin, in a way likely to confuse customers about affiliation, origin, sponsorship or approval. It protects unregistered marks as well as registered ones, and it also covers false advertising.
provisions.counselNote: This is the claim for an unregistered product or project name, and the one a competitor or fork would face. It also reaches misleading claims about partnerships or endorsements, which fintech marketing can create.

provisions.title: Dilution by blurring or tarnishment of famous marks
provisions.summary: Lets the owner of a famous mark, one widely recognised by the general consuming public of the United States, obtain an injunction against use that dilutes it by blurring or tarnishment, without proof of confusion. Subsection (c)(3) excludes nominative and descriptive fair use, except as a designation of source for the user's own goods.
provisions.counselNote: Dilution protection is limited to famous marks, so most project names rely on confusion claims. The fair use exclusion supports careful 'compatible with' wording, but it is not a licence to use another company's logo.

provisions.title: Cyberpiracy prevention
provisions.summary: Makes a person liable to the owner of a mark who, with bad faith intent to profit from the mark, registers, traffics in or uses a domain name. Liability for using a domain name falls on its registrant or the registrant's authorised licensee, and the owner may proceed in rem against the domain name in defined cases.
provisions.counselNote: Developers and vendors often register domains for launches. Records of who holds each domain support both enforcement and the bank's control over its brand.

provisions.title: Construction and definitions
provisions.summary: Defines trademark, service mark, certification mark, collective mark, domain name and use in commerce. It also sets the grounds for abandonment: discontinued use with intent not to resume, where three consecutive years of nonuse is prima facie evidence, or conduct that makes the mark generic or otherwise loses its significance.
provisions.counselNote: These definitions decide whether a name is a mark at all and whether it still is one. Clearance and portfolio reviews should check actual use, not only registration.

provisions.title: Trademarks
provisions.summary: Gives no permission to use the licensor's trade names, trademarks, service marks or product names, except reasonable and customary use to describe the origin of the work and to reproduce the content of the NOTICE file.
provisions.counselNote: A bank product that uses an Apache-licensed project's name needs its own trademark clearance, separate from the licence review. The licence does not settle the name question.

provisions.title: Limitations on grant scope
provisions.summary: States that the licence grants no rights in the trademarks, service marks or logos of any contributor, except as may be needed to meet the notice requirements in s.3.4.
provisions.counselNote: A file-level copyleft licence still excludes trademarks, so an MPL component in a product does not license the contributor's brand. Use a separate brand agreement if the bank needs one.

provisions.instrument: GNU General Public License v3.0 only
provisions.title: Additional terms
provisions.summary: Lets a licensor add a permitted term declining to grant rights under trademark law for some trade names, trademarks or service marks. Any added terms must be stated in the relevant source files or in a notice showing where to find them.
provisions.counselNote: A GPL project may decline trademark rights in its notice, so the trademark position is not always silent. Check the notice before adopting a GPL component whose name the bank wants to use.

provisions.instrument: Abitron Austria GmbH v. Hetronic International, Inc.
provisions.title: Lanham Act claims limited to US use in commerce
provisions.summary: Held that the Lanham Act's infringement provisions for registered marks and for unregistered marks (§§ 1114(1)(a), 1125(a)(1)) reach only infringing use in commerce in the United States. Use abroad falls outside them, even if it causes confusion or other effects in the United States.
provisions.counselNote: A name used only outside the United States is not caught by these US claims, but the same name used in US markets may be. Clearance should follow where the product is actually offered.

provisions.instrument: Jack Daniel's Properties, Inc. v. VIP Products LLC
provisions.title: Rogers test and source-identifying use
provisions.summary: Held that the Rogers test for expressive works does not apply where the accused user relies on the mark as a designation of source for its own goods. The ordinary likelihood-of-confusion analysis applies instead, with parody as one factor.
provisions.counselNote: A parody or joke name is not an automatic defence when it is used as a product's own brand. This matters for marketing, merchandise and playful product names.

provisions.instrument: Barcamerica International USA Trust v. Tyfield Importers, Inc.
provisions.title: Naked licensing and abandonment
provisions.summary: Reported as a Ninth Circuit decision holding that a mark owner who licenses the mark without controlling the quality of the licensee's goods or services can abandon it (reported; check).
provisions.counselNote: Brand licences to partners need written quality control to keep the mark protected. Check the current Ninth Circuit position before relying on this case.

provisions.title: Unsupervised use of a mark by licensees
provisions.summary: Reported as a Ninth Circuit naked licensing decision, cited with Barcamerica for the point that unsupervised licensing can abandon a mark (reported; check).
provisions.counselNote: The same risk arises with informal groups or partners that use a name without supervision. Written terms and monitoring matter more than the label on the licence.

checklist: **Clear the name first:** Search the federal register, state registers, company names, domain names and app stores before any launch or rename (good practice).
**Decide who owns each mark:** Record whether the bank, a subsidiary, a vendor or a foundation holds each name, and keep that in a marks register.
**Write trademark terms into every licence:** Say which names a licensee may use and which are reserved, and for code the bank publishes, state that the licence gives no name rights.
**Control partner use of the bank's marks:** Issue approved logo files and usage rules, and require approval of quality, so the marks are not licensed naked.
**Check fork and dependency names:** Confirm that an upstream project's name in a fork, package or product is used only to describe it, and record the upstream name and licence in the SBOM.
**Track use of each mark:** Keep a dated record of actual use, so that three years of nonuse is caught before it becomes a question of abandonment (§ 1127).
**Register the core marks:** File for the product and bank names that matter most, and keep the filings current (good practice).
**Watch for look-alike names:** Monitor the register, app stores and domain registrations for confusingly similar names, and set a takedown route before a launch.
**Use third-party names carefully:** Describe compatibility with 'compatible with' and the other party's name only, with no logo and no suggestion of endorsement.
itAngle: **Names in code:** Product names, package names, namespaces and logos appear in repositories, manifests and build metadata, so a rename is a code change with release and documentation impact.
**Upstream names in forks:** When you fork a project, change the package name, binary names and user-facing strings that use the upstream mark, and keep the upstream licence notices intact.
**SBOM identity:** Record the supplier, name and version of each component as published, so a renamed fork is not mistaken for the original, and keep its licence identifier with it.
**Brand checks in CI:** Run a check that flags the bank's logos, names or forbidden upstream names in builds, documentation and app store metadata before release (good practice).

**Owned accounts:** Keep domain names, documentation sites, package registry accounts and app store listings in an inventory, registered to the bank rather than to an individual developer (good practice).
virtualBankNotes: **Brand control with partners:** Fintech and affiliate use of the bank's name needs written rules, approval and monitoring, because loose licensing can put the marks at risk (naked licensing; reported; check).

**Sponsorship confusion:** A partner product that uses the bank's name or logo may suggest a sponsorship the bank has not approved. That is the core confusion question under § 1125(a)(1)(A) (drafting inference).
**Disclosure of roles:** Partner pages and app store listings should state the bank's role accurately, so customers can tell what the bank provides and what the partner provides (good practice).
**Vendor deliverables:** Vendor contracts should say who owns names, logos and brand assets made for the bank, and whether the vendor may name the bank as a customer (drafting inference).
**Records:** Keep the marks register, brand approvals and monitoring reports in the third-party risk file, so the bank can show its controls over partner use (good practice).
productNotes: **Clear the name before it is announced:** Ask counsel to search registers, company names, domains and app stores before a product, SDK, API or app name goes public, since a rename after launch is the costliest fix (15 U.S.C. § 1125(a)(1)(A)). Make the search a standing step for every new name (good practice).

**Keep partner names to description:** Marketing may name a wallet, card scheme or other partner only to say that a bank product is compatible with it, with no logo, no stylised version and no suggestion of endorsement (15 U.S.C. § 1125(a)(1)(A)). Check every partner reference in the copy review (good practice).

**Use an upstream name only to describe:** Before a bank fork, package or product carries an open source project's name, get counsel's view, because a code licence does not license the name (Apache-2.0 s.6). Ask whether the name is needed only to say what the product does (good practice).

**Tell counsel about a rename or upstream change early:** Forks such as OpenSearch, OpenTofu and Valkey took new names after upstream changes (reported; check). A change to a dependency that affects a product name, package name or logo is a decision for counsel and marketing together (good practice).
pitfalls: **Launching unchecked:** Choosing a product or project name without clearance, then learning of a prior user or registrant after launch, when a rebrand is most expensive.
**Reading a licence as a name grant:** Treating a permissive licence as permission to use the project's name in marketing or product names (Apache-2.0 s.6).
**Forks under the old name:** Shipping a fork under the upstream name, which exposes the bank to a claim and confuses users about who maintains the product.
**Loose partner use:** Letting partners or vendors use the bank's marks without rules or quality control, which can lead to naked licensing (reported; check).
**Overreading dilution:** Assuming dilution protection applies to any name, when § 1125(c) covers only famous marks.
**Stray domains:** Leaving a launch domain or app store account in an individual employee's name, where it can be lost or transferred when that person leaves.

points: **Registration first:** an EU trade mark is a single right registered with the EUIPO under Regulation (EU) 2017/1001, and rights come mainly from registration rather than use, so clear and file a project name before launch.

**Registration first:** UK marks are registered under the Trade Marks Act 1994; an unregistered name is protected only through passing off, which needs goodwill, so register the project name before release.

**Registration without use:** since 2019 a Canadian mark can be registered without first being used, and registration gives the owner the exclusive right to use it throughout Canada (Trademarks Act s.19) (reported; check).

hongKong.summary: Hong Kong treats a registered trade mark as a property right under the Trade Marks Ordinance (Cap. 559 s.10(1)). An unregistered name has no statutory infringement action and is left to passing off (Cap. 559 s.10(3)). The biggest difference from the US is that statutory infringement needs a registration, so the bank should register its marks before launch in Hong Kong (good practice).
keyPoints: **Property right:** A registered trade mark is a property right and personal property (Cap. 559 s.10(1), s.27(1)).
**Unregistered names:** The Ordinance gives no proceedings to stop infringement of an unregistered mark, but it keeps the law of passing off (Cap. 559 s.10(3)).

**Infringement test:** Identical signs for identical goods or services infringe, identical signs for similar goods or services infringe where confusion is likely, and similar signs for identical or similar goods or services do too (Cap. 559 s.18(1)-(3)).

**Non-use revocation:** Any person may apply to revoke a registration that the owner has not genuinely used in Hong Kong for a continuous 3 years, unless there are valid reasons for non-use (Cap. 559 s.52(1)-(2)).

**Transactions:** An assignment must be in writing and signed (Cap. 559 s.27(4)), and an unregistered transaction can be ineffective against a conflicting interest acquired in ignorance of it (Cap. 559 s.29(3)(a)).

sections.heading: Registration, rights and passing off
sections.lede: A Hong Kong registration gives statutory rights, while an unregistered name depends on passing off.
points: **Application and date:** An application is filed with the Registrar (Cap. 559 s.38), and once accepted and not successfully opposed the mark is registered as of the filing date (Cap. 559 s.47(1), s.48).
**Term and renewal:** Registration lasts 10 years and can be renewed for further 10-year periods on request and payment, and a mark not renewed is removed from the register (Cap. 559 s.49, s.50).

**Refusal grounds:** A mark that is not distinctive, is descriptive or has become customary in the trade is refused, unless it had acquired distinctiveness through use before filing (Cap. 559 s.11(1)(b)-(d), s.11(2)).

**Passing off:** Passing off protects unregistered goodwill against a misrepresentation that causes, or is likely to cause, damage, and the Ordinance treats it as a ground for refusing registration, but only if the owner of the earlier right objects in opposition proceedings (Cap. 559 s.12(5)(a), (6)) (reported; check).
sections.takeaway: Register the bank's core names and logos in Hong Kong before launch, and do not rely on goodwill alone to protect an unregistered name (good practice).

sections.heading: Infringement, prior use and licensees
sections.lede: Infringement turns on identity or likely confusion, and the own-name, prior-use and licensee rules shape who can act.
points: **Well-known marks:** A mark entitled to protection under the Paris Convention as a well-known mark is protected against an identical or similar sign used without due cause in a way that takes unfair advantage of, or is detrimental to, its distinctive character or repute, for any goods or services (Cap. 559 s.18(4)).
**Own name:** A registered mark is not infringed by a person's use of its own name, address or place of business, provided the use accords with honest practices (Cap. 559 s.19(3)(a)).

**Prior use:** A registered mark is not infringed by continuous prior unregistered use in Hong Kong from a date before the earlier of the registrant's first use in Hong Kong and its registration (Cap. 559 s.19(4)).

**Threats:** A person threatened over use other than applying the mark to goods or packaging, or supplying services, can seek a declaration, an injunction and damages, unless the threatener shows that the acts infringe, or would infringe if done, and the threatened person cannot then show that the registration is invalid or liable to be revoked in a relevant respect; a notice that a mark is registered is not a threat (Cap. 559 s.26(1)-(5)). Proceedings are barred if the owner, or a licensee with power to sue, starts an infringement action within 28 days of the threat and pursues it with due diligence (Cap. 559 s.26(6)).

**Licensees:** Unless the licence provides otherwise, a licensee may call on the owner in writing to sue an infringer, and may sue in its own name if the owner refuses or does nothing for one month (Cap. 559 s.35(2)-(3)).
sections.takeaway: Check that any use of a name that is not the bank's own is covered by a licence or a clear right, because the own-name defence does not reach it (drafting inference).

sections.heading: Keeping, recording and licensing a mark
sections.lede: A mark can be lost through non-use, and a licence or assignment that is not in writing, signed or recorded can fail against others.
points: **Use that starts late:** Use that starts within 3 months before a revocation application is generally disregarded, unless preparations for it began before the owner became aware that an application might be made (Cap. 559 s.52(4)-(5)).
**Use outside Hong Kong:** Export-only packaging, and services supplied outside Hong Kong, can count as use for this purpose (Cap. 559 s.52(3)(b)-(c)).

**Licences in writing:** A licence is not effective unless it is in writing and signed by the grantor, and it binds a later owner of the mark unless the licence provides otherwise (Cap. 559 s.33(3), (5)).

**Registering transactions:** A new owner or licensee who does not apply to register the transaction within 6 months cannot recover damages or profits for infringement in the gap, unless the court is satisfied that an application was not practicable within 6 months and an application was made as soon as practicable afterwards (Cap. 559 s.29(4)(a)-(b)).

**False claims of registration:** Falsely representing that a sign is registered, knowing or having reason to believe it is false, is an offence with a fine at level 3, and using 'registered' or '註冊' in Hong Kong counts as a representation of registration here unless it is shown that the reference is to registration elsewhere than in Hong Kong and that the mark is in fact so registered for those goods or services (Cap. 559 s.94(2)).
sections.takeaway: Record each assignment and licence of a mark in writing, sign it, register it within 6 months, and keep marketing free of registration claims the bank cannot support (good practice).

provisions.title: Registered mark as property right; passing off preserved
provisions.summary: A registered trade mark is a property right obtained by registration, and its owner has the rights and remedies the Ordinance provides. No proceedings lie for infringement of an unregistered mark, but the law of passing off is unaffected.
provisions.counselNote: A brand the bank has used but not registered in Hong Kong is protected only through passing off, which turns on goodwill and misrepresentation (reported; check).

provisions.title: Infringement of registered trade mark
provisions.summary: Use in the course of trade of an identical sign for identical goods or services infringes. Similar signs infringe where confusion is likely, and well-known marks are protected against unfair advantage or detriment for any goods or services.
provisions.counselNote: Product and channel names need clearance against the register before launch, because the infringement test turns on identity and likely confusion.

provisions.title: Revocation for non-use
provisions.summary: Any person may apply to the Registrar or the court to revoke a registration that the owner has not genuinely used in Hong Kong, or used with its consent, for a continuous period of at least 3 years, unless there are valid reasons for non-use. Use starting within 3 months before the application is generally disregarded.
provisions.counselNote: A bank that registers marks it does not yet use, such as for a planned product, can lose them to a third party's application.

provisions.title: Registration of transactions
provisions.summary: Assignments of a registered mark, licences under it and security interests are registrable transactions. A new owner or licensee who does not apply to register the transaction within 6 months cannot recover damages or profits for the gap, and it can be ineffective against a conflicting interest acquired in ignorance of it.
provisions.counselNote: Co-branded licences and vendor-held marks should be registered promptly, or the bank may not recover profits for the gap.

provisions.title: Own name, address and prior use
provisions.summary: A registered mark is not infringed by use of a person's own name, address or place of business, or a predecessor's name, where the use accords with honest practices. It is also not infringed by continuous prior unregistered use in Hong Kong from before the earlier of first use and registration.
provisions.counselNote: Legacy brand use may survive a later registration, so the bank should document its own prior use in Hong Kong.

provisions.title: Groundless threats of infringement proceedings
provisions.summary: A person threatened with infringement proceedings over use other than applying the mark to goods or packaging, or supplying services, may seek a declaration that the threats are unjustifiable, an injunction and damages. The threatener has a defence if it shows that the acts would infringe, unless the registration is shown to be invalid or liable to revocation in a relevant respect. A notice that a mark is registered is not a threat.
provisions.counselNote: A demand letter from the bank that threatens proceedings over use outside the goods, packaging and services limb can give the recipient this claim, so the bank's letters should be drafted with care.

provisions.title: Licensee's right to sue
provisions.summary: A licensee may call on the owner in writing to take infringement proceedings. If the owner refuses or does not act within one month, the licensee may sue, but generally cannot proceed unless the owner is joined or the court gives leave.
provisions.counselNote: A brand licensee or vendor should have a clear clause on who enforces the mark, so the bank is not left to chase an infringer alone.

provisions.title: Falsely representing a mark as registered
provisions.summary: Falsely representing that a sign is a registered trade mark, or making a false representation about the goods or services covered by a registration, is an offence if the person knows or has reason to believe it is false. The fine is level 3. In Hong Kong, the word 'registered' or '註冊', or another word or symbol referring to registration, is treated as a representation of registration in Hong Kong unless it is shown to refer to an actual registration elsewhere for those goods or services.
provisions.counselNote: Marketing that describes a product name as registered needs a Hong Kong registration behind it, or a foreign registration for those goods or services that the claim is shown to refer to, or the bank may commit an offence.

provisions.title: Excluded services of regulated persons
provisions.summary: The false trade description offence for services does not reach goods or services sold or supplied by a person regulated under the Banking Ordinance (Cap. 155), where that sale is itself regulated under an Ordinance listed in the item.
provisions.counselNote: Whether a particular bank service falls within this exclusion is a question of fact, so the bank should not assume that its marketing claims are outside the offence.

bankNotes: **Service names:** The false trade description offence for services does not reach services sold by a regulated bank where that sale is itself regulated under the Banking Ordinance (Cap. 362 Sch. 4, item 1), but whether a particular service falls within that test is a question of fact (drafting inference).
**Registration before launch:** Register marks for the bank's product and channel names before public launch, and check every app store listing and domain name against the register (good practice).

**Domain names and listings:** Disputes over .hk domain names are reported to be decided under the domain registry's dispute resolution policy, with the Hong Kong International Arbitration Centre as the dispute resolution provider (reported; check), so the bank should keep domain and listing ownership in its own accounts (good practice).

glossary.definition: The federal trademark statute, in Title 15 of the U.S. Code (15 U.S.C.). It covers registered and unregistered marks, infringement, false designation of origin and dilution.
Bona fide use of a mark in the ordinary course of trade, not made merely to reserve a right in the mark (§ 1127).
The core infringement test: whether use of a mark is likely to confuse customers about source, sponsorship, affiliation or approval (§ 1114(1)(a); § 1125(a)(1)(A)).
Using another's mark to refer to that owner's product, such as saying a product is 'compatible with' it. It is excluded from dilution liability (§ 1125(c)(3)(A)).
Loss of a mark through discontinued use with no intent to resume, or through conduct that makes it generic or otherwise loses its significance (§ 1127).
Licensing a mark without quality control over the licensee's goods or services. It can lead to abandonment (reported; check).
Registering, trafficking in or using a domain name in bad faith to profit from another's mark (§ 1125(d)(1)(A)).
A new project started from a copy of existing open source code. A fork may keep or change the upstream name, but the licence does not decide that question.
A mark used by someone other than its owner to certify regional or other origin, material, quality, accuracy or other characteristics (§ 1127).
Harm to a famous mark's distinctiveness through blurring or tarnishment. Protection needs no proof of confusion (§ 1125(c)(1)).
The common law action that protects unregistered goodwill against a misrepresentation that causes, or is likely to cause, damage (reported; check).
The defence in s.19(4) of the Trade Marks Ordinance (Cap. 559) for continuous unregistered use in Hong Kong from before the earlier of the registrant's first use in Hong Kong and its registration.

title: How open source licences work
oneLiner: An open source licence is a copyright permission with conditions, and its duties usually start only on distribution or network use.
keyPoints: Open source licences are the rules that let the bank use, change and share code that others wrote. Each one grants a permission, attaches conditions and says what follows if a condition fails.

**Permission with conditions:** Without a licence, copying, changing and distributing code need the owner's permission under the Copyright Act (17 U.S.C. § 106). A court can treat a broken licence condition as infringement, as in Jacobsen v. Katzer, 535 F.3d 1373 (Fed. Cir. 2008).

**Contract too:** A licence can also be enforced as a contract. In Artifex Software, Inc. v. Hancom, Inc. (N.D. Cal. 2017), the court refused to dismiss a claim that the GPL was an enforceable contract, on the facts pleaded, and the case then settled.

**Triggers:** Duties start on specific acts: distributing or conveying the code and, under AGPL-3.0 s.13, offering a modified version to remote users. Running unmodified GPL-3.0 code internally carries no conditions (GPL-3.0 s.2).

**Families:** Licences run from permissive (MIT, Apache-2.0) through copyleft (GPL, LGPL, MPL) to [[network copyleft]] (AGPL-3.0). Source-available licences such as SSPL and BUSL restrict use and are not open source.
**Counsel's role:** Record the licence and SPDX identifier for each component, check the trigger before approving distribution or network use, and keep notices with the code.

conceptMap.caption: A licence grants permission to copy, change and share. Its conditions decide what the user owes, and a broken condition can end the grant.

items.label: Permission to copy, change and share
items.note: The grant that the licence adds to the default position

items.label: Conditions on the user
items.note: Notices and the same licence on distribution; source code under s.3

items.label: Conveying or distribution
items.note: The usual trigger for the copyleft duties

items.label: Modified version run over a network
items.note: The network copyleft trigger

items.label: Patent licence
items.note: Some licences grant patent rights as well

items.label: Termination and cure
items.note: A broken condition can end the grant, subject to reinstatement

items.label: Warranty disclaimer
items.note: Permissive licences like MIT give no warranty

items.label: Trade names and marks
items.note: No trademark rights are granted

deepDive.heading: What counts as open source
deepDive.lede: The label has more than one definition, and the tests differ in what they ask.

visual.caption: Three tests. Only the first two describe open source or free software in the usual sense.

items.label: Open Source Definition (OSI)
items.note: Free redistribution, source code, derived works, no discrimination against fields of endeavour

items.label: Four freedoms (FSF)
items.note: Run, study and change, redistribute, distribute modified versions

items.label: Source-available
items.note: Code is visible, but use or commercial activity is restricted, e.g. SSPL, BUSL, Elastic License 2.0

points: **Open Source Definition:** The OSI's definition sets ten criteria, including free redistribution, access to source code and no discrimination against any person, group or field of endeavour (OSI Open Source Definition).

**Four freedoms:** The Free Software Foundation describes [[free software]] as software whose users may run, study and change it, redistribute it, and distribute modified versions. These are its views, not law.

**Source-available:** Licences such as SSPL, BUSL, Elastic License 2.0 and the Commons Clause publish code but restrict use, so they fall outside the open source definition. The OSI does not treat SSPL as open source (reported; check).
**Why it matters:** Internal policies often use the word 'open source'. Ask which test the policy means, and whether it reaches source-available code.
deepDive.takeaway: Approve by licence and by act, not by label.

deepDive.heading: A licence as permission and as contract
deepDive.lede: A licence can work as a copyright permission, as a contract, or as both, and the label affects the remedy.
points: **Permission:** Jacobsen v. Katzer, 535 F.3d 1373 (Fed. Cir. 2008), held that the Artistic License's attribution and change notices were conditions limiting the licence, so breaking them could support a copyright infringement claim and not only a breach of contract.

**Contract:** In Artifex Software, Inc. v. Hancom, Inc. (N.D. Cal. 2017), the court refused to dismiss a claim that the GPL was an enforceable contract, on the facts pleaded. The case then settled, so it sets no rule.

**Third parties:** Software Freedom Conservancy v. Vizio, Inc. (Cal. Super. Ct., filed 2021) reportedly lets a purchaser pursue the GPL as a third-party beneficiary. No final judgment is confirmed as at November 2026 (reported; check).
**Practical point:** Assume a licensor can argue both copyright and contract, and keep compliance records that would satisfy either (good practice).

deepDive.heading: Licence families, from permissive to network copyleft
deepDive.lede: The families differ mainly in what they require when code is passed on or run as a service.

visual.caption: Each layer adds a condition. Lower layers can reach more of the bank's own code.
