items.label: Public domain dedications
items.note: No conditions; CC0-1.0 s.4(a) leaves the affirmer's patent and trademark rights untouched

items.label: Permissive
items.note: Keep notices; the bank's own code need not be released

items.label: Weak (file-level) copyleft
items.note: Changed covered files or the library carry the duties; a larger work can differ

items.label: Strong copyleft
items.note: A work based on the program, when distributed, is licensed as a whole under the GPL

items.label: Network copyleft
items.note: Also reaches a modified version offered to remote users

points: **[[Permissive licence|permissive licence]]:** MIT, BSD, ISC and Apache-2.0 mainly ask for notices. They do not require the bank's own code to be released.
**Weak copyleft:** LGPL, MPL-2.0 and EPL-2.0 attach their duties to the licensed files or library, so the bank's own code in a larger work can keep its own terms if the rules are met.
**Strong copyleft:** GPL-2.0 requires that any work containing or derived from the program, when distributed, be licensed as a whole at no charge under the GPL (GPL-2.0 s.2(b)).
**Network copyleft:** AGPL-3.0 adds a duty for a modified version that remote users interact with (AGPL-3.0 s.13).
**Source-available:** SSPL, BUSL, Elastic License 2.0 and the Commons Clause restrict use or commercial activity, so treat them as commercial terms.

deepDive.heading: What triggers the duties
deepDive.lede: Most duties attach to an act: using, modifying, distributing or running a service.

visual.caption: Identify the act first. A duty applies only once that act has happened.

items.label: Use internally, unmodified
items.note: Running GPL-3.0 code in-house (GPL-3.0 s.2)

items.label: Modify
items.note: Once passed on, changed files carry notices (GPL-2.0 s.2(a); Apache-2.0 s.4(b))

items.label: Distribute or convey
items.note: Source or a written offer; the licence applies to the work (GPL-2.0 s.3; GPL-3.0 s.6)

items.label: Run as a network service
items.note: No conveying without a copy (GPL-3.0 s.0), except AGPL-3.0 s.13

points: **Internal use:** Running unmodified GPL-3.0 code carries no conditions at all (GPL-3.0 s.2). Internal changes can still matter later if the code is shipped.

**Modification:** Changing covered code for the bank's own use carries no conditions; the duties start when the changed version is passed on. Modified files must then carry change notices (GPL-2.0 s.2(a)); under GPL-3.0 the work must carry a prominent notice that it was modified, with a relevant date (GPL-3.0 s.5(a)), and a conveyed modified work must be licensed as a whole under GPL-3.0 (GPL-3.0 s.5(c)).

**Distribution:** Object code distributed under GPL-2.0 must come with the source, or with a written offer valid for at least three years (GPL-2.0 s.3(b)). GPL-3.0 s.6 gives comparable routes, but allows a written offer only for object code in a physical product (GPL-3.0 s.6(b)).

**[[Conveying|conveying]]:** Under GPL-3.0, conveying is propagation that enables others to make or receive copies. Mere interaction with a user over a network, with no copy transferred, is not conveying (GPL-3.0 s.0).
**Network copyleft:** AGPL-3.0 s.13 requires a modified version to offer its Corresponding Source to remote users. Running an unmodified version triggers nothing under that section.
deepDive.takeaway: Ask which act the bank is performing before deciding which duties apply.

deepDive.heading: Linking, derivative works and compatibility
deepDive.lede: Whether linking creates a derivative work is unsettled in US courts. Compatibility decides whether two licences can share one program.

visual.caption: Compatibility runs one way. Check each pair before code is combined.

items.label: Apache-2.0 code in a GPL-3.0 program
items.note: FSF view: Apache-2.0 is compatible with GPLv3

items.label: Apache-2.0 code in a GPL-2.0 program
items.note: FSF view: Apache-2.0 is not compatible with GPLv2

items.label: GPL-3.0 code with AGPL-3.0 code
items.note: GPL-3.0 s.13 and AGPL-3.0 s.13 allow the combination; the AGPL network duty then reaches the combined work

points: **Linking:** The FSF treats static and dynamic linking to GPL code as making a combined work, and says that for other ways programs communicate, such as pipes, sockets or plug-ins, the answer depends on the facts. No US court has adopted that view.

**Derivative works:** A derivative work is one based on a preexisting work and recast, transformed or adapted (17 U.S.C. § 101). Courts have not settled when software that links to another program becomes one.

**One-way fit:** Compatibility is usually one way. Code under one licence can go into a program under another only if the second licence allows it. The FSF considers Apache-2.0 compatible with GPLv3 but not GPLv2.
**GPL and AGPL:** GPL-3.0 s.13 lets the bank combine GPL-3.0 and AGPL-3.0 code into one work. The AGPL network requirements then apply to the combination as such.
**Practical point:** Record each combination in the component inventory and obtain a documented compatibility decision before linking (good practice).
deepDive.takeaway: Treat compatibility as an architecture decision, not a legal afterthought.

deepDive.heading: Versions, termination and cure
deepDive.lede: A licence can end if its conditions are broken, but the GPL family gives a route back.

items.label: Violation
items.note: Any attempt otherwise to propagate or modify is void (GPL-3.0 s.8)

items.label: Violation stops
items.note: Lasts until the holder explicitly and finally terminates it

items.label: No notice within 60 days
items.note: Reinstated permanently if the holder does not notify the violation before 60 days after it stops

items.label: First notice, cured within 30 days
items.note: Applies only to the first notice from that holder

points: **GPL-2.0 s.4:** Any attempt to copy, modify, sublicense or distribute otherwise terminates the licence automatically. Parties who have received copies from the violator keep theirs while they stay in full compliance.

**GPL-3.0 s.8:** Provides the cure route: provisional reinstatement once the violation stops, permanent reinstatement if no notice arrives within 60 days after the violation stops, and permanent reinstatement after a cure within 30 days of the first notice.
**Kernel statement:** Kernel developers who signed the Linux Kernel Enforcement Statement agreed to apply GPLv3-style cure terms to their own contributions to the kernel (reported; check).
**Enforcement culture:** The Principles of Community-Oriented GPL Enforcement, published by SFC and the FSF in 2015, put compliance before litigation (reported; check).
deepDive.takeaway: Treat a licence notice as a clock: the 30-day cure window starts when the notice arrives.

deepDive.heading: Versions, notices and what no licence means
deepDive.lede: Small details decide what the bank may do with a release.
points: **[[Or later version|or later version]]:** Where a program names a GPL version, a recipient may choose a later one only if the program also says 'any later version' (GPL-2.0 s.9). Where it names no version, any published version may be chosen (GPL-2.0 s.9).

**[[Dual licensing|dual licensing]]:** A licensor can offer the same code under a commercial licence and a copyleft licence, but only if it owns the copyright or holds the rights to grant both (drafting inference).

**No licence:** Code without a licence keeps the default position: copying, changing and distributing need the owner's permission (17 U.S.C. § 106). Publishing code in a public repository does not by itself grant open source rights (drafting inference).

**Notices:** MIT requires the copyright and permission notice in all copies or substantial portions of the software (MIT full text). Stripping licence notices can raise issues under 17 U.S.C. § 1202 (reported; check).

**No counterparty:** Permissive licences disclaim warranty, and MIT provides the software 'AS IS' (MIT full text). Plan support and indemnity separately with a vendor or in-house team (good practice).

provisions.title: Exclusive rights of the copyright owner
provisions.summary: Gives the owner the exclusive rights to do, and to authorize, the acts of reproducing the work, preparing derivative works, distributing copies, and performing or displaying it publicly, subject to §§ 107 to 122.
provisions.counselNote: Every open source licence is a grant of some of these rights. Without a licence, copying, changing or distributing the code needs the owner's permission.

provisions.title: Definition: derivative work
provisions.summary: Defines a derivative work as a work based upon one or more preexisting works, recast, transformed or adapted in any form, such as a translation or adaptation. A work of original editorial revisions or elaborations can also qualify.
provisions.counselNote: The definition decides when a modified or combined program is one the licence reaches. Courts have not settled how it applies to software that links to other code.

provisions.title: Writing requirement for transfers
provisions.summary: A transfer of copyright ownership is not valid unless it is in a writing signed by the owner of the rights conveyed or the owner's agent. A non-exclusive licence is not a transfer of ownership under § 101, so it needs no signed writing.
provisions.counselNote: A non-exclusive open source licence needs no signed writing, but an assignment to the bank, or from a contractor, does.

provisions.title: Licence conditions limit the scope of the permission
provisions.summary: The Federal Circuit held that the attribution and change-notice terms of the Artistic License were conditions limiting the licence. A user who broke them could be sued for copyright infringement, and not only for breach of contract.
provisions.counselNote: A failure to comply with a notice or attribution condition can take the bank outside the licence, which exposes it to infringement claims and injunctions.

provisions.instrument: Artifex Software, Inc. v. Hancom, Inc.
provisions.title: GPL enforceable as a contract on the facts pleaded
provisions.summary: The court refused to dismiss a claim that the GPL was an enforceable contract, on the facts pleaded. The defendant had used the software without complying with the GPL or taking a commercial licence, and the case then settled.
provisions.counselNote: Licensors can plead contract as well as copyright, so the bank's compliance records should show compliance on both footings.

provisions.instrument: Software Freedom Conservancy v. Vizio, Inc.
provisions.title: Purchaser's claim as third-party beneficiary of the GPL
provisions.summary: A nonprofit sued as a purchaser of Vizio TVs, claiming to be a third-party beneficiary of the GPL with a right to source code. Pre-trial rulings reportedly let the claim proceed. No final judgment is confirmed as at November 2026.
provisions.counselNote: The case tests who can enforce the GPL. A bank that distributes GPL code in devices or apps should allow for enforcement by purchasers as well as copyright holders, although that theory is not settled (drafting inference).

provisions.title: Modification, notices and licensing of derivative works
provisions.summary: Permits modification and distribution of the program if the modified files carry prominent change notices and any work that contains or is derived from the program is licensed as a whole under the GPL. Mere aggregation on a storage medium does not bring other works under the licence.
provisions.counselNote: This section sets the strong copyleft scope for GPL-2.0 code. Counsel should check whether a combined product is a work based on the program before distribution.

provisions.title: Definitions: covered work, modify and convey
provisions.summary: Defines conveying as propagation that enables others to make or receive copies. Mere interaction with a user through a computer network, with no transfer of a copy, is not conveying. Defines modify and modified version.
provisions.counselNote: Conveying is the trigger for most GPL-3.0 duties. Hosting a service that users reach over a network is not conveying unless a copy is transferred.

provisions.title: Basic permissions, including running unmodified code
provisions.summary: Gives unlimited permission to run the unmodified program and to make, run and propagate covered works that are not conveyed. The bank may convey covered works to contractors who make modifications exclusively for it, on terms that bar copies outside that relationship.
provisions.counselNote: Internal use of unmodified GPL-3.0 code carries no conditions. Contractor work is permitted only on the controlled terms this section sets out.

provisions.title: Termination and reinstatement
provisions.summary: Makes any attempt to propagate or modify other than as the licence allows void and automatically terminates the licensee's rights. Rights are reinstated provisionally when the violation stops, and permanently if the holder gives no notice within 60 days after the violation stops or the violation is cured within 30 days of the first notice.
provisions.counselNote: The cure windows are short and run from notice. A compliance team needs a route for handling licensor notices within 30 days.

provisions.instrument: GNU Affero General Public License v3.0
provisions.title: Remote network interaction
provisions.summary: Requires that a modified version offer all users who interact with it remotely over a network an opportunity to receive its Corresponding Source. Combination with GPL-3.0 code is also permitted under this section.
provisions.counselNote: The duty applies to modified versions only. Running an unmodified version triggers nothing under this section, but a change to an AGPL service that remote users reach can start the source offer.

provisions.title: Permission, notice condition and disclaimer
provisions.summary: Grants permission to use, copy, modify, merge, publish, distribute, sublicense and sell the software, subject to including the copyright and permission notice in all copies or substantial portions. The software is provided 'AS IS', without warranty.
provisions.counselNote: The only real condition is the notice. The no-warranty clause means the bank has no licensor warranty or indemnity to rely on.

provisions.title: Standard licence identifiers
provisions.summary: Provides standard short identifiers, such as GPL-2.0-only or MIT, and expressions that combine them, so that software licences can be recorded consistently in code and in inventories.
provisions.counselNote: Records that use SPDX identifiers can be read by scanners and by counsel in the same terms, which speeds up licence review.

provisions.title: Ten criteria for open source
provisions.summary: Sets ten criteria a licence must meet to count as open source under the OSI's definition. They include free redistribution, access to source code, derived works, and no discrimination against persons, groups or fields of endeavour.
provisions.counselNote: The definition is a standard set by a non-governmental body. It is useful for policy, but it is not law and does not bind a court.

checklist: **Classify every component:** Record each licence, its family and its SPDX identifier, and flag any source-available or network copyleft licence for legal review.
**Confirm the act before the duty:** Ask whether the use is internal, modified, distributed or run as a network service, because each act attracts different duties.
**Set an AGPL rule:** Require legal sign-off before a modified AGPL-3.0 component runs in a customer-facing service, and plan the source offer (good practice).
**Read the 'or later' wording:** Check whether a GPL program names a version and allows later versions, and record which version the bank relies on.
**Decide compatibility before linking:** Document each licence combination and get a written decision before code is linked or bundled into one product.
**Keep notices with the code:** Carry licence texts and copyright notices into the product, the About screen, the container image and the release package.
**Prepare a cure route:** Name who receives licensor notices, the deadline to respond and the engineering owner, so that a 30-day GPL-3.0 cure window is not missed.
**Route source-available code to contract review:** Send SSPL, BUSL and Elastic License 2.0 code to commercial review and the vendor process, not the open source queue.
**Check ownership for dual licences:** Before accepting a dual-licence offer, confirm who owns the copyright and holds the right to grant both licences.
**Record every licence decision:** Keep each approval with the licence text, version, date and reviewer, so that the bank can show its basis at audit.
itAngle: **SPDX in manifests:** Declare licences as SPDX expressions in package manifests, such as GPL-2.0-only or GPL-2.0-or-later, so that scanners and counsel read the same answer.
**Transitive dependencies:** Scanners need to walk the full dependency tree, because a permissive top-level package can pull in a copyleft library several levels down.
**Linking is a build decision:** Static linking, dynamic linking, plugin loading and separate processes change the combined-work analysis, so record how each component is linked in the build.

**Network services:** Track which services run modified AGPL-3.0 code. AGPL-3.0 s.13 requires the source offer to be prominent, with the source available from a network server at no charge through a standard or customary means of copying software; the offer itself might be a link in the service's user interface or API response (drafting inference on the form).
**Notices in artefacts:** Generate licence and notice files during the build and ship them in mobile apps, container images and firmware, not only in the repository.
virtualBankNotes: **Approval tiers:** Set licence approval tiers by family and by act, so that permissive libraries clear fast and AGPL or source-available code goes to counsel.
**Customer-facing code:** AGPL-3.0 code in online banking or in APIs raises the network duty for any modified version, so engineering and legal should agree before deployment.

**Contractors and affiliates:** GPL-3.0 s.2 allows the bank to give covered code to a contractor who modifies it only for the bank, on terms that bar copies outside that relationship. Treat transfers to affiliates as distribution unless a licence term says otherwise (drafting inference).

**Third-party oversight:** The interagency guidance on third-party relationships is technology-neutral and does not deal with open source as such. Vendors that supply or support open source components fall within it, while the components themselves usually do not (drafting inference).
**Examiner questions:** Examiners may ask for a current inventory of components, licences and approvals. The FFIEC development booklet covers open source components (reported; check the wording).
productNotes: **Say how the product will use the code:** Tell counsel whether the code stays inside the bank, is modified, goes to customers or runs as a service for users, because each act brings different duties (GPL-3.0 s.2; AGPL-3.0 s.13).

**Send the licence, not the label:** A vendor or colleague who says 'open source' does not settle the question, so send the licence text or its SPDX identifier with the request (OSI Open Source Definition). Source-available terms such as SSPL, BUSL and Elastic License 2.0 go to commercial review, not the open source queue (reported; check).

**Keep licence notices in the product:** Ask engineering to ship licence texts and copyright notices in the app, the About screen, the container image or the release package (MIT full text). Stripping them can also breach 17 U.S.C. § 1202(b) when it is done knowing it will enable infringement.

**Send licensor letters to counsel the same day:** A notice from a copyright holder can start a short cure clock, so the product or engineering lead who receives it should pass it on at once (GPL-3.0 s.8).
pitfalls: **Source-available as open source:** Approving SSPL, BUSL or Elastic License 2.0 code under an open source policy, when those licences restrict use and are not open source.
**Wrong trigger:** Treating every use as distribution, or assuming that a modified AGPL program run for remote users carries no source duty.
**Version drift:** Assuming a later GPL version applies when the program names a version but does not say 'any later version' (GPL-2.0 s.9).
**Notices lost in the build:** Stripping copyright and licence notices during packaging, which breaks licence conditions and can raise issues under 17 U.S.C. § 1202 (reported; check).
**Views as law:** Treating FSF or OSI positions on linking or compatibility as settled law, when no US court has adopted the FSF position on linking.
**Slow cure:** Starting remediation only after a licensor's notice arrives, which can leave the 30-day GPL-3.0 cure window missed.

points: **Cyber Resilience Act:** free and open-source software not supplied in a commercial activity is outside scope, and open-source software stewards have lighter duties (Regulation (EU) 2024/2847, Art. 24).

**Product liability:** software is a product, and free and open-source software developed or supplied outside a commercial activity is excluded (Directive (EU) 2024/2853), for products placed on the market from 9 December 2026.

**Broadly the same:** a licence works as a copyright permission with conditions, because programs are literary works (CDPA 1988 s.3(1)(b)); with no leading UK ruling on open source licences, the licence text and ordinary contract and copyright principles govern (drafting inference).
**No open source statute:** Canada has no general open source statute, so licences are enforced as contracts or through copyright.
**Moral rights in the background:** moral rights cannot be assigned (Copyright Act s.14.1(2)), which affects how a licence's credit or notice terms are drafted.

hongKong.summary: No Hong Kong statute deals with open source licences as such (reported; check), so a licence works as a permission under the Copyright Ordinance (Cap. 528 s.22(2)) and as a contract. The bank needs a licence for each act it does with code, and Hong Kong adds offences for dealing in and possessing infringing programs in a trade or business. A practical difference is that the reasonableness tests in Cap. 71 ss.7 to 9 do not apply to a contract so far as it relates to the creation or transfer of a right or interest in copyright, so an upstream disclaimer may fall outside them, while the bank's own customer terms for its services do not (Cap. 71 Sch. 1 para 1(c); drafting inference).
keyPoints: **Permission under copyright:** Copying, adapting and issuing a program need the owner's licence, so an open source licence is the permission that makes the bank's use lawful (Cap. 528 s.22(1)-(2), s.23(1), s.24(1)).
**Ending the permission:** Once a licence no longer authorises an act, further copying, issuing copies or adapting the program without licence infringes copyright (Cap. 528 ss.22-24, s.29).
**Business use triggers offences:** Dealing in or possessing infringing copies of a program for a trade or business can be a criminal offence (Cap. 528 s.118(1)(d), (f), (2A)).

**Contract too:** Offer and acceptance may be given by electronic records, so terms accepted online can form a contract (Cap. 553 s.17(1)-(2)). Acceptance by conduct alone falls outside that section and is a common-law question.

**Disclaimers:** The reasonableness tests in Cap. 71 ss.7 to 9 do not apply to a contract so far as it relates to the creation or transfer of a right or interest in copyright or other IP (Cap. 71 Sch. 1 para 1(c)). Whether a non-exclusive open source licence creates such an interest is arguable (drafting inference). The bank's own customer terms remain subject to ss.7 and 8 (Cap. 71 ss.7-8).

sections.heading: What the licence permits
sections.lede: A licence grants some of the owner's exclusive rights, so its scope decides what the bank may do with the code.
points: **Restricted acts:** The owner's exclusive rights cover copying, issuing copies to the public, communicating the work to the public and making adaptations (Cap. 528 s.22(1)(a), (b), (fa), (g)).

**Copies in any form:** Copying covers reproduction in any material form, including electronic storage, and it includes copies that are transient or incidental to another use (Cap. 528 s.23(2), (6)). A cache or a loaded program can therefore be a copy (drafting inference).

**Issue of copies:** Issuing copies to the public includes issuing them in electronic form (Cap. 528 s.24(2), (4)). A build shipped to customers therefore needs the licence to cover it (drafting inference).

**Adaptation of programs:** For a program, an adaptation is an arrangement or altered version, or a translation, and a translation includes conversion into a different computer language or code (Cap. 528 s.29(3)(b), (4)). Porting code to another language is an adaptation.
sections.takeaway: Map each planned act, such as building, modifying, shipping or hosting, to a licence term before engineering starts (good practice).

sections.heading: Lawful users and their statutory rights
sections.lede: A person with a contractual right to use a program has statutory back-up and adaptation rights, and the licence can limit them.
points: **Who is a lawful user:** A lawful user is a person with a contractual right to use the program (Cap. 528 s.60(2)).
**Back-up copies:** A lawful user may make a back-up copy where it is necessary for the lawful use (Cap. 528 s.60(1)).
**Copying and adapting:** A lawful user may copy or adapt a program where it is necessary for the lawful use, including to correct errors (Cap. 528 s.61(1)-(2)).

**Exclusion:** An agreement may exclude the back-up right in s.60 (Cap. 528 s.60(3)). Section 61 has no equivalent words, so whether a licence can exclude it is a question of construction (drafting inference).
**Reach of the offences:** For offences under s.118(1), the lawful-user test applies to a contractual right to use a program in any place in or outside Hong Kong (Cap. 528 s.118A(a)).
sections.takeaway: Do not treat the statutory lawful-user rights as a safe harbour where the licence says otherwise, and state any exclusion in the contract in plain words (good practice).

sections.heading: Offences and time limits
sections.lede: The criminal exposure follows trade or business activity, and the prosecution clock runs for three years.
points: **Dealing offence:** Selling, offering for sale or possessing an infringing copy with a view to sale, in the course of a trade or business, is an offence (Cap. 528 s.118(1)(d), (f)).

**Business possession of programs:** Possessing an infringing copy of a computer program for a trade or business, with a view to its use by anyone in that business, is an offence (Cap. 528 s.118(2A)-(2B)). Printed copies are excluded (Cap. 528 s.118(2C)), and so is a program technically required for the viewing or listening of a work by a member of the public (Cap. 528 s.118(2D)).
**Civil remedies:** Infringement is actionable by the copyright owner, who may obtain damages, injunctions and accounts (Cap. 528 s.107(1)-(2)).
**Time limit:** No prosecution may be started more than three years after the offence was committed (Cap. 528 s.120A).
sections.takeaway: Ask whether each use of third-party code is in the course of the bank's business before assessing offence risk, because the dealing and possession offences turn on that test (good practice).

provisions.title: Acts restricted by copyright
provisions.summary: The owner has the exclusive right to copy the work, issue copies to the public, communicate it to the public and make adaptations. Copyright is infringed by a person who, without the owner's licence, does or authorises another to do any of those acts.
provisions.counselNote: This is the starting point for every open source question: the licence is the owner's permission to do these acts, and anything outside it is infringement.

provisions.title: Copying, including electronic and transient copies
provisions.summary: Copying means reproducing the work in any material form, and includes storing it electronically. It also includes copies that are transient or incidental to some other use of the work.
provisions.counselNote: Engineers may not think of a loaded or cached program as a copy. Under this section it can be one, so the licence must cover the act.

provisions.title: Adaptation of a computer program
provisions.summary: For a computer program, an adaptation is an arrangement or altered version of the program, or a translation of it. A translation includes a version converted into or out of a computer language or code, or into a different one.
provisions.counselNote: Porting a library to another language or framework is an adaptation, so a licence that only covers use will not clear it.

provisions.title: Lawful user: back-up copy of a program
provisions.summary: A lawful user, meaning a person with a contractual right to use the program, may make a back-up copy where it is necessary for lawful use. An agreement may exclude this section.
provisions.counselNote: Engineering teams often assume a back-up right exists. It applies only to a contractual user, and the contract can take it away.

provisions.title: Lawful user: copying or adapting a program
provisions.summary: A lawful user may copy or adapt a program where that is necessary for lawful use, including to correct errors in it. This section does not apply to copying permitted under section 60.
provisions.counselNote: This is the statutory route for fixing bugs in licensed code. Because it has no express words of exclusion, the licence wording needs care.

provisions.title: No right to be identified for a computer program
provisions.summary: The right to be identified as author does not apply to a computer program, or to a computer-generated work or the design of a typeface.
provisions.counselNote: Any attribution duty in open source code comes from the licence or the contract, not from a statutory right of identification.

provisions.title: Criminal offences: dealing and business possession
provisions.summary: It is an offence, without the owner's licence, to sell or offer for sale an infringing copy in a trade or business, or to possess one with a view to sale. It is also an offence to possess an infringing copy of a computer program for a trade or business with a view to its use in that business. Printed copies of programs are excluded.
provisions.counselNote: The business possession offence is the one that reaches an internal team using unlicensed code in a product. Counsel should ask whether each use is in the course of the bank's business.

provisions.title: Three-year time limit for prosecutions
provisions.summary: No prosecution under the Ordinance may be commenced after three years from the date the offence was committed.
provisions.counselNote: The criminal route is a short-term exposure. Section 120A limits prosecutions only; civil claims in tort or contract run for six years under the Limitation Ordinance (Cap. 347 s.4(1)), so the bank's records should cover the whole period of use.

provisions.title: Electronic offer and acceptance
provisions.summary: An offer and its acceptance may be expressed by electronic records, and a contract is not denied validity only because an electronic record was used to form it.
provisions.counselNote: Click-through or package-level terms can bind the bank as a contract. Procurement should keep the accepted version of any licence the bank agrees to online.

provisions.title: IP contracts outside the reasonableness tests
provisions.summary: Sections 7, 8 and 9 do not apply to any contract so far as it relates to the creation or transfer of a right or interest in copyright or other intellectual property.
provisions.counselNote: An upstream disclaimer in a licence is not tested under these sections. The bank's own terms for customers are still tested, so the two should not be confused.

bankNotes: **Vendor and support contracts:** The HKMA expects an authorised institution to discuss an outsourcing of a banking-related business area with it in advance, and to be satisfied that the SA-2 section 2 issues are addressed before it starts (HKMA SPM SA-2, para 1.3.2). This is guidance, not law. A support contract for one component is not usually outsourcing, but a vendor that runs a banking-related function on open source code may be (drafting inference).

**Personal data in hosted code:** Where a provider processes customer personal data for the bank, the bank must adopt contractual or other means to protect the data and to stop it being kept longer than necessary (Cap. 486 Sch. 1, DPP 2(3) and DPP 4(2)). This is a statutory duty, not guidance.
**Approval tiers:** Set licence approvals by family and by act, so that permissive libraries clear quickly and network copyleft or source-available code goes to counsel (good practice).

glossary.definition: Software distributed under a licence that meets the Open Source Definition, which sets ten criteria including free redistribution and access to source code (OSI Open Source Definition).

The Free Software Foundation's term for software whose users have four freedoms: to run, study and change it, to redistribute it, and to distribute modified versions. This is the FSF's view, not a legal test.
Code published for reading or use under terms that restrict use or commercial activity. It is not open source under the OSI definition; SSPL, BUSL and Elastic License 2.0 are examples.
A licence that requires works based on the licensed code to be released on the same terms when they are distributed. GPL, LGPL, MPL and AGPL differ in how far the requirement reaches.
A licence that mainly asks for notices, such as MIT or Apache-2.0, and does not require the user's own code to be released.
The GPL-3.0 term for propagation that enables others to make or receive copies. It is the usual trigger for GPL-3.0 duties, and mere network interaction is not conveying (GPL-3.0 s.0).
A standard short code, such as MIT or GPL-2.0-only, that names a licence in a form that software tools can read (ISO/IEC 5962:2021).

The option to use a later version of a licence, which GPL-2.0 allows where the program names a version and says 'any later version', or, where it names no version, any version ever published (GPL-2.0 s.9).
Offering the same code under two licences, often a copyleft licence and a commercial one. The licensor must hold the rights needed to grant both.
A copyleft licence that also reaches a modified version used over a network, as AGPL-3.0 s.13 provides for remote users.
A person with a contractual right to use a computer program. Only a lawful user gets the back-up and adaptation rights in ss.60 and 61 (Cap. 528 s.60(2)).
For a computer program, an arrangement or altered version of it, or a translation, which includes conversion into a different computer language or code (Cap. 528 s.29(3)(b), (4)).

intro: **Pick a licence and how the bank uses the code:** the finder shows what that licence asks for in those uses, with the licence's own words one tap away, and whether two licences can go into one program.

**Triggers decide everything:** most licences ask nothing of code that stays inside the bank. Duties start when copies go to others, and for the AGPL when a modified version serves users over a network.

**Read the actual licence:** the text that ships with a component governs, and variants exist. FSF and OSI positions shown here are their views, not law, and courts have decided few of these questions.

uses.label: Give copies to others
uses.hint: Mobile apps, SDKs, on-premises software, devices

uses.label: Run it behind an online service
uses.hint: Customer websites, app back ends, APIs

uses.label: Link or bundle it into a larger program
Give it to a contractor or affiliate

families.label: Public domain dedications
families.blurb: The author gives up rights as far as the law allows; CC0 adds a fallback licence.

families.label: Permissive
families.blurb: Use for any purpose; keep the notices. Apache-2.0 adds a patent licence.

families.label: Weak copyleft
families.blurb: Changes to the licensed files or library stay open; the rest of the program can use its own licence.

families.label: Strong copyleft
families.blurb: A distributed program that contains or is based on the code must carry the same licence and come with source.

families.label: Network copyleft
families.blurb: Like the GPL, plus source for users of a modified version over a network.

families.label: Source-available (not open source)
families.blurb: Source you can read, with limits on use, usually on offering it as a service.

families.label: Content licences
families.blurb: Made for documents and data, not code.

licences.name: BSD Zero Clause License
licences.summary: The licence lets anyone use, copy, modify and distribute the software for any purpose, with or without fee. It attaches no conditions at all: it asks for no notice or licence text, and it disclaims warranties and liability.
licences.trigger: No use or distribution triggers a licence duty, because the licence attaches no conditions to either (0BSD, full text).
licences.patent: The licence is silent on patents and grants no express patent licence (0BSD, full text).

duties.text: Give copies to others without a licence text, since the licence requires none; keep the copyright line where bank policy asks, as good practice (0BSD, full text).
Treat copies given to contractors and affiliates as permitted, because the licence sets no limit on who may receive them (0BSD, full text).

watch: The absence of an attribution duty does not remove the bank's own need for a record: note the author and source in the approval file (good practice).
Individuals often apply this licence to their own code, so confirm who holds the copyright before relying on it (17 U.S.C. § 201(a); drafting inference).
The disclaimer covers all warranties and liability, so the bank carries the quality and security risk unless it tests the code (0BSD, full text).

licences.name: MIT License
licences.summary: The licence lets anyone use, copy, modify, merge, publish, distribute, sublicense and sell copies of the software, free of charge. Its one condition is that the copyright notice and the permission notice appear in all copies or substantial portions of the software.
licences.trigger: Making any copy or substantial portion of the software, including a copy given to a contractor or shipped in a product, sets off the notice condition (MIT, full text).
licences.patent: The licence is silent on patents and grants no express patent licence (MIT, full text).

duties.text: Keep the copyright notice and the permission notice in every copy or substantial portion that goes out, in the source files or in the documentation shipped with a binary (MIT, full text).
Keep the same notices on internal copies and on copies given to a contractor, since the condition speaks of all copies and does not limit itself to copies leaving the bank (MIT, full text).
Keep the notices in modified versions as well, because the condition attaches to any substantial portion of the software, altered or not (MIT, full text).

watch: Whether a missing notice is a breach of a condition or of a promise is for the courts to decide, so treat a missing notice as a defect to fix at once (drafting inference).

Build tools, minifiers and packagers that strip headers can remove the notice, and stripping it to hide use can engage the rule on copyright management information (17 U.S.C. § 1202(b); reported; check).
The licence says nothing about the licensor's patents, unlike Apache-2.0 s.3, so the bank should not assume a patent licence (drafting inference).

licences.name: BSD 2-Clause "Simplified" License
licences.summary: The licence lets anyone use, copy, modify and redistribute the software in source or binary form, with or without modification. Its two conditions are to keep the copyright notice, the conditions and the disclaimer in source redistributions, and to reproduce them in the documentation or other materials that come with a binary.
licences.trigger: Redistribution in source or binary form sets off the two conditions; the licence attaches no condition to use alone (BSD-2-Clause, full text).
licences.patent: The licence is silent on patents and grants no express patent licence (BSD-2-Clause, full text).

duties.text: Keep the copyright notice, the conditions and the disclaimer in the source files of any source redistribution (BSD-2-Clause, condition 1).
Reproduce the same notice, conditions and disclaimer in the documentation or other materials that come with each binary release (BSD-2-Clause, condition 2).
Keep the notice in modified source as well, because condition 1 applies to any redistribution of source, altered or not (BSD-2-Clause, condition 1).

watch: The binary condition is easy to miss: an app or device build that ships the library with no documentation or about screen fails condition 2 (drafting inference).
The "Simplified" name is a label only: check that the SPDX identifier matches the file header, since the BSD-3-Clause text adds a non-endorsement condition (BSD-2-Clause, full text).
No patent grant or termination appears in the text, so contributors' patents are not licensed in terms (drafting inference).

licences.name: BSD 3-Clause "New" or "Revised" License
licences.summary: The licence lets anyone use, copy, modify and redistribute the software in source or binary form, with or without modification. It has the same two notice conditions as BSD-2-Clause and adds a third: the names of the copyright holder and contributors may not be used to endorse or promote products derived from the software without written permission.
licences.trigger: Redistribution in source or binary form sets off conditions 1 and 2, and using the holder's or contributors' names to endorse or promote a derived product sets off condition 3 (BSD-3-Clause, full text).
licences.patent: The licence is silent on patents and grants no express patent licence (BSD-3-Clause, full text).

duties.text: Keep the copyright notice, the conditions and the disclaimer in the source files of any source redistribution (BSD-3-Clause, condition 1).
Reproduce the notice, conditions and disclaimer in the documentation or other materials that come with each binary release (BSD-3-Clause, condition 2).
Do not use the upstream holder's or contributors' names to endorse or promote a bank product built on the code, without written permission (BSD-3-Clause, condition 3).

watch: Condition 3 bites on marketing: a press release, app listing or support page that suggests the upstream project backs the bank's product can breach it, so state the origin accurately and no more (drafting inference).
BSD-2-Clause and BSD-3-Clause differ only by condition 3, so an approval record should name the variant that the file header carries (BSD-3-Clause, full text).
No patent grant or termination appears in the text, so contributors' patents are not licensed in terms (drafting inference).

licences.name: ISC License
licences.summary: The licence lets anyone use, copy, modify and distribute the software for any purpose, with or without fee. Its one condition is that the copyright notice and the permission notice appear in all copies, and it disclaims warranties and liability.
licences.trigger: Making any copy of the software, in any form, sets off the notice condition (ISC License, full text).
licences.patent: The licence is silent on patents and grants no express patent licence (ISC License, full text).

duties.text: Keep the copyright notice and the permission notice in every copy, including internal copies and copies given to a contractor (ISC, full text).
Where the code ships in binary form, put the notices where they appear with the product, such as the documentation or about screen, as good practice (ISC, full text).
Keep the upstream notices in modified versions and add the bank's own notice beside them, without deleting the upstream notice (good practice; ISC, full text).

watch: ISC reads like MIT but is shorter; its notice condition is the only one, so an approval file should not record it as a no-condition licence like 0BSD (drafting inference).
The disclaimer protects the authors: no warranty or liability is accepted, so the bank's own customer terms must carry any warranty it gives (drafting inference).
No express patent grant appears, so the authors' patents are not licensed in terms (ISC, full text).

licences.name: zlib License
licences.summary: The licence lets anyone use the software for any purpose, including commercial use, and alter and redistribute it freely. It requires that the origin not be misrepresented, that altered source be plainly marked, and that the licence notice stay in source distributions.
licences.trigger: Distributing the software or altered source, or claiming the code as one's own, sets off the conditions; the licence does not address internal use directly (zlib License, full text).
licences.patent: The licence is silent on patents and grants no express patent licence (zlib License, full text).

duties.text: Do not claim that the bank wrote the original software; an acknowledgement in the product documentation is welcome but not required (zlib License, condition 1).
Mark altered source versions plainly as altered, and do not present them as the original software (zlib License, condition 2).
Keep the licence notice in every source distribution; it may not be removed or altered (zlib License, condition 3).

watch: An internal fork is an altered source version, so mark it as altered even where no copy leaves the bank, as good practice (drafting inference).
Compare the licence text in each file with the zlib text, since reworded terms are a different licence and need their own approval (drafting inference).
The "as-is" disclaimer and the absence of a patent grant leave warranty and patent risk to the bank's own review (zlib License, full text).

licences.name: Boost Software License 1.0
licences.summary: The licence lets any person or organisation use, reproduce, display, distribute and transmit the software, and prepare derivative works, free of charge. Its one condition is that the licence statement appears in all source copies and derivative works, but not in copies that are solely machine-executable object code.
licences.trigger: Copying or distributing source code or derivative works, or any copy that is not solely object code, sets off the notice condition (BSL-1.0, full text).
licences.patent: The licence is silent on patents and grants no express patent licence (BSL-1.0, full text).

duties.text: Keep the copyright notices and the full licence statement in every source copy and derivative work, including internal ones, since the condition is not limited to distribution (BSL-1.0, full text).
A binary-only release need not carry the statement, because copies that are solely object code generated by a language processor are exempt; keep it where policy requires (BSL-1.0, full text).

watch: The exemption is narrow: a source file inside a bundle, or a header-only library copied into the bank's source tree, is a source copy and must keep the statement (drafting inference).
A device or on-premises product that receives only object code relies on the exemption, so check that no source copy reaches the product through the build pipeline (good practice).
The licence is silent on patents, so the authors' patents are not licensed in terms (BSL-1.0, full text).

licences.name: Apache License 2.0
licences.summary: The licence grants a perpetual, worldwide, royalty-free copyright licence and an express patent licence from each contributor, to use, modify and distribute the work in source or object form (Apache-2.0 s.2, s.3). Its conditions apply on redistribution: a copy of the licence, marked changes, retained notices and the NOTICE file's attributions (s.4). Section 6 separately withholds any right to use the project's marks beyond describing its origin (s.6).
licences.trigger: Distributing the work or derivative works in source or object form sets off the section 4 conditions; running the work internally or as a hosted service does not (Apache-2.0 s.4).
licences.patent: Section 3 gives an express patent licence from each contributor for the claims its contribution necessarily infringes, and that licence ends for any licensee who sues alleging the work infringes a patent (Apache-2.0 s.3).

duties.text: Give every recipient a copy of the Apache licence with the code or product (Apache-2.0 s.4(a)).

When you redistribute a changed version, mark each changed file with a prominent notice that it was changed, and keep the copyright, patent, trademark and attribution notices in derivative source (Apache-2.0 s.4(b)-(c)).
Carry the attribution notices from any NOTICE file in a NOTICE file, the documentation, or the display where third-party notices normally appear (Apache-2.0 s.4(d)).

Before the bank starts patent litigation alleging that the work, or a contribution in it, infringes a patent, check whether the termination in section 3 would end its patent licence to the work (Apache-2.0 s.3).
Do not use the project's names or marks beyond describing the origin of the work and reproducing the NOTICE file (Apache-2.0 s.6).

watch: Section 3 ends the patent licence to the work if the bank sues anyone alleging that the work infringes, so the bank's own enforcement decisions can cut off its licence (Apache-2.0 s.3).
A contribution the bank sends upstream is under Apache-2.0 unless the bank says otherwise, so check the inbound terms before pushing a patch (Apache-2.0 s.5).
The bank may add its own terms to its modifications, but only if its use of the original work still complies with the licence (Apache-2.0 s.4).

licences.name: The Unlicense
licences.summary: The licence dedicates the software to the public domain, so anyone may copy, modify, publish, use, compile, sell or distribute it for any purpose, in source or binary form. It asks for no attribution and disclaims warranties and liability.
licences.trigger: Nothing sets off a licence duty: the dedication covers every use, copy and distribution (Unlicense, full text).
licences.patent: The dedication is silent on patents and grants no patent licence (Unlicense, full text).

duties.text: Confirm the dedication works where the bank ships or hosts the code, since the text has no drafted fallback licence for places that do not recognise a dedication (drafting inference; Unlicense, full text).
Record the source, the author and the dedication in the approval file, since no notice has to travel with the code and provenance would otherwise be lost (good practice; Unlicense, full text).

watch: The text has no drafted fallback licence like CC0-1.0 s.3: if a court does not give effect to the dedication, the bank must rely on its short statement that anyone is free to copy, modify and distribute the software (Unlicense, full text).

A dedication is only as good as the author's title, so confirm the author owned the rights, especially for code written by an employee (17 U.S.C. § 201(b)) or by a contractor, whose work is made for hire only in the categories listed in 17 U.S.C. § 101 (drafting inference).
The licence says nothing about trademarks or patents, so the bank's use of the author's name needs its own check (drafting inference).

licences.name: Creative Commons Zero v1.0 Universal
licences.summary: The affirmer waives copyright and related rights in the work worldwide, so anyone may copy, modify, distribute and use it for any purpose, including commercially. If the waiver fails, a fallback licence applies on the same terms, and the affirmer's patent and trademark rights are not waived.
licences.trigger: Nothing sets off a licence duty, because the waiver applies to every copy, use and distribution (CC0-1.0 s.2).
licences.patent: CC0 grants no patent licence, and section 4(a) says the affirmer's patent and trademark rights are not waived, licensed or otherwise affected (CC0-1.0 s.4(a)).

duties.text: Check that the affirmer owned the rights it waived, since the waiver reaches only the rights the affirmer holds (CC0-1.0 Preamble).
Clear any third-party rights in the material before release, since the affirmer disclaims responsibility for them (CC0-1.0 s.4(c)).
Do not treat CC0 as a patent or trademark licence: the affirmer's rights in both survive, so check patents and marks separately (CC0-1.0 s.4(a)).

watch: The waiver is a dedication, not a licence, so the fallback licence in section 3 is the only licence language if the waiver fails (CC0-1.0 s.3).
No attribution is required, but the bank's own policy may still want the origin recorded (good practice).
Fedora stopped allowing CC0 for code in 2022 because of the patent and trademark point (reported; check).

licences.name: Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International
licences.summary: The licence lets anyone share and adapt the material, worldwide and royalty-free, provided the creator is credited and changes are indicated. It licenses no patent, trademark, moral or personality rights, and it disclaims warranties and liability.
licences.trigger: Sharing the material in whole, in part or in adapted form sets off the attribution conditions in section 3(a) (CC-BY-4.0 s.3(a)).
licences.patent: Patent and trademark rights are not licensed under the licence (CC-BY-4.0 s.2(b)(2)).

duties.text: Keep the creator's name, a copyright notice, a reference to the licence and to the disclaimer, and a link to the material where reasonably practicable (CC-BY-4.0 s.3(a)(1)(A)).
Indicate any changes you made and keep any earlier indication of modification (CC-BY-4.0 s.3(a)(1)(B)).
State that the material is licensed under CC BY 4.0 and include the licence text or a link to it (CC-BY-4.0 s.3(a)(1)(C)).
Make sure any licence you apply to adapted material does not stop recipients from complying with CC BY 4.0 (CC-BY-4.0 s.3(a)(4)).
Do not add terms or technical measures that restrict others from exercising the licensed rights (CC-BY-4.0 s.2(a)(5)(B)).

watch: Credit is the main burden: where the bank shares a dataset or model card in an app or product, the credit line must appear where users can see it (drafting inference; CC-BY-4.0 s.3(a)(2)).
CC BY 4.0 is drafted for creative and data material, so its terms do not address software points such as source code or patents (drafting inference).
Personality, publicity and privacy rights in images or voices depicted in the material are not licensed (CC-BY-4.0 s.2(b)(1)).

licences.name: Mozilla Public License 2.0
licences.summary: Permits use, modification and distribution, including in larger works that carry other terms. Its main condition is file-level copyleft: distributed MPL-covered files stay under the MPL, with their source available.
licences.trigger: Distributing Covered Software, in source or executable form, to anyone outside the bank (s.3); internal use alone does not.
licences.patent: Express patent licence from each Contributor for its Patent Claims (s.2.1(b)); all your s.2.1 rights from every Contributor, copyright as well as patent, end if you start patent litigation (other than a declaratory judgment action, counter-claim or cross-claim) against any entity alleging that a Contributor Version directly or indirectly infringes a patent (s.5.2).

duties.text: Distribute MPL-covered files in source form under the MPL, and leave the licence notices in them intact (s.3.1, s.3.4).
For any executable copy, make the MPL source available at no more than the cost of distribution, and tell recipients how to get it (s.3.2(a)).
A larger work may carry other terms, but the MPL files keep MPL terms; GPL-family secondary licences apply only where the file is not marked Incompatible With Secondary Licenses (s.3.3; Exhibit B).

watch: The Exhibit B notice ('Incompatible With Secondary Licenses') blocks the GPL-family option for that file (s.1.5; Exhibit B); check file headers before combining with GPL code.
Licence change risk: HashiCorp moved Terraform from MPL-2.0 to the Business Source License 1.1 in August 2023 (reported; check). Record the version you rely on.

licences.name: Eclipse Public License 2.0
licences.summary: Permits use, modification and distribution, including in commercial products, with copyright and patent licences from each contributor. Its main condition is that distributed copies of the Program are also made available in source form under EPL-2.0.
licences.trigger: Distributing the Program, in any form, to anyone outside the bank (s.3.1); internal use alone does not.
licences.patent: Express, royalty-free patent licence from each contributor for its licensed patents (s.2(b)); it ends if the recipient sues alleging that the Program itself, not a combination with other software or hardware, infringes the recipient's patents (s.7).

duties.text: When you distribute the Program, make its Source Code available and state that it is governed by EPL-2.0, with a reasonable way to obtain it (s.3.1(a), s.3.2).
If you distribute under a different licence, it must disclaim warranties and must not limit recipients' rights in the Source Code under EPL-2.0 (s.3.1(b)).
When you distribute copies of the Program, keep the EPL-2.0 copyright, patent and attribution notices in the Program files, including when you combine them with other code (s.3.3).

watch: The GPL-2.0 'Secondary License' route is open only where the initial Contributor attaches the Exhibit A notice (s.1 defines the term; s.3.2(a) and Appendix); without that notice, do not treat the code as GPL-2.0.
Patent litigation over the Program ends the patent licences (s.7); route any patent dispute with a contributor through counsel first.

licences.name: GNU Lesser General Public License v2.1 only
licences.summary: Lets a proprietary program link to the library, and lets the library be modified and shared under the same licence. Its main condition is that a distributed modified library stays under LGPL-2.1 with source, and a combined work must let users relink or replace the library.
licences.trigger: Distributing the library, a modified library, or a combined work containing it to anyone outside the bank (s.2, s.6); internal use alone does not.
licences.patent: No express patent grant; if a patent licence or court order would contradict the licence, you may not distribute at all (s.11).

duties.text: When you distribute a modified library, license the whole under LGPL-2.1 and mark the changed files with notices of the change and date (s.2(b)-(c)).

For a work that uses the library, give prominent notice that the library is used, supply a copy of the licence, and let users modify the work for their own use and reverse engineer it for debugging such modifications (s.6).
Applying the GNU GPL-2.0 to a copy instead is allowed, but the change is irreversible for that copy and its derivatives (s.3).

watch: Whether linking creates a combined work is unsettled in US courts; the FSF's view that it does is a view, not law.
Check file headers for 'or later' wording; LGPL-2.1-only and LGPL-2.1-or-later differ, and the -only version has no later-version option.

sources.label: GNU Lesser General Public License v2.1 only

licences.name: GNU Lesser General Public License v3.0 only
licences.summary: Adds to GPL-3.0 permission to convey a combined work on terms of the user's choice, provided the library stays modifiable and users can reverse engineer for debugging. Its main conditions are notices, a copy of the licences, and a relinking or source route for the library (s.4).
licences.trigger: Conveying the library, or a combined work containing it, to anyone outside the bank (s.4); internal use alone does not.
licences.patent: The licence incorporates GPL-3.0 (Preamble), so GPL-3.0 s.11 (patent licence from contributors) and s.10 (no patent suits over the Program) apply.

duties.text: In a combined work, give prominent notice that the library is used and that it is covered by LGPL-3.0, and include the GNU GPL-3.0 and LGPL-3.0 texts (s.4(a)-(b)).
Let the terms of the combined work permit modification of the library and reverse engineering for debugging such modifications (s.4).

Header-file material may be conveyed under your own terms, but if the incorporated material is more than numerical parameters, data layouts, accessors, or small macros, inline functions and templates of ten lines or fewer, you must give prominent notice that the Library is used and include the GNU GPL and LGPL-3.0 texts (s.3(a)-(b)).

watch: Check file headers: LGPL-3.0-only and LGPL-3.0-or-later differ in which version applies, and the SPDX identifier must match the file.
Because the licence incorporates GPL-3.0, read its patent and conveying terms as GPL-3.0 terms, not as a plain weak-copyleft licence.

sources.label: GNU Lesser General Public License v3.0 only

licences.name: GNU General Public License v2.0 only
licences.summary: Permits use, modification and distribution, with source code and the same licence for any work based on the program. Its main condition is that anything you distribute that contains or is derived from the program must be licensed as a whole under GPL-2.0-only.
licences.trigger: Distributing the program, or a work based on it, to anyone outside the bank (s.2(b), s.3); internal use alone does not.
licences.patent: No express patent grant; if a patent licence or court order would contradict the licence, you may not distribute the program at all (s.7).

duties.text: When you distribute a modified version, mark the modified files with prominent notices stating that you changed them and the date of the change (s.2(a)).
License any distributed work that contains or is derived from the program as a whole, at no charge, under GPL-2.0-only (s.2(b), s.6).
With object code, provide complete source, or a written offer valid for at least three years to supply it (s.3(a)-(b)).

watch: Copying, modifying or distributing outside the licence terminates your rights (s.4), and the text has no reinstatement clause like GPL-3.0 s.8 (drafting inference).
GPL-2.0-only code cannot be merged into a GPL-3.0 work, and the 'only' version does not allow a later GPL (see the compatibility pairs for this licence).

sources.label: GNU General Public License v2.0 only

licences.name: GNU General Public License v3.0 only
licences.summary: Permits use, modification and conveying, with the same licence for conveyed copies and combined works. Its main condition is that when you convey a covered work you must provide its Corresponding Source under GPL-3.0; running the program for users over a network is not conveying (s.0).
licences.trigger: Conveying a covered work to anyone outside the bank (s.0, s.6); internal use and network interaction without a transfer of copies are not conveying (s.0, s.2).
licences.patent: Express patent licence from each contributor for its essential patent claims (s.11), and you may not sue over patent claims that the Program infringes (s.10).

duties.text: When you convey object code, provide the Corresponding Source under GPL-3.0 with it, or by one of the routes in s.6.
When you convey a modified version in source form, mark it with prominent notices stating that you modified it and the date, and that it is released under GPL-3.0 (s.5(a)-(b)).
Do not impose further restrictions on recipients, and do not charge a royalty or licence fee for exercising the granted rights (s.10).

You may give copies to a contractor only to make modifications exclusively for you or to provide facilities for running them, on terms that bar the contractor from copying them outside its relationship with you (s.2).

watch: Affiliates: the FSF says copying within one company is not distribution, and that whether a move to a majority-owned, controlled subsidiary is distribution turns on local copyright law, though US law appears not to treat it as distribution (reported; check); affiliates are separate legal persons, so treat transfers between them, including to a subsidiary, as conveying (drafting inference).
Cure: a violation stopped and cured within 30 days of the first notice from a copyright holder reinstates the licence (s.8).

sources.label: GNU General Public License v3.0 only

licences.name: GNU Affero General Public License v3.0 only
licences.summary: Permits the same use, modification and conveying as GPL-3.0, plus a duty to offer source to remote users of a modified version. Its main condition is that users who interact with a modified version over a network must be offered its Corresponding Source (s.13).
licences.trigger: Conveying copies (s.6), or letting users interact remotely with a modified version over a network (s.13); running an unmodified version over a network triggers nothing under s.13.
licences.patent: Same as GPL-3.0: express patent licence from each contributor (s.11) and no patent suits over the Program (s.10).

duties.text: If you modify the program and users interact with it remotely, offer them the Corresponding Source of your version at no charge, from a network server, through a standard or customary means of copying software (s.13).
When you convey copies, provide the Corresponding Source under AGPL-3.0 by one of the routes in s.6.
When you convey a modified version, mark it with prominent notices that you modified it and the date (s.5(a)).

watch: Internal users count: employees who use a modified version over the bank's network are users interacting remotely, so the s.13 offer is owed to them (drafting inference; check the wording).

GPL-3.0 and AGPL-3.0 code may be combined into one work in either direction. Each part keeps its own licence, but the AGPL network source offer reaches the combination, including the GPL-3.0 code in it (GPL-3.0 s.13; AGPL-3.0 s.13).

Added terms can be enforced against AGPL licensees: Neo4j, Inc. v. PureThink LLC held that the AGPL's further-restrictions term did not let a licensee strip a Commons Clause that the licensor had added (reported; check).

sources.label: GNU Affero General Public License v3.0 only

licences.name: Server Side Public License, v 1
licences.summary: Permits use, modification and distribution of the program, with a source-release condition for services. If you offer the program to others as a service, you must release the source of the service stack, including the software used to make it available (reported; check).
licences.trigger: Offering the program to third parties as a service (s.13) (reported; check); internal use does not on its face fall within that trigger (drafting inference).
licences.patent: Patent terms are not covered here; check the licence text before relying on any patent position.

duties.text: Before offering the program to third parties as a service, release the Service Source Code: the program and all software used to make the service available (s.13) (reported; check).
Keep internal use separate from any offer to third parties; the release duty attaches to a service offered to others (reported; check).

watch: OSI does not treat SSPL as open source (reported; check), so do not describe it as open source in policies, SBOMs or vendor questionnaires.
The release duty reaches all software used to make the service available, so the scope can extend well beyond the licensed program (reported; check).

licences.name: Business Source License 1.1
licences.summary: Makes the source available and allows non-production use, with production use limited unless the licensor's Additional Use Grant allows it. Each version converts to an open-source Change License after its Change Date, which the licence caps at four years from first public release (reported; check).
licences.trigger: Production use, or any use outside the Additional Use Grant, of a version that has not yet reached its Change Date (reported; check).
licences.patent: Patent terms are not covered here; check the licence text before relying on any patent position.

duties.text: Before running the software in production inside the bank, check the Additional Use Grant; production use is limited unless the grant allows it (reported; check).
Check whether offering the software as a service to others falls within the Additional Use Grant; the licensor sets that limit (reported; check).
Track each version's Change Date; after it, that version is available under its Change License instead (reported; check the text).

watch: Change Dates and Change Licenses vary by version, so each release needs its own date check (reported; check).

Not open source: it is source-available, and the OSI has not approved it (reported; check). HashiCorp moved Terraform from MPL-2.0 to BUSL-1.1 in August 2023, and OpenTofu forked the last open version (reported; check).

licences.name: Elastic License 2.0
licences.summary: Lets you use, copy, distribute and modify the software, with limits; the main limit is that you may not provide the software to others as a hosted or managed service (reported; check). It is source-available, not open source.
licences.trigger: Offering the software to third parties as a hosted or managed service, or removing the licence notices (check the licence text).
licences.patent: Patent terms are not covered here; check the licence text before relying on any patent position.

duties.text: Do not offer the software to third parties as a hosted or managed service, which the licence restricts (reported; check the licence text).
Keep the licence and copyright notices intact in every copy and modified version you distribute (check the licence text).

watch: Source-available, not open source: the OSI does not approve it, so do not describe it as open source. Elastic moved Elasticsearch and Kibana to this family in 2021 and added AGPLv3 as an option in August 2024 (reported; check).
Choice of licence can change between versions; the version you hold is governed by its own terms (check the licence text).

licences.name: Commons Clause License Condition v1.0
licences.summary: A condition added to another licence, usually a permissive one, that bars selling the software. It is attached to another licence and does not stand alone; the condition reaches hosting or support services whose value derives entirely or substantially from the software (reported; check).
licences.trigger: Selling the software, or a hosted or support service whose value derives entirely or substantially from it (reported; check).
licences.patent: The condition says nothing about patents, so the patent terms of the underlying licence apply (drafting inference; check).

duties.text: Do not sell the software, or any copy of it, since the Commons Clause bars selling it (reported; check).
Do not offer, for a fee or other consideration, a hosted or support service whose value derives entirely or substantially from the software (reported; check).

watch: The condition travels with the code: Neo4j, Inc. v. PureThink LLC held that a licensee could not strip a Commons Clause added to AGPL code, and that calling the fork free and open source was false advertising (reported; check).
Not open source: do not describe code under this condition as open source in policies or vendor terms.

compat.note: MIT imposes only a notice condition, so MIT code can sit in an Apache-2.0 work with its notice kept (MIT, full text).
MIT code can join a GPL-2.0-only work, which must then be licensed as a whole under GPL-2.0 (GPL-2.0 s.2(b)).
MIT code can join a GPL-3.0 work, which is then conveyed under GPL-3.0 with the MIT notice kept (GPL-3.0 s.5).
The BSD-3-Clause notice and no-endorsement conditions can be met inside a GPL-2.0 work, which is then licensed as a whole under GPL-2.0 (GPL-2.0 s.2(b)).
The FSF view is that Apache-2.0 is compatible with GPL-3.0 (a view, not law); the combined work is conveyed under GPL-3.0 with the Apache notices kept (Apache-2.0 s.4).
The FSF view is that Apache-2.0 is incompatible with GPL-2.0; Apache's patent termination (Apache-2.0 s.3) adds a restriction GPL-2.0 forbids (GPL-2.0 s.6).

Apache-2.0 files can ship inside a project whose own code is MIT, but they stay under Apache-2.0 (its patent licence, NOTICE file and change notices), so the whole cannot be offered under MIT alone (Apache-2.0 s.4). MIT code into an Apache-2.0 project is straightforward.
LGPL-2.1 s.3 lets you apply GPL-2.0 to a copy, irreversibly for that copy, so the library can then join a GPL-2.0-only work.
LGPL-3.0 incorporates GPL-3.0 (Preamble), so the library can join a GPL-3.0 work, which is then conveyed under GPL-3.0.

MPL-2.0 s.3.3 lets a larger work carry other terms, and s.1.12 lists GPL-2.0 or any later version as a Secondary License; MPL files may also be distributed under the GPL in that larger work unless they are marked Incompatible With Secondary Licenses (s.1.5, s.3.3).
A larger work may be distributed under Apache-2.0 (MPL-2.0 s.3.3), provided the MPL files keep MPL terms and their source is available (s.3.1-3.2).

EPL-2.0 lets the code be made available under GPL-2.0, its Secondary License, only where the initial Contributor attaches the Exhibit A notice (EPL-2.0 s.1, s.3.2(a); Appendix). Without that notice, the EPL code cannot be relicensed under GPL-2.0-only.

GPL-2.0-only code cannot move to GPL-3.0: it names no later version (GPL-2.0 s.9) and GPL-2.0 bars further restrictions (s.6). Code marked "GPL-2.0 or any later version" can go into a GPL-3.0 program.

GPL-3.0 adds terms GPL-2.0 does not allow, such as the installation information duty for user products (GPL-3.0 s.6), and GPL-2.0 s.6 bars any further restriction on recipients; GPL-2.0-only also has no later-version option.
GPL-3.0 s.13 lets GPL-3.0 code be combined with AGPL-3.0 code into one work; the AGPL network requirement then applies to the combination as such.

AGPL-3.0 s.13 lets AGPL code be combined with GPL-3.0 code into one work, but the AGPL part keeps its terms, including the network source offer for modified versions, so the whole is not under GPL-3.0 alone.
The combined work must be conveyed under GPL-3.0, which bars further restrictions (GPL-3.0 s.10), so it cannot be distributed under Apache-2.0 as a whole.
A GPL-2.0-only work must be licensed as a whole under GPL-2.0 (GPL-2.0 s.2(b)) and recipients receive GPL-2.0 terms (s.6), so the combined work cannot be distributed as MIT.
CC0 places no conditions on use, so CC0 material can join a GPL-3.0 work; CC0 s.4(a) keeps patent and trademark rights unaffected, which the GPL does not change.
SSPL code keeps its own terms, including the s.13 service release duty (reported; check), and GPL-3.0 s.10 bars further restrictions, so SSPL code cannot be relicensed under GPL-3.0.
BUSL code keeps the licensor's terms until its Change Date, so it cannot be relicensed under Apache-2.0 before then; after it, the Change License applies (reported; check the text).
Elastic-2.0 code keeps its own limits, including the managed-service restriction (reported; check the licence text), so it cannot be relicensed under Apache-2.0 as a whole.

The Commons Clause condition travels with the code and cannot be stripped; Neo4j v. PureThink treated it as enforceable against AGPL licensees (reported; check), so Apache-2.0 cannot take the code without the condition.
CC BY-4.0 is a content licence whose attribution condition can be met in a GPL-3.0 work, but it is not written for software; check whether the material is code or content.
The Unlicense dedicates the work to the public domain with no conditions, so it can sit in an MIT-licensed work, with the combined work's own MIT notice.

licenceKit.caveat: A study aid, not legal advice. Duties are summarised; the licence text governs, and the facts of each use matter. Check the version and any added terms on the component itself.

title: Permissive licences
oneLiner: Permissive licences grant broad rights for light conditions: keep the notice, and under Apache-2.0 meet the patent, change and NOTICE terms.
keyPoints: Permissive licences let anyone use, copy, modify and redistribute code, including in closed-source products, on light conditions such as keeping the copyright notice (MIT, full text).
**Conditions:** MIT and ISC require the notice in copies, BSD-2-Clause adds the binary form, and Apache-2.0 adds change-marking and NOTICE-file duties (Apache-2.0 s.4).
**Patents:** The MIT and BSD texts say nothing about patents. Apache-2.0 gives an express patent licence that ends if you sue alleging the Work infringes a patent (Apache-2.0 s.3).
**Names:** BSD-3-Clause bars using contributors' names to endorse derived products without written permission, and Apache-2.0 withholds trademark rights (BSD-3-Clause cl.3; Apache-2.0 s.6).
**No conditions:** 0BSD and MIT-0 impose no notice duty, and Unlicense and CC0-1.0 dedicate code to the public domain. CC0 still leaves patent and trademark rights in place (CC0-1.0 s.4(a)).
**Counsel's job:** Approve only known licence texts, record each one by SPDX identifier, and make sure notices ship inside every app, image and SDK (good practice).

conceptMap.caption: Permissive licences grant broad rights and ask for little back. The conditions that matter are the notice, the names and, under Apache-2.0, the patent and file-change terms.

items.label: Copyright notice
items.note: Must travel with copies

items.label: Express patent licence
items.note: Ends if you sue claiming the Work infringes a patent

items.label: Patent silence
items.note: No patent terms in the text

items.label: Names and marks
items.note: No endorsement or trademark rights

items.label: Changed files and NOTICE
items.note: Mark changes, carry the NOTICE text

items.label: Public domain route
items.note: CC0 keeps patent and mark rights

deepDive.heading: A permission under copyright, not a transfer
deepDive.lede: The author keeps the copyright, and the licence says what others may do with the code.
points: **Copyright base:** Code is protected once it is fixed in a tangible medium (17 U.S.C. § 102(a)). The owner holds the exclusive rights in § 106, and a permissive licence authorises some of them (17 U.S.C. § 106).

**Non-exclusive:** The author can license the same code to others. A [[Non-exclusive licence]] is not a transfer of ownership, so the signed-writing rule for transfers does not apply to it (17 U.S.C. § 204(a)).

**Enforceable terms:** Licences are often accepted by download or in a package. The Seventh Circuit held that shrink-wrap terms are enforceable unless they are objectionable on general contract grounds (ProCD, Inc. v. Zeidenberg, 86 F.3d 1447 (7th Cir. 1996)).

**Ideas stay free:** Copyright never protects an idea, procedure or method of operation (17 U.S.C. § 102(b)). A licence cannot create that protection, so a method in permissive code is a patent question, not a licence question.
**Scope:** Terms that the courts treat as conditions limit the licence itself. Breaking one can be infringement, not only breach of contract (Jacobsen v. Katzer, 535 F.3d 1373 (Fed. Cir. 2008)).

deepDive.heading: Same family, different conditions
deepDive.lede: The short texts look alike, but their conditions differ in ways that matter at release.

visual.caption: Conditions only. Read the full text before approving any variant.

items.label: MIT
items.note: No patent or name terms

items.label: ISC
items.note: Shorter wording, same condition

items.label: BSD-2-Clause
items.note: Binary notice goes in documentation or other materials

items.label: BSD-3-Clause
items.note: No use of contributors' names to promote derived products

items.label: Zlib
items.note: Origin not to be misrepresented; acknowledgement not required

items.label: BSL-1.0
