items.note: Production use limited until the Change Date (reported; check)

items.label: Elastic License 2.0
items.note: Not open source; read its use limits (reported; check)

points: **Definition:** Open source needs free redistribution and no discrimination against any field of endeavour, among ten criteria in the Open Source Definition (OSI Open Source Definition).
**SSPL:** MongoDB adopted the Server Side Public License in October 2018 and withdrew it from OSI review in March 2019; the OSI does not treat it as open source (reported; check).
**BUSL 1.1:** The Business Source License limits production use, and each version converts to a Change License on its Change Date (reported; check).
**Elastic License 2.0:** Elastic moved Elasticsearch and Kibana to SSPL and Elastic License 2.0 in early 2021, so these terms are source-available rather than open (reported; check).
**Commons Clause:** A condition added to an existing open licence, barring 'selling' the software, including hosted or support services that derive substantially from it (reported; check).
**Counsel's test:** Ask whether the licence text, not the vendor's marketing, permits the bank's intended use, and label the component to match (good practice).

deepDive.heading: Business Source License: time-limited restrictions
deepDive.lede: BUSL 1.1 restricts production use for each version until that version converts, unless the Additional Use Grant allows it.
points: **Production use:** Production use is limited unless the licensor's [[Additional Use Grant|Additional Use Grant]] allows it (reported; check). Internal bank use needs a check against that grant.
**Change Date:** Each version converts to a Change License on its Change Date, so the restriction on that version is time-limited (reported; check).
**Maximum period:** The licence sets a maximum of four years after first public release for the Change Date, so read the text for the actual term (reported; check).
**Versions:** Restrictions run version by version, so an older version can become open while a newer one is still restricted (drafting inference).
**HashiCorp example:** Terraform moved from MPL-2.0 to BUSL 1.1 on 10 August 2023, and OpenTofu was forked under the Linux Foundation (reported; check).

deepDive.heading: The Commons Clause and further restrictions
deepDive.lede: Adding a sale ban to AGPL code is contested: the text bars further restrictions, but a reported court holding went the other way on removal (reported; check).

visual.caption: How the dispute was reported to run (reported; check).

items.note: To AGPL-licensed code, barring hosted sales

items.label: Licensee removes the condition
items.note: Then offers the code commercially

items.label: Court reportedly holds the condition enforceable against removal
items.note: Read through the further-restrictions term (reported)

points: **Added terms:** AGPL s.7 limits added terms to listed kinds, such as attribution or trademark requests, and treats other non-permissive terms as [[further restrictions|Further restrictions]] (AGPL-3.0 s.7).
**Bar on restrictions:** A party that conveys the work may not impose further restrictions on the rights the licence grants, such as a fee, royalty or other charge (AGPL-3.0 s.10).
**Court view:** In Neo4j, Inc. v. PureThink LLC the courts reportedly held that a licensor adding the Commons Clause to AGPL code could stop a licensee removing it under that term (reported; check).
**Misdescription:** The courts reportedly also held that calling the fork 'free and open source' was false advertising (reported; check).
**Appeal:** A further appeal, No. 24-5538, is reported pending as at November 2026 (reported; check).

points: **Pattern:** Several vendors moved from permissive, weak copyleft or AGPL-3.0 terms to source-available ones, and some later re-added an open licence as an option (reported; check).
**Forks:** OpenSearch, OpenTofu and Valkey were each forked under a new name after the change, and each fork's own licence and governance then matter (reported; check).
**Why it matters:** A bank that depends on one of these components inherits the vendor's licensing decisions, which it does not control (drafting inference).
**Adding an option:** Adding AGPLv3 as an option does not change the terms of versions already released under the other licence (drafting inference).
**Ownership change:** A change of control can bring a new owner with a different licensing approach, so review the licence after any deal (drafting inference).

deepDive.heading: What a change does to code already held
deepDive.lede: A licence change looks forward, and the rights already granted usually stay.

visual.caption: The terms attach to the version, not to the project name.

items.label: Versions released before the change
items.note: Keep the terms they were released under

items.label: Versions released after the change
items.note: Terms apply from release

items.label: Forks
items.note: Set by the forking group

points: **Versions:** A licence change normally applies to new versions. Code received under the earlier licence keeps those terms (drafting inference; check each licence's own wording).
**Irrevocability:** Under AGPL-3.0 the rights granted are irrevocable, provided the stated conditions are met (AGPL-3.0 s.2).
**Termination risk:** A breach of the AGPL terminates the licensee's rights until they are reinstated, and reinstatement can follow a cure within 30 days of a first notice (AGPL-3.0 s.8).
**Contributors:** A vendor can relicense only code it has rights to, so a change in a project with many outside contributors depends on their agreements (drafting inference).
**Records:** Keep a record of the version and licence of each deployed copy, so the bank can answer for older releases after a change (good practice).

deepDive.heading: Protecting the bank
deepDive.lede: The aim is to know which terms apply and to have a fallback.

visual.caption: A practical sequence for each network-facing component.

items.label: Inventory
items.note: Components, licences, versions and vendors

items.label: Read the terms
items.note: Network, change and use clauses

items.label: Contract
items.note: Notice of changes, exit and transition terms

items.label: Fallback
items.note: An open fork or replacement, tested

deepDive.takeaway: Know which licence applies to each network-facing component, and have a tested way out before the vendor changes its terms.
points: **Inventory:** Record each network-facing component with its licence, version and the vendor's history of licence changes.
**Clauses:** Require notice of any licence change and of any new source-available component, with a right to exit (good practice).
**Fallback:** For each critical source-available component, identify an open fork or replacement and test the migration (good practice).
**Service model:** Check whether the bank's service is offered to others, since that is the trigger for SSPL-style service-source duties (reported; check).
**Escalation:** Send any notice from a copyright holder to counsel at once, as AGPL cure periods run from the first notice (AGPL-3.0 s.8; good practice).

provisions.instrument: GNU Affero General Public License v3.0
provisions.title: Remote network interaction
provisions.summary: If you modify the program, your modified version must prominently offer the users who interact with it remotely through a computer network an opportunity to receive its Corresponding Source, at no charge, from a network server. The section also lets you combine the covered work with a GPL-3.0 work and convey the combined work, with the GPL-3.0 part staying under GPL-3.0 and the AGPL terms still applying to the covered part. GPL-3.0 s.13 adds that the AGPL network clause then applies to the combination as such.
provisions.counselNote: The duty arises from modification plus remote use, and no distribution is needed. Count staff, partners and customers who use a modified service remotely as users, and build the source offer before launch.

provisions.instrument: GNU Affero General Public License v3.0
provisions.title: Definitions: convey and propagate
provisions.summary: Defines 'convey' as any propagation that enables others to make or receive copies, and states that mere interaction with a user through a computer network, with no transfer of a copy, is not conveying. 'Propagate' covers copying, distribution and making available to the public.
provisions.counselNote: A bank can run an AGPL program as a hosted service without conveying it. Only the network duty in s.13 then applies, and only if the bank has modified the program.

provisions.instrument: GNU Affero General Public License v3.0
provisions.title: Basic permissions
provisions.summary: Grants unlimited permission to run the unmodified program. Covered works that the licensee does not convey may be made, run and propagated without conditions, so long as the licence remains in force. Output is covered only if it is itself a covered work.
provisions.counselNote: Running an unmodified AGPL program for staff or customers creates no s.13 duty. Confirm that the deployed copy matches the upstream release, because any patch can change the answer.

provisions.instrument: GNU Affero General Public License v3.0
provisions.title: Additional terms and further restrictions
provisions.summary: Lets the holder of material add certain terms to it, such as requests for attribution, marking of modified versions or trademark limits. All other non-permissive additional terms are treated as further restrictions under s.10. A recipient may remove such a term only where the Program carries a notice that it is governed by the licence along with that term.
provisions.counselNote: On the text, a sale ban added to AGPL code is a further restriction, which a recipient may remove only where the Program carries a notice that it is governed by the licence along with that term. The reported Neo4j holding points the other way on removal, so treat any added sale ban as a live dispute (drafting inference; reported; check).

provisions.instrument: GNU Affero General Public License v3.0
provisions.title: Termination, provisional reinstatement and cure
provisions.summary: Any propagation or modification not expressly allowed is void and terminates the licence. Rights are reinstated provisionally once the violation stops, and permanently if the copyright holder gives no notice within 60 days after the violation stops, or if the licensee cures within 30 days of a first notice.
provisions.counselNote: A missed notice can put the bank's rights in a component at risk. Route any notice from a copyright holder to counsel on receipt and log the date, because the cure period runs from the first notice.

provisions.instrument: GNU Affero General Public License v3.0
provisions.title: Automatic licensing and no further restrictions
provisions.summary: Each recipient of a conveyed covered work receives a licence from the original licensors. The party conveying the work may not impose further restrictions on the rights granted, such as a licence fee or royalty, and may not start litigation alleging that a patent claim is infringed by the program.
provisions.counselNote: The text bars further restrictions, while the reported Neo4j holding went the other way on removal, so review any sale ban a vendor adds before the bank accepts the code (drafting inference; reported; check).

provisions.title: Exclusive rights in copyrighted works
provisions.summary: Gives the copyright owner the exclusive rights to reproduce the work, to prepare derivative works, to distribute copies, and to perform or display the work publicly, subject to the sections that follow.
provisions.counselNote: Making a modified version is preparing a derivative work, so the bank needs a licence for it. The licence's terms then set what the bank may do and what it must give back.

provisions.ref: N.D. Cal.; appeal No. 24-5538 (reported; check the citation)
provisions.title: Commons Clause added to AGPL code
provisions.summary: As reported, the courts held that a licensor adding the Commons Clause to AGPL-licensed code could stop a licensee removing it under the AGPL's further-restrictions term, and that calling the fork 'free and open source' was false advertising. A further appeal is reported pending as at November 2026.
provisions.counselNote: This is the main reported authority on layering a sale ban onto AGPL code. Check the reported holding and any appellate outcome before relying on it in a vendor negotiation.

provisions.title: Offering the program as a service
provisions.summary: As reported, offering the program as a service requires releasing the 'Service Source Code', meaning the program and all software used to make the service available. The OSI does not treat SSPL as open source.
provisions.counselNote: A service built on SSPL code can pull the surrounding stack into scope. Ask engineering which software makes a hosted service available before the bank offers one to others. Read the full licence before relying on this summary.

provisions.title: Production limits and Change Date
provisions.summary: As reported, the licence is source-available. Production use is limited unless the licensor's Additional Use Grant permits it. Each version converts to a Change License on its Change Date, with the licence setting a maximum of four years after first public release.
provisions.counselNote: Read the Additional Use Grant for the bank's intended use, and record each version's Change Date in the component register. The licensor sets the grant, so the bank should not assume it covers internal platforms.

provisions.title: Ban on selling the software
provisions.summary: As reported, the 2018 condition is added to an existing open licence and bars 'selling' the software, including hosting or support services whose value derives entirely or substantially from it.
provisions.counselNote: Ask vendors whether any component they supply carries the condition, since it limits the hosted or support services they may offer on that code.

provisions.instrument: The Open Source Definition (Open Source Initiative)
provisions.title: Ten criteria for open source
provisions.summary: Lists ten criteria, including free redistribution, access to source code, no discrimination against persons, groups or fields of endeavour, and a licence that is not specific to a product and does not restrict other software. On the OSI's view, licences that restrict some fields of use do not qualify (a view, not law).
provisions.counselNote: Use the definition to test a vendor's claim of open source. Treat any component that fails it as source-available in policy, scanning and board reporting.

provisions.instrument: Interagency Guidance on Third-Party Relationships: Risk Management (Federal Reserve, FDIC, OCC)
provisions.title: Life-cycle risk management for third parties
provisions.summary: Sets out risk management across the life cycle of third-party relationships, from planning and due diligence through contract, monitoring and termination. It is technology-neutral and does not deal with open source as such. The agencies expect banks to manage each stage of a third-party relationship.
provisions.counselNote: A vendor's relicensing changes the relationship and should trigger reassessment, contract review and exit planning. Log it as a third-party event in the risk register (drafting inference).

checklist: **Inventory network-facing software:** List every component that users reach over a network, including online banking, APIs, admin consoles and partner portals, with its licence and version.
**Classify each licence:** Show open source, network copyleft and source-available components separately in policy, scanning and board reporting.
**Track modifications:** Keep a patch record against the upstream release tag for every AGPL component, so the bank knows when s.13 applies.
**Build the source offer before launch:** For a modified AGPL service, publish a prominent, free link to the Corresponding Source of the deployed version, approved by counsel.
**Read BUSL terms for the intended use:** Confirm that the Additional Use Grant covers the bank's production use, and record each version's Change Date.
**Pin versions and watch for licence changes:** Check licence files at every upgrade, and gate builds on any new or changed licence.
**Write vendor notice clauses:** Require notice of any licence change or new source-available component, with a right to exit and a transition period.
**Prepare a fork or exit plan:** For each critical source-available component, name an open alternative and test the migration.
**Escalate copyright-holder notices at once:** Send any notice of an AGPL violation to counsel on receipt, because cure periods run from the first notice.
itAngle: **Scanner blind spots:** Licence scanners may report source-available terms as open source. Check the licence file and the declared licence field together, and review any non-OSI licence by hand.

**Patch-level modification:** A patched container image, a forked module or a local change to a vendored AGPL library is a modified version. Diff against the upstream tag in CI so the source offer tracks what actually runs.

**Source offer mechanics:** Place the offer where remote users can see it, such as a footer link in a web console, and point it to the exact commit for the deployed version (drafting inference from AGPL-3.0 s.13).
**Infrastructure as code:** Provider and module versions can move to a new licence on upgrade, so pin versions and read the licence before each bump.

**Service boundaries:** Under SSPL-style terms, the software that makes a service available may include the orchestration, monitoring and deployment code around the database (reported; check). Map that stack when the component is first adopted.
virtualBankNotes: **Third-party life cycle:** A vendor's move to source-available terms changes the risk of the relationship. The interagency guidance (88 Fed. Reg. 37920) expects banks to reassess third-party relationships through their life cycle, so log the change as a trigger.
**Continuity:** A critical service built on a source-available component needs a documented fallback and a tested exit, so a licence change does not become an outage risk (good practice).

**NYDFS overlay:** Where the bank is covered by the NYDFS Cybersecurity Regulation (23 NYCRR Part 500), its third-party service provider policy under section 500.11 should cover licence changes in its monitoring (good practice).

**Examiner questions:** Examiners may ask which components the bank runs under non-OSI terms and who approved them. Keep the register and approvals retrievable (reported; check the FFIEC Development, Acquisition and Maintenance booklet).

**Vendor-built services:** When a vendor offers a managed service on source-available code, the vendor's licence limits what it may offer. The contract should say who carries the risk if those limits change (good practice).
productNotes: **Raise a change to an AGPL service at design time:** A modified AGPL-3.0 program that remote users reach must offer them its source, even though nothing is distributed (AGPL-3.0 s.13). Any customisation of such a component starts that duty, so design reviews should flag it.

**Running it unchanged is not the trigger:** Running an unmodified AGPL-3.0 program over a network triggers no source duty, but a patch or fork does (AGPL-3.0 s.2; AGPL-3.0 s.13). Keep a record of each patch against the upstream release.

**Ask about the vendor's licence history:** Several database and infrastructure vendors moved to source-available terms between 2018 and 2025 (reported; check). Ask for the licence history before a component is chosen, and write in a notice-of-change clause with a right to exit (good practice).

**Do not call source-available code open source:** Product copy, partner decks and board papers should not describe SSPL, BUSL or Elastic License 2.0 code as open source, since those licences restrict use (reported; check).
pitfalls: **Calling it open source:** Filing source-available components as open source in policy, scanner output or board papers.
**Ignoring remote staff:** Assuming AGPL duties reach only customers, and missing modified internal portals and partner tools that users reach over a network.
**Assuming relicensing reaches old code:** Treating a licence change as removing rights already granted, when the terms of earlier releases usually stay (drafting inference).
**Trusting a fork:** Assuming a community fork is clear of obligations without reading its licence, its trademark position and its governance.
**Missing cure periods:** Letting a copyright holder's notice sit, when the AGPL-3.0 s.8 cure period runs from the first notice.
**Accepting added terms:** Taking AGPL code from a vendor that has added a sale ban, without checking it against AGPL-3.0 s.7 and s.10.

points: **Licence text controls:** there is no EU-level ruling on AGPL-3.0 s.13 or on source-available terms, so the licence text and national contract and copyright law govern (drafting inference).

**Reverse engineering limits:** a licence cannot stop a lawful user from decompiling for interoperability or from observing, studying or testing a program (Directive 2009/24/EC, Arts. 5(3), 6, 8), which bears on hosted-service terms.
**Broadly the same:** AGPL-3.0 s.13 operates as a licence condition on copyright, and programs are literary works (CDPA 1988 s.3(1)(b)), so the US analysis carries over.
**Lawful-user rights:** observe-study-test, back-up and decompilation rights (CDPA 1988 ss.50A-50C) should be checked against any source-available licence restriction on reverse engineering.

**Broadly the same:** no Canadian decision on AGPL-3.0 s.13 or source-available terms is identified, and Canada has no general open source statute, so licences are enforced as contracts or through copyright (drafting inference).

**Interoperability exceptions:** adaptation for compatibility and reproduction for interoperability are permitted (Copyright Act ss.30.6, 30.61), and s.41.12 excepts interoperability from the anti-circumvention rules.

hongKong.summary: Under Hong Kong copyright, making a work available online so that the public can access it at a time and place they choose is a restricted act, whether or not anyone downloads a copy. No Hong Kong decision on the AGPL network clause or on source-available terms is reported (reported; check), so the licence text and the vendor contract decide most questions.
keyPoints: **Making available is restricted:** Making a work available online so that the public may access it is a restricted act, whether or not anyone downloads a copy (Cap. 528 ss.22(1)(fa), 28A(2)(c), 28A(3)). Whether letting users interact with a hosted program makes the program itself available is not settled (drafting inference).
**Host determines content:** A host communicates a work when it determines the content of the communication. Clicking a link or providing mere facilities does not (Cap. 528 s.28A(4)-(6)).
**Modified versions:** Communicating an adaptation is restricted too, separately from the AGPL s.13 duty (Cap. 528 s.29(2); AGPL-3.0 s.13).

**AGPL trigger:** Section 13 needs a modified program that remote users interact with, and then an offer of Corresponding Source, with no distribution needed (AGPL-3.0 s.13). No Hong Kong decision applies it (reported; check).
**Source-available terms:** SSPL, BUSL and similar licences are not open source, and no Hong Kong decision enforcing them is reported (reported; check).

sections.heading: Making a program available over a network
sections.lede: Under Hong Kong copyright the question is who communicates the work to the public, not where the server sits.
points: **Communication:** Electronic communication of a work to the public is restricted, and it includes making the work available so that members of the public can access it from a place and at a time they choose (Cap. 528 s.28A(1)-(3)).
**Who communicates:** The person who determines the content of the communication is the one who communicates it. A party that only provides facilities does not (Cap. 528 s.28A(4)-(5)).
**Direct access:** Facilities primarily designed for direct access to a work without permission are not mere facilities (Cap. 528 s.28A(6)).
**Private access:** Access limited to staff or named partners may not amount to making the work available to the public, but the bank should not assume that without advice (drafting inference).
sections.takeaway: Ask who controls what the service delivers and who can reach it before deciding whether the network analysis applies.

sections.heading: Modified programs and the AGPL source offer
sections.lede: Changing the code before running it for remote users adds a copyright act and a licence duty.
points: **Adaptation over a network:** Doing a s.28A act in relation to an adaptation is restricted, whether or not the adaptation was recorded at that time (Cap. 528 s.29(2)).
**Program adaptation:** Porting a service into another computer language or code is a translation, which counts as an adaptation of a program (Cap. 528 s.29(3)(b), (4)).
**Source offer:** A modified version must prominently offer its remote users the opportunity to receive its Corresponding Source, at no charge, from a network server (AGPL-3.0 s.13).
**Users:** The offer is not confined to outside customers, so staff or partners who use a modified service remotely are probably users too (drafting inference).

**Lawful use:** A licensed user may adapt a program where necessary for lawful use (Cap. 528 s.61(1)-(2)), so a source-available term that bars modification of a hosted program should be read against that right (drafting inference).
sections.takeaway: Before modifying an AGPL service, decide who the remote users are and how the source offer will be made.

sections.heading: Source-available terms and later changes
sections.lede: A vendor can change the terms for later versions, and the bank's rights follow the licence that came with each copy.
points: **Enforcement:** Source-available terms bind the bank as a contract and as a copyright licence. A breach of a licence term founds copyright remedies only where the act done falls outside the licence, such as copying or adapting beyond it (Cap. 528 s.107(1)-(2); drafting inference).
**Versions:** A licence change normally applies to later versions, so code already received keeps the earlier terms (drafting inference; read each licence's wording).

**Reverse engineering:** Hong Kong has no express decompilation exception, so a term that bars reverse engineering may still be overridden by s.61 where copying or adapting is necessary for lawful use, and whether a licence can cut that back is a question of construction; the circumvention exception in s.273D is narrow (Cap. 528 s.273D(1); drafting inference).
**Service model:** Whether the bank's service is offered to others matters under some source-available terms, such as SSPL's service-source duties (reported; check).
sections.takeaway: Know which licence governs each network-facing version, and secure notice and exit rights in the vendor contract.

provisions.title: Communication to the public
provisions.summary: Electronic communication of a work to the public is restricted, including making it available online so that the public can access it from a place and at a time they choose. A host communicates a work when it determines the content, while links and mere facilities do not.
provisions.counselNote: Code sent to users' browsers or devices is made available to them, but whether remote use of a hosted program's functions makes the program itself available is not settled, so the bank's hosting terms need checking (drafting inference).

provisions.title: Acts done in relation to an adaptation
provisions.summary: Doing an act in s.23, 24, 25, 27 or 28A, or making an adaptation, in relation to an adaptation of the work is also a restricted act. It does not matter whether the adaptation was recorded when the act is done.
provisions.counselNote: Sending or making available a modified program over a network is restricted here, while the AGPL duty can arise from remote interaction alone, so both analyses are needed.

provisions.title: Lawful user copying and adapting
provisions.summary: A lawful user may copy or adapt a program where that is necessary for lawful use, including to correct errors. The section has no express words allowing an agreement to exclude it.
provisions.counselNote: A user licensed to run a hosted program may adapt it where necessary for lawful use, which bears directly on source-available terms that restrict modification.

provisions.title: Interference with rights management information
provisions.summary: Removing or altering electronic rights management information is actionable only where the defendant knows or has reason to believe that the act induces, enables, facilitates or conceals an infringement. A notice that identifies the work, author or owner can be such information.
provisions.counselNote: Author, copyright and licence notices in AGPL code can be rights management information (s.274(3)(a)-(b)), so the bank's build and deployment should keep them intact (drafting inference).

bankNotes: **Vendor contracts:** The HKMA's outsourcing guideline (SA-2) expects written agreements with vendors, covering confidentiality and HKMA access. Guidance is not law, but a licence-change clause belongs alongside those terms (good practice).

**Hosted personal data:** A bank that engages a data processor must adopt contractual or other means to prevent unauthorised access to the personal data it transfers (Cap. 486 Sch. 1, DPP 4(2)). A source-available host's terms must still meet that test (drafting inference).

glossary.definition: Copyleft that applies when users interact with a modified program over a network, not only when copies are distributed. The AGPL-3.0 is the main example (AGPL-3.0 s.13).
All the source code needed to generate, install, run and modify an object-code work, including the scripts that control those activities (AGPL-3.0 s.1).
Propagation that enables others to make or receive copies. Mere interaction with a user through a computer network is not conveying (AGPL-3.0 s.0).

Terms that a licensee may not add to the rights a licence grants. The AGPL treats most non-permissive additional terms as further restrictions, which s.10 bars and s.7 lets a recipient remove (AGPL-3.0 s.7, s.10).
Software whose source code can be read, but whose use, copying or redistribution is limited. It is not open source under the OSI's definition.
Under the SSPL, the program and all software used to make a service available to others, which must be released when the program is offered as a service (reported; check).
MongoDB's 2018 source-available licence. The OSI does not treat it as open source, and it extends service-source duties to hosted services (reported; check).
A source-available licence that limits production use unless the Additional Use Grant allows it, and converts each version to a Change License on its Change Date (reported; check).
The licensor's permission, set in a BUSL 1.1 licence, to use the software in production beyond the default limit (reported; check).
The date on which a BUSL 1.1 version converts to its Change License, ending its production limits (reported; check).
A licence condition, from 2018, that bars selling the software, including hosted or support services whose value derives substantially from it (reported; check).
Elastic's source-available licence, used alongside SSPL for Elasticsearch and Kibana from early 2021. It is not open source (reported; check).
Making a work available by wire or wireless means so that members of the public can access it from a place and at a time they choose. It is a restricted act (Cap. 528 s.28A(3)).

title: Using open source: policy, SBOMs and compliance
oneLiner: Open source use is an inventory problem first: know what is in each product, under which licence, and who approved it.
keyPoints: Using open source is a licensing decision for every component, so the bank needs a record of what it uses, how it uses it and which licence applies.

**Policy tiers:** Approval should scale with risk. Permissive components that stay internal pass a light check, while copyleft, network copyleft and source-available code goes to counsel (good practice).

**SBOMs:** A [[SBOM|Software bill of materials]] lists the components in a product. Executive Order 14028 (2021) pushed SBOMs for software sold to the federal government, and NTIA's minimum elements set the baseline data fields.

**Bank expectations:** Regulators expect third-party and secure development controls, citing interagency guidance and the FFIEC booklets. NYDFS regulation mandates written secure development procedures (23 NYCRR 500.8).
**Supply chain:** Log4Shell (2021) and the xz Utils backdoor (2024) showed that one shared component can reach many products, so scanning must cover indirect dependencies.
**Records:** Keep the approval, the licence texts and the attribution and source-offer files with each release, so the bank can show what it shipped and why (good practice).

deepDive.heading: Policy and approval tiers
deepDive.lede: A policy that applies one process to every component will be bypassed. Tier by licence, and by how the bank uses the code.

visual.caption: Tiers follow the licence family and the use. The same component can pass in one place and need review in another.

items.label: Tier 1: permissive, internal
items.note: MIT, BSD or Apache-2.0 code kept inside the bank

items.label: Tier 2: permissive, shipped
items.note: Keep licence texts and notices with each product

items.label: Tier 3: copyleft
items.note: GPL, LGPL, MPL or EPL code that is distributed

items.label: Tier 4: network or source-available
items.note: AGPL, SSPL, BUSL or Elastic code, or any unlicensed code

points: **Use drives the duty:** Internal use, shipping, publishing, network use and contractor use each trigger different licence terms, so the test is the use, not the name of the component.

**Permissive code:** Apache-2.0 requires recipients to get the licence and the bank to keep notices when it redistributes the work (Apache-2.0 s.4). MIT needs the notice in all copies (MIT, full text).
**Copyleft code:** Distributing GPL-2.0 object code requires source or a written offer (GPL-2.0 s.3), so shipped copyleft components go to counsel and the product owner.
**Network code:** A modified AGPL-3.0 program must offer its source to users who interact with it over a network (AGPL-3.0 s.13). Source-available licences are not open source (reported; check).
**No licence:** Code with no licence keeps its copyright, so the bank needs the owner's permission to copy or change it (17 U.S.C. § 106).

deepDive.heading: Programme office and intake
deepDive.lede: The programme office turns the policy into a queue that engineers will actually use.

visual.caption: Intake to release. Each step leaves a record that the next step relies on (good practice).

items.label: Intake
items.note: Component, version, use, product and owner recorded

items.label: Licence and security check
items.note: Licence identifier, known vulnerabilities and pinned version

items.label: Approval
items.note: The tier sets who signs off, and on what conditions

items.label: Build and inventory
items.note: SBOM generated from the build, not typed by hand

items.label: Release
items.note: Notices, source offers and the SBOM kept with the version

items.label: Monitor
items.note: New advisories or licence changes reopen the review

points: **Programme office:** A small group owns the policy, the approved-component list and the exceptions, and reports to the bank's technology and legal committees (good practice).
**Intake before merge:** Engineers record the component, version, use, product and owner before the code is merged, not after release (good practice).
**Approval by tier:** Counsel reviews copyleft, network and source-available components, and security reviews known vulnerabilities in any tier (good practice).
**Exceptions:** Each exception needs a written reason, an owner and an expiry date, so a temporary approval does not become permanent (good practice).
**Approved list:** Keep a list of approved components and versions that the build can check against (good practice).
deepDive.takeaway: A short intake that engineers complete beats a long policy that they route around.

deepDive.heading: Inventory, SBOMs and scanning
deepDive.lede: An SBOM answers the question 'what is in this product?', and it misleads once it goes stale.

visual.caption: NTIA's 2021 [[minimum elements|Minimum elements]] for an SBOM. CISA published a draft update in 2025, and whether a final version has issued is reported as unconfirmed (reported; check).

items.label: Data fields
items.note: Plus other unique identifiers, dependency relationships, the SBOM author and a timestamp

items.label: Automation support
items.note: Machine-readable formats that ties the SBOM to the build

items.label: Practices and processes
items.note: How the SBOM is produced, updated and shared with customers

points: **Why it matters:** Executive Order 14028 (12 May 2021) directed software supply-chain measures, including SBOMs for software sold to the federal government.
**Standard licence identifiers:** SPDX is ISO/IEC 5962:2021, so licence identifiers in an SBOM can be checked against a published list (SPDX ISO/IEC 5962:2021).
**Scanning:** Run licence and vulnerability scans in the build and at release, and record each result against the component version (good practice).
**Vendor SBOMs:** Ask vendors for an SBOM that matches the version the bank receives, not an older one, and check that it covers their own third-party components (good practice).

items.label: FFIEC development booklet
items.note: Covers third-party and open source components (reported; check)

items.label: PCI DSS requirement 6.3.2
items.note: Inventory of bespoke software and third-party components (reported)

items.label: Executive Order 14306
items.note: Removed the validated attestation requirement (reported)

points: **Federal attestations:** Executive Order 14306 amended Executive Order 14144 (January 2025) and removed its validated attestation requirement (reported; check). OMB Memorandum M-26-05 (January 2026) is reported to have rescinded M-22-18 and M-23-16 (reported; check).

**Secure development:** NIST SP 800-218, the Secure Software Development Framework (version 1.1, February 2022), is a common reference for secure development questions. A draft revision was published for comment in December 2025 (reported).

**Third parties:** The interagency guidance, 88 Fed. Reg. 37920 (9 June 2023), covers the whole life cycle of third-party relationships. It is technology-neutral and does not single out open source, but the vendors that support or host open source fall within it (drafting inference).

**Applications:** NYDFS requires written procedures for secure development of in-house applications and for assessing externally developed ones (23 NYCRR 500.8). Section 500.11 requires a policy on third-party service providers.

deepDive.heading: Maintainers and supply-chain risk
deepDive.lede: A clean licence does not make a component safe.
points: **Log4Shell:** The flaw CVE-2021-44228 was disclosed on 9 December 2021. A single widely reused library reached products whose teams had never chosen it directly (drafting inference).

**xz Utils:** A backdoor in versions 5.6.0 and 5.6.1 (CVE-2024-3094) was disclosed on 29 March 2024. Maintainers and project governance are therefore a risk factor at intake, not only the code (good practice).
**Indirect dependencies:** Scanning must reach transitive dependencies, base images and framework packages, because the bank may ship a component it never chose (good practice).
**Maintenance:** Track whether a component is still maintained, and plan a replacement or a fork before a project goes quiet (good practice).
**Licence change:** An upstream licence change can make a pinned version the last one the bank may use, which affects releases already shipped (good practice).

deepDive.heading: Attribution, notices and source offers
deepDive.lede: Notices are the cheapest compliance duty, and the easiest to lose in a build.
points: **Copyright management information:** Licence headers can be copyright management information (17 U.S.C. § 1202(c)(6)). Intentionally removing or altering them, knowing that it will induce, enable, facilitate or conceal infringement, is prohibited (§ 1202(b)). Reasonable grounds to know suffice only for civil claims.
**Apache-2.0 notices:** Recipients get a copy of the licence, modified files carry a notice, and attribution notices from any NOTICE file travel with the derivative work (Apache-2.0 s.4).

**Written offers:** GPL-2.0 allows distribution with a [[written offer|Written offer]] valid for at least three years (GPL-2.0 s.3). For physical products, GPL-3.0 ties the written offer to spare parts or customer support for the product model (GPL-3.0 s.6(b)).
**Release bundle:** Keep the notice bundle, the source offer and the SBOM with each shipped version, so a question about a past release can be answered (good practice).

deepDive.heading: Export controls and sanctions
deepDive.lede: Publishing code raises export questions as well as licensing ones.
points: **Published code:** Software that is published is outside the Export Administration Regulations (15 C.F.R. § 734.3(b)(3), § 734.7) (reported; check the eCFR).

**Encryption:** Since a rule of 29 March 2021, publicly available encryption source code needs a notification only where it implements non-standard cryptography (15 C.F.R. § 742.15(b)) (reported; check).
**Bank code:** Any cryptography the bank builds into code it publishes deserves an export review before release (good practice).

**Sanctions:** GitHub restricted accounts in sanctioned regions in 2019, and announced an OFAC licence for developers in Iran in January 2021 (reported). Screen contributors and vendors under the bank's sanctions programme (good practice).

provisions.title: Integrity of copyright management information
provisions.summary: Bars intentionally removing or altering copyright management information without authority, where the person knows that this will induce, enable, facilitate or conceal infringement, or, for civil remedies, has reasonable grounds to know (§ 1202(b)). Copyright management information includes the title, the author, the owner and the terms and conditions for use (§ 1202(c)).
provisions.counselNote: Licence headers and notices in shipped code can be copyright management information. A build step that strips them needs a review before it runs in a release pipeline.

provisions.title: Redistribution
provisions.summary: Lets recipients reproduce and distribute the work, modified or not, in source or object form. The conditions are that recipients get a copy of the licence, modified files carry notices that they were changed, copyright and attribution notices are kept, and any NOTICE file's attribution notices appear in at least one listed place.
provisions.counselNote: These are the duties the bank meets when it ships an app, SDK or container that contains Apache-2.0 code. The notice duties are easy to miss in a release, so the release checklist should test them.

provisions.title: Permission notice and warranty disclaimer
provisions.summary: Grants broad permission to use, copy, modify, merge, publish, distribute, sublicense and sell the software. The copyright notice and permission notice must be included in all copies or substantial portions, and the software is provided as is, without warranty.
provisions.counselNote: The conditions are light, but the notice duty applies to every copy, including copies inside container images and app bundles. The disclaimer means the bank has no warranty from the author.

provisions.title: Application security
provisions.summary: Requires written procedures for the secure development of in-house applications, and for evaluating, assessing or testing the security of externally developed applications.
provisions.counselNote: Open source components sit between these two limbs, so counsel should document how the procedure covers them (drafting inference). Examiners look for the procedure and for evidence that it is followed.

provisions.title: Third-party service provider security policy
provisions.summary: Requires a written policy on the security of third-party service providers, which the covered entity applies to vendors that access its systems or data.
provisions.counselNote: Commercial support vendors and hosted services built on open source are third-party service providers (drafting inference). Their contracts should carry the security duties the policy sets (good practice).

provisions.instrument: Federal Reserve, FDIC and OCC: Interagency Guidance on Third-Party Relationships: Risk Management
provisions.title: Risk management across the life cycle of third-party relationships
provisions.summary: Sets out risk management across the whole life cycle of third-party relationships, replacing the agencies' earlier guidance. It is technology-neutral and does not deal with open source as such. The agencies have proposed a revision in 2026 (reported; check).
provisions.counselNote: An open source project is usually not a business arrangement, but the vendor that supports, patches or hosts it is. Map those vendors into the third-party inventory (drafting inference).

provisions.instrument: FFIEC IT Examination Handbook: Development, Acquisition, and Maintenance booklet
provisions.title: Software development, acquisition and supply-chain risk
provisions.summary: Covers software development, acquisition and supply-chain risk, including third-party and open source components. It was transmitted by OCC Bulletin 2024-26 and SR 24-6 (reported; check the booklet's wording).
provisions.counselNote: Examiners use the booklet to test how the bank governs software it builds and buys. An open source inventory that is kept current lets the bank answer those questions quickly (good practice).

provisions.title: Secure Software Development Framework (SSDF)
provisions.summary: Sets out practices for secure software development, from organisational preparation through to the response to vulnerabilities. A draft revision (version 1.2) was published for comment in December 2025 (reported).
provisions.counselNote: Vendors and open source projects are often asked to show SSDF-aligned practices, which gives the bank a common baseline for due diligence (good practice).

provisions.title: Software supply-chain measures and SBOMs
provisions.summary: Directed measures to improve the security of the software supply chain, including SBOMs for software sold to the federal government.
provisions.counselNote: It is an executive order for federal buyers, not a rule for banks, but it set much of the SBOM vocabulary that vendors now use in bank due diligence (drafting inference).

provisions.instrument: NTIA, The Minimum Elements for a Software Bill of Materials (SBOM)
provisions.title: Minimum elements for an SBOM
provisions.summary: Sets data fields (supplier, component name, version, other unique identifiers, dependency relationship, author of the SBOM data and timestamp), automation support (SPDX, CycloneDX and SWID tags), and practices and processes for producing and sharing SBOMs.
provisions.counselNote: This is the baseline the bank can ask vendors to meet in due diligence. CISA's 2025 draft update should be checked before it is cited as current (reported; check).

provisions.title: Licence compliance programmes
provisions.summary: The international standard for open source licence compliance programmes. It gives a company a benchmark against which to check its own programme.
provisions.counselNote: Using OpenChain as the benchmark for the programme office gives the bank a recognised yardstick when it sets policy, and when it asks vendors about their own programmes (good practice).

provisions.instrument: PCI Security Standards Council, PCI DSS v4.0.1
provisions.title: Inventory of bespoke and custom software and third-party components
provisions.summary: Requires an inventory of bespoke and custom software and of the third-party components in it. The requirement has been mandatory since 31 March 2025 (reported; check).
provisions.counselNote: Card issuers and acquirers answer to this requirement for cardholder data environments. An SBOM kept current from the build is the natural evidence for it (drafting inference).

provisions.title: Notification for publicly available encryption source code
provisions.summary: Since a rule of 29 March 2021, publicly available encryption source code needs a notification to BIS and the NSA only where it implements non-standard cryptography. Published software is outside the EAR (§§ 734.3(b)(3), 734.7) (reported; check the eCFR).
provisions.counselNote: A bank that publishes an SDK or sample code with custom cryptography should run this check before release. The regulation text should be read in full before any release decision relies on it.

checklist: **Set the tiers:** Write the approval tiers by licence family and by use, and publish them to every engineering team (good practice).
**Keep an inventory:** Record each component, version, licence, product and owner, and generate the list from the build (PCI DSS requirement 6.3.2; good practice).
**Gate new dependencies:** Block a new dependency in the pipeline until its intake record and tier approval exist (good practice).
**Scan every release:** Check licences and known vulnerabilities for each release, including indirect dependencies and base images (good practice).
**Ship the notices:** Include licence texts, NOTICE files and copyright notices in each app, SDK and container image (Apache-2.0 s.4; MIT, full text).

**Hold the source offers:** Keep written source offers for at least three years after each distribution (GPL-2.0 s.3(b)). For GPL-3.0 object code in a physical product, the offer must also run for as long as spare parts or customer support are offered (GPL-3.0 s.6(b)).
**Vet vendors:** Ask vendors for their SBOM and open source policy in due diligence, and map them into the third-party inventory (88 Fed. Reg. 37920).
**Set exception rules:** Require a written reason, an owner and an expiry date for every exception, and review open exceptions each quarter (good practice).
**Keep the release record:** Retain approvals, SBOMs, scan results and notice bundles with each release for as long as the product is supported (good practice).
**Review before publishing:** Check published code for encryption, secrets and internal hostnames before release, and confirm any notification under 15 C.F.R. § 742.15(b) (reported; check).
itAngle: **Pipeline gates:** Put licence and vulnerability checks in CI so that a new dependency or a changed licence fails the build until the approval record exists (good practice).
**Generated SBOMs:** Produce the SBOM from the build in SPDX or CycloneDX, so each shipped image or binary carries its own list of components (NTIA minimum elements; SPDX ISO/IEC 5962:2021).
**Pinned versions:** Commit lockfiles and pin versions, so that the SBOM, the scan and the approval all describe the code that actually ships (good practice).
**Transitive reach:** Scan the whole dependency graph, including base images and build-time packages, because a component the team never chose can still reach production (good practice).
**Notice automation:** Generate the third-party notices from the SBOM, and check that they land in each app bundle, container image and SDK package (Apache-2.0 s.4; good practice).
virtualBankNotes: **Third-party inventory:** Open source components may not be vendors, but the companies that support, host or patch them belong in the third-party inventory under the interagency guidance (88 Fed. Reg. 37920; drafting inference).

**NYDFS scope:** A NYDFS-regulated bank or fintech must keep written secure development procedures for in-house applications and an assessment process for externally developed ones (23 NYCRR 500.8), with its third-party policy under 500.11.
**Examiner requests:** Keep the inventory, approval records and SBOMs in a form examiners can read, because the FFIEC booklet tests how software is governed (reported; check).

**Sanctions and access:** Contributors and vendors may be located in sanctioned regions. Screen them under the bank's sanctions programme (good practice), since a platform may restrict developers there (reported).

**Federal rules:** Federal attestation duties for vendors have been rolled back (reported; check), but banks still ask vendors for the same secure development evidence in their own due diligence (good practice).
productNotes: **Send the component before the merge:** Tell counsel the component, its version, how the product uses it and whether it ships to customers or runs as a service before the code is merged, because the use decides the approval tier (good practice).

**Plan for notices at release:** Apache-2.0 and MIT code shipped in an app, SDK or container needs its licence text and notices with each copy, so product should put the notices into every release, in a NOTICE file or in a display where such notices normally appear (Apache-2.0 s.4(d); MIT, full text).

**Flag any modified network service early:** A modified AGPL-3.0 program that remote users interact with must offer its source to them, so tell counsel before engineers change an AGPL component behind a customer-facing feature (AGPL-3.0 s.13).

**Do not copy code with no licence:** Code published with no licence keeps its copyright, so a designer, engineer or marketer cannot paste it into a feature without the owner's permission (17 U.S.C. § 106).
pitfalls: **Inventory gaps:** Relying on a manually kept list, which misses indirect dependencies and the components that come in through base images.
**Approval after release:** Letting a component ship and approving it afterwards, so the tier decision is made without the product context.
**Silent exceptions:** Granting exceptions without an owner or an expiry date, so temporary approvals become permanent.
**Stripped notices:** Build steps that drop licence headers or NOTICE files, creating breach risk under the licence and, if done knowingly, under 17 U.S.C. § 1202(b).
**Trusting a licence label:** Treating the licence identifier as the whole story, and missing the maintenance, governance and licence-change history of the project.
**Stale vendor SBOMs:** Accepting a vendor SBOM produced once and never refreshed, so that it no longer describes the version the bank runs (good practice).

points: **Cyber Resilience Act reporting:** manufacturers must report actively exploited vulnerabilities from 11 September 2026, with most obligations from 11 December 2027 (Regulation (EU) 2024/2847).

**Open source outside commerce:** free and open-source software not supplied in a commercial activity is outside the Cyber Resilience Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/2847), and the Product Liability Directive excludes it on the same basis (Directive (EU) 2024/2853).
**Same use analysis:** programs are literary works (CDPA 1988 s.3(1)(b)), so intake and approval steps carry over from the US.

**Lawful-user checks:** back-up, decompilation and observe-study-test rights (CDPA 1988 ss.50A-50BA) override any licence term, which is void so far as it would prohibit or restrict them (CDPA 1988 s.296A).

**Broadly the same:** no Canadian statute requires SBOMs or licence scanning; for a bank, OSFI's third-party and technology risk guidelines (B-10 and B-13) may also bear on supply-chain expectations (drafting inference; check the current guideline text).
**User exceptions:** adaptation for compatibility and back-up copies (Copyright Act s.30.6) and interoperability reproduction (s.30.61) bear on what a review must allow for.

hongKong.summary: Hong Kong makes it a criminal offence to possess an infringing copy of a computer program, without the owner's licence, for use in a trade or business (Cap. 528 s.118(2A)-(2B)). Unlike the US treatment in this stage, which turns mainly on what the bank ships, this reaches unlicensed internal use, so the bank's own installed software is the main exposure (drafting inference). A copy made within the lawful-user rules is not an infringing copy at all, so it falls outside the offence (Cap. 528 ss.35(2), 60-61; drafting inference).
keyPoints: **Business use offence:** Possessing an infringing copy of a program, without the owner's licence, for the purpose of or in the course of a trade or business, with a view to its use in that business, is a criminal offence (Cap. 528 s.118(2A)-(2B)).
**Penalty:** On indictment the fine is level 5 for each infringing copy, and the term of imprisonment is up to four years (Cap. 528 s.119(1)).

**Officers:** A director, manager or similar officer commits the offence too where the company's offence was committed with their consent or connivance, or is attributable to them (Cap. 528 s.125(1)).

**Defences:** The accused has a defence if they prove they did not know and had no reason to believe the copy was infringing (Cap. 528 s.118(3)). An employee given the copy by the employer for use at work also has a defence, unless they could make or influence the decision to acquire, use or remove it (Cap. 528 s.118(3A)-(3B)).
**Click acceptance:** An offer and its acceptance may be expressed by electronic records, so a licence accepted by click can bind the bank (Cap. 553 s.17(1)-(2)).

sections.heading: Business use is the trigger
sections.lede: The offence turns on use in a trade or business, so the bank's internal copies carry the exposure.
points: **Trigger:** The copy must be possessed for the purpose of, or in the course of, a trade or business, with a view to its use in that business (Cap. 528 s.118(2A)). A production system or staff workstation running an unlicensed program would meet that test (drafting inference).
**Programs in scope:** The business use offence covers computer programs, and also movies, television dramas and certain sound and visual recordings (Cap. 528 s.118(2B)).
**Excluded copies:** Printed copies of a program are outside the offence, and so are programs that are technically required to view or listen to a work (Cap. 528 s.118(2C)-(2D)).

**Who is exposed:** Because the employee defence does not cover staff who decide on acquiring or removing software, IT managers and procurement staff carry the risk alongside the bank and its officers (Cap. 528 s.118(3B), s.125(1); drafting inference).
sections.takeaway: Inventory the licence for each program installed in a business function, including test and staging copies, before the bank relies on it (good practice).

sections.heading: Lawful users and their limits
sections.lede: A person with a contractual right to use a program has statutory back-up and adaptation rights, but those rights stop short of the business use offence.
points: **Lawful user:** A lawful user is a person with a contractual right to use the program (Cap. 528 s.60(2)).
**Back-up copies:** A lawful user may make a back-up copy where it is necessary for the lawful use, but an agreement to the contrary can exclude that right (Cap. 528 s.60(1), (3)).
**Copy or adapt:** A lawful user may copy or adapt a program where that is necessary for the lawful use, including to correct errors (Cap. 528 s.61(1)-(2)).
**Exclusion of s.61:** Section 61 has no equivalent words to s.60(3), so whether a licence can exclude it is a question of construction (drafting inference).
**Cross-border reach:** For s.118(1) offences, a contractual right to use a program in any place in or outside Hong Kong counts as a lawful user right (Cap. 528 s.118A(a)).
sections.takeaway: Write any restriction on back-up, copying or adaptation into the licence in plain words, and do not treat the statutory rights as a safe harbour for business use (good practice).

sections.heading: Terms, acceptance and designated systems
sections.lede: Terms accepted online can bind the bank, and a designated critical computer system carries statutory notice duties.
points: **Electronic acceptance:** An offer and its acceptance may be expressed by electronic records, and a contract is not invalid only because an electronic record was used (Cap. 553 s.17(1)-(2)).

**Method of acceptance:** Section 17 leaves intact the common-law rule that the offeror may prescribe how acceptance is to be communicated (Cap. 553 s.17(3)), so a vendor can require a specific click or confirmation step.
**Acceptance by conduct:** Acceptance by conduct alone is not covered by s.17 and is a common-law question (drafting inference).

**Negligence liability:** Except for a contract so far as it relates to the creation or transfer of a right or interest in copyright or other intellectual property, which ss.7 to 9 do not reach (Cap. 71 Sch. 1, para 1(c)), no contract term can exclude liability for death or personal injury from negligence, and other negligence liability can be excluded only so far as the term is reasonable (Cap. 71 s.7(1)-(2)).

**Designated systems:** A designated critical infrastructure operator must notify a computer-system security incident to the Commissioner as soon as practicable, and within 12 hours after becoming aware of it where the core function is disrupted or likely to be, or otherwise within 48 hours after becoming aware (Cap. 653 s.28(2)(a); Sch. 6, item 1).
sections.takeaway: Record each electronic acceptance with the version accepted, and if a critical computer system is designated, plan any material change so that it can be notified within one month (Cap. 653 s.22(1); good practice).

provisions.title: Business possession of infringing programs
provisions.summary: Makes it an offence to possess an infringing copy of a computer program, without the copyright owner's licence, for the purpose of or in the course of a trade or business and with a view to its use in that business. Printed copies and programs technically required to view or listen to a work are excluded.
provisions.counselNote: This is the risk that sits with the bank's own installed software, not only with what it ships. Its licence inventory should cover each business function, including test and staging systems.

provisions.title: Penalties on indictment
provisions.summary: On conviction on indictment, an offence under s.118(1) or (2A) carries a fine at level 5 for each infringing copy and imprisonment for four years. Officers can also be liable where the company's offence was committed with their consent or connivance, or is attributable to them (s.125(1)).
provisions.counselNote: The fine runs per copy, so the number of unlicensed installations drives the exposure. A manager who approves a non-compliant installation can share the liability (Cap. 528 s.125(1)).

provisions.title: Lawful user: back-up copies
provisions.summary: A lawful user, meaning a person with a contractual right to use the program, may make a back-up copy where that is necessary for the lawful use. The section is subject to any agreement to the contrary.
provisions.counselNote: A licence term that limits back-up copies works as written, because the section yields to any agreement. Vendor licences should be read for such a term before the bank relies on the right.

provisions.title: Lawful user: copying and adapting
provisions.summary: A lawful user may copy or adapt a program where that is necessary for the lawful use, including to correct errors. The section has no express words allowing an agreement to exclude it.
provisions.counselNote: Whether a licence can cut back this right is not settled by the text, so counsel should not assume that an adaptation restriction is void or enforceable without a view on construction.

provisions.title: Contracts formed by electronic records
provisions.summary: An offer and its acceptance may be expressed by electronic records, and a contract is not invalid only because an electronic record was used. The section does not affect the common-law rule that the offeror may prescribe how acceptance is communicated.
provisions.counselNote: Click-through terms in a vendor portal or in the bank's own tooling can bind the bank. Procurement should record the version accepted and who accepted it.

provisions.title: Negligence liability that cannot be excluded
provisions.summary: Except for a contract so far as it relates to the creation or transfer of a right or interest in copyright or other intellectual property (Cap. 71 Sch. 1, para 1(c)), a contract term or notice cannot exclude liability for death or personal injury from negligence. Other negligence liability can be excluded only so far as the term meets the requirement of reasonableness.
provisions.counselNote: The reasonableness test may not reach a pure IP licence, because ss.7 to 9 of Cap. 71 do not apply to a contract so far as it relates to the creation or transfer of a right or interest in copyright or other intellectual property (Cap. 71 Sch. 1, para 1(c); drafting inference).

provisions.instrument: Protection of Critical Infrastructures (Computer Systems) Ordinance (Cap. 653)
provisions.title: Incident notification for designated operators
provisions.summary: A designated critical infrastructure operator must notify a computer-system security incident to the Commissioner. Schedule 6 sets 12 hours where the core function is disrupted or likely to be disrupted, and otherwise 48 hours, with a written report within 14 days.
provisions.counselNote: This applies only if the bank, or a system of its, has been designated by written notice, so confirm designation first. If it applies, the deadlines run from awareness of the incident, which makes early triage a legal matter.

provisions.title: Operational Resilience
provisions.summary: A non-statutory guideline issued on 31 May 2022 to implement the Basel Committee's principles for operational resilience. Banks were to build a resilience framework by 31 May 2023 and be operationally resilient by 31 May 2026.
provisions.counselNote: The 2026 date has passed, and a later HKMA letter moves the focus to sustaining resilience. Examiners are likely to test vendor dependencies and scenario testing, so vendor contracts should support both.

provisions.title: Outsourcing
provisions.summary: Non-statutory guidance on outsourcing (dated 28 December 2001). It expects an authorised institution to discuss with the HKMA, in advance, a plan to outsource a banking-related business area, and to address the section 2 issues before implementing it (para 1.3.2).
provisions.counselNote: The guideline is the main source of the HKMA's expected clauses in vendor contracts, in particular supervisory access and inspection rights. Build the HKMA discussion into procurement timelines.

provisions.title: Security of personal data at data processors
provisions.summary: Where a data user engages a data processor, in or outside Hong Kong, it must adopt contractual or other means to prevent unauthorised or accidental access, processing, erasure, loss or use of the data transferred to the processor.
provisions.counselNote: This is why every vendor that touches customer personal data needs security terms in its contract, whether it is a cloud provider, a support firm or a hosted service built on open source.

bankNotes: **Operational resilience:** The HKMA's OR-2 guideline set 31 May 2026 as the date for banks to be operationally resilient, and a June 2026 HKMA letter moved the focus to sustaining that resilience. The guideline is guidance, not law.

**Outsourcing:** The HKMA's outsourcing guideline says an authorised institution should discuss with the HKMA, in advance, a plan to outsource a banking-related business area (para 1.3.2). It is guidance, not law.

**Personal data processors:** A bank that engages a data processor must use contractual or other means to protect the personal data it transfers (Cap. 486 Sch. 1, DPP 4(2)) and to stop the processor keeping it longer than necessary (Cap. 486 Sch. 1, DPP 2(3)).

**Supply chain controls:** No Hong Kong statute requires SBOMs or licence scanning as such, so the bank's open source approval steps carry over; the HKMA's technology risk guidance (TM-G-1), which covers the management of technology service providers, is the supervisory reference for them (drafting inference).

glossary.definition: A machine-readable inventory of the components in a software product, with their suppliers, versions and dependency relationships. NTIA's 2021 minimum elements set its baseline.
NTIA's 2021 list of data fields, automation support and practices for an SBOM (NTIA, 12 July 2021). CISA's 2025 draft update is reported and needs checking.
Automated scanning that identifies the open source components in code or in a build, and reports their licences and known vulnerabilities.
The team that owns an organisation's open source policy, approves components and exceptions, and keeps the inventory current (good practice).
A standard format for software package data, including licence identifiers, published as ISO/IEC 5962:2021.
A machine-readable SBOM format, one of the automation formats that NTIA's minimum elements name alongside SPDX and SWID tags.
The ISO/IEC 5230:2020 standard for open source licence compliance programmes, used as a benchmark for a company's own programme.
A promise to supply the corresponding source code on request, valid for at least three years, under GPL-2.0 s.3(b) or GPL-3.0 s.6(b).
Information such as the title, author, owner and terms of use conveyed with a copyrighted work. Removing it without authority can breach 17 U.S.C. § 1202(b).
A component pulled in by another component rather than chosen directly. Inventories and scans that stop at direct dependencies miss many of them.
NIST SP 800-218, a set of secure software development practices, version 1.1 of February 2022.
A vendor or other party that the bank relies on for services. Both the interagency guidance and 23 NYCRR 500.11 address such providers.
A person with a contractual right to use a computer program (Cap. 528 s.60(2)). Only a lawful user has the statutory back-up and copy-or-adapt rights in ss.60 and 61.

An operator designated under the Protection of Critical Infrastructures (Computer Systems) Ordinance (Cap. 653), which imposes organisational, preventive and incident-reporting duties for its designated computer systems.

intro: **What this is:** counsel's checklist for approving one open source component, or reviewing the components in a release: from the request, through the licence and what it asks for the bank's use, to security, export and the records. Each step says what to check, why, who owns it and what goes on the file, with the legal force of each source on its pill.

**Start with the profile:** say what is coming in, its licence, how the bank will use it and the context. The list then shows only the steps that apply (a step shows when any option it depends on is picked; steps for every case always show). Ticks, open issues and notes stay in this browser and go into the downloads.

**Where the duties come from:** the licence binds whoever copies, changes or distributes the code under it, and most duties start only when the code leaves the bank or, for the AGPL, when a modified version serves users over a network. The Licence finder on stage 7 sets out what each common licence asks.
**Model wording:** some steps carry wording to adapt (contract clauses, notices, written offers). It is a template to fit to the facts, never the licence's own text.
