phases.title: Intake and triage
phases.lede: Capture what is being asked for and route it by risk, so permissive code for internal use moves fast and the hard cases reach counsel.

phases.title: Identify the licence
phases.lede: Find the licence that actually governs the code, record it in a standard form, and treat silence as a refusal.

phases.title: Map the obligations to the use
phases.lede: A licence asks for little until its trigger happens. Match each trigger to how the bank will really use the code.

phases.title: Security, maintenance and inventory
phases.lede: Open source comes with no supplier: the bank has to check the code is genuine, maintained and patched, and keep it on its inventory.

phases.title: Provenance and AI
phases.lede: Know where the code came from, including code an AI assistant suggested, and who is behind the projects the bank depends on.

phases.title: Export controls and sanctions
phases.lede: Encryption and cross-border use bring in the export rules and sanctions, even for code anyone can download.

phases.title: Before release
phases.lede: When code leaves the bank, the notices, licence texts and any source must go with it.

phases.title: Records and monitoring
phases.lede: Keep the file and look again when the version, the use or the licence changes.

items.title: Log the request: component, version, source, purpose
detail: **One route:** Send every request for an open source component through a single intake form, so the office sees it before any build uses it (good practice).
**Identity:** Record the exact name, version, download source and registry. Licence terms and vulnerability reports attach to a specific version (drafting inference).
**Use:** Record how the bank will use it: inside the bank, shipped, online or modified. Most licence duties attach only on distribution, and GPL-3.0 treats conveying as the trigger (GPL-3.0 s.0).
evidence: Intake record: component, version, source, purpose, requester
Routing decision and date

sources.label: OpenChain (ISO/IEC 5230)
sources.note: Licence compliance programme standard; good practice.

items.title: Check whether an approved component already does the job
detail: **Reuse first:** Search the approved component list before admitting a new one. Each extra component adds a licence to identify, a notice to keep and a vulnerability feed to watch (good practice).
**Same job, lighter licence:** If an approved component does the job under a permissive licence, a copyleft option adds duties the bank may not need (good practice).
**Duplicates:** Two components that do the same job double the review, patch and notice work for the same benefit (drafting inference).
evidence: Search of the approved component list, with the result
Reason a new component is needed

sources.label: OpenChain (ISO/IEC 5230)
sources.note: Good practice in a licence compliance programme.

items.title: Route the request by risk tier
detail: **Auto-approve:** Permissive licences such as MIT, BSD and Apache-2.0 can be approved for internal use, because their duties are mainly notices (Apache-2.0 s.4). The tiering itself is good practice, not a legal rule.

**Review:** Send copyleft (GPL, LGPL, MPL, EPL), AGPL and source-available licences to counsel, because their duties turn on distribution, network use or source disclosure (GPL-3.0 s.6; AGPL-3.0 s.13).
**Escalate:** Send code with no licence to Legal, since without a licence the bank has no permission to copy, modify or distribute it (17 U.S.C. § 106).
evidence: Tier assigned to each request: auto, review or escalate
Approver and date for each tier decision

sources.label: GNU Affero General Public License v3.0

items.title: Confirm a build tool stays out of what is shipped
detail: **Output:** A build tool's licence usually does not claim the code it produces, so compiling or testing with the tool usually does not make the bank's product subject to that licence (drafting inference; check the tool's licence text).

**Runtime libraries:** Check for runtime code copied into the build. The GCC Runtime Library exception lets programs compiled with GCC combine with the runtime libraries it covers on their own terms, provided all the compiled code came from an eligible compilation process, for example one with no GPL-incompatible plug-in (GCC-exception-3.1).
**Test tools:** Keep test and lint tools out of release packages, so their notices never ship by accident (good practice).
evidence: Tool list with licence and whether its output ships
Any runtime library copied into a build

items.title: Ask the vendor or contractor for its open source list
detail: **Ask early:** Request a software bill of materials and a licence list for every open source component in what the vendor delivers, before signing (NTIA minimum elements, 2021).
**Contract duty:** Make the list a deliverable under the contract, updated with each release, so the vendor owes it rather than offering it as a courtesy (good practice).

**Bank oversight:** The Interagency Guidance on Third-Party Relationships (2023) expects banks to manage vendor risk across the relationship, but it does not address open source as such (88 Fed. Reg. 37920).
evidence: Vendor SBOM and licence list for the deliverable
Contract clause making the list a deliverable
wording: [Vendor] will give [Bank] a list of every open source component in the [Deliverable], with each component's name, version, supplier and licence identifier, and will update the list with each release.

sources.label: NTIA minimum elements for an SBOM (2021)
sources.ref: Minimum Elements for a Software Bill of Materials (SBOM)
sources.note: Data fields for an SBOM; a federal reference, not a bank rule.

items.title: Discuss vendor outsourcing with the HKMA before it starts
detail: **Advance discussion:** Where a vendor runs a banking-related function on the component, the HKMA expects the bank to discuss the outsourcing with it in advance (HKMA SA-2 para 1.3.2).

**Guidance status:** This is guidance, not law. It covers outsourcing a banking-related business area, back office included, or changing the scope of such outsourcing, and the bank should be satisfied that the SA-2 section 2 issues are addressed before it implements the arrangement.
**Timing:** Build the HKMA discussion into procurement timelines, so that it does not come after the contract is signed (good practice).
evidence: Record of the HKMA discussion, with its date
Outsourcing scope note showing which banking-related functions the vendor runs

items.title: Identify the licence from repository, package data and headers
detail: **Primary sources:** Read the LICENSE file, the package metadata and the file headers, and check that they agree. Where they differ, treat the licence as unresolved until counsel decides (good practice).
**Scanner:** Run a licence scanner over the full source tree and record its name and version. A scanner finds leads to check, and a person confirms each result (good practice).
evidence: LICENSE file text and package metadata, with paths
Scanner name, version and report date

items.title: Record the licence as an SPDX identifier or expression
detail: **Standard name:** Record each licence by its SPDX identifier, such as Apache-2.0 or GPL-2.0-only, so every team uses one name (ISO/IEC 5962:2021).
**Expressions:** Use SPDX operators for dual licences and exceptions, such as MIT OR Apache-2.0 or GPL-2.0-only WITH Classpath-exception-2.0 (ISO/IEC 5962:2021).
**Version suffix:** Keep the '-only' or '-or-later' suffix. A notice that allows a later version gives the user a different choice from one that does not (GPL-2.0-only, Appendix).
evidence: SPDX expression for each component, in the intake record
Exceptions listed by SPDX identifier

items.title: Resolve conflicts between declared and detected licences
detail: **Hold the stricter reading:** Where the declared and detected licences differ, use the more restrictive one until counsel resolves the conflict (good practice).
**Resolve with evidence:** Check the upstream project, the release archive and the file headers. Where a conflict remains, get the copyright holder's written statement (good practice).
**Record the outcome:** Note the resolved licence, the evidence and the date, so a later scan does not reopen the question (good practice).
evidence: Declared and detected licence, side by side
Resolution, evidence and date

items.title: Treat code without a licence as all rights reserved
detail: **No permission:** Copyright gives the author the exclusive right to reproduce, adapt and distribute the work, so code with no licence carries no permission to do those things (17 U.S.C. § 106).
**Ask or drop:** Ask the author or owner for a written licence before any copy is made, or drop the component (good practice).

**Unclear claims:** A licence named only in a README or on a web page can leave the version, the files covered or who granted it unclear. Treat the component as unlicensed until the owner confirms the terms (good practice).
evidence: Written licence from the owner, or record of the decision to drop
Date of request and reply

items.title: Trace a copied snippet to its source and licence
detail: **Copying is copying:** A snippet from a website, forum answer or sample copies the author's expression, so the author's rights apply unless a licence says otherwise (17 U.S.C. § 106(1)).
**Record the source:** Keep the URL, the access date and any licence text the page shows, so counsel can check the terms that applied when the code was copied (good practice).
**Attribution:** Where the licence of the source asks for attribution, keep the notice with the copied code (good practice).
evidence: URL, access date and any licence text shown on the page
Location in the codebase where the snippet is used

items.title: Check the exact version and whether it says only or or later
detail: **Exact version:** Record the version of each copyleft licence, such as GPL-2.0 or LGPL-3.0, because each version has its own terms and compatibility turns on the version.
**Only or later:** A notice offering 'any later version' lets the user choose a later release. The '-only' identifier means that one version applies (GPL-2.0-only, Appendix).
**Check before combining:** Settle the version and the only or later wording before testing whether two components can sit in one work (good practice).
evidence: Version and SPDX identifier, as in the SBOM entry
Note of whether the licence says only or or later

items.title: Check for linking exceptions
detail: **Read the exception:** A linking exception is an extra permission added to the GPL, such as the Classpath exception or the GCC Runtime Library exception. It changes which combinations are allowed, so read the exact text (Classpath-exception-2.0; GCC-exception-3.1).
**Scope:** Check which files or library the exception covers. The GCC exception applies to files that carry its notice, and code the exception does not name keeps the GPL terms (GCC-exception-3.1).
**Other exceptions:** The LLVM Exception relaxes some Apache-2.0 conditions for compiled forms and for combinations with GPLv2 code (LLVM-exception).
evidence: Exception name and SPDX identifier, with the file it covers
Counsel note on the combination it permits

items.title: Read source-available terms as restrictions, not open source
detail: **Not open source:** SSPL, BUSL, Elastic License 2.0 and Commons Clause are source-available. OSI does not treat SSPL as open source (OSI Open Source Definition; reported; check).
**Production use:** BUSL 1.1 limits production use except as the licensor's Additional Use Grant allows, and each version converts on its Change Date (reported; check).

**Hosting and service:** SSPL s.13 requires a party offering the program as a service to release the service source code. Commons Clause bars selling the software, including hosting or support whose value derives substantially from it (reported; check).
evidence: Licence text with any Additional Use Grant or Change Date
Counsel note on production and hosting limits

items.title: Read the model or dataset licence and its use policy
detail: **Licence and policy:** Read the model licence and any acceptable use policy together. Use restrictions can bind the bank even where the licence itself is permissive (good practice).
**Scale thresholds:** The Llama 4 Community License needs a separate licence from Meta for licensees with over 700 million monthly active users (reported; check).
**Open label:** Do not assume an open-weights model is open source. The OSI's Open Source AI Definition 1.0 (28 October 2024) sets its own test, separate from the weights' licence (reported; check).
evidence: Model licence and use policy, with version and date
Thresholds and restricted uses noted

sources.label: Llama 4 Community License
sources.ref: Licence terms, 700 million monthly active users

items.title: Hold a licence for every installed copy used in the business
detail: **Offence:** Possessing an infringing copy of a computer program, without the owner's licence, for use in a trade or business is a criminal offence (Cap. 528 s.118(2A)-(2B)). Printed copies and programs needed only to view or hear a work are outside it (s.118(2C)-(2D)), so the main exposure is unlicensed installed software used inside the bank (drafting inference).

**Penalty and officers:** On indictment the fine is level 5 for each infringing copy and the term is up to 4 years (Cap. 528 s.119(1)). A director, manager or similar officer also commits the offence where it was committed with their consent or connivance, or is attributable to them (s.125(1)).

**Defences:** It is a defence for the accused to prove they did not know, and had no reason to believe, that the copy was infringing (s.118(3)). An employee given the copy by the employer for use at work also has a defence, unless they could make or influence the decision to acquire, use or remove it (s.118(3A)-(3B)).
evidence: Inventory of installed software checked against licence records, by product and copy count
Licence file for each product used in the business, with the date of the last check

items.title: Keep copyright and licence notices
detail: **Keep the notice:** The MIT licence requires the copyright notice and the permission notice in all copies or substantial portions of the software (MIT full text).
**Apache notices:** On distribution, Apache-2.0 s.4 requires a copy of the licence, prominent marks on changed files, retained notices and the NOTICE file's attribution (Apache-2.0 s.4).

**Stripping risk:** Licence headers can count as copyright management information, so removing them can engage 17 U.S.C. § 1202(b) where the bank knows or has reasonable grounds to know that infringement follows (17 U.S.C. § 1202(b), (c); drafting inference).
evidence: Notice file for each release, with copyright lines
Header check report for modified files

items.title: Apache-2.0: NOTICE file, changed-file marks, patent termination
detail: **Changed files:** If the bank distributes modified files, mark each one with a prominent notice that the bank changed it, and keep the original copyright, patent, trademark and attribution notices (Apache-2.0 s.4(b)-(c)).

**NOTICE file:** If the work has a NOTICE file, pass its attribution notices on in at least one place: the NOTICE file, the documentation or a display where such notices normally appear (Apache-2.0 s.4(d)).

**Patent termination:** The patent licence ends if the bank sues alleging that the Work or a Contribution infringes a patent. Check the bank's litigation plans before any suit touching the code (Apache-2.0 s.3).
evidence: Changed-file list with notices added
Copy of the NOTICE file and where its text appears

items.title: Confirm internal use stays internal
detail: **Copies inside the bank:** GPL-3.0 treats conveying as propagation that lets others make or receive copies (GPL-3.0 s.0). Copies used only within the bank are generally treated as not conveyed (drafting inference; FSF view).

**Contractors:** Giving GPL-3.0 code to a contractor falls within the licence's contractor permission only if the contractor modifies or runs it exclusively on the bank's behalf, under the bank's direction and control, on terms that bar copies of the bank's copyrighted material outside that relationship; otherwise the copy is conveyed on the usual terms. Either way, the bank must comply with the licence for code whose copyright it does not control (GPL-3.0 s.2).

**Affiliates:** The FSF's view is that copies within one organisation are not distribution (FSF view, not law). Affiliates are separate legal persons, so treat a copy to one as distribution unless the licence says otherwise (drafting inference).
evidence: Map of internal copies: sites, staff, affiliates, contractors
Contract terms for contractors who run or modify the code

items.title: Map every route by which copies leave the bank
detail: **Every route:** List each channel by which a copy leaves the bank, such as an app store, an SDK, an on-premises install, device firmware or a partner's build. Each route can be conveying or distribution with licence duties (GPL-3.0 s.0; Apache-2.0 s.4).
**Partners and customers:** A copy handed to a partner or customer counts even when the bank did not build the final product, so include them in the map (GPL-3.0 s.0).
**Records:** Keep one route list per release, with the channel, the recipient class and the licence duties it triggers (good practice).
evidence: Route list per release: channel, recipient, licence
Owner and date for each route

items.title: GPL code shipped to others: source for the whole work
detail: **Whole work:** Distributing a work that contains or derives from GPL-2.0 code requires licensing the whole work under the GPL, at no charge to every third party (GPL-2.0-only s.2).

**Source with object code:** Give complete corresponding source with object code, or a written offer valid for at least three years (GPL-2.0-only s.3). Under GPL-3.0 the written offer is available only for object code in a physical product, and a download must offer equivalent access to the source (GPL-3.0-only s.6(b), (d)).

**Modified GPL-3.0 code:** Mark the changes with prominent notices and dates, and license the whole work under GPL-3.0 when it is conveyed, as source or, through s.6, as object code (GPL-3.0-only ss.5-6).
evidence: Source package or written offer, with the release version
Licence file and change notices for the release

items.title: LGPL, MPL and EPL: meet the file or library-level duties
detail: **LGPL relinking:** When a combined work built on LGPL code is distributed, its terms must permit modification of the work for the customer's own use and reverse engineering for debugging such modifications. In practice that often means a shared library or relinking route (LGPL-2.1-only s.6; LGPL-3.0-only s.4).
**MPL file level:** Covered MPL files stay under MPL-2.0 when distributed in source form, while a Larger Work may combine them with material under other terms (MPL-2.0 s.3.1, s.3.3).
**EPL duties:** Distributing EPL-2.0 code requires making the Program available as source code and telling recipients how to obtain it (EPL-2.0 s.3.1).
evidence: Relink or shared-library route for each LGPL library
MPL file list and EPL source statement

sources.label: GNU Lesser General Public License v2.1
GNU Lesser General Public License v3.0

items.title: AGPL behind an online service: modified versions and source offers
detail: **Trigger:** AGPL-3.0 s.13 applies only where the bank modifies the program and users interact with it remotely over a network. Running an unmodified copy behind an API triggers nothing under s.13 (AGPL-3.0 s.13).
**Source offer:** The licence requires a modified version to offer every remote user its Corresponding Source, from a network server at no charge (AGPL-3.0 s.13).
**Mixed code:** AGPL-3.0 s.13 lets AGPL code be combined with GPL-3.0 code, and the GPL-3.0 part keeps its own terms (AGPL-3.0 s.13).
evidence: List of AGPL components and whether any is modified
Source offer link or endpoint, with the version

sources.label: GNU Affero General Public License v3.0

items.title: Source-available code behind a service: check hosting limits
detail: **Service source:** SSPL s.13 requires a party that offers the program as a service to release the service source code, meaning the program and the software used to make the service available (reported; check).

**Hosting limits:** Commons Clause bars selling the software, including hosting or support whose value derives substantially from it (reported; check). Read the licence text before any hosted offering.
**Internal or customer-facing:** Running the code only for bank staff is a different question from giving customers access to it through the service (drafting inference; check the licence text).
evidence: Licence text and version for each source-available component
Hosting model and whether customers reach the code

items.title: Track the bank's changes and decide whether to contribute them
detail: **Change notices:** Where the bank distributes a modified copy, mark the changes with prominent notices and dates, as GPL-3.0 s.5(a) and GPL-2.0 s.2(a) require. Apache-2.0 s.4(b) asks for the same on modified files (GPL-3.0-only s.5; GPL-2.0-only s.2; Apache-2.0 s.4).
**Change register:** Keep a list of the bank's changes by file and by version, so each release can show what changed and which notices apply (good practice).

**Upstream decision:** Decide whether to offer fixes upstream. Contributing can cut the cost of keeping a fork current, but each contribution follows the project's licence and contribution terms (good practice).
evidence: Change register by file and version
Upstream decision and reason

items.title: Check the licences in one program are compatible
detail: **Test the direction:** Compatibility is often one-way, so ask whether each component's licence can sit inside the combined work's licence, not the reverse (good practice).

**Apache and GPLv2:** The FSF views Apache-2.0 as compatible with GPLv3 but not GPLv2. A common reason given is Apache's extra terms, such as patent termination (Apache-2.0 s.3), which GPL-2.0 s.6 bars as further restrictions (FSF view, not law).
**Version first:** The answer turns on exact versions and on any only or or-later wording, so settle those first (GPL-2.0-only, Appendix).
evidence: Compatibility note for each pair, with the reason
Version and licence table for the program

items.title: Check patent grants, retaliation clauses and the bank's own patents
detail: **Grants:** Apache-2.0 s.3, GPL-3.0 s.11 and MPL-2.0 s.2.1 each grant recipients a licence under the contributors' patent claims that their code would infringe (Apache-2.0 s.3; GPL-3.0-only s.11; MPL-2.0 s.2.1).

**Retaliation:** If the bank sues alleging that the Work infringes a patent, its Apache-2.0 patent licence ends (Apache-2.0 s.3). If the bank starts litigation alleging that a Contributor Version infringes a patent, its grants from Contributors under MPL-2.0 end (MPL-2.0 s.5.2).

**Own patents:** A contribution can license the bank's own patents to recipients where it infringes them, under Apache-2.0 s.3 or GPL-3.0 s.11. Check the bank's patents before release (good practice).
evidence: Patent clause in each component licence
Bank patents or applications the code may touch

items.title: Do not use the project's marks beyond naming its origin
detail: **Apache-2.0 limit:** Apache-2.0 s.6 gives no permission to use the licensor's trade names or marks, except as required for reasonable and customary use in describing the origin of the work and reproducing the NOTICE file (Apache-2.0 s.6).

**MPL and GPL:** MPL-2.0 s.2.3 grants no rights in a Contributor's trademarks, service marks or logos. GPL-3.0 s.7(e) lets a licensor decline trademark rights in some names (MPL-2.0 s.2.3; GPL-3.0-only s.7).

**Product naming:** Use the project's name only to say the product is built on it. Using a registered name in commerce in a way likely to cause confusion can infringe (15 U.S.C. § 1114(1)) (good practice).
evidence: Name-use review for product, app store and website copy
Attribution text and where it appears
wording: [Product] is built on [Project], an open source project maintained by [Owner]. [Project] is a trademark of [Owner], and [Bank] is not affiliated with [Owner].

items.title: Put licence compliance into the vendor contract
detail: **Warranty:** Ask the vendor to warrant that its open source use complies with the licences, and that its SBOM and licence list are complete (good practice).
**Remediation:** Require the vendor to fix licence and security problems within an agreed period, and to replace a component it cannot bring into compliance (good practice).
**Indemnity:** Ask for an indemnity against third-party claims that open source in the deliverable breaches its licence or infringes, and read the carve-outs for open source (good practice).
evidence: Clauses: warranty, SBOM, remediation, indemnity
Vendor reply and agreed open source list
wording: [Vendor] warrants that the [Deliverable] complies with the licences of every open source component it contains, and will deliver an updated software bill of materials with each release.

sources.label: NTIA minimum elements for an SBOM (2021)
sources.ref: Minimum Elements for a Software Bill of Materials (SBOM)

items.title: Check licence terms against the lawful-user rights and the interoperability limits
detail: **Lawful user:** A person with a contractual right to use a program may make a back-up copy where necessary for that use, and may copy or adapt it where necessary for lawful use, including to correct errors (Cap. 528 s.60(1)-(2), s.61(1)-(2)). An agreement can exclude the back-up right (s.60(3)), but section 61 has no equivalent words, so whether a licence can exclude it is a question of construction (drafting inference).

**No decompilation exception:** The Ordinance has no express decompilation or reverse-engineering exception. Reverse engineering that copies or adapts the program therefore needs the owner's licence or a statutory exception, such as the lawful-user rule or fair dealing for research or private study (Cap. 528 ss.38, 61; drafting inference), so any licence term on debugging should be checked against section 61 (good practice).

**Interoperability:** Circumventing an effective technological measure for interoperability is excused only on its conditions, which include that the copy is not infringing and that the analysis is not itself an infringement (Cap. 528 s.273D(1)(b)-(e)). The exception excuses circumvention, not copying or adapting.
evidence: Licence clause review noting the back-up, adaptation and error-correction terms
Record of any interoperability work, showing each condition was met

items.title: Scan for known vulnerabilities and record the result
detail: **Scan the exact version:** Run a composition scan on the version the bank will use and keep the report with the approval. A licence review alone says nothing about known flaws (good practice).
**Expect late findings:** Log4Shell (CVE-2021-44228) was disclosed on 9 December 2021, and the xz Utils backdoor (CVE-2024-3094) on 29 March 2024, so a clean scan is dated (good practice).
**Re-scan later:** Repeat the scan at each new version and when an advisory affects a component already approved (good practice).
evidence: Scan report with date, tool version and version scanned
Open CVE list and the decision on each

items.title: Check the project is maintained
detail: **Read the activity:** Check release dates, commit history and open security issues over the past year, and record them in the approval file (good practice).
**Count the maintainers:** A project with one maintainer depends on that person staying active. Ask whether a foundation or company stands behind it (good practice).
**Learn from xz Utils:** The backdoor in versions 5.6.0 and 5.6.1 was disclosed on 29 March 2024 (CVE-2024-3094). Review who can publish releases and sign them (good practice).
evidence: Release and maintainer summary with dates
Bus factor record for the approval file

items.title: Confirm the package is the real project
detail: **Check the name:** Typosquatting uses a near copy of a popular package name. Compare the publisher and repository link with the project's own website before installing (good practice).
**Guard internal names:** Dependency confusion lets a public package shadow an internal package with the same name. Pin the registry source for internal names (good practice).
**Verify signatures:** Where the project publishes signatures or checksums, check them and record the result in the approval file (good practice).
evidence: Publisher name, package URL and checksum
Signature check result

items.title: Pin versions and pull from a trusted mirror
detail: **Pin exact versions:** Use lock files and fixed versions so the build tested is the build shipped (good practice).
**Use a scanned mirror:** Pull packages through an internal mirror that the bank scans, rather than directly from public registries (good practice).
**Make builds reproducible:** Where the build can be reproduced, the bank can show that a shipped binary came from the approved source (good practice).
evidence: Pinned versions and hashes in the lock file
List of approved registries and mirrors

items.title: Add the component to the product's SBOM
detail: **Record the minimum fields:** Each entry should carry the supplier, component name, version, other unique identifiers, dependency relationship, SBOM author and a timestamp (NTIA, 12 July 2021).
**Pick a machine format:** The NTIA paper names SPDX, CycloneDX and SWID tags as formats that support automation (NTIA, 12 July 2021).
**Match the licence field:** Record the licence as an SPDX identifier so the SBOM and the approval file agree (SPDX, ISO/IEC 5962:2021).
evidence: SBOM entry: supplier, name, version, licence
SBOM export in SPDX or CycloneDX

sources.label: NTIA minimum elements for an SBOM (2021)

items.title: For critical systems, plan support, patching and exit
detail: **Name the support route:** Decide whether the component has commercial support, a vendor or only community fixes, and record who patches it and how fast (good practice).

**Oversee the vendor:** The interagency guidance expects a bank to manage third-party relationships across their life cycle (88 Fed. Reg. 37920). It does not mention open source as such, so vendors that supply open source are best treated as in scope (drafting inference).

**Plan the exit:** Record how the bank would replace the component, including a fork or commercial alternative. A NYDFS-regulated bank also needs written procedures for evaluating externally developed applications (23 NYCRR 500.8).
evidence: Support and patch route with response times
Exit or replacement plan with owner

items.title: Keep the PCI DSS inventory of third-party components
detail: **Inventory the components:** Requirement 6.3.2 requires an inventory of bespoke and custom software and of the third-party components in it (PCI DSS v4.0.1, requirement 6.3.2; reported).
**Keep it current:** The requirement has applied since 31 March 2025 (reported; check), so a new open source library should reach the inventory before it enters a card environment (good practice).
**Share the records with the SBOM:** Use the same component records for the card inventory and the product SBOM, so the two match (good practice).
evidence: Component list for each card-environment application
Version and owner for each open source item

items.title: Container images: check the base image and every layer
detail: **Review every layer:** Each layer adds packages, and each package has its own licence and CVE status, so review the whole image and not only the application (good practice).
**Check the base image:** Confirm the base image's publisher, tag and update cadence, and whether its distribution carries licence terms of its own (good practice).
**Mind distribution:** If the image goes to customers, each copyleft package in it brings its own duties, such as a source offer (GPL-2.0 s.3).
evidence: Image layer list and base image tag
Licence list for operating system packages

items.title: Check end-of-life dates and the upgrade path
detail: **Unsupported runtimes:** A framework or base image past end of life gets no security fixes, so a scan finding against it may never close (good practice).
**Set a date:** Record the end-of-life date in the approval file and set a review trigger before it arrives (good practice).
**Check the vendor contract:** Where a vendor supplies the runtime, check that it covers upgrades, since end of life can fall inside the contract term (good practice).
evidence: End-of-life date and support end for the version
Upgrade path and target date

items.title: Put security and retention terms in vendor and hosting contracts
detail: **Security terms:** A bank that gives personal data to a data processor, in or outside Hong Kong, must adopt contractual or other means to prevent unauthorised or accidental access, processing, erasure, loss or use (Cap. 486 Sch. 1 s.4, DPP 4(2)).
**Retention:** The same kind of term must stop the processor keeping the data longer than necessary for the processing (Cap. 486 Sch. 1 s.2, DPP 2(3)).

**Processor test:** A data processor processes personal data on behalf of another and not for its own purposes (DPP 2(4)). A vendor that uses the data for its own purposes falls outside that definition, and the analysis then changes (drafting inference).
evidence: Vendor contract clauses on security, retention and return or erasure of data
Register of hosts and processors that receive personal data from the component

items.title: Check whether the bank or a system is designated as critical infrastructure
detail: **Material changes:** If the bank or a system is designated under the Protection of Critical Infrastructures (Computer Systems) Ordinance, a material change to the design, configuration, security or operation of a critical computer system must be notified to the regulator within 1 month (Cap. 653 s.22(1), (2)(a)).

**Incidents:** A computer-system security incident must be notified within 12 hours where the core function is disrupted or likely to be disrupted, and otherwise within 48 hours, with a written report within 14 days (Cap. 653 s.28; Sch. 6).

**Regulator:** The HKMA is the designated authority for authorized institutions, so material changes are notified to it, but incidents are notified to the Commissioner of Critical Infrastructure (Computer-system Security) (Cap. 653 Sch. 2; s.6; s.22(1); s.28(1)).
evidence: Written confirmation of the designation status of the bank and each system, with the date checked
Change and incident log recording the date of awareness and the date of each notice

sources.label: Protection of Critical Infrastructures (Computer Systems) Ordinance (Cap. 653)

items.title: Check AI-suggested code for matches to licensed code
detail: **Run the match check:** Scan AI-suggested code against open source before it enters the codebase, using a duplication filter or scanner, and record the result (good practice).

**Stripping headers is a risk:** Removing a licence header from copied code can engage § 1202(b)(1), which bars intentional removal of copyright management information (17 U.S.C. § 1202(b)(1)). Courts have accepted that licence terms can be such information in some cases (reported; check).
**Recent case:** A court is reported to have dismissed the § 1202(b) claim against an AI coding tool. Verbatim output still needs a licence check (Doe v. GitHub, Inc.; reported; check).
evidence: Match scan result for each AI-suggested block
Duplication filter setting in the coding assistant

items.title: Use only approved AI coding tools with the agreed settings
detail: **Approved list only:** Limit AI coding assistants to those on the approved list, with duplication filters on and the agreed settings locked (good practice).
**Keep confidential code out of prompts:** Do not paste confidential or customer code into prompts unless the vendor contract allows that use (good practice).
**Check the indemnity conditions:** Some vendors defend output claims only while built-in filters and guardrails stay on. Microsoft's Copilot Copyright Commitment is one example (reported; check).
evidence: Approved tool list and agreed settings
Vendor terms on training use and indemnity

items.title: Record human authorship for AI-assisted code the bank wants to own
detail: **Prompts alone are not enough:** The Copyright Office says a prompt alone does not give the user enough control to be an author. Human expression in the output, or human selection and arrangement, can be protected (Copyright Office, Part 2, 29 January 2025).

**Record the human contribution:** The Copyright Office says applicants should disclose AI-generated material that is more than de minimis and exclude it from the claim (88 Fed. Reg. 16190). Keep a record of human edits and selection.
**Courts need a human author:** The D.C. Circuit held that the Copyright Act requires human authorship for registration (Thaler v. Perlmutter, 130 F.4th 1039).
evidence: Record of human edits, selection and arrangement
Disclosure text for any registration

sources.label: Copyright Office
sources.ref: Copyright and Artificial Intelligence, Part 2: Copyrightability (29 January 2025)

items.title: For critical dependencies, review the project's governance
detail: **Foundation or single vendor:** A foundation-hosted project usually has a neutral process for licence and maintainer decisions. A single-vendor project depends on that company's choices (good practice).

**Licence-change history:** Elastic, Redis and HashiCorp each moved products away from open licences, and Elastic and Redis later added AGPL-3.0 as an option (reported; check). Check the history before relying on a critical dependency.
**Plan the fallback:** Identify which fork or foundation project would carry the code if the licence changes (good practice).
evidence: Governance model and foundation status
Licence-change history of the project

sources.label: Elastic, Redis and HashiCorp licence changes

items.title: Classify encryption in the component and the product
detail: **Published software sits outside:** Software that is published is not subject to the EAR, but published encryption software classified under ECCN 5D002 stays subject to it unless the publicly available source code rule releases it (15 C.F.R. § 734.3(b)(3); § 734.7(b); § 742.15(b); reported; check).
**Classify the encryption:** Record whether the component provides encryption functions and how the product uses them, before any release (good practice).
**Licence is not a classification:** An open licence does not decide export status, which turns on the software's content and how it is made available (good practice).
evidence: Encryption classification record for the component
Product classification and release decision

items.title: If the bank publishes encryption source, check the notification rule
detail: **Only non-standard cryptography:** Since a BIS rule of 29 March 2021, publicly available encryption source code needs a notification only where it implements non-standard cryptography (15 C.F.R. § 742.15(b); reported; check).
**Send the notice where needed:** Where the rule applies, send the notification to BIS and the NSA's ENC Encryption Request Coordinator, and record the date (reported; check).
**Record the analysis:** Write down why the code uses standard cryptography or why it does not, so the decision can be shown later (good practice).
evidence: Decision on publishing encryption source
Notification copy and date, if required

items.title: Check sanctions exposure for contributors, hosting and users
detail: **Screen the parties:** Check contributors, hosting providers and users against the sanctions lists before giving them access, because OFAC rules apply to the bank's dealings (good practice).
**Platform restrictions:** GitHub restricted accounts in sanctioned regions in 2019, and on 5 January 2021 announced an OFAC licence to serve developers in Iran (reported; check).
**Document the decision:** Record whether access from sanctioned places is allowed and on what basis (good practice).
evidence: Screening record for contributors and hosts
Decision on access from sanctioned places

sources.label: GitHub sanctions restrictions and OFAC licence

items.title: Generate the attribution notice and ship it
detail: **Notice for every component:** Include each component's copyright notice and licence text. Where a NOTICE file exists, carry its attribution notices (Apache-2.0 s.4(a), (d)).

**Make it reachable:** Put the notice where users can find it, such as an about screen or a file in the package (good practice). Where users reach the code over a network, a modified AGPL program needs a source offer (AGPL-3.0 s.13).
**Reconcile with the scan:** A notice that omits a component found in the scan is a gap at release. Reconcile the two before sign-off (good practice).
evidence: Attribution notice file with all licence texts
About screen or NOTICE file for the release

items.title: Prepare source or a written offer where copyleft requires it
detail: **GPL-2.0 release:** Object code must come with complete source, or with a written offer valid for at least three years (GPL-2.0 s.3(b)).

**GPL-3.0 release:** Convey the Corresponding Source with the object code, including the scripts that build and install it, or, for a physical product only, with a written offer; a download must offer equivalent access to the source through the same place, or on another server that clear directions point to (GPL-3.0 s.6(b), (d)).

**File and network scope:** MPL-2.0 requires the source of the MPL-covered files, changed or not, when they go out in executable form (MPL-2.0 s.3.2). AGPL-3.0 s.13 adds a network offer for modified versions.
evidence: Corresponding source package and build scripts
Written offer text with three-year validity

items.title: Check app store terms against the licence
detail: **Store terms can conflict:** App store usage rules can clash with copyleft terms. Check the store's terms against the licence before submission (good practice).
**Precedent:** VLC was removed from Apple's App Store in January 2011 after a complaint that the store terms conflicted with the GPL (reported; check).
**Record the decision:** If the terms and the licence cannot both be met, record the decision and the option chosen, such as a different distribution route (good practice).
evidence: Store terms review with date
Licence conflict decision and distribution route

items.title: Record the legal sign-off and any conditions
detail: **Name the approver:** Record who approved the release, the version and the basis for approval (good practice).
**Write conditions as tasks:** Each condition, such as a notice on the about screen or a source offer, needs an owner and a date (good practice).
**Set an expiry:** Set an expiry or a review trigger, so that a new version or a licence change reopens the approval (good practice).
evidence: Sign-off record with conditions and expiry
Named owner and review date

items.title: Keep the approval file
detail: **Core contents:** Keep the licence, the intended use, the decision, the scan results and the owner in one file for each component, so that a later question can be answered quickly (good practice).
**Use a known model:** OpenChain (ISO/IEC 5230) is a licence compliance programme standard, and this file fits its approach (good practice).
**Keep it after use ends:** Retain the file for as long as the bank's records policy requires after the last release that used the component (good practice).
evidence: Licence, use, decision, scans and owner for each component
Approval conditions and review dates

items.title: Re-review on new versions, new uses or licence changes
detail: **Set triggers:** Re-review on a new version, a new use such as moving from internal use to shipped copies, and any change in the licence or in who owns the project (good practice).
**Distribution changes the duties:** A change from internal use to distribution can turn a quiet licence into active duties, such as conveying source with object code (GPL-3.0 s.6).
**Check each version:** A project may change its licence in a new version, so check the licence of the version in use and not only the project name (good practice).
evidence: Trigger list with dates
Re-review record for each change

items.title: Plan for a licence change and a fork
detail: **Recent history:** Elastic (2021), Redis (2024) and HashiCorp (2023) each moved products to source-available terms, and foundation-hosted forks followed; Elastic (2024) and Redis (2025) later added AGPL-3.0 as an option (reported; check).
**Pin the last open version:** Keep the last version released under an open licence, with its licence file, so the bank can keep running that code if the licence changes (good practice).
**Test the fork path:** Identify the fork or replacement, check its licence and governance, and test a build before any change happens (good practice).
evidence: Pinned last open version and its licence
Fork or replacement candidate and owner

sources.label: Elastic, Redis and HashiCorp licence changes

items.title: Handle a compliance complaint or GPL enforcement letter
detail: **Cure first:** If the bank gets its first notice of a GPL-3.0 violation and cures it within 30 days of receipt, the licence is reinstated (GPL-3.0 s.8).
**Preserve the evidence:** Keep the build, the release package and the correspondence, so the bank can show what it shipped and when it fixed it (good practice).
**Community approach:** The 2015 Principles of Community-Oriented GPL Enforcement put compliance before litigation, which shapes how the community responds to a complaint (Principles, 2015).
evidence: Complaint record with dates
Preserved source and build evidence

items.label: Intake record
items.note: Component, version, source, purpose, owner

items.label: Licence and scan report
items.note: SPDX identifier, scan results, conflicts resolved

items.label: SBOM entry
items.note: The component in the product inventory

items.label: Approval note
items.note: Decision, conditions, review date

items.label: Attribution notice
items.note: Notices and licence texts that ship with the product

items.label: Source package or written offer
items.note: Where copyleft requires it

documentsNote: A component used only inside the bank needs the first four; anything shipped or served to customers needs the last two as well.

reviewKit.caveat: A study aid for counsel, not legal advice. Licences are read on their own words and the facts of the use; FSF and OSI positions are views, not law.

title: Releasing code and contributing
oneLiner: Before the bank publishes code, settle title, clean the code and choose a licence whose patent and copyleft terms the bank accepts.
keyPoints: Releasing code is a grant of rights. The licence tells outsiders what they may do, so the bank must own the code, or hold a licence to it, before it grants anything.

**Ownership:** Under the Copyright Act (17 U.S.C. § 201(b)), code written by employees within the scope of their jobs belongs to the bank as a work made for hire, unless the parties agree otherwise in writing. Contractor and vendor code needs a signed transfer or a licence first (17 U.S.C. § 204(a)).

**Licence choice:** Apache-2.0 gives an express patent licence and ends it for a licensee who sues claiming the work infringes a patent. MIT says nothing about patents. Copyleft licences add duties on whoever distributes the code.

**Clean-up:** Secrets, customer data, internal hostnames and security-sensitive logic come out before the first public push. Published code can no longer meet the secrecy test for a trade secret (18 U.S.C. § 1839(3)).
**Contributions:** Outside code reaches the project by sign-off (DCO) or by a contributor licence agreement (CLA). Only an assignment moves title to the bank (17 U.S.C. § 204(a)).
**Counsel's role:** Approve the release in writing, and record the licence, the provenance and the export answer. Keep the bank's names and marks outside the grant (Apache-2.0 s.6).

conceptMap.caption: What the bank must own, clean and license before publication. Each item is settled before the code goes public, because a public push is hard to take back.

centre.note: Owned, cleaned and licensed before it is published
