deepDive.heading: Own it before publishing
deepDive.lede: Only code the bank owns, or may license, should leave the bank.

visual.caption: Who owns the code, and the paperwork the bank needs before it publishes.

items.label: Employee
items.note: The bank is the author, and owns the rights unless the parties agreed otherwise in a signed writing (17 U.S.C. § 201(b))

items.label: Contractor
items.note: Usually not a work made for hire, so title needs a signed writing (§ 204(a)) or a licence to publish

items.label: Vendor deliverable
items.note: Read the ownership and licence-back terms before publishing what a vendor built

items.label: Third-party code
items.note: Keep its licence terms and notices with every copy (Apache-2.0 s.4(c))

points: **Employees:** Under the Copyright Act (17 U.S.C. § 201(b)), code an employee writes within the scope of employment is a work made for hire, so the bank is the author and, unless the parties agreed otherwise in a signed writing, owns the rights.

**Contractors:** Software from an independent contractor usually falls outside the nine work made for hire categories, so the bank needs a signed transfer for title (17 U.S.C. §§ 101, 204(a)) or a licence to publish it.
**Third-party code:** Code copied from another project keeps that project's licence, and its notices must stay with it (Apache-2.0 s.4(c)). Record the source and the licence for each piece.
**Vendor terms:** Check the vendor contract for ownership and licence-back terms before the bank publishes what a vendor built (good practice).
**Staff side work:** Code that staff wrote for another employer, or for their own projects, is not the bank's to release (good practice).
deepDive.takeaway: Settle title for each part of the code before the release review starts.

deepDive.heading: Clean the code before it leaves
deepDive.lede: A public push is easy to make and hard to take back.

visual.caption: What comes out of the code, and what stays with it.

items.label: Secrets and credentials
items.note: Including history, config files and test fixtures (good practice)

items.label: Personal and customer data
items.note: Test data, logs and seed files are common sources

items.label: Internal names and systems
items.note: Hostnames, internal URLs, ticket references and codenames

items.label: Security-sensitive logic
items.note: Fraud, risk and anti-abuse rules that help attackers once published

items.label: Licence and copyright notices
items.note: Removing them can breach 17 U.S.C. § 1202(b)

points: **Secrets:** Scan the full history, not only the latest commit, and rotate any key that has appeared in it (good practice).

**Trade secrets:** Under the Economic Espionage Act (18 U.S.C. § 1839(3)), information counts as a trade secret only while its owner keeps it secret by reasonable measures. Code the bank publishes cannot later be treated as a secret for what was shown.

**Notices:** The ban on removing copyright management information applies where the person intends the removal and knows, or for civil claims has reasonable grounds to know, that it will enable infringement (17 U.S.C. § 1202(b)). Licence headers may count as that information (drafting inference; reported).
**Third-party notices:** Check a third-party licence before stripping anything from its code, since some licences make keeping notices a condition of redistribution (Apache-2.0 s.4(c)).
**Sign-off on the scan:** Let a named reviewer sign off the scan result, and keep the record with the release file (good practice).

deepDive.heading: Pick a licence on purpose
deepDive.lede: The licence sets what outsiders may do and what they must keep.

visual.caption: How five common licences differ at release. Read the trigger, not only the name.

items.label: Apache-2.0
items.note: Express patent licence, ended if the licensee sues claiming the work infringes a patent (s.3); trade names excluded (s.6)

items.label: MIT
items.note: Notice must go with copies; no patent language (MIT full text)

items.label: MPL-2.0
items.note: MPL files, changed or not, stay under MPL-2.0 and their source goes with executables; the bank's own files can differ (s.3.1-3.3)

items.label: GPL-3.0
items.note: Modified code conveyed to others must be licensed as a whole under GPL-3.0 (s.5(c))

items.label: AGPL-3.0
items.note: Modified versions used remotely must offer their source (s.13)

points: **Apache-2.0:** Each contributor grants a patent licence for the claims its contribution necessarily infringes. That licence ends for a licensee who sues alleging the work infringes a patent (Apache-2.0 s.3). Choose it where patent terms matter.
**MIT:** Short and permissive. It has no patent language, so the bank gets no express patent licence from it (MIT full text).

**Copyleft:** Conveying means propagation that enables others to make or receive copies (GPL-3.0 s.0), so purely internal use does not convey the code. Once the bank conveys modified GPL code, the whole work must be licensed under GPL-3.0 (s.5(c)).

**Network copyleft:** AGPL-3.0 s.13 applies only if the bank modifies the program and remote users interact with the modified version. An unmodified network service triggers nothing under that section.
**No licence:** Code with no licence keeps the default rule. Others may read it, but copying, changing or sharing it needs permission (17 U.S.C. § 106).
**Dual licensing:** Offering the same code under a commercial licence works only if the bank owns all of it, or holds consent from every other contributor (good practice).

deepDive.heading: Take in outside contributions
deepDive.lede: Decide how outside code reaches the project before the first contribution arrives.

visual.caption: Two routes to the project, with different effects on title. Confirm the route before any contribution is merged.

items.label: Sign-off (DCO)
items.note: The contributor certifies the right to submit the code; title stays with the contributor (good practice)

items.label: Licence CLA
items.note: The contributor keeps title and licenses it to the project (drafting inference: check the form)

items.label: Assignment CLA
items.note: Must be in a signed writing (17 U.S.C. § 204(a))

points: **Sign-off:** A sign-off is light and fast. It shows that the contributor could submit the code, so it suits a project whose licence is already clear (good practice).
**Licence CLA:** A [[CLA|Contributor licence agreement (CLA)]] that only licenses rights leaves the contributor owning the code, so the bank holds a licence, not title (good practice).
**Assignment CLA:** An assignment moves title, and it must be in a signed writing (17 U.S.C. § 204(a)). Use it only where the bank needs to own the project's code outright.
**Corporate CLA:** Have the employer sign when its staff contribute, and check that the signer has authority to bind the company (good practice).

**Staff contributions:** Staff should contribute to outside projects only under written approval that names the code and the licence. The bank's title to staff code follows the ownership rules in the ownership stage (good practice).

deepDive.heading: Governance, trademarks and project names
deepDive.lede: A project needs rules for decisions, reports and names before it has users.
points: **Trademarks:** Apache-2.0 s.6 gives no permission to use the licensor's names or marks, beyond describing the origin of the work and reproducing its NOTICE content. Say the same in the project's readme (good practice).
**Project names:** Clear the name by search before launch. Projects that changed licence have seen forks take new names, such as OpenTofu and Valkey (reported; check).

**Foundations:** A foundation such as the Linux Foundation can hold a project's marks and set its governance rules. Read its charter and trademark policy before the bank hands over a name (good practice).
**Security reports:** Publish a security policy that says where to report a vulnerability and how the project will respond before any disclosure (good practice).
**Compliance reference:** OpenChain (ISO/IEC 5230:2020) is the standard for licence compliance programmes, and it is a useful reference for the bank's own release process (good practice).
deepDive.takeaway: A name and a security contact are part of the release, not an afterthought.

deepDive.heading: The release path, in order
deepDive.lede: Each step depends on the one before it, so run them in this order.

visual.caption: The release path for one component, in the order it is run.

items.label: Confirm title
items.note: Trace each file to an employee, a contractor transfer or a vendor term

items.label: Clean the code
items.note: Secrets, personal data and internal names out; notices kept

items.label: Choose the licence
items.note: Record why, and what the licence grants and requires

items.label: Check export
items.note: Record whether the code implements encryption, and which kind

items.label: Approve in writing
items.note: Business owner, security and counsel

items.label: Publish with notices
items.note: Licence, NOTICE file and changed-file notices travel with the code

points: **Export:** Software that is published is generally outside the Export Administration Regulations (15 C.F.R. § 734.3(b)(3); reported; check). Encryption source that implements [[non-standard cryptography]] may still need a notification (15 C.F.R. § 742.15(b); reported; check).
**Approval:** Counsel approves the release in writing, after the title, scan and licence checks are signed off (good practice).
**Record:** Keep the licence choice, the scan results, the export answer and the approver's name in one release record (good practice).
**Publishing:** The repository should carry the licence file, the NOTICE file where one applies, and changed-file notices (Apache-2.0 s.4(a), (b), (d)).
deepDive.takeaway: A complete release record is the evidence an examiner or a buyer will ask for later.

provisions.title: Initial ownership and works made for hire
provisions.summary: Copyright vests first in the author or authors. For a work made for hire, the employer or other person for whom the work was prepared is the author and owns the rights, unless the parties agree otherwise in a signed writing. Joint authors are co-owners.
provisions.counselNote: This decides whether the bank can release employee code without more paperwork. Contractor and vendor code needs its own route to title.

provisions.title: Exclusive rights in copyrighted works
provisions.summary: The copyright owner has exclusive rights to reproduce the work, prepare derivative works, distribute copies, and perform or display it publicly, subject to the sections that follow. Those rights apply to code that carries no licence.
provisions.counselNote: Code published with no licence keeps these rights reserved, so outsiders may look at it but may not copy, change or share it without permission.

provisions.title: Execution of transfers of copyright ownership
provisions.summary: A transfer of copyright ownership, other than by operation of law, is not valid unless an instrument of conveyance, or a note or memorandum of the transfer, is in writing and signed by the owner of the rights or its authorised agent. A certificate of acknowledgement is not required for the validity of a transfer, but it is prima facie evidence of execution when properly issued (§ 204(b)).
provisions.counselNote: A contractor's code stays with the contractor until a signed transfer says otherwise. Check the signature block and the signatory's authority before relying on it.

provisions.title: Removal or alteration of copyright management information
provisions.summary: Bars intentional removal or alteration of copyright management information without authority, and distribution of copies knowing it was removed. The person must know, or for civil claims have reasonable grounds to know, that this will induce, enable, facilitate or conceal infringement. Copyright management information includes the terms and conditions for use of the work.
provisions.counselNote: Licence headers and notices may count as copyright management information (drafting inference; reported), so a clean-up that strips them can carry risk. Keep the notices unless counsel has decided otherwise.

provisions.title: Definition of trade secret
provisions.summary: Defines a trade secret as financial, business, technical or other information, expressly including programs and codes, that the owner has kept secret by reasonable measures and that derives independent economic value from not being generally known or readily ascertainable.
provisions.counselNote: Code the bank publishes no longer meets the secrecy element for what is shown, so the release review is also a trade secret decision (drafting inference).

provisions.title: Grant of Patent License
provisions.summary: Each contributor grants a perpetual, worldwide, royalty-free patent licence for the claims its contribution necessarily infringes, alone or in combination with the work. The licence for a licensee ends if that licensee sues, alleging that the work or a contribution infringes a patent.
provisions.counselNote: This patent grant is the main reason to choose Apache-2.0 for code with patent value. It also means the bank grants every user a licence under the patent claims it can license that its contribution necessarily infringes, alone or combined with the work, and loses the patent licences other contributors grant it if it brings patent litigation alleging the work infringes.

provisions.title: Redistribution
provisions.summary: A redistributor must give recipients a copy of the licence, mark modified files, keep the copyright, patent, trademark and attribution notices in the source form of derivative works, and reproduce the NOTICE file's attribution notices where the work has one.
provisions.counselNote: These duties arise on distribution. Internal use does not distribute copies, but publishing a release does, so the notices must travel with the release.

provisions.title: Trademarks
provisions.summary: The licence grants no permission to use the licensor's trade names, trademarks, service marks or product names, except reasonable and customary use to describe the origin of the work and to reproduce the content of the NOTICE file.
provisions.counselNote: A bank's release does not license its name or logo to forks. Say so in the readme, and keep brand assets out of the repository.

provisions.title: Responsibilities
provisions.summary: Distributing covered software in source form keeps it under MPL-2.0, and executable distributions must make the source available. A larger work that combines covered software with other code may be distributed on the larger work's own terms, provided the covered software still complies with the licence.
provisions.counselNote: File-level copyleft lets the bank keep its own files private, but changes to covered files must be shared when distributed. Track which files are covered.

provisions.instrument: GNU Affero General Public License v3.0
provisions.title: Remote Network Interaction; Use with the GNU General Public License
provisions.summary: If a user modifies the program, the modified version must prominently offer all users interacting with it remotely through a network an opportunity to receive its Corresponding Source. Running an unmodified version over a network triggers nothing under this section.
provisions.counselNote: An internal or customer-facing service built on a modified AGPL program can be obliged to offer its source to those who use it remotely. Check modifications before any such service goes live.

provisions.title: MIT License
provisions.summary: Permits use, copying, modification, merger, publication, distribution, sublicensing and sale of the software, provided the copyright notice and permission notice are included in copies or substantial portions. The software is provided as is, with a disclaimer of warranty and of liability.
provisions.counselNote: MIT gives broad rights on one condition, which is keeping the notice. It contains no patent language, so where a patent grant matters the bank should choose a licence that has one.

provisions.title: Licence terms as conditions of the grant
provisions.summary: The Federal Circuit held that the attribution and change-notice terms of the Artistic License were conditions limiting the scope of the licence. A user who broke them could be sued for copyright infringement, not only for breach of contract.
provisions.counselNote: Notice and attribution terms in a bank's own release can carry copyright remedies, so write the conditions clearly and state what counts as compliance.

provisions.title: Encryption source code with non-standard cryptography
provisions.summary: Software that is published is generally outside the Export Administration Regulations (reported; check the eCFR). Since a rule of 29 March 2021, publicly available encryption source code needs a notification only where it implements non-standard cryptography.
provisions.counselNote: Most release code needs no export step, but any release that implements encryption needs a recorded answer before the first public push. The test turns on the implementation, not on the licence.

checklist: **Confirm title:** Trace each file to an employee, a signed contractor transfer, a vendor deliverable term or a licence the bank holds.
**Scan the full history:** Run secret and credential scanning on every commit and branch, and rotate any key found, before the first public push.
**Remove personal and customer data:** Check test fixtures, seed files, logs and sample configuration for personal or account data.
**Strip internal references:** Remove internal hostnames, URLs, ticket numbers and codenames, and keep the licence and copyright notices intact.
**Record third-party code:** List each third-party component with its licence, source and notices, and keep the NOTICE content and changed-file notices (Apache-2.0 s.4).
**Choose and record the licence:** Note why Apache-2.0, MIT, MPL-2.0 or a copyleft licence was picked, and whether a patent grant matters to the bank.
**Set the contribution route:** Pick a DCO sign-off or a CLA, and confirm who signs for the bank and for any corporate contributor.
**Clear the project name:** Run a clearance search on the name, and state in the readme that the bank does not license its own names or marks (Apache-2.0 s.6).
**Check export:** Record whether the code implements encryption, and if so whether it uses non-standard cryptography (15 C.F.R. § 742.15(b); reported; check).
**Approve in writing:** Get sign-off from the business owner, security and counsel, and keep the approval with the release record.
itAngle: **Repository audit:** Run secret scanning across all branches, tags and history before the first public push. A secret in old history stays readable once the repository is public (good practice).
**Licence metadata:** Add a LICENSE file and SPDX identifiers in source headers, so that scanners and downstream tools read the same licence. SPDX is ISO/IEC 5962:2021.

**Dependency gate:** Before release, check every dependency's licence against the release licence. A copyleft dependency can change what the release must carry and how it is distributed (good practice).
**Packages and images:** Ship the licence file and NOTICE content inside each package, container image and source archive, so that the Apache-2.0 s.4 copies travel with the binary.
**Contribution gates:** Require a DCO sign-off check or a signed-CLA check in continuous integration, so a pull request cannot merge without the route the bank chose (good practice).
virtualBankNotes: **Third-party oversight:** Interagency guidance on third-party relationships (88 Fed. Reg. 37920) is technology-neutral and does not single out open source. Where a vendor supplies or supports code the bank publishes, treat that vendor relationship under the guidance (drafting inference).

**Secure development:** If the bank is covered by NYDFS Part 500, 23 NYCRR 500.8 requires written procedures for the secure development of in-house applications. A release of in-house code should follow the same written process, and the release record should show it (drafting inference).
**Data and secrets:** A release that exposes customer data or working credentials is a security incident for the bank to investigate, whatever the licence says (good practice).
**Brand and fraud:** A bank's name or product code on a public repository invites lookalikes and phishing sites. Keep the reporting route clear in the readme and the security policy (good practice).
**Examiner evidence:** Examiners may ask who approved a release, what was removed and which licence applied. Keep the release record where it can be produced quickly (good practice).
productNotes: **Ask before any public push:** Tell counsel before a sample app, SDK or demo repository goes public, since a public push cannot be fully recalled and forks may keep copies (good practice).

**Bring the title trail with the code:** Name the authors of each part, including contractors and vendors, and send each contractor or vendor deliverable with its signed transfer of title, or with a licence to publish it where title stays with the vendor, because contractor code stays with the contractor without a transfer (17 U.S.C. §§ 101, 204(a)).

**Let product name the sensitive parts:** Ask engineering and product to flag secrets, customer data, internal hostnames and fraud or anti-abuse rules, and do not strip licence headers to tidy the repository (17 U.S.C. § 1202(b); Apache-2.0 s.4(c)).

**Agree the licence and the name early:** Apache-2.0 gives an express patent grant that ends for a licensee who sues claiming the work infringes a patent (Apache-2.0 s.3), so product should settle that choice with counsel, and the readme should say that the bank does not license its names or marks (Apache-2.0 s.6).
pitfalls: **Publishing first:** Pushing a repository public to test a feature before title and scan checks run. A public push cannot be fully recalled, and forks may keep copies (good practice).
**Silent release:** Publishing code with no licence file, so users may read it but cannot copy or change it (17 U.S.C. § 106).
**Name and logo:** Using the bank's name or logo as the project name or in the repository. Apache-2.0 s.6 does not license those marks to forks or users.
**Licence mixing:** Combining Apache-2.0, GPL and MPL code in one release without checking which terms the combined work must carry (good practice; see the copyleft stage).

**Stripping notices:** Removing copyright or licence headers to make code look clean. That can breach 17 U.S.C. § 1202(b) where the knowledge test is met, and it can break the licence's own conditions (Apache-2.0 s.4(c)).
**Dual licence without title:** Selling a commercial licence for code that staff or contractors still own, or that carries another licensor's terms (drafting inference).

points: **Open-source stewards:** the Cyber Resilience Act's open-source software stewards have lighter duties (Regulation (EU) 2024/2847, Art. 24), which matters for a bank that hosts a community project.

**Employee code:** the employer exercises the economic rights in programs an employee creates in the course of duties or on instructions, unless agreed otherwise (Directive 2009/24/EC, Art. 2(3)), so confirm ownership before release.
**Employee works:** the employer is first owner of works made in employment, subject to agreement (CDPA 1988 s.11(2)).
**Employee inventions:** inventions made in normal duties belong to the employer, with compensation for outstanding benefit (Patents Act 1977 ss.39-41; Shanks v Unilever [2019] UKSC 45).

**Employer ownership:** the employer owns works made in the course of employment absent agreement (Copyright Act s.13(3)), but Nexus Solutions Inc. v. Krougly, 2026 ONCA 199, held it did not own software the employee was not asked or expected to write (reported; check).
**Moral rights:** moral rights can be waived but not assigned (Copyright Act s.14.1), so release and contributor terms should take a waiver, not an assignment, of moral rights.

hongKong.summary: In Hong Kong the employer owns code that an employee writes in the course of employment, and the developer keeps copyright in commissioned code unless the contract expressly says otherwise (Cap. 528 ss.13, 14(1), 15(1)). Publishing code can also destroy patent novelty, and the six-month relief is narrow (Cap. 514 ss.9B, 11A). The main difference from the US rule in this stage is that Hong Kong gives an employee an award for exploitation that neither side could reasonably have contemplated (Cap. 528 s.14(2); drafting inference).
keyPoints: **Employee code:** The employer is the first owner of code an employee writes in the course of employment, subject to any agreement to the contrary and to an award for unexpected exploitation (Cap. 528 s.14(1)-(2)).

**Commissioned code:** Unless the agreement expressly says who owns the copyright, the developer keeps it, and the bank gets only an exclusive licence for the purposes both sides had in mind (Cap. 528 s.15(1)-(2)).

**Publication is disclosure:** Anything made available to the public before the material date of the application is part of the state of the art, and the six-month exception covers only an evident abuse or a prescribed display (Cap. 514 ss.9B(2), 11A(1)-(2)).

**Personal data:** Using personal data for a new purpose needs the data subject's prescribed consent, so real customer data should not go into test data or code samples (Cap. 486 Sch. 1, DPP 3(1); drafting inference).

**Attribution:** The right to be identified and the integrity right do not apply to a computer program, so any attribution or integrity duty must come from the licence or the contract (Cap. 528 ss.91(2)(a), 93(2)).

sections.heading: Title before publication
sections.lede: Settle who owns each part of the code before anything leaves the bank.
points: **Employees:** Code written in the course of employment belongs to the bank unless an agreement says otherwise (Cap. 528 s.14(1)(a)).

**Award:** An employee is owed an award if the bank exploits the code in a way neither side could reasonably have contemplated when it was made, unless the parties agreed otherwise (Cap. 528 s.14(2)).
**Contractors:** Commissioned code stays with the developer unless the contract expressly names the bank as the owner (Cap. 528 s.15(1), s.13).
**Written transfers:** An assignment of copyright is effective only if it is in writing and signed by or for the assignor (Cap. 528 s.101(3)).
**Outside contributions:** A licence leaves title with the contributor, so the bank needs an assignment where it must own contributed code outright (good practice).
sections.takeaway: Collect a signed transfer or a licence for each contractor part, and the employer's records for each employee part, before the release review starts (good practice).

sections.heading: Publication and patent novelty
sections.lede: A public push can destroy novelty for any invention in the code, and the relief is narrow.
points: **Novelty:** An invention is new only if it does not form part of the state of the art, which comprises everything made available to the public before the material date (Cap. 514 s.9B(1)-(2)).

**Six-month exception:** A disclosure is disregarded only if it occurred no earlier than six months before filing and was due to an evident abuse against the applicant, or to a display at a prescribed exhibition or meeting (Cap. 514 s.11A(1)-(2)).
**Display evidence:** For an exhibition display, the filing must state the display at the time, and the request to record the application must give the prescribed details (Cap. 514 s.11A(3)).
**Other patent routes:** The same kind of exception applies to a standard (O) patent and to a short-term patent (Cap. 514 ss.37B, 109).
sections.takeaway: Settle the patent filing decision before any public push, because the six-month exception is narrow (good practice).

sections.heading: Personal data and secrets
sections.lede: Code, fixtures and sample data can carry personal data, and the data protection principles apply to what the bank releases.
points: **New purpose:** Personal data may not be used for a new purpose without the data subject's prescribed consent (Cap. 486 Sch. 1, DPP 3(1)).

**Security:** The bank must take all practicable steps to protect personal data against unauthorised access, having regard to the kind of data and the harm that could result (Cap. 486 Sch. 1, DPP 4(1)).
**Test data:** Applying these principles to source code and test data is a drafting inference, so fixtures should be synthetic (good practice).
**Secrets:** Customer data or working credentials in a public repository should be treated as a security incident to investigate, whatever the licence says (good practice).
sections.takeaway: Have the release owner sign off that fixtures, logs and sample configuration hold only synthetic data and no credentials, and keep that sign-off with the release record (good practice).

sections.heading: Moral rights, waivers and attribution
sections.lede: Moral rights do not reach computer programs, so attribution for code is a contract matter.
points: **Identification:** The right to be identified as author does not apply to a computer program (Cap. 528 s.91(2)(a)).
**Integrity:** The right to object to derogatory treatment does not apply to a computer program (Cap. 528 s.93(2)).

**Other works:** Documentation and other non-program works in the repository may carry moral rights, which can be waived by a signed writing but not assigned (Cap. 528 ss.98(2)-(3), 105; drafting inference).
**Contributor terms:** Release and contributor terms should take any waiver and any attribution promise that the bank needs (good practice).
sections.takeaway: Put any attribution promise and any moral rights waiver in the release or contributor terms, not in an assumed statutory right (good practice).

provisions.title: Employee works
provisions.summary: The employer is the first owner of copyright in a literary work made by an employee in the course of employment, subject to any agreement to the contrary. Where the work is exploited in a way neither side could reasonably have contemplated, the employer must pay the employee an award, unless the parties agreed otherwise.
provisions.counselNote: Code written by staff is the bank's by default, but the award right means the bank should record what it expects to do with the code, so the exploitation test can be answered later.

provisions.title: Commissioned works
provisions.summary: Copyright in a commissioned work belongs to the person the commissioning agreement expressly entitles. Whatever the agreement says, the commissioner has an exclusive licence for the purposes reasonably contemplated when the work was commissioned, and may restrain exploitation it could reasonably object to.
provisions.counselNote: Contractor code is the highest-risk title gap before a release. An express assignment in the contract is the only clean route to owning it outright.

provisions.title: Assignments must be in writing
provisions.summary: An assignment of copyright is not effective unless it is in writing and signed by or on behalf of the assignor.
provisions.counselNote: An unsigned transfer from a contractor or vendor leaves the bank without title, however clear the intent. Ask for the signed document before the code is published.

provisions.title: Novelty and the state of the art
provisions.summary: An invention is new only if it does not form part of the state of the art. The state of the art comprises everything made available to the public, in Hong Kong or elsewhere, before the material date of the application.
provisions.counselNote: Publishing code that embodies an unfiled invention can remove patent protection for it. Product and engineering should flag any novel method in the code before a public push.

provisions.title: Non-prejudicial disclosure for standard (R) patents
provisions.summary: A disclosure is not counted against novelty if it occurred no earlier than six months before the filing date and was due to an evident abuse against the applicant, or to a display at a prescribed exhibition or meeting. A display needs a statement at filing and the prescribed details in the request.
provisions.counselNote: The window is six months and the grounds are narrow, so an ordinary open source release is unlikely to qualify, because it needs an evident abuse or a display at a prescribed exhibition or meeting. Filing decisions must come before the code goes public.

provisions.title: Use of personal data for a new purpose
provisions.summary: Personal data may not be used for a new purpose without the data subject's prescribed consent, subject to the exceptions in the principle.
provisions.counselNote: Test fixtures and sample data drawn from live customer records are a new use of personal data. Engineering should replace them with synthetic records before any public release.

provisions.title: No integrity right in programs
provisions.summary: The right to object to derogatory treatment does not apply to a computer program or to a computer-generated work.
provisions.counselNote: The author of a program cannot rely on the integrity right when the code is changed or released under another licence. Any protection for the author has to come from the licence terms.

provisions.title: Waiver of moral rights
provisions.summary: A moral right may be waived by an instrument in writing signed by the person giving it up. A waiver may cover specific works, a class of works or future works, and may be conditional or revocable.
provisions.counselNote: Release and contributor terms are the place to take a waiver for documentation and other non-program material. An assignment of the moral right is not possible, so the bank should not draft one.

provisions.title: General Principles for Technology Risk Management
provisions.summary: Non-statutory guidance (version 1, 24 June 2003) setting baseline expectations for technology risk governance, information security, system development and change management, and operations.
provisions.counselNote: This is the baseline the HKMA uses to judge whether IT controls are adequate. A release record that shows who approved each step fits its change management expectations, though the guideline is old and is read with later modules.

bankNotes: **Technology change control:** The HKMA's TM-G-1 guideline sets the baseline it uses to judge whether IT controls are adequate, so the release record should show who approved each change. The guideline is guidance, not law.

**Vendor code:** Where a vendor builds code that the bank intends to publish, the HKMA's outsourcing guideline (SA-2) applies only if the arrangement is outsourcing of a banking-related business area (drafting inference). The guideline is guidance, not law.

glossary.definition: A sign-off line in which a contributor certifies the right to submit the code under the project's licence. It is lighter than a CLA and does not by itself move title (good practice; check the project's current text).
A signed agreement under which a contributor licenses rights in its contributions to the project, or in some forms assigns them. An assignment must be in a signed writing (17 U.S.C. § 204(a)).
A licence that requires distributed modifications to be licensed on the same terms, as a whole. Under GPL-3.0 s.5(c), the entire work must be licensed under the GPL when it is conveyed.
Offering the same code under two licences, typically an open source licence and a commercial one. It works only where the offeror owns or controls all the rights in the code (good practice).

Information conveyed with a copy of a work that identifies the work, its authors and owners, and the terms of use. Its intentional removal can breach 17 U.S.C. § 1202(b) where the knowledge test is met (§ 1202(c)).
An optional Apache-2.0 text file that carries attribution notices. A redistributor must reproduce those notices where they apply (Apache-2.0 s.4(d)).

One of GPL-2.0, LGPL-2.1, AGPL-3.0 or a later version of them (MPL-2.0 s.1.12). Where MPL-2.0 covered software is combined with code under such a licence, it may also be distributed under that licence, unless the file carries the Exhibit B notice that it is incompatible with secondary licences (MPL-2.0 s.3.3).
A written promise to supply source code with object code. GPL-2.0 s.3(b) accepts an offer valid for at least three years, and GPL-3.0 s.6(b) allows one only for object code in a physical product.

A work prepared by an employee within the scope of employment, or a commissioned work in one of nine listed categories under a signed writing. The employer or hiring party is the author (17 U.S.C. §§ 101, 201(b)).
Cryptography outside the standard set. Whether it is implemented decides whether published encryption source code needs a notification to US authorities (15 C.F.R. § 742.15(b); reported; check).
A work made on the commission of a person under an agreement with its author, to which s.15 of the Copyright Ordinance (Cap. 528) applies.

An exhibition or meeting prescribed under the Patents Ordinance (Cap. 514) at which an invention may be displayed without the display counting against novelty, subject to the six-month limit in s.11A.

intro: **What this is:** counsel's checklist for publishing the bank's code, or letting staff contribute to outside projects: the business case, title to the code, cleaning it, the licence, contributions coming in, patents and trademarks, export, governance and launch.

**Start with the profile:** say what is going out, under what licence, how outside contributions will come in and what the code contains. The list then shows only the steps that apply. Ticks, open issues and notes stay in this browser and go into the downloads.

**Why it matters:** once code is public it cannot be called back. Secrets, customer data and security-sensitive logic must come out first, and the licence the bank chooses grants rights, including patent rights under some licences, to everyone who receives the code.
**Model wording:** some steps carry wording to adapt (policy lines, sign-off text, contributor terms). It is a template, never a licence's own text.

options.label: A contribution to an outside project
An SDK, API client or sample code
A public fork of an outside project
Dual licensing with a commercial option
A foundation's licence
options.hint: The project will be hosted by a foundation

options.label: Security-sensitive logic
options.hint: For example fraud or AML rules

options.label: Code written by contractors or vendors
Hong Kong law applies
options.hint: The bank, its developers or the users are in Hong Kong

phases.title: The business case
phases.lede: Be clear why the bank is releasing, who sponsors it and who signs off, because publishing is permanent.

phases.title: Who owns what is released
phases.lede: The bank can only license what it owns or may relicense: check every author and every third-party file.

phases.title: Clean the code
phases.lede: Remove what must never be public, including from the history, before the first push.

phases.title: Choose the licence
phases.lede: The licence decides what others may do with the code and what the bank gives away with it, patents included.

phases.title: Contributions in
phases.lede: Decide how outside code comes in, so the bank can keep licensing the project as it intends.

phases.title: Patents and trademarks
phases.lede: Publication is prior art and some licences grant patent rights; the project name needs clearing and protecting.

phases.title: Export and sanctions
phases.lede: Public encryption code can need a notification; hosting platforms bring their own sanctions rules.

phases.title: Governance
phases.lede: A public project needs owners, rules for contributors and a way to report security issues.

phases.title: Launch and after
phases.lede: Launch under the bank's control, then keep the project maintained or close it cleanly.

items.title: Record why the bank is releasing and who sponsors it
detail: **Name the purpose:** Record whether the release is for recruiting, setting a standard or building an ecosystem. The purpose sets the licence and the upkeep the bank must fund (good practice).
**Name the sponsor:** Record the business owner who answers for the project after launch, including security reports and licence questions. Without one, nobody holds those duties (good practice).
**Keep the decision:** File the purpose, sponsor and date with the release request, so a later review can test whether the release still serves its aim (good practice).
evidence: Release purpose statement signed by the sponsor
Named business owner and date

items.title: Get sign-off from the business owner, security and legal
detail: **Name each approver:** Obtain written sign-off from the business owner, Security and Legal, each on the risks it owns. One team's approval does not cover the others (good practice).
**Set approval tiers:** Set the tier for each release by its licence, the data it touches and any patent or mark issue. Higher tiers go to senior sign-off (good practice).
**Tie approval to the version:** Each approval should state what it covers, the version and any condition. An approval given for one version does not cover a later one (good practice).
evidence: Approval form per tier with names and dates
Conditions and the version each approval covers

items.title: Check the request against the bank's open source policy
detail: **Read the outbound rules:** Check the release against the bank's open source policy on outbound code: the licences it allows, who approves, and which names may appear (good practice).
**Confirm the policy version:** Record the policy version and any exception in force on the release date. An exception granted for one project does not extend to another (good practice).
**Escalate gaps:** Where the policy is silent, such as a new model licence or a dual licence, refer the point to Legal rather than deciding it within the team (good practice).
evidence: Policy check note citing the policy version
Exceptions in force, if any

items.title: Staff contribution: confirm it is within the contribution policy
detail: **Check the scope:** Confirm the contribution fits the bank's contribution policy. A small fix or documentation is usually simpler to approve than a new feature (good practice).

**Separate bank time from personal time:** Code an employee writes within the scope of employment is a work made for hire, and the bank is its author and owner (17 U.S.C. § 101; § 201(b)). Off-duty code may not be (drafting inference).

**Check the outside licence:** A contribution to an Apache-2.0 project is under that licence unless the submitter states otherwise (Apache-2.0 s.5). Read the outside project's own rules before submitting.
evidence: Contribution approval with scope and time record
Outside project's licence and contribution rules noted

items.title: List who wrote the code
detail: **List every author:** Record each employee, contractor, vendor and outside contributor who wrote code in the release, using version control history and team records. Gaps in this list become gaps in title (good practice).

**Check employment status:** Code by an employee within the scope of employment is a work made for hire, so the bank is the author (17 U.S.C. § 101; § 201(b)). Code by anyone else needs a signed assignment or it stays with its writer (§ 204(a)).
**Keep the list with the release:** The copyright notice and attribution in the release should name the correct owner, so the author list is the source for them (good practice).
evidence: Author list from commit history with employment status
Work-for-hire confirmation for employee authors

items.title: Confirm written assignments from contractors and vendors
detail: **Check for a signed writing:** A transfer of copyright needs a writing signed by the owner (17 U.S.C. § 204(a)). Contractor code is usually not a work made for hire, so get a signed assignment before release (§ 101; § 201(b)).
**Check the wording:** The assignment should transfer ownership of the code, not just a licence, and should cover code written before the agreement was signed (good practice).

**Note the termination risk:** A grant by an author executed on or after 1 January 1978 can be terminated in a five-year window, notwithstanding any contrary agreement (17 U.S.C. § 203(a)(3), (a)(5)). Long-lived code carries that risk.
evidence: Signed assignment or agreement for each contractor and vendor
Vendor list cross-checked to the author list
wording: [Contractor] assigns to [Bank] all right, title and interest, including copyright, in the deliverables and in all code written for [Bank] before this agreement, and will sign any further document needed to record the assignment.

items.title: Inventory third-party code and confirm its licence allows release
detail: **Inventory the components:** List each third-party component in the release with its licence identifier and version. Code with no licence gives no permission to copy, so it cannot go out until its owner grants one (drafting inference).

**Test each licence against the outbound one:** A permissive component fits most outbound choices. Conveying a modified GPL-3.0 work, in source or object form, requires licensing the whole work under GPL-3.0 (GPL-3.0 s.5(c), s.6).

**Keep the notices:** Keep each component's copyright and licence notices in the release. Removing them can also engage the copyright management information rules (17 U.S.C. § 1202(b); reach to licence notices reported; check).
evidence: Component list with SPDX identifiers and versions
Compatibility note for each copyleft component

items.title: Handle AI-assisted code: authorship and match checks
detail: **Record the human authorship:** Human authorship is required for copyright protection (Thaler v. Perlmutter, 130 F.4th 1039 (D.C. Cir. 2025)). Prompts alone are not enough control, but human expression in the output, or human selection and arrangement, can be protected.

**Disclose in any registration:** The Copyright Office's policy expects AI-generated material that is more than de minimis to be excluded from the claim and described in the application (agency policy, not statute) (88 Fed. Reg. 16190 (16 March 2023)).
**Check for matches:** Scan AI-suggested code for verbatim matches to licensed code before release, since copied code brings its original licence terms with it (good practice).
evidence: Record of AI-assisted sections and the human edits
Match-scan report on the AI-suggested code

sources.label: Copyright Office
sources.ref: Copyright and Artificial Intelligence, Part 2: Copyrightability (29 January 2025)

sources.label: Copyright Office
sources.ref: Statement of policy, 88 Fed. Reg. 16190 (16 March 2023)

items.title: For a fork, keep the upstream licence and notices
detail: **Keep the upstream licence:** A fork stays under the licence of the code it came from. Keep the licence text, copyright notices and any NOTICE file in the release (Apache-2.0 s.4(a), (c), (d)).
**Mark the changes:** Apache-2.0 requires modified files to carry notices that they were changed (Apache-2.0 s.4(b)). GPL-3.0 requires prominent notices of modification with a date (GPL-3.0 s.5(a)).
**Rename the project:** The upstream marks may be used only to name the origin of the work (Apache-2.0 s.6). A new name avoids confusion with the upstream project (good practice).
evidence: Upstream licence and NOTICE files in the release
List of changed files with dates

items.title: Settle who owns the code before release
detail: **Employees:** Code an employee writes in the course of employment belongs to the employer, subject to any agreement to the contrary. The employer may owe an award for exploitation that neither side could reasonably have contemplated (Cap. 528 s.14(1)-(2)).

**Contractors:** Code commissioned from a contractor belongs to the contractor unless the agreement expressly says otherwise. The bank then has only an exclusive licence for the purposes both sides contemplated, plus a power to restrain objectionable exploitation (s.15(1)-(2)).

**Written assignments:** An assignment of copyright is effective only in writing signed by or for the assignor (s.101(3)). An electronic signature counts only if the method identifies the signer, shows approval, is reliable and suits the purpose, and the other party consents to it (Cap. 553 s.6(1)).
evidence: Employee and contractor IP clauses, with the signed copies on file
Signed assignment, or signed electronic record, for each transfer of code

items.title: Scan the full history for secrets and rotate any found
detail: **Scan the whole history:** Scan every branch, tag and past commit, not only the current tree. A key deleted in a later commit stays in the history and in every clone (good practice).
**Rotate, then clean:** Rotate each credential found and treat it as exposed before rewriting history. Rewriting history alone does not make a published secret safe (good practice).
**Protect the trade secret:** Code and credentials can be trade secrets only while the owner keeps them secret (18 U.S.C. § 1839(3)). Publishing them ends that status (drafting inference).
evidence: Full-history secret scan report with date and tool
Rotation record for each credential found

items.title: Remove customer, production and personal data
detail: **Remove customer and personal data:** Delete customer records, production extracts and personal data from fixtures, logs, screenshots and samples. Data that is published cannot be recalled from copies others have made (good practice).
**Use synthetic data:** Replace examples and test data with generated values, and check that they cannot be traced to a real customer (good practice).
**Review logs and configuration:** Logs, error dumps and configuration files often hold data the test files do not. Review them separately (good practice).
evidence: Data review sign-off by Engineering and Security
List of files removed or replaced

items.title: Remove internal hostnames, addresses and architecture details
detail: **Search for internal names:** Remove internal hostnames, addresses, network ranges, service names and diagrams that show how the bank's systems connect. That map helps an attacker target the bank (good practice).

**Check the build and deploy files:** Build files, container definitions, pipelines and infrastructure code often hold internal addresses and account names. Review them with the source code (good practice).
**Involve Security:** Security reviews the cleaned release and signs off any architecture notes that remain (good practice).
evidence: Security review record for the cleaned release
List of addresses and hostnames removed

items.title: Review security-sensitive logic before release
detail: **Review the logic:** Fraud, AML and sanctions rules and scoring thresholds show how the bank detects crime. Publishing them can help someone design around the control, so remove or generalise them (good practice).
**Keep regulator material out:** Confidential supervisory information must stay out of code, comments and test data. Ask Legal to confirm what is covered (good practice).

**Decide the trade secret point first:** Valuable logic that is kept secret can be a trade secret, and publication ends that status (18 U.S.C. § 1839(3)(B); drafting inference). Decide before release, not after.
evidence: Security-sensitive logic review and decision
Legal confirmation that regulator-confidential material is absent

items.title: Decide whether to publish the commit history
detail: **Compare the options:** A squashed history removes past secrets, names and deleted files, but also the record of who wrote what. A full history keeps that record, but must be scanned first (good practice).
**Keep the attribution record:** If history is squashed, keep the author list and the licence record elsewhere, so that the notices and attribution survive (good practice).
**Record the choice:** The release notes should say which history was published, so that a reader knows what the public repository contains (good practice).
evidence: Decision record: squashed or full history
Scan result for the history published

items.title: Keep personal data out of code and test data
detail: **New purpose:** Using personal data for a new purpose needs the data subject's prescribed consent (Cap. 486 Sch. 1 s.3, DPP 3(1)). Real customer records should therefore not go into test data, fixtures or sample code.

**Security:** The bank must take all practicable steps to protect personal data against unauthorised access, having regard to the kind of data and the harm that could result (Cap. 486 Sch. 1 s.4, DPP 4(1)).
**Practice:** Replace real records with synthetic data before the code leaves the bank, and scan the release for personal data before it is published (good practice).
evidence: Scan report for personal data in the release, with the result
Record of the synthetic data set used for testing

items.title: Choose the outbound licence and record why
detail: **Tie the licence to the aim:** Recruiting and standards favour a permissive licence such as Apache-2.0 or MIT. Copyleft keeps derivatives open, which suits some aims and not others (good practice).
**Follow the ecosystem norm:** A project community expects the licence it already uses. A licence outside that norm can keep contributors away even where it is sound (good practice).

**Record the reason:** File the choice and its reasons with the release, stating the licence as an SPDX identifier. OSI approval means the licence passed OSI's review against its ten criteria, which is a view, not law.
evidence: Licence decision note with business aims
SPDX identifier of the chosen licence

items.title: Apache-2.0: understand the patent licence it grants
detail: **Read the two grants:** Apache-2.0 grants a copyright licence (s.2) and a patent licence from each contributor. The patent licence covers only claims that the contribution necessarily infringes alone or in combination with the Work (Apache-2.0 s.3).

**Review the bank's own patents:** Once the bank releases under Apache-2.0, the grant can reach its patent claims that its contribution necessarily infringes. Review pending applications first (drafting inference).
**Know the termination:** The patent licence ends for a recipient who sues, alleging that the Work infringes a patent (Apache-2.0 s.3). That protects the bank against claims over its own release.
evidence: Patent review record before release
Licence file with the Apache-2.0 text and NOTICE file

items.title: Copyleft outbound: confirm the bank wants reciprocity
detail: **Confirm the reciprocity:** A GPL-3.0 work conveyed in source or object form must be licensed as a whole under GPL-3.0, so recipients keep the same freedoms (GPL-3.0 s.5(c), s.6). Check that the bank wants that outcome.

**Note the network term:** AGPL-3.0 s.13 requires a modified version to offer its source to users who interact with it remotely over a network. A bank that modifies an AGPL-3.0 program and runs the modified version as a service must offer its source to remote users (AGPL-3.0 s.13).

**Consider the file-level option:** MPL-2.0 is file-level copyleft. MPL files, changed or not, must be made available in source form when the bank distributes them in executable form, but a larger work may be distributed under other terms (MPL-2.0 s.3.2, s.3.3).
evidence: Reciprocity decision record with the licence chosen
Notes on modified-version and network duties

sources.label: GNU Affero General Public License v3.0

items.title: Dual licensing: confirm the bank can license every part
detail: **Check the ownership:** A dual licence lets the bank offer the same code on commercial terms, so it must hold rights in every part. Copyright vests in each author (17 U.S.C. § 201(a)), so each contributor's code needs an assignment or a grant the bank can relicense.
**Get each grant in writing:** A transfer of copyright needs a writing signed by the owner (17 U.S.C. § 204(a)). Written grants let the bank show it may relicense the code (good practice).
**Exclude third-party code:** The bank cannot relicense code it does not own, even under a commercial licence. Remove or license that code separately first (good practice).
evidence: Chain-of-title record for each contributed part
Written grants covering commercial relicensing

items.title: Add the licence file, SPDX headers and copyright notices
detail: **Add the full licence text:** Put the complete licence in a LICENSE file at the top of the repository, and give recipients a copy with each distribution (Apache-2.0 s.4(a)). A header alone does not carry the full terms.
**Use SPDX identifiers:** Add an SPDX-License-Identifier line to each source file, and a copyright line naming the bank as owner of the code it wrote (ISO/IEC 5962:2021; good practice).
**Keep the notices:** Headers and notices can be copyright management information. Removing or altering them may engage 17 U.S.C. § 1202(b); whether licence headers count is reported; check.
evidence: LICENSE and NOTICE files in the release
Header check report across all source files
wording: Copyright [year] [Bank legal name]. Licensed under the [licence name]; see the LICENSE file. SPDX-License-Identifier: [licence identifier]

items.title: Documentation and data: choose a content licence
detail: **Choose the attribution terms:** CC BY-4.0 requires anyone who shares the material to keep the creator's name, a copyright notice, a reference to the licence and a link where the licensor supplied them, the link only where reasonably practicable, and in every case to say if they modified the material, keep any earlier note of changes, and state that it is under CC BY 4.0, with the licence text or a link to it (CC-BY-4.0 s.3(a)(1)).
**Check the waiver:** CC0-1.0 does not waive trademark or patent rights held by the person waiving (CC0-1.0 s.4(a)). Fedora stopped allowing CC0 for code in 2022 for that reason (reported; check).
**Keep the licences apart:** A content licence on documentation does not change the licence of the code it describes. Keep the two licence files separate (good practice).
evidence: Content licence file in the documentation folder
Attribution text for each CC BY release

items.title: Models and weights: choose the licence and use terms
detail: **Read the licence as a licence:** Many model licences carry use limits that open source licences do not. The Llama 4 Community License requires a separate licence above 700 million monthly active users (reported; check).
**Read the use policy with the licence:** An acceptable use policy sets limits on use beyond copyright, so read it together with the licence and record the version reviewed (good practice).
**Do not rely on the label:** OSI's Open Source AI Definition 1.0 (28 October 2024, reported; check) is OSI's view, not law. Judge the release by the licence's actual terms (good practice).
evidence: Model licence and use policy with version and date
Decision on the licence and any use limits

items.title: SDK: separate the SDK licence from the service terms
detail: **Separate the two sets of terms:** The SDK licence governs copying and use of the code (Apache-2.0 s.2). The API service terms govern use of the bank's service, so keep them in separate documents (good practice).
**Ship the licence with the code:** Give each recipient the SDK licence text with the distribution, as Apache-2.0 requires (Apache-2.0 s.4(a)).

**Limit added terms:** Apache-2.0 lets a downstream distributor add terms only for its own modifications or for derivative works as a whole (Apache-2.0 s.4). The bank as licensor is not bound by that rule, but terms that restrict use of the SDK would make it something other than a plain Apache-2.0 release (drafting inference). Keep API restrictions out of the SDK licence.
evidence: SDK licence and API terms, each dated and separate
Licence text shipped with each SDK package

items.title: Set up DCO sign-off and a check in CI
detail: **Require sign-off on every commit:** Each contributor adds a Signed-off-by line, which certifies the Developer Certificate of Origin 1.1 for that commit and records who made the statement (good practice).

**Know what the DCO does not do:** It is not a licence, carries no express patent grant and does not transfer copyright, which needs a writing signed by the owner (17 U.S.C. § 204(a)). Cover those points elsewhere (drafting inference).
**Enforce it in CI:** Set the pipeline to reject any commit without a valid sign-off, and apply the same check to the bank's own repositories so the rule is not optional (good practice).
evidence: CI configuration and a rejected test commit
Contributor guide section on sign-off

items.title: Set up individual and corporate CLAs
detail: **Choose a licence or an assignment:** A contributor who grants a licence keeps ownership, while an assignment moves it. A transfer of copyright ownership is not valid unless an instrument signed by the owner records it (17 U.S.C. § 204(a)).

**Cover the contributor's employer:** Work prepared by an employee within the scope of employment is usually owned by the employer (17 U.S.C. § 201(b)). A corporate CLA signed by an authorised officer should therefore cover staff who contribute for the company (drafting inference).
**Keep the signed forms:** File each signed individual or corporate CLA with the contributor's name, the version signed and the date, before the first accepted change (good practice).
evidence: Signed ICLA or CCLA with version and date
Register of signatories checked against commit authors
wording: [Contributor] grants [Bank] a perpetual, worldwide, non-exclusive, no-charge, royalty-free licence to use, reproduce, modify, distribute and sublicense its Contributions under the [project licence], and confirms that it has the right to do so.

sources.label: Apache Software Foundation individual and corporate CLA models

items.title: Say clearly that outside contributions are not accepted
detail: **State it where contributors look:** Say in the README and contribution notes that outside pull requests and patches are not accepted, so no one spends effort on code the bank will not merge (good practice).
**Close the channels:** Turn off outside pull requests in the repository settings where the host allows it, and say whether issues are read or answered (good practice).

**Do not merge unsolicited code:** A patch sent in without a signed written transfer does not pass copyright to the bank (17 U.S.C. § 204(a)). Decline such patches rather than merge them (good practice).
evidence: README and contribution notes with the statement
Export of the repository settings with the date

items.title: Review inbound contributions for licences and secrets
detail: **Scan each incoming change:** Run secret detection and a licence or snippet scan on every pull request before merge, since copied code can carry a licence the release does not allow (good practice).
**Block on a missing record:** Do not merge until the DCO sign-off or signed CLA is on file for that contributor, and treat a missing record as a blocking defect (good practice).

**Keep notices with matched code:** Where a contribution copies third-party code, keep its licence and notices. Removing copyright management information can engage 17 U.S.C. § 1202(b), and Apache-2.0 s.4(c) requires notices to be retained.
evidence: Scanner report attached to each pull request
Record of the sign-off or CLA check before merge

items.title: Review the bank's patents and pending inventions first
detail: **Check the release date against filings:** Publishing code or a paper can be prior art against the bank's own later patent. An inventor's own disclosure is excluded only if it was made one year or less before the effective filing date (35 U.S.C. § 102(b)(1)).
**Clear the patents before publication:** List each pending invention and each granted patent the code touches, and decide whether to file before the release (good practice).

**Expect an eligibility challenge:** Software claims are tested for an abstract idea and an inventive concept under 35 U.S.C. § 101 and Alice Corp. v. CLS Bank International, 573 U.S. 208 (2014), so the filing should state the technical improvement (drafting inference).
evidence: Patent list with filing status and dates
Release date set against the earliest filing date

sources.label: Alice Corp. v. CLS Bank International

items.title: Understand the patent licence the release or contribution grants
detail: **Apache-2.0 grants a patent licence:** Each contributor licenses the patent claims its contribution necessarily infringes. That licence ends if the licensee sues over patent infringement by the work (Apache-2.0 s.3).

**MIT has no patent clause:** The MIT text grants no express patent licence, so a release under it should not be presented as a patent grant. MPL-2.0 s.2.1(b), by contrast, licenses the contributor's patent claims over its contribution (drafting inference).

**GPL-3.0 conditions its patent licence:** A party conveying a covered work while knowingly relying on a patent licence, where the source is not publicly available free of charge, must make the source so available, give up the licence for that work or extend it to recipients (GPL-3.0 s.11).

**Name the licensed claims:** Where the bank contributes, its patent licence reaches the claims its contribution necessarily infringes, so the approval should say which claims those are (good practice).
evidence: Licence choice with the patent position recorded
List of claims the release or contribution may license

items.title: Clear and register the project name and set a trademark policy
detail: **Clear the name before launch:** Use in commerce of a name likely to cause confusion can infringe a registered mark (15 U.S.C. § 1114(1)), and unregistered names are protected against false designation of origin (15 U.S.C. § 1125(a)).

**Write a trademark policy:** Say who may use the name and logo and for what. Apache-2.0 s.6 grants no mark rights beyond describing the origin of the work, so the policy has to carry the rest (good practice).
**Keep control of licensed marks:** Licensing a mark without quality control can abandon it, and forks have renamed themselves, as OpenSearch, OpenTofu and Valkey did (reported; check).
evidence: Clearance search report and filing receipt
Trademark policy published with the project

sources.label: Barcamerica International USA Trust v. Tyfield Importers, Inc.

items.title: Control use of the bank's own names and logos
detail: **Keep brand use under the brand policy:** Contributors must not use the bank's logo or marks on repositories, packages or talks without approval. Factual attribution of the bank as the source is the only use the policy should allow (good practice).

**Do not rely on the licence for the brand:** Apache-2.0 s.6 gives no permission to use the licensor's trade names or marks beyond describing the origin of the work. The bank's protection rests on its own marks and the Lanham Act (drafting inference).

**Watch for false endorsement:** A project presented as the bank's, or as approved by it, can give rise to a claim for likely confusion as to affiliation, origin, sponsorship or approval (15 U.S.C. § 1125(a)(1)(A)).
evidence: Brand policy extract for open source use
Review log for repository names and logos

items.title: File any patent before the code is published
detail: **Novelty:** Anything made available to the public before the material date is part of the state of the art, so publishing code that embodies an invention can defeat novelty (Cap. 514 s.9B(1)-(2)).

**Narrow relief:** The six-month rule covers only an evident abuse against the applicant, or a display at an official or officially recognised international exhibition (for a standard patent (R), a prescribed exhibition or meeting) (ss.11A, 37B, 109). Do not plan a release on the basis that it applies (good practice).
**Timing:** Decide on filing before the code goes to a public repository, a public demo or a store listing (drafting inference).
evidence: Filing record, or a dated decision not to file, made before first publication
Planned publication dates for the component

items.title: Register project names used as brands in Hong Kong
detail: **Registration:** A registered trade mark is a property right (Cap. 559 s.10(1)). An unregistered name is protected only by passing off, because the Ordinance gives no infringement action for it (s.10(3)), so a name that matters as a brand should be registered in Hong Kong (drafting inference).

**Markings:** Do not describe an unregistered mark as registered, or use the registered symbol for it. Using the word 'registered' in Hong Kong is treated as a representation of registration here, unless it refers to a registration elsewhere that in fact exists for those goods or services (s.94(2)), and a false representation made knowing, or having reason to believe, that it is false is an offence with a level 3 fine (s.94(1)).
**Name search:** Run a search before the name appears in public material, so the bank does not build a brand on a name it cannot register (good practice).
evidence: Name search result, with its date
Trade mark filing receipt, or a dated decision not to file

items.title: Classify encryption and file any notification
detail: **Classify the encryption:** List each function in the released code that encrypts data, and record how the bank classifies it under the Export Administration Regulations before release (good practice).

**Published source is generally outside the EAR:** Software that is published is not subject to the EAR (15 C.F.R. § 734.3(b)(3)) (reported; check the eCFR). Unpublished builds and binaries need their own classification (drafting inference).

**Check for non-standard cryptography:** Publicly available encryption source needs a notification only where it implements non-standard cryptography, sent to BIS and the NSA's ENC Encryption Request Coordinator (15 C.F.R. § 742.15(b)) (reported; check the eCFR).
evidence: Encryption classification record for each component
Notification confirmation, if one was filed

items.title: Check hosting and sanctions questions
detail: **Screen contributors and users:** Check contributors, maintainers and known users against sanctions lists before accepting or hosting their work (good practice).

**Check the hosting platform's position:** Find out whether the platform restricts accounts in sanctioned regions. GitHub restricted such accounts in 2019 and in January 2021 announced an OFAC licence to serve developers in Iran (reported; check).
**Record the outcome:** Keep the screening result, the reviewer and the date with the release file, and screen again when the contributor list changes (good practice).
evidence: Screening log for contributors and maintainers
Hosting platform terms check with the date

items.title: Name maintainers and set response times
detail: **Name at least two maintainers:** Give named maintainers authority to merge changes and to release security fixes, so one departure does not stop the project (good practice).
**Publish response times:** State how quickly the project answers security reports and pull requests, and what it will not support, so users can plan (good practice).

**Name a takedown contact:** Give one person the handling of copyright takedown notices and licence complaints. The notice-and-takedown safe harbour for hosts depends on acting on valid notices and on a designated agent registered with the Copyright Office (17 U.S.C. § 512(c)(1)(C), (c)(2)).
evidence: Maintainer list with merge rights
Published response-time statement

items.title: Publish contribution guide and code of conduct
detail: **Explain the contribution route:** Set out the sign-off or CLA step, the review path and the coding rules, so contributors meet the release's terms on the first attempt (good practice).

**State the licence rule:** Say that contributions are licensed under the outbound licence unless the contributor states otherwise. Apache-2.0 s.5 takes the same position for contributions to Apache-licensed work (good practice).
**Publish a code of conduct:** Name who enforces it and how reports are handled. Staff conduct stays under the bank's own policies, which the code should not replace (drafting inference).
evidence: Published contribution guide with the date
Code of conduct with a named enforcement contact

sources.label: Community governance practice
sources.ref: contribution guide and code of conduct

items.title: Publish a security policy and disclosure route
detail: **Publish a SECURITY.md file:** Give a private route for reporting vulnerabilities and say how and when the bank will respond. Reporters should not need to open a public issue (good practice).

**Agree timing before disclosure:** Coordinate a fix window with the reporter before details are published, and keep the route monitored, since unanswered reports are a common cause of early disclosure (good practice).

**Apply the bank's own secure development rules:** Where the released code is developed in-house by a bank regulated by NYDFS, the written secure development procedures under 23 NYCRR 500.8 cover it (drafting inference).
evidence: Published SECURITY.md with the contact route
Disclosure timeline agreed for the first release

items.title: Foundation hosting: transfer assets and marks under its rules
detail: **Transfer copyright in writing:** Where the foundation takes ownership of the code, rather than a non-exclusive licence to it, the transfer is valid only if an instrument signed by the owner records it (17 U.S.C. § 204(a)). A patent assignment must be in writing, and recording it within three months, or before a later purchase, protects it against later buyers (35 U.S.C. § 261).

**Read the foundation's IP rules:** Foundations such as FINOS, the Linux Foundation and the Apache Software Foundation set their own contribution and IP terms, which may require particular licences or contributor paperwork (good practice).

**Keep the governance terms:** Decide what the bank keeps, such as maintainer seats, marks and an exit right, before the transfer, because the foundation's rules govern the project afterwards (good practice).
evidence: Signed copyright assignment and any recorded patent assignment
Foundation IP policy and the bank's retained rights

items.title: Set up the repository under the bank's organisation account
detail: **Use the organisation account:** Host the repository under the bank's organisation rather than a personal account, so ownership and access survive staff changes (good practice).
**Require two-factor sign-in:** Make two-factor sign-in mandatory for every member with write access, and keep admin rights to a short, named list (good practice).
**Protect the main branch:** Require reviewed pull requests and passing checks before merge, and block force pushes to the release branch (good practice).
evidence: Repository settings export with the date
Admin and write access list

items.title: Agree the announcement and what staff may say
detail: **Review the announcement:** Clear the text with legal and communications before release, so it matches the licence terms and the bank's public statements (good practice).

**Avoid unsupported claims:** Do not describe the code as secure, tested or compliant unless the evidence is on file. A false statement about qualities in commercial advertising can be challenged under 15 U.S.C. § 1125(a)(1)(B).
**Set who speaks for the bank:** Name who may comment publicly, and make clear that personal posts by staff are not the bank's statements (good practice).
evidence: Approved announcement text with reviewers named
List of spokespeople

items.title: Record the final legal sign-off and any conditions
detail: **Record the approval details:** Write down who approved the release, the date, the version and the licence chosen, so the decision can be traced later (good practice).
**List each condition:** For each condition, such as attribution, a CLA on file or a clean scan, name an owner and a deadline. A release with an open condition is not cleared (good practice).
**Set re-review triggers:** State what would reopen the sign-off, such as a new contributor group, a new version with new code or a change in an upstream licence (good practice).
evidence: Signed sign-off record with version and date
Conditions list with owners and deadlines

items.title: Staff contributions: corporate CLA authority and identity
detail: **Confirm who may sign:** Only officers with delegated authority should sign a corporate CLA, and the signatory should match the bank's delegation records (good practice).
**Contribute under the bank identity:** Staff should commit with corporate email addresses, so each DCO sign-off or CLA record can be tied to an employee (good practice).

**Check the employer's ownership:** Work prepared by an employee within the scope of employment is usually owned by the bank (17 U.S.C. § 201(b)). Work done in personal time needs a check against the bank's policy (drafting inference).
evidence: Delegation list for CLA signatories
Contributor identity check record

items.title: Monitor dependencies, vulnerabilities and licence changes
detail: **Track dependency advisories:** Scan the released code's dependencies at each release and follow advisories. Log4Shell (CVE-2021-44228) was disclosed on 9 December 2021, and the xz Utils backdoor (CVE-2024-3094) on 29 March 2024 (good practice).

**Watch for licence changes:** Upstream projects have moved to source-available terms, as HashiCorp did with Terraform on 10 August 2023 and Redis did in March 2024 (reported; check). Each change should trigger a re-review.
**Give the duty an owner:** Name the person and the schedule for monitoring, since the bank keeps this duty after launch (good practice).
evidence: Monitoring schedule and named owner
Advisory and licence-change log

sources.label: NTIA minimum elements for an SBOM (2021)

items.title: Plan archiving or handover if the bank stops maintaining
detail: **Say what happens next:** Publish a notice that says whether the project will be maintained, archived or handed over, and when, so users can plan their own move (good practice).
**Hand over before archiving:** Transfer maintainer rights, and any marks, to a successor before the bank stops, because an archived project receives no fixes (good practice).

**Do not describe archiving as a withdrawal:** A licence already granted is governed by its own terms. Apache-2.0 s.2 makes the copyright licence irrevocable, so the notice should not say that archiving withdraws it (drafting inference).
evidence: Archive or handover notice template
Handover plan with the named successor

items.title: Keep the release file
detail: **Keep the file together:** Store the approvals, scan reports, licence decision and sign-off in one place, indexed by project and version (good practice, in line with OpenChain).

**Keep it for the claim period:** A copyright claim must be brought within three years after it accrues (17 U.S.C. § 507(b)), and patent damages reach back six years (35 U.S.C. § 286). Keep the file for longer than the last release of the code (drafting inference).
**Keep the compliance evidence:** Retain the notices, the attribution file and any source offer that a licence required, because they show compliance if a dispute arises (good practice).
evidence: Release file index with version and dates
Retention rule for the file
