title: Software IP in deals and vendor contracts
oneLiner: Deals and vendor contracts decide who owns the code, which licences survive the transaction, and who pays when title or open source fails.
keyPoints: Software IP shapes both sides of a deal: what the bank acquires or licenses, and whether the code keeps running after signing. Diligence and contracts must answer both.
**Chain of title:** The Copyright Act (17 U.S.C.) requires a signed writing for any transfer of copyright (§ 204(a)), so code without one may still belong to its author.
**Open source:** Copyleft duties usually follow distribution or conveying, and network duties follow modified services, so a scan must match each licence to how the target uses it.
**Assignability:** Non-exclusive patent licences are personal and need consent to transfer unless the licence allows it (In re CFLC, Inc., 89 F.3d 673 (9th Cir. 1996)).
**Vendor contracts:** The bank is usually the licensee, so its contract must cover affiliates, regulators and outsourcers, disclose open source, and allocate IP indemnity risk (good practice).
**Continuity:** The Bankruptcy Code (11 U.S.C.) lets a licensee of IP keep its rights when a debtor rejects the licence (§ 365(n)), but escrow and exit terms do the practical work (good practice).

conceptMap.caption: Diligence finds the defects. Deal documents and vendor contracts decide who carries them.

deepDive.heading: Chain of title in code and patents
deepDive.lede: Ownership follows the author unless a signed writing or a work-made-for-hire rule moves it.

visual.caption: A contractor's copyright assignment can be terminated decades later.

items.label: Assignment signed
items.note: Writing signed by the author (§ 204(a))

items.label: Notice served
items.note: Notice must be recorded in the Copyright Office

items.label: Window opens
items.note: Exact date depends on publication (§ 203(a)(3))

items.label: Window closes
items.note: Termination must take effect within the window

points: **Staff code:** A work an employee prepares within the scope of employment is a [[work made for hire]], so the bank owns it without a further transfer (17 U.S.C. §§ 101, 201(b)).
**Contractor code:** Software from an independent contractor usually falls outside the nine work-for-hire categories, so the bank needs a signed assignment (17 U.S.C. §§ 101, 204(a)).

**Termination:** An author's grant can be terminated in a window that opens about 35 years after the grant, and the agreement cannot override that right (17 U.S.C. § 203(a)(3), (a)(5)). Record which key code is contractor-written (good practice).

**Recordation:** Recording a copyright transfer gives constructive notice only if the work is identified and registered, and it sets priority between conflicting transfers (17 U.S.C. § 205(c)-(d)). The earlier transfer prevails if recorded within one month of execution (two months outside the United States) or before the later transfer is recorded.

**Patents:** The Patent Act (35 U.S.C.) requires assignments in writing. An unrecorded assignment is void against a later purchaser or mortgagee for value without notice, unless it is recorded within three months or before the later purchase (35 U.S.C. § 261).
deepDive.takeaway: Ask for the signed writings, not just a clause saying staff assign their work.

deepDive.heading: Open source in the target's products
deepDive.lede: Licence duties attach to conveying, modification or network use, so the scan must match each licence to the use.

visual.caption: Obligations rise from notices alone to source for network users.

items.label: Permissive (MIT, Apache-2.0)
items.note: Keep licence and notice text; no copyleft

items.label: Weak copyleft (LGPL, MPL-2.0)
items.note: Source for covered files, and relinking for LGPL combined works

items.label: Strong copyleft (GPL)
items.note: Source with conveyed copies

items.label: Network copyleft (AGPL-3.0)
items.note: Source offered to remote users of modified versions

points: **Trigger:** Under the GPL, conveying means propagating copies to others, and mere interaction over a network is not conveying (GPL-3.0 s.0).
**Internal running:** The GPL lets you run and propagate covered works you do not convey without conditions, so code run only inside the bank creates no conveying (GPL-3.0 s.2).

**Network copyleft:** If a modified AGPL-3.0 version is used remotely, it must offer its Corresponding Source to those users (AGPL-3.0 s.13). Running an unmodified version over a network triggers nothing under that section.

**Affiliates:** The FSF treats copying inside one company as not distribution, and says that whether a move to a majority-owned, controlled subsidiary is distribution turns on local copyright law, though US law appears not to treat it as distribution (reported; check). Treat affiliate transfers as distribution unless the licence says otherwise (drafting inference).
**Scan scope:** Manifest-based scanning misses copied and vendored code, so the scan must reach the source tree and the build output (good practice).
deepDive.takeaway: Map each component to how the target conveys or hosts it, not just to its licence name.

deepDive.heading: Patents, trade secrets and litigation
deepDive.lede: Diligence tests whether the target can keep what it claims and whether its own practices create exposure.
points: **Prior use:** A good-faith commercial use in the United States at least a year before the earlier of the effective filing date or a qualifying public disclosure is a defence to infringement, but it must be proved by clear and convincing evidence (35 U.S.C. § 273(a)-(b)).

**Trade secrets:** The Defend Trade Secrets Act (DTSA) protects code only where the owner has taken reasonable measures to keep it secret (18 U.S.C. § 1839(3)(A)). Publishing code under an open licence ends its secrecy (drafting inference).

**Registration:** No US infringement suit over a United States work may be brought until preregistration or registration has been made, or registration has been refused (17 U.S.C. § 411(a)). Statutory damages and fees generally cannot be claimed for infringement that began before a late registration (§ 412).

**Patent defence:** The Federal Circuit reportedly held USAA's mobile deposit claims ineligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101 on 12 June 2025, wiping out about $218 million of jury damages against PNC (reported; check). Banks are frequent patent defendants.
**Export:** Ask whether the target publishes non-standard cryptography in source code, since that needs a notification (15 C.F.R. § 742.15(b)) (reported; check the eCFR).
**AI tools:** Ask whether staff or contractors have pasted confidential code into third-party AI tools, since that can weaken the reasonable measures the target relies on (good practice).
deepDive.takeaway: Treat secrecy and registration as facts to prove, not as assumptions.

deepDive.heading: Asset deal, share deal or licence
deepDive.lede: The structure decides which assignments, consents and recordals the deal needs.

visual.caption: Each structure moves IP and consents differently.

items.label: Asset deal
items.note: Signed writings for copyright (§ 204(a)); recorded patent assignments

items.label: Share deal
items.note: Check change-of-control and assignment clauses

items.label: Licence in
items.note: Non-exclusive patent licences are personal

items.label: SaaS
items.note: Continuity depends on the vendor's terms and exit plan

points: **Asset deal:** Copyright passes only by a signed writing and patents only by a written assignment, so each transfer needs its own document and recordal (17 U.S.C. § 204(a); 35 U.S.C. § 261).
**Share deal:** The target keeps its IP and contracts, so the main risks are existing title defects and clauses that a change of control triggers (good practice).

**Personal licences:** A [[personal licence]] needs the licensor's consent to transfer. Under federal law, a non-exclusive patent licence is personal unless it allows transfer (In re CFLC, Inc., 89 F.3d 673 (9th Cir. 1996)).

**Copyright licences:** Gardner v. Nike, Inc., 279 F.3d 774 (9th Cir. 2002), reportedly held that an exclusive copyright licensee could not sublicense without the owner's consent, a rule since criticised and not followed everywhere (reported; check).

**Entity transactions:** Where a covered work is propagated as a result of a transaction that transfers control of an organisation, substantially all its assets, or subdivides or merges it, each party that receives a copy also receives the predecessor's GPL licences, as an [[entity transaction]] (GPL-3.0 s.10).
deepDive.takeaway: Choose the structure after mapping the consents, not before.

deepDive.heading: Warranties, indemnities and insurance
deepDive.lede: Known defects need specific protection, because general warranties and insurance often leave them out.

items.label: Diligence finding
items.note: Title gap, copyleft use or AI-generated code

items.label: Specific protection
items.note: Named in the agreement and payable whatever the warranty says

items.label: Remediation covenant
items.note: Fix with a deadline, before or after closing

items.label: Closing deliverables
items.note: Signed, recordable and filed after closing

points: **Open source warranty:** Ask the seller to warrant a complete list of components, licences and compliance, and check that list against the scan (good practice).
**Insurance gap:** [[R&W insurance]] usually excludes matters known from diligence, so known open source or title defects need a special indemnity or escrow (reported; check market practice).
**Non-infringement:** Knowledge qualifiers can narrow a non-infringement warranty, so ask for an unqualified title warranty on owned code (good practice).

**AI code:** The Copyright Office says applicants must disclose AI-generated material that is more than de minimis and claim only the human contribution (88 Fed. Reg. 16190). Ask the seller to list AI-generated code.
**Sufficiency:** A sufficiency-of-IP warranty asks whether the business has what it needs to run. Define the business and the key assets in the agreement (good practice).
deepDive.takeaway: Price the known risks through specific terms, and keep the general warranty for the unknown.

deepDive.heading: Vendor contracts where the bank is the licensee
deepDive.lede: The bank's contract should keep its use secure, reveal what sits inside the code, and allow an exit.
points: **Scope:** Grant use by affiliates, outsourcers, contractors and regulators, and check whether the licence covers the bank's customers where they use deliverables (good practice).

**Ownership of deliverables:** Customisations belong to the vendor or its own staff unless the contract assigns them in writing (17 U.S.C. §§ 201(b), 204(a)). State who owns each deliverable and what licence the bank receives.

**Open source disclosure:** Require a list of open source components and licences in each deliverable, a warranty of compliance, and approval before copyleft code enters. Limit the IP indemnity carve-outs to what the bank changes or combines (good practice).

**SBOM and vulnerabilities:** NTIA's 2021 minimum elements list fields such as supplier, component name, version, dependency relationships and timestamp, which make a useful contract template (good practice). Set vulnerability notice times too.

**Bank data and AI:** Prohibit training AI models on bank data without written consent, and bind vendor AI tools to the bank's confidentiality terms (good practice). NYDFS's October 2024 industry letter covers diligence on AI vendors and is guidance, not a new rule.

**Audit exposure:** Licence metrics can change under a vendor's new pricing. Oracle's move to a per-employee Java SE metric from 23 January 2023 is reported as an example (reported; check), so fix the metric and audit terms in the contract.
deepDive.takeaway: Negotiate the audit and metric terms before the vendor's pricing model changes.

deepDive.heading: Bankruptcy and continuity
deepDive.lede: A vendor's insolvency can cut off the bank's licence unless the contract plans for it.

visual.caption: Rejection does not end the licence on its own, but it does not supply the code or the service either.

items.label: Licensor enters bankruptcy
items.note: The licence is at risk

items.label: Debtor rejects the licence
items.note: Rejection is a breach, not a termination

items.label: Bank keeps its IP rights
items.note: Trademarks are outside the Code's definition of IP

items.label: Continuity plan
items.note: Escrow, data export and exit terms

points: **Rejection:** Mission Product Holdings, Inc. v. Tempnology, LLC, 587 U.S. 370 (2019), held that rejecting a contract is a breach, not a termination, so a trademark licensee kept its rights.

**Section 365(n):** A licensee of intellectual property may keep its rights after rejection, under a [[section 365(n) election]] (11 U.S.C. § 365(n)). Trademarks are not in the Code's definition of intellectual property.
**Escrow:** Release events usually include insolvency and failure to support, but a source code deposit alone may not run a SaaS service (reported; check market practice).
**No mandate:** No US bank regulation mandates escrow. The interagency guidance treats business continuity and exit as contract matters (drafting inference).
**SaaS continuity:** Continuity needs the environment, configuration, data export and access credentials, plus a tested exit plan (good practice).
deepDive.takeaway: Test the exit before the vendor needs it.

provisions.title: Ownership of copyright
provisions.summary: Copyright vests first in the author, and an employer is the author of a work made for hire unless a signed writing says otherwise. Ownership can be transferred in whole or in part, and each exclusive right can be owned separately.
provisions.counselNote: The bank's ownership of staff code rests on this section. Separately owned exclusive rights can be carved out in a deal, so check which rights a vendor actually holds.

provisions.title: Execution of transfers of copyright ownership
provisions.summary: A transfer of copyright ownership, other than by operation of law, is not valid unless the instrument, or a note or memorandum of the transfer, is in writing and signed by the owner of the rights conveyed. A non-exclusive licence is not a transfer and needs no writing.
provisions.counselNote: Vendor and contractor code is not the bank's until a signed writing exists. Ownership does not pass by an unsigned statement of work or by conduct alone, so check the signature chain on each key deliverable.

provisions.title: Termination of transfers and licences granted by the author
provisions.summary: An author's grant of a transfer or licence, other than a work made for hire and executed on or after 1 January 1978, can be terminated in a five-year window that opens about 35 years later. Notice must be served 2 to 10 years before the effective date and recorded, and the right applies despite any contrary agreement.
provisions.counselNote: Contractor-written code the bank acquires or licenses can be recaptured by the author decades later. Diligence should record that exposure, because the contract cannot waive it.

provisions.title: Recordation of transfers and other documents
provisions.summary: A transfer can be recorded in the Copyright Office. Recording gives constructive notice once the work is identified and registered. An earlier transfer recorded within one month of execution generally prevails over a later one.
provisions.counselNote: Record copyright assignments at closing or sooner, so that the bank's title is protected against a later transfer by the same author.

provisions.title: Ownership; assignment
provisions.summary: Patent assignments must be in writing. An assignment is void against a later purchaser or mortgagee for value without notice unless it is recorded within three months of its date or before the later purchase.
provisions.counselNote: Patent title in a deal is only as good as its recorded chain. Put recording deadlines on the closing checklist.

provisions.title: Employee inventions: employment agreements
provisions.summary: An employment-agreement clause requiring assignment does not apply to an invention the employee developed entirely on their own time without the employer's equipment, supplies, facilities or trade secret information, unless it relates to the employer's business or results from work for the employer. A clause going further is unenforceable.
provisions.counselNote: Staff side projects in California can fall outside the bank's assignment clause, so diligence should check the target's assignment wording against this section.

provisions.title: Employee inventions: written notification
provisions.summary: An employer whose employment agreement requires assignment of inventions must also give the employee written notice, when the agreement is made, that the agreement does not apply to inventions that qualify under section 2870.
provisions.counselNote: The notice is a duty the employer must meet, so a missing notice is a diligence point (drafting inference: the text does not say the clause then fails).

provisions.title: Immunity for disclosure to officials or an attorney
provisions.summary: Protects confidential disclosure of a trade secret to a government official or an attorney to report a suspected violation of law, and in sealed court filings. Employers must give notice of this immunity in agreements with employees, a term that includes contractors and consultants, for agreements entered into or updated after 11 May 2016, or lose exemplary damages and attorney fees against an employee who was not notified.
provisions.counselNote: Contractor and vendor confidentiality agreements need the notice or a cross-reference to a reporting policy, or the bank loses exemplary damages and fees against them.

provisions.title: Automatic licensing of downstream recipients
provisions.summary: Each conveyance gives the recipient a licence from the original licensors, and no further restrictions may be imposed. An entity transaction, meaning a transfer of control, substantially all assets, a subdivision or a merger, passes the predecessor's licences to each party that receives a copy.
provisions.counselNote: In an acquisition the GPL licences pass to the successor, so the buyer inherits both the rights and any copyleft duties attached to the code it receives.

provisions.title: Grant of patent license
provisions.summary: Each contributor grants a perpetual, royalty-free patent licence to make, use and sell the work, limited to claims the contribution necessarily infringes. The licence terminates for a licensee that sues the work or a contribution for patent infringement.
provisions.counselNote: A bank that starts patent litigation over software it uses under Apache-2.0 can lose the patent licence to that code, so the litigation strategy must consider the open source licences in use.

provisions.title: Non-exclusive patent licences are personal
provisions.summary: The court held that a non-exclusive patent licence is personal under federal law and cannot be transferred without the licensor's consent, unless the licence allows transfer.
provisions.counselNote: Asset deals can need consent for patent licences the target has in-licensed, so check the licence terms before choosing the structure.

provisions.instrument: Mission Product Holdings, Inc. v. Tempnology, LLC
provisions.title: Rejection is breach, not termination
provisions.summary: The Supreme Court held that a debtor's rejection of a contract is a breach, not a termination, so a trademark licensee kept its rights to use the mark.
provisions.counselNote: Rejection does not by itself end the bank's rights as a licensee, but it does not supply the code, data or service, so escrow and exit terms are still needed.

provisions.title: Interagency Guidance on Third-Party Relationships: Risk Management
provisions.summary: The three bank agencies' guidance on managing third-party relationships across their whole life cycle. It is technology-neutral and does not deal with open source as such. The agencies proposed a revision in 2026 (reported; check).
provisions.counselNote: Vendors that supply or support open source are third parties under this guidance, so the agencies expect the bank's diligence and contract terms to reach them (drafting inference).

checklist: **Map the chain of title:** For each core product, list its authors, employers, contractors and vendors, and match each to a signed writing or a work-for-hire basis.
**Demand present assignments:** Require 'hereby assign' wording from contractors and vendors, signed before work starts, and check it against the California notice rules.
**Scan the source, not only the manifests:** Reconcile the scan with the target's component inventory and SBOM, and include vendored and copied code.
**Classify copyleft exposure:** Sort each component by whether the target conveys it, modifies it, or runs it as a network service (AGPL-3.0 s.13).
**Check consents before the structure:** Read each licence and key contract for assignment, change-of-control and sublicensing terms, then choose the asset or share route.
**Prepare recordable assignments:** Draft copyright and patent assignments that identify the works or patents, and set a recordal deadline after closing (17 U.S.C. § 205(d); 35 U.S.C. § 261).
**Negotiate special indemnities:** Ask for a named indemnity or escrow for each known title, open source or AI defect, because R&W insurance usually excludes it.
**Set vendor licence scope:** Cover affiliates, outsourcers and regulators, and require an open source list, an SBOM and vulnerability notice times in each deliverable.
**Plan for vendor failure:** Agree escrow or SaaS exit terms, a tested data export, and the bank's rights if the vendor becomes insolvent.
**Protect bank data from training:** Prohibit vendors from using bank data to train AI models without written consent, and bind their AI tools to the bank's confidentiality terms.
itAngle: **Scan the dependency graph:** Composition-analysis scanners read declared licences from manifests, but copied snippets and vendored code need file or snippet matching, so ask the vendor for its scan settings.
**Generate the SBOM in the build:** An SBOM produced in the pipeline, in SPDX or CycloneDX form, is more reliable than a hand-written list, and each release can be compared with the last.

**Trace authorship in version control:** Match commit identities to employees, contractors and vendors to support the chain-of-title review. Expect gaps where contributors used personal addresses or had no signed agreement.
**Check the release path:** Confirm that the vendor signs its build artefacts and records its dependencies, because the bank inherits the supply-chain risk of the code it acquires (good practice).
**Test the escrow deposit:** Ask for a build of the deposited source in a clean environment. A deposit that cannot be built or run is of little value when the vendor fails (good practice).
virtualBankNotes: **Third-party guidance:** The agencies' 2023 guidance (88 Fed. Reg. 37920) covers the whole life cycle of third-party relationships, so open source vendors and their support contracts fall within the bank's programme (drafting inference).

**Model risk:** Vendor models and AI tools may fall within model risk guidance, which the agencies replaced on 17 April 2026 (Federal Reserve SR 26-2; OCC Bulletin 2026-13). Keep the inventory of models and their owners current.
**NYDFS duties:** For covered entities, 23 NYCRR 500.8 covers evaluating the security of externally developed applications, and 500.11 requires a third-party service provider security policy.
**Examiner requests:** Keep vendor diligence files, SBOMs and open source reviews retrievable and tied to each deal, because examiners ask for them as evidence of control (good practice).

**Partner use of marks:** A fintech partner that uses the bank's name or logo needs quality control. Without it, the mark may be abandoned through naked licensing (Barcamerica International USA Trust v. Tyfield Importers, Inc., 289 F.3d 589 (9th Cir. 2002)) (reported; check).
productNotes: **Bring the vendor build to counsel early:** Send the statement of work and the ownership and licence-back terms before the product team commits to a build, because a contractor's code is not the bank's until a signed writing says so (17 U.S.C. §§ 101, 204(a)).

**Ask vendors for an open source list:** Require the vendor's list of open source components and licences in each deliverable, and approval before any copyleft code enters, so the product team does not inherit a licence it never saw (good practice).

**Agree the licence metric before usage grows:** Licence metrics can change under a vendor's new pricing, as Oracle's move to a per-employee Java SE metric showed, so agree the metric and audit terms before the product scales (reported; check).

**Plan the exit with the contract:** Ask for escrow or SaaS exit terms and a tested data export. A licensee of IP can keep its rights after a vendor's rejection in bankruptcy if it makes the election in 11 U.S.C. § 365(n), but rejection does not supply the code, data or service (drafting inference).
pitfalls: **Relying on the warranty alone:** Known defects are usually excluded from R&W insurance and are hard to recover under a general warranty, so take special indemnities (reported; check).
**Assuming a share deal avoids consents:** A share deal leaves the contracts in place, but change-of-control clauses can still be triggered (good practice).
**Unsigned contractor code:** Code from a contractor without a signed assignment stays with the contractor, whatever the statement of work says (17 U.S.C. § 204(a)).
**Scanning manifests only:** Manifest-level scans miss vendored and copied code, so copyleft can reach a product unnoticed (good practice).
**Treating assignments as permanent:** An author's termination right under 17 U.S.C. § 203 cannot be waived by agreement (§ 203(a)(5)), so plan for it in long-lived code.
**Escrow without a build test:** A deposit that cannot be built or run gives little protection when the vendor fails (good practice; reported market practice).

points: **Employee code only:** the employer's rights under Art. 2(3) cover employee programs, so contractor code still needs its own written transfer in diligence (Directive 2009/24/EC, Art. 2(3)).
**European patents:** the Unified Patent Court opened on 1 June 2023 and litigates many European patents in one forum, so diligence on patent-heavy targets should check UPC exposure.

**Employee code and inventions:** the employer is first owner of employee works, subject to agreement (CDPA 1988 s.11(2)), and of employee inventions made in normal duties (Patents Act 1977 ss.39-41), so trace both.
**Outside the UPC:** the UK is not part of the Unified Patent Court (opened 1 June 2023), so UK patents need separate diligence.

**Employer ownership limit:** the employer owns works made in employment absent agreement (Copyright Act s.13(3)), but Nexus Solutions Inc. v. Krougly, 2026 ONCA 199, limits that to software the employee was asked or expected to write (reported; check).
**Moral rights in deal papers:** moral rights can be waived but not assigned (Copyright Act s.14.1), so deal documents should take waivers from authors.

hongKong.summary: The Copyright Ordinance and the signed writing rule decide who owns code and patents after a deal, and patent and trade mark transactions must be registered to protect the new owner. The two biggest differences from the US position are that a commissioner who does not take the copyright still has an exclusive licence for the purposes both sides could reasonably have contemplated (Cap. 528 s.15(2)), where a US commissioner without an assignment usually has at most an implied non-exclusive licence, and that a new patent or trade mark owner who does not apply to register within six months loses damages and profits for the gap.
keyPoints: **Written transfers only:** An assignment of copyright is not effective unless it is in writing and signed by or for the assignor (Cap. 528 s.101(3)). A patent assignment or mortgage is void unless it is in writing and signed (Cap. 514 s.50(6)), and a trade mark assignment is not effective unless it is in writing and signed (Cap. 559 s.27(4)).

**Commissioned code:** Unless the agreement expressly provides for the copyright, the developer keeps it. The commissioner gets an exclusive licence for the purposes both sides could reasonably have contemplated when the work was commissioned, and can restrain any exploitation it could reasonably object to (Cap. 528 s.15(2)(a)-(b)). The Ordinance has no work-made-for-hire rule for commissioned works, so the commissioner does not own the code by default (drafting inference).

**Employee code:** The employer is the first owner of copyright in a work made by an employee in the course of employment, subject to any contrary agreement (Cap. 528 s.14(1)). Subject to any agreement to the contrary, the employer must pay an agreed or tribunal-set award if the work is exploited in a way neither side could have contemplated (Cap. 528 s.14(2)).

**Six-month registration window:** A new patent owner or exclusive licensee who does not apply to register the transaction within six months cannot recover damages or an account of profits for infringements in the gap, unless the court is satisfied that registration was not practicable within the six months and that an application was made as soon as practicable afterwards (Cap. 514 s.87). The trade mark rule is the same (Cap. 559 s.29(4)).

**Insolvent vendors:** A liquidator may disclaim unprofitable contracts with the court's leave, within 12 months of the winding up starting (Cap. 32 s.268(1)). The other party may then apply to rescind the contract and prove for damages (Cap. 32 s.268(5)). There is no Hong Kong equivalent of US Bankruptcy Code s.365(n) (reported; check).

sections.heading: Chain of title in code, patents and marks
sections.lede: Ownership moves only as the law and the signed paperwork allow, so the bank's title is only as good as its documents.
points: **Author starts as owner:** Commissioned code stays with the developer unless the contract expressly says who owns the copyright (Cap. 528 s.15(1)). Look for an express assignment in every development contract (drafting inference).

**Employee work:** The employer owns copyright in an employee's work made in the course of employment, unless the contract says otherwise (Cap. 528 s.14(1)). Inventions made in the course of an employee's normal duties, or of duties outside them that were specifically assigned, belong to the employer, as between them, where the circumstances in either case were such that an invention might reasonably be expected to result from those duties (Cap. 514 s.57(1)(a)); a special obligation to further the employer's interests also brings the invention within s.57(1)(b).
**Assignment formality:** An assignment of copyright is not effective unless it is in writing and signed by or for the assignor (Cap. 528 s.101(3)). An oral transfer does not pass the copyright.

**Prior licences:** A licence granted by the copyright owner binds a later owner, unless the buyer took in good faith, for valuable consideration and without notice of the licence (Cap. 528 s.101(4)). Licences already granted over acquired code generally pass with it (drafting inference).
**Exclusive copyright licences:** An exclusive licensee has the same rights as an assignee for matters after the grant, but not against the copyright owner (Cap. 528 s.112(1)-(2)).
sections.takeaway: Before signing, make the contract name the owner of each deliverable, and attach an express assignment for any code the bank must own (good practice).

sections.heading: Registration of patent and trade mark transactions
sections.lede: A transfer or licence that is not registered loses priority to a later party, and it also limits the damages the new owner can claim.
points: **Registrable transactions:** Assignments, licences, mortgages and court transfers of a patent can be registered (Cap. 514 s.52(3)). An earlier unregistered transaction loses to a later one if the later party acquired without knowledge of it and the earlier one was not registered (Cap. 514 s.52(1)-(2)).

**Six-month clock:** The six months run from the date of the transaction, and the new owner must apply to register within that time to keep its claim for damages or an account of profits (Cap. 514 s.87(a)).

**Trade mark rule:** A registrable trade mark transaction is ineffective against a later party with a conflicting interest who acquired it without knowledge, until an application to register is made (Cap. 559 s.29(3)(a)).

**Right to sue for past infringement:** An assignment of a patent, or an exclusive patent licence, may pass the right to sue for earlier infringements, so the deal should say whether that right passes (Cap. 514 s.50(7)).

**Practicability exception:** The six-month bar does not apply if the court is satisfied that registration was not practicable in time and an application was made as soon as practicable afterwards (Cap. 514 s.87(b); Cap. 559 s.29(4)(b)).
sections.takeaway: Diary the six-month deadline from each completion date, and file every registrable patent or trade mark transaction within it (good practice).

sections.heading: Vendor contracts and continuity
sections.lede: Vendor contracts must deal with personal data, and a vendor's insolvency can take away the bank's rights under a contract.
points: **Processor retention:** A bank that gives processing to a data processor, in Hong Kong or abroad, must adopt contractual or other means to stop the processor keeping the personal data longer than needed (Cap. 486 Sch. 1, DPP 2(3)).

**Processor security:** The bank must adopt contractual or other means to prevent unauthorized or accidental access, processing, erasure, loss or use of personal data transferred to a processor (Cap. 486 Sch. 1, DPP 4(2)).

**Disclaimer in a winding up:** The liquidator can disclaim an onerous contract or other unsaleable property, and the disclaimer ends the company's rights and liabilities in it (Cap. 32 s.268(1)-(2)).

**The other party's remedy:** After a disclaimer, the counterparty can apply to the court to rescind the contract and to recover damages, which can be proved as a debt in the winding up (Cap. 32 s.268(5), (7)).
sections.takeaway: Write into the vendor contract the processor's deletion and return duties, security terms, step-in rights and a transition period, so the bank keeps service and its data if the vendor fails (good practice).

provisions.title: Commissioned works
provisions.summary: Copyright in a commissioned work belongs to whoever the agreement expressly entitles; without such a term the author owns it (s.13). Either way the person who commissioned the work has an exclusive licence for the purposes both sides could reasonably have contemplated, and may restrain uses it could reasonably object to.
provisions.counselNote: This is the first clause to check in any development contract. A bank that pays for code gets a licence, not ownership, unless the contract assigns the copyright.

provisions.title: Employee works
provisions.summary: The employer is the first owner of copyright in a work made by an employee in the course of employment, subject to any agreement to the contrary. Where the work is exploited in a way neither side could have contemplated, the employer must pay the employee an award.
provisions.counselNote: Employee code belongs to the bank by default, but the unforeseen-exploitation award can be claimed. Staff contracts and IP policies should cover both points.

provisions.title: Assignment and licences
provisions.summary: An assignment of copyright must be in writing and signed by or for the assignor. A licence from the copyright owner binds later owners, except a good-faith purchaser for value who had no notice of it.
provisions.counselNote: The writing rule is the first test of any acquisition of code. In a share or asset deal, existing licences over the code usually bind the buyer.

provisions.title: Patent transactions and the right to sue
provisions.summary: An assignment or mortgage of a patent, or a right in one, is void unless it is in writing and signed. An assignment or exclusive licence can also pass the right to sue for earlier infringements.
provisions.counselNote: Patent deal documents should say expressly whether past infringement claims pass with the patent. Silence leaves the point open.

provisions.title: Priority of unregistered transactions
provisions.summary: An unregistered patent transaction loses to a later transaction if the later party acquired its rights without knowing of the earlier one and the earlier one was not registered. The rule covers assignments, licences, mortgages and court transfers.
provisions.counselNote: A patent chain of title needs a registration check at each step. A buyer who does not search the register can lose to a later transferee.

provisions.title: Registration and infringement damages
provisions.summary: A new patent owner or exclusive licensee who does not apply to register within six months cannot recover damages or an account of profits for infringements in the gap. The court can excuse the delay if registration was not practicable and an application followed as soon as practicable.
provisions.counselNote: The six-month deadline is short for a bank that buys patents from many sellers. Build it into the completion checklist.

provisions.title: Registration of trade mark transactions
provisions.summary: An unregistered trade mark transaction is ineffective against a later party with a conflicting interest who acquired it without knowledge. A new owner or licensee who does not apply to register within six months cannot recover damages or an account of profits for the gap.
provisions.counselNote: Trade mark licences to group companies or vendors are registrable transactions. Missing the registration step weakens both the licence and the remedies.

provisions.title: Data processors: no longer than necessary
provisions.summary: A data user who engages a data processor, in or outside Hong Kong, must adopt contractual or other means to stop the processor keeping the personal data longer than needed for the processing. A data processor is a person who processes data on another's behalf and not for its own purposes.
provisions.counselNote: The Ordinance requires contractual or other means to stop retention beyond what is necessary, so retention and return-or-erase terms are the usual way to meet that duty. If the vendor uses the data for its own purposes, it is not a processor and the analysis changes.

provisions.title: Security terms for data processors
provisions.summary: A data user who engages a data processor must adopt contractual or other means to prevent unauthorized or accidental access, processing, erasure, loss or use of the data transferred for processing.
provisions.counselNote: Every vendor that touches customer data, including cloud and SaaS providers, must be bound by contractual or other means that prevent unauthorized access, processing, erasure, loss or use, and a contract is the usual way to do that.

provisions.instrument: Companies (Winding Up and Miscellaneous Provisions) Ordinance (Cap. 32)
provisions.title: Disclaimer of onerous property in a winding up
provisions.summary: With the court's leave, a liquidator may disclaim unprofitable contracts and other unsaleable property within 12 months. The disclaimer ends the company's rights and liabilities in the property but does not otherwise affect third parties. The other party may apply to rescind the contract.
provisions.counselNote: A vendor's insolvency can end the bank's licence unless the contract plans for it. The Ordinance does not name licences as such, so the bank's position depends on the contract's terms.

bankNotes: **Outsourcing discussion:** The HKMA expects an authorised institution to discuss with it, in advance, any plan to outsource a banking-related business area, including back office work, or to change the scope of that outsourcing (SA-2, para 1.3.2). This is guidance, not law, but the bank should build the discussion into its procurement timetable.

**Vendor clauses:** SA-2 is the main source of the HKMA's expected vendor clauses, including supervisory inspection and access rights. The digital bank guideline adds its own paragraph on advance discussion of material outsourcing.

**Operational resilience:** The HKMA's operational resilience module (OR-2) expects vendor dependencies to be mapped and critical operations tested in severe scenarios. The framework deadline of 31 May 2026 has passed, so examiners are likely to test these points.

glossary.definition: The documented sequence of transfers from each author or inventor to the current owner. Diligence checks each link, including the signed writings that a copyright transfer requires (17 U.S.C. § 204(a)).
A work prepared by an employee within the scope of employment, or a commissioned work in one of nine listed categories where both parties sign a written agreement to that effect (17 U.S.C. § 101).

A transaction that transfers control of an organisation or substantially all its assets, subdivides it or merges it. Under GPL-3.0 s.10, where a covered work is propagated as a result of the transaction, each party that receives a copy also receives its predecessor's licences.
Filing a transfer with the Copyright Office (17 U.S.C. § 205) or the USPTO (35 U.S.C. § 261) to give notice and set priority against later transfers.
The five-year period in which an author may end a grant the author made, which opens about 35 years after the grant (17 U.S.C. § 203(a)(3)).

Representations and warranties insurance, a policy that covers losses from breaches of a seller's warranties. It usually excludes matters the buyer knew from diligence (reported; check market practice).
A seller's promise to pay for a named risk, such as a copyleft finding or a title defect, whether or not a general warranty was breached (good practice).
A deposit of source code with a neutral agent, released on defined events such as insolvency or failure to support (reported; check market practice).

The licensee's right under 11 U.S.C. § 365(n) to keep its rights in licensed intellectual property after the debtor-licensor rejects the licence in bankruptcy. Trademarks are not in the Code's definition of intellectual property.

A licence the licensee cannot transfer without the licensor's consent. Under federal law, non-exclusive patent licences are personal unless the licence allows transfer (In re CFLC, Inc., 89 F.3d 673 (9th Cir. 1996)).
An assignment, licence, mortgage or similar transfer that can be entered on the register. Registration protects the new party against later transactions (Cap. 514 s.52; Cap. 559 s.29(2)).
A literary, dramatic, musical or artistic work, or a film, made by an employee in the course of employment. The employer is its first copyright owner unless agreed otherwise (Cap. 528 s.14(1)).

intro: **What this is:** counsel's checklist for software IP diligence when the bank buys a company or a code base, licenses software in, signs up to a SaaS service, has software built for it, or builds with a fintech partner.

**Start with the profile:** say what the deal is, what the target or vendor has, and what the bank needs from it. The list then shows only the steps that apply. Ticks, open issues and notes stay in this browser and go into the downloads.

**What it protects:** the bank's right to use and own what it pays for, free of claims, open source surprises and vendor failure. The M&A volume covers the asset purchase agreement itself; the Canadian and Hong Kong volumes cover vendor contracts in those places.
**Model wording:** some steps carry wording to adapt (representations, indemnities, contract clauses). It is a template to fit to the deal.

options.label: Buying a code base or other assets
A fintech partnership or joint build
Its product offered as a hosted service
Code from contractors or offshore teams
Staff in California or similar states
Custom work the bank will own
Bank data used to build, train or improve
Hong Kong law applies
options.hint: The bank, its developers or the users are in Hong Kong

phases.title: Scope
phases.lede: Agree what the deal covers and what matters to the bank's plan before asking for documents.

phases.title: Ownership and chain of title
phases.lede: Check that every person who wrote the code or made the inventions has passed their rights to the target, in writing.

phases.title: Open source
phases.lede: Find out what open source is in the products and whether the way they are shipped or hosted has set off duties.

phases.title: Patents
phases.lede: Check what the patents are worth, what binds them, and what others' patents threaten the business.

phases.title: Trade secrets and people
phases.lede: Trade secrets survive only if they were kept secret and the people who know them are bound.

phases.title: AI and data
phases.lede: Models, training data and AI-written code carry their own licence and authorship questions.

phases.title: Contracts and licences
phases.lede: Read the licences in and out, and set the terms the bank needs as a licensee.

phases.title: Security and regulators
phases.lede: A bank also needs secure development evidence, export checks and access for its regulators.

phases.title: Deal terms
phases.lede: Turn what diligence found into representations, indemnities and price.

phases.title: Closing and after
phases.lede: Collect the deliverables, record the transfers and bring the target under the bank's policies.

items.title: Map the software and IP the deal covers
detail: **List the assets:** Map each product, code base, patent, mark, data set and model in the deal, and the entity that holds it. Rights often sit in a subsidiary or with a contractor, not the named seller (good practice).

**Trace title:** Record how each code base reached its holder. Copyright vests first in the author and passes to a new owner by a signed writing, unless the transfer is by operation of law (17 U.S.C. § 201(a); § 204(a)).
**Note the licences:** Mark which open source and inbound licences each product depends on, since the target can transfer only the rights it holds (good practice).
evidence: Asset map: product, code base, patent, mark, data, model
Holder and transfer route for each item

items.title: Send the IP data-room request list
detail: **Ask for title:** Request each registration, assignment and licence, with dates and signatures, so that title can be checked rather than described (good practice).
**Ask for the code:** Request the open source inventory, scan reports, contractor agreements and invention assignments, and say which code each one covers (good practice).
**Ask for claims:** Request any IP claim, demand letter, settlement and open source compliance notice within the look-back period the deal sets (good practice).
evidence: Standard request list issued with the NDA
Response log with dates and reviewer

sources.label: Deal practice
sources.note: Drafting inference; not a source of law.

items.title: Decide what is material to the bank's plan
detail: **Tie it to the plan:** Decide which products and code matter most to the bank's use, such as a critical service or a customer app, and focus the review there (good practice).
**Set the triggers:** Set the risks that make an item material, such as copyleft in shipped code or a patent on a core process (good practice).
**Record the cut-off:** Write down what was left out and why, so that a later question about an unreviewed item can be answered (good practice).
evidence: Materiality note signed by Legal and the business owner
Out-of-scope list with reasons

sources.label: Interagency Guidance on Third-Party Relationships (2023)
sources.note: Agencies expect risk management across the life cycle; the guidance is not law.

sources.label: Deal practice
sources.note: Drafting inference; not a source of law.

items.title: Check registrations, assignments and recordals
detail: **Search the registers:** Search the USPTO assignment records and the Copyright Office records for each registered patent, mark and work, and match each hit to the asset map (good practice).

**Check patent recording:** An assignment of a patent is void against a later buyer or mortgagee for value without notice unless it is recorded within three months or before that later purchase (35 U.S.C. § 261).
**Check copyright recordals:** Recording gives constructive notice only if the document identifies the work and the work is registered, and priority turns on timing (17 U.S.C. § 205(c)-(d)).
evidence: USPTO assignment search printout with date
Copyright Office search and recordal certificates

items.title: Check employee invention and confidentiality agreements
detail: **Read the wording:** Check that each agreement says "hereby assign" or equivalent. A promise to assign in future leaves title with the inventor until a separate assignment is signed (FilmTec Corp. v. Allied-Signal, Inc., 939 F.2d 1568 (Fed. Cir. 1991)).
**Check the signatures:** Confirm a signed agreement is on file for every current and former engineer named in the code history (good practice).
**Flag state limits:** Note each employee in a state with an invention-assignment limit, since a clause can be unenforceable as to some inventions (Cal. Lab. Code § 2870(b)).
evidence: Signed agreement for each named inventor and author
Gap list of missing or promise-only wording

sources.label: Board of Trustees of Leland Stanford Junior University v. Roche Molecular Systems, Inc.

items.title: Check state-law limits and notices
detail: **Read the Labor Code:** California stops an assignment clause from reaching an invention made on the employee's own time, without employer resources, unless it relates to the business or results from work for it (Cal. Lab. Code § 2870(a)).
**Check the notices:** The employer must give written notice of § 2870 when the agreement is made, and may require confidential disclosure of inventions under § 2871 (Cal. Lab. Code § 2872; § 2871).

**Check other states:** Several other states have similar statutes with different terms, so check each one for an employee in that state before relying on the clause (Minn. Stat. § 181.78; reported; check).
evidence: List of employees by state with the clause in force
Notice of § 2870 in each agreement

items.title: Check contractor and offshore assignments
detail: **Do not rely on work-for-hire:** Software from an independent contractor usually falls outside the nine categories of commissioned work, so "work made for hire" wording alone is weak (17 U.S.C. § 101).
**Require a signed writing:** A transfer of copyright is not valid unless the owner signs a writing, so get a signed assignment from each contractor (17 U.S.C. § 204(a)).
**Check local law:** Offshore developers may be subject to their own rules on assignment and moral rights, so ask local counsel to confirm the chain of title (good practice).
evidence: Signed assignment for each contractor and team
Local-law note for each offshore team

sources.label: Deal practice
sources.note: Drafting inference; not a source of law.

items.title: Check founders assigned pre-formation IP
detail: **Find early code:** Search the code history for work done before the company was formed, and for side projects by the founders (good practice).
**Check the assignment:** Confirm a signed assignment of that work to the target exists. Without one, the founder may still own the copyright (17 U.S.C. §§ 201(a), 204(a)).
**Check joint work:** Where two people wrote code together, ask whether it is a joint work, since joint authors are co-owners of the copyright (17 U.S.C. § 201(a)).
evidence: Code history search with pre-formation commits flagged
Signed founder assignments

items.title: Look for joint ownership and co-development
detail: **Spot co-ownership:** Joint authors of a code base are co-owners of its copyright, so check whether a partner or other company contributed code to the asset (17 U.S.C. § 201(a)).

**Check the licensing rules:** Co-owners of copyright may each license non-exclusively but must account for profits, and an exclusive licence needs all of them (Davis v. Blige, 505 F.3d 90 (2d Cir. 2007); reported; check).
**Check patents:** Absent agreement, each joint owner of a patent may make, use and sell it without the others' consent or accounting (35 U.S.C. § 262).
evidence: Co-ownership map with contribution record
Co-owner licence and accounting terms

items.title: Check government rights and funding terms
detail: **Check funding:** Ask whether government money paid for any code or invention, since a government contract can set rights in the work (reported; check the data-rights and patent clauses).
**Note the title point:** Bayh-Dole does not vest title in a federal contractor's invention, so the contractor's own assignment still matters (Stanford v. Roche, 563 U.S. 776 (2011)).
**Read each contract:** Check the data-rights and patent terms in each government contract, since the terms vary from one contract to the next (reported; check).
evidence: Funding source list by product and code
Data-rights and patent clause extracts

sources.label: Board of Trustees of Leland Stanford Junior University v. Roche Molecular Systems, Inc.

items.title: Use written, signed assignments for each IP right
detail: **Copyright:** An assignment of copyright is effective only in writing signed by or for the assignor (Cap. 528 s.101(3)).

**Patents and marks:** A patent assignment or mortgage is void unless it is in writing and signed (Cap. 514 s.50(6)), and a trade mark assignment is not effective unless it is in writing and signed (Cap. 559 s.27(4)).

**Commissioned code:** Commissioned code stays with the author unless the agreement expressly says who owns it (Cap. 528 s.15(1)), so the deal should name the owner in the contract (drafting inference).
evidence: Signed assignment for each IP right on the target's register
Schedule of contractor and commissioned code, with the contract reference for each

items.title: Get a code scan and the open source inventory
detail: **Scan the code:** Run a software composition scan on the target's code and builds, and compare the result with the target's own list (good practice).

**Require an SBOM:** Ask for a software bill of materials with the supplier, component, version, dependency and timestamp fields that the NTIA minimum elements list (NTIA, Minimum Elements for an SBOM, 2021).
**Test the results:** Check the scan against the code itself, since scanners can miss copied snippets and report unknown versions (good practice).
evidence: Scanner report with version and date
SBOM with the NTIA data fields

sources.label: NTIA minimum elements for an SBOM (2021)
sources.ref: Minimum Elements for a Software Bill of Materials, 12 July 2021

sources.label: Deal practice
sources.note: Drafting inference; not a source of law.

items.title: Assess copyleft in products that are distributed
detail: **Find the trigger:** GPL duties start when the bank conveys a covered work, such as giving copies to customers. Internal use is not conveying (GPL-3.0 s.0; s.6).

**Check the source offer:** A GPL-3.0 product that conveys object code must provide the Corresponding Source by one of the methods in s.6: for a download, equivalent access to the source from the same place; for object code in a physical product, the source on a durable medium or a written offer valid for at least three years and for as long as spare parts or customer support are offered; plus installation information for User Products (GPL-3.0 s.6).
**Check the whole work:** Under GPL-2.0, code that contains or is derived from the program must be licensed as a whole under the GPL when distributed (GPL-2.0 s.2(b)).
evidence: Distribution map: which products convey which licensed code
Source offer and notice text per product

items.title: Assess AGPL and SSPL in hosted services
detail: **Check the modification:** AGPL-3.0 s.13 applies only if the program is modified and users interact with it over a network. Running an unmodified version triggers nothing under s.13 (AGPL-3.0 s.13).
**Offer the source:** A modified AGPL program offered online must prominently give remote users an opportunity to receive its Corresponding Source at no charge (AGPL-3.0 s.13).
**Read SSPL carefully:** SSPL-1.0 requires release of the service source code for a program offered as a service. OSI does not treat SSPL as open source (SSPL-1.0 s.13; reported; check).
evidence: Modification record for each hosted AGPL program
Source-offer link or notice in the service

sources.label: GNU Affero General Public License v3.0

items.title: Agree remediation before or after closing
detail: **Fix before close:** Require the target to remove or re-license non-compliant code before closing. A GPL-2.0 breach can end the licence, and GPL-3.0 reinstates a licence provisionally once the breach stops, permanently if the holder gives no notice within 60 days after the breach stops, or if a first notice is cured within 30 days (GPL-2.0 s.4; GPL-3.0 s.8).
**Hold money back:** Where a fix falls after closing, use a price escrow or special indemnity sized to the cost of rewriting or re-licensing the code (good practice).
**Write the duty:** Set a covenant with a date, a named owner and evidence of completion, so the obligation can be enforced (good practice).
evidence: Remediation covenant with dates and owner
Escrow or special indemnity terms

sources.label: Deal practice
sources.note: Drafting inference; not a source of law.

items.title: Ask the vendor for its open source list and obligations
detail: **Ask for the list:** Require the vendor to name each open source component in what it delivers, with its licence and version, and to flag any copyleft or source-available term (good practice).
**Make it a duty:** Put the list and the vendor's compliance duty in the contract, with an audit right and a duty to report changes (good practice).
**Check the flow-down:** Make sure the vendor meets each licence's own duties, such as notices and source offers, since a breach can still reach the bank if it ships the code (good practice).
evidence: Vendor component list with licence and version
Contract clause on compliance duties and audit right

sources.label: Interagency Guidance on Third-Party Relationships (2023)
sources.note: Agencies expect vendor oversight; the guidance is not law.

items.title: Review the portfolio, status, fees and encumbrances
detail: **Check status:** Confirm each application or patent is live and its fees are paid. A patent term runs 20 years from the US filing date, subject to the payment of fees (35 U.S.C. § 154(a)(2)).

**Check encumbrances:** Search for security interests, pledges and licences on each patent. An interest that works as an assignment or grant is void against a later mortgagee for value without notice unless recorded (35 U.S.C. § 261).

**Read the claims:** Read the claims of the software patents the bank needs, since eligibility under § 101 is a live question for software (Alice Corp. v. CLS Bank International, 573 U.S. 208 (2014)).
evidence: Portfolio schedule with status and next fee date
Encumbrance search log by patent

sources.label: Alice Corp. v. CLS Bank International

items.title: Assess freedom to operate for key products
detail: **Name the products:** Limit the search to the products that matter most to the bank's plan, and map the patent claims to the features those products use (good practice).
**Expect suits:** Banks are frequent patent defendants. USAA's mobile deposit claims were held ineligible under § 101 against PNC Bank in June 2025 (35 U.S.C. § 101; reported; check).

**Weigh the defences:** Note any claim open to a § 101 challenge, and whether a prior commercial use defence under 35 U.S.C. § 273 applies to in-house processes, which needs clear and convincing evidence (35 U.S.C. § 273).
evidence: Claim chart for each key product
Defence notes: § 101 and § 273 prior use

items.title: Review patent licences and change-of-control terms
detail: **Check assignability:** A non-exclusive patent licence is personal and cannot be assigned without the licensor's consent, unless the licence allows it (In re CFLC, Inc., 89 F.3d 673 (9th Cir. 1996)).

**Read change of control:** A deal can trigger a consent right or termination even where the licence is silent on assignment, so read the change-of-control terms against the deal structure (drafting inference).
**Check the licensed scope:** Confirm which affiliates, products and fields the licence covers, since a licence held by the target may not reach the bank after closing (good practice).
evidence: Licence schedule with consent and change-of-control terms
Consent requests and replies

sources.label: Deal practice
sources.note: Drafting inference; not a source of law.

items.title: Check pledges, OIN membership and standards commitments
detail: **Check pledges:** Find any covenant not to sue, pledge or standards commitment the target gave on its patents, since it may bind the bank once it owns the portfolio (good practice).
**Check the OIN:** The Open Invention Network holds a royalty-free non-aggression commitment covering a defined list of Linux packages, so confirm whether the target joined it (reported; check).
**Check standards terms:** A commitment made to a standards body can limit the licence terms the bank may set, so read it before relying on the portfolio (good practice).
evidence: List of pledges, covenants and standards commitments
OIN membership confirmation, if any

sources.label: Deal practice
sources.note: Drafting inference; not a source of law.

items.title: Assess trade secret protection
detail: **Test reasonable measures:** A trade secret needs the owner's reasonable measures to keep it secret, and independent economic value from not being generally known (18 U.S.C. § 1839(3)(A)-(B)).
**Check access controls:** Review how source code is stored, who can read it and what confidentiality terms those people signed. Weak controls weaken the trade secret claim (good practice).

**Note the reverse engineering point:** Reverse engineering and independent derivation do not count as improper means, so a rival's lawful rebuild of a shipped product is not misappropriation under the DTSA (18 U.S.C. § 1839(6)(B)), though a licence term barring reverse engineering can still bind a licensee (Bowers v. Baystate Technologies, Inc., 320 F.3d 1317 (Fed. Cir. 2003)).
evidence: Trade secret register with access controls
Confidentiality terms for each holder

sources.label: Deal practice
sources.note: Drafting inference; not a source of law.

items.title: Check key departures and confidentiality exposure
detail: **List key people:** Identify engineers and founders who are leaving or have left, and check what confidentiality and assignment terms each signed (good practice).

**Check the immunity notice:** Agreements with employees and contractors that govern trade secrets, entered into or updated after 11 May 2016, must give notice of the DTSA immunity or cross-refer to a policy. Without it, exemplary damages and fees are unavailable against that person (18 U.S.C. § 1833(b)(3)-(4)).

**Check non-competes:** California voids employee non-competes, so a key engineer based there cannot be bound by one as an employee, though a founder or other owner who sells the business or their whole ownership interest in it can agree one with the buyer (Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code §§ 16600, 16601).
evidence: Departure list with agreements on file
Notice text in each confidentiality agreement

items.title: Check who holds source code
detail: **List the holders:** Record every person, contractor, escrow agent and hosting provider that holds a copy of the source code or its credentials, and the terms that cover each (good practice).
**Cut stale access:** Check that former staff and contractors no longer hold repository access or keys, and that access is logged (good practice).
**Check escrow:** Where a third party holds a copy, confirm the release conditions and the verification steps in the escrow agreement (good practice).
evidence: Holder list with access and terms
Access removal confirmation with date

sources.label: Deal practice
sources.note: Drafting inference; not a source of law.

items.title: Inventory AI models, training data and their licences
detail: **List the models:** Record each AI model, its version, its provider and where it runs, including models inside the target's products and build tools (good practice).

**Read the model terms:** Check each licence and use policy, since open weights often carry user thresholds and use limits, such as the separate Llama 4 licence above 700 million monthly active users (reported; check).

**Trace the training data:** Ask what each model was trained on and under what rights, since courts have treated training on pirated copies differently from training on lawfully acquired books (Bartz v. Anthropic PBC, N.D. Cal. 23 June 2025).

**Do not assume open means free:** Treat a model as open source only if it meets the OSI Open Source AI Definition 1.0, and read its licence before assuming it can be used commercially (reported; check).
evidence: AI model register: name, version, provider, licence
Training data source and rights statement per model

sources.label: Open Source Initiative
sources.note: Reported; check. A definition of open source, not a statute.

sources.label: Deal practice
sources.note: Drafting inference; not a source of law.

items.title: Assess AI-generated code and authorship claims
detail: **Test authorship:** Ask which code an AI tool generated and how much human selection or change a person made, since a prompt alone gives too little control to make the user the author (Copyright Office, Part 2, 29 January 2025).

**Check registrations:** Confirm that any copyright claim covers only human authorship and discloses more-than-de minimis AI material, since the Copyright Act requires human authorship for registration (88 Fed. Reg. 16190; Thaler v. Perlmutter, 130 F.4th 1039 (D.C. Cir. 2025)).

**Watch for verbatim output:** Scan AI-suggested code for copies of licensed code, since a copy keeps its licence duties even where a copyright management information claim fails (Doe v. GitHub, Inc., reported; check).
evidence: List of AI-assisted code with the tool and settings used
Scan report for matches to licensed code

sources.label: Copyright Office
sources.ref: Copyright and Artificial Intelligence, Part 2: Copyrightability (29 January 2025)
sources.note: Guidance, not law; the answer is case by case.

items.title: Confirm no training or improvement on bank data without consent
detail: **Set the default:** Require the target or vendor to confirm in writing that bank data is not used to train, tune or improve any model without the bank's consent (good practice).
**Limit retention:** Confirm that prompts, outputs and bank data are kept only as long as the contract allows, and that the vendor deletes them on request (good practice).

**Expect supervisory questions:** Examiners may ask how the bank oversees AI vendors, since NYDFS's 2024 letter covers diligence on AI vendors and the bank's own AI use (NYDFS industry letter, 16 October 2024).
evidence: Vendor written confirmation on use of bank data
Retention and deletion terms in the contract

sources.label: NYDFS industry letter
sources.ref: Cybersecurity Risks Arising from Artificial Intelligence (16 October 2024)

sources.label: Deal practice
sources.note: Drafting inference; not a source of law.

items.title: Review inbound licences: scope, transfer, change of control
detail: **Find the transfer terms:** Check whether each inbound licence passes to the buyer on an asset sale or change of control, since a non-exclusive patent licence is personal and not assignable without the licensor's consent unless its terms allow it (In re CFLC, Inc., 89 F.3d 673 (9th Cir. 1996)).

**Read the copyright licences:** A non-exclusive copyright licence needs no signed writing, but courts have generally treated it as personal, so it passes only with the licensor's consent unless its terms allow transfer (Harris v. Emus Records Corp., 734 F.2d 1329 (9th Cir. 1984)), while an exclusive grant is a transfer that needs a signed writing (17 U.S.C. §§ 101, 204(a)).
**Record the consents:** List each licence that needs consent and whether its terms treat a change of control as an assignment (good practice).
evidence: Inbound licence schedule: scope, term, transfer and consent terms
Consent list for each licence

sources.label: Deal practice
sources.note: Drafting inference; not a source of law.

items.title: Review customer licences: exclusivity, source access, MFN
detail: **Look for exclusivity:** Find any exclusive licence or option the target granted, since an exclusive grant is a transfer of copyright ownership that must be in a signed writing and can limit the bank's plans for that code (17 U.S.C. §§ 101, 204(a)).
**Check source access:** Find each promise to give customers or escrow agents source code or rights to modify it, since such promises can limit what the bank can keep proprietary (good practice).
**Check most-favoured terms:** Record any most-favoured-customer clause that could reach the bank's own deal terms after closing (good practice).
evidence: Outbound licence register with exclusivity and source terms
List of most-favoured and source-access promises

sources.label: Deal practice
sources.note: Drafting inference; not a source of law.

items.title: Licence scope: affiliates, outsourcers, regulators, recovery sites
detail: **Name who may use it:** Check that the licence covers affiliates, outsourcers, auditors, regulators and recovery sites, since a licence limited to one entity can bar use by the people who run the bank (good practice).

**Check sublicensing:** Confirm the right to let outsourcers use the software for the bank, since courts have not applied one rule on whether a licensee may sublicense without consent (Gardner v. Nike, Inc., 279 F.3d 774 (9th Cir. 2002); reported; check).

**Match the vendor guidance:** Interagency guidance expects a bank to oversee the parties its vendors use, so the licence should let the bank see and approve them (Interagency Guidance, 88 Fed. Reg. 37920, 9 June 2023).
evidence: Scope matrix: entity, site and user types covered
Sublicence and subcontractor consent terms

sources.label: Deal practice
sources.note: Drafting inference; not a source of law.

items.title: Ownership of customisations and deliverables
detail: **Assign the work:** Check that the vendor assigns custom code to the bank in a signed writing, since software from an independent contractor usually falls outside the work made for hire categories (17 U.S.C. §§ 101, 201(b), 204(a)).
**Carve out the vendor's tools:** Exclude the vendor's pre-existing libraries and tools from the assignment, and take a licence to them so the bank can keep running the code (good practice).
**Limit the licence-back:** Where the vendor keeps rights to general know-how, limit the licence to the bank's own use and confirm that it survives termination (good practice).
evidence: Assignment clause and signed instrument
Schedule of vendor pre-existing materials and licence-back

items.title: IP indemnity: scope, carve-outs and control of defence
detail: **Test the carve-outs:** Check whether the indemnity excludes modifications, combinations and open source, since those carve-outs often leave the bank exposed to the claims it most needs covered (good practice).
**Control the defence:** Require the vendor to defend and settle claims, with the bank's consent to any admission or payment and a right for the bank to step in if the vendor stops (good practice).
**Check AI output cover:** Some vendors make output indemnities depend on settings such as content filters being on, so record any such condition as a contract term (reported; check).
evidence: Indemnity clause with carve-outs and defence control
Conditions tied to AI filters or settings

sources.label: Deal practice
sources.note: Drafting inference; not a source of law.

items.title: Source code escrow or SaaS continuity
detail: **Set the release events:** Check that release events cover insolvency, ceasing business and failure to support, and that the bank may use the code when one occurs (market practice; reported; check).

**Test the deposit:** Verify that the deposit builds and runs, and include the environment, configuration, data and credentials needed, since source code alone rarely keeps a SaaS service running (market practice; reported).

**Plan for the vendor's bankruptcy:** A licensee of intellectual property can keep its rights when the licensor rejects the licence (11 U.S.C. § 365(n)), and Tempnology held that rejection is a breach, so a trademark licensee keeps its rights (587 U.S. 370 (2019)).
evidence: Escrow or continuity agreement with release events
Verification report on the test build and deposit

sources.label: Bankruptcy Code (11 U.S.C.)
sources.note: Statute; no text held in the volume's extracts.

sources.label: Mission Product Holdings, Inc. v. Tempnology, LLC

items.title: Licence audit and metric risk
detail: **Read the metric:** Record how the licence counts use, such as per employee, per core or per installation, and whether the vendor can audit the bank's counts (good practice).
**Check the audit clause:** Limit audits by notice period, frequency, an independent auditor and a confidentiality duty, and fix how any shortfall is priced (good practice).
**Expect metric changes:** Oracle moved its Java SE subscriptions to a per-employee metric from 23 January 2023, an example of how a metric change can produce a large claim (reported; check).
evidence: Licence metric schedule and count method
Audit clause and result of the last audit

sources.label: Deal practice
sources.note: Drafting inference; not a source of law.

items.title: SBOM, vulnerability notice and secure development duties
detail: **Ask for an SBOM:** Require an SBOM that carries the NTIA minimum data fields: supplier, component, version, other identifiers, dependency relationships, author and timestamp (NTIA, 12 July 2021).

**Set notice duties:** Require prompt notice of known vulnerabilities and a fix timeline (good practice). For NYDFS-regulated firms, 23 NYCRR 500.11 requires a written third-party service provider policy, which these terms can support (drafting inference).

**Write in secure development:** Require the vendor to follow secure development practice and give evidence on request, as 23 NYCRR 500.8 contemplates for externally developed applications (good practice).
evidence: SBOM in SPDX or CycloneDX format, dated
Vulnerability notice and fix commitments in the contract

sources.label: NTIA minimum elements for an SBOM (2021)
sources.ref: The Minimum Elements for a Software Bill of Materials (12 July 2021)

sources.label: Deal practice
sources.note: Drafting inference; not a source of law.

items.title: AI terms: no training on bank data; output indemnity
detail: **Ban training on bank data:** Write into the contract that prompts, outputs and bank data are not used to train or improve models, and that the vendor flows the same limit down to its own providers (good practice).
**Ask for an output indemnity:** Ask whether the vendor defends claims over generated output, and on what conditions such as filters or settings (good practice; reported; check).

**Test the training rights:** Fair use for training turns on the facts, as the 2025 decisions in Bartz and Kadrey v. Meta Platforms, Inc. show, so ask the vendor for its training data rights position (Copyright Office, Part 3, pre-publication, 9 May 2025).
evidence: AI terms schedule: training, output and retention
Vendor indemnity letter and its conditions

sources.label: Copyright Office
sources.ref: Copyright and Artificial Intelligence, Part 3: Generative AI Training (pre-publication, 9 May 2025)
sources.note: Pre-publication version; check for a final text.

sources.label: Deal practice
sources.note: Drafting inference; not a source of law.

items.title: Test exclusion clauses and service terms against Hong Kong law
detail: **IP carve-out:** Sections 7 to 9 of the Control of Exemption Clauses Ordinance do not apply to a contract so far as it relates to the creation or transfer of a right or interest in IP (Cap. 71 Sch. 1 para 1(c)). The services, support or hosting parts of the same contract stay within those sections, so the carve-out must be applied clause by clause (drafting inference).

**Services:** Where a service contract is silent, the supplier must use reasonable care and skill (Cap. 457 s.5), and where the customer deals as consumer the supplier cannot exclude those liabilities by a contract term (s.8(1)).
**Consumers:** The court's unconscionability powers apply only where a party deals as consumer (Cap. 458 s.5(1)), so a business-to-business software licence would not generally fall within them.
evidence: Clause mark-up showing which parts sit inside the IP carve-out
Services terms checked against the implied terms

items.title: Discuss outsourcing with the HKMA and cover IP disputes in arbitration
detail: **Regulator:** Where the deal outsources a banking-related function to the vendor, discuss the outsourcing with the HKMA in advance (HKMA SA-2 para 1.3.2). This is guidance, not law.

**Arbitration:** IP disputes, including those over ownership, validity, infringement and transactions in an IP right, can be arbitrated (Cap. 609 s.103C, s.103D(1)). An award binds the parties and those claiming through them (s.73(1)).

**Licensees:** A third-party licensee does not become a person claiming through a party just by holding a licence, although its contract and operation-of-law rights are preserved (s.103E(2)-(3)). Check the clause that binds each licensee (drafting inference).
evidence: Record of the HKMA discussion, with its date
Arbitration clause showing that IP disputes are in its scope

items.title: Review secure development evidence and testing
detail: **Ask for the framework:** Ask whether the vendor follows NIST SP 800-218, the Secure Software Development Framework v1.1 (February 2022), and for evidence of its practice (NIST SP 800-218).

**Read the testing record:** Review test reports, code review records and fix times for critical findings, since NYDFS 500.8 requires written procedures for assessing the security of externally developed applications (23 NYCRR 500.8).

**Do not rely on federal forms:** Federal secure software attestation duties have been rolled back (reported; check), so ask the vendor for its own evidence rather than a federal form (good practice).
evidence: Secure development questionnaire and evidence pack
Test and review records with dates

sources.label: NIST
sources.ref: SP 800-218, Secure Software Development Framework v1.1 (February 2022)

items.title: Check export classification and sanctions
detail: **Classify the code:** Classify any encryption in the target's code, since published software is outside the EAR but unpublished code can remain subject to it (15 C.F.R. §§ 734.3(b)(3), 734.7; reported; check).
