**Screen the parties:** Screen the target's customers, contributors and hosting providers against sanctions lists, since OFAC sanctions reach dealings with sanctioned persons and places (GitHub restricted sanctioned-region accounts in 2019; reported).
**Price the exposure:** Where the target has dealt in sanctioned places, ask for a written disclosure and a specific indemnity before closing (good practice).
evidence: Export classification record for encryption and controlled items
Sanctions screen of customers and hosts

sources.label: Deal practice
sources.note: Drafting inference; not a source of law.

items.title: Secure regulator access and audit rights
detail: **Write in access:** Require the vendor to give the bank, its auditors and its regulators access to records, sites and staff, and to cooperate in examinations (good practice).
**Match the guidance:** The interagency third-party guidance expects a bank to manage risk across the life of a vendor relationship, including audit and oversight (88 Fed. Reg. 37920, 9 June 2023).
**Limit subcontracting:** Require notice of, and a right to object to, material subcontractors, and extend the same access to them (good practice).
evidence: Audit and regulator access clause
Subcontractor list with notice terms

sources.label: Deal practice
sources.note: Drafting inference; not a source of law.

items.title: Draft IP reps: ownership, non-infringement, open source, sufficiency
detail: **Cover title:** Give a representation that the target owns each asset free of liens, and that every author and contractor assigned rights in a signed writing (17 U.S.C. § 204(a)).

**Cover infringement and open source:** Give representations on infringement, on open source use and on copyleft in distributed code, and tie any knowledge qualifier to a named group of people (good practice).
**Cover sufficiency:** Give a representation that the assets are sufficient for the business as run today, and state what it leaves out (good practice).
evidence: Draft IP representations with the knowledge group named
Disclosure schedule keyed to the asset map

sources.label: Deal practice
sources.note: Drafting inference; not a source of law.

items.title: Price known issues into special indemnities
detail: **Find the known issues:** List each open source breach, claim or contributor dispute found in diligence, since general representations do not usually cover what the buyer already knows (good practice).

**Set a special indemnity:** Give the buyer a specific indemnity for each known issue, with its own cap, survival period and control of defence, rather than relying on general representations (good practice).
**Hold back the cost:** Consider an escrow or price holdback sized to the remediation cost, released once remediation is verified (good practice).
evidence: Known-issues list with exposure estimate
Special indemnity terms and holdback amount

sources.label: Deal practice
sources.note: Market practice; not a source of law.

items.title: Check R&W insurance exclusions
detail: **Read the exclusions:** Check whether the policy excludes matters known from diligence, such as open source non-compliance, since insurers usually exclude what diligence has already found (reported; check).
**Size the gap:** Map each excluded matter to a special indemnity or price adjustment, so the buyer does not carry an uninsured known risk (good practice).
**Check the claims period:** Confirm the retention and the period for claims, since a short period can end cover before a copyleft or title defect surfaces (good practice).
evidence: Policy exclusion list reviewed against the findings
Gap table: excluded matter and remedy

items.title: Add AI and data reps: training data, AI code, bank data
detail: **Cover training data:** State that the target holds the rights to the training data it used, or has a licence covering that use, since fair use for training depends on the facts (Bartz v. Anthropic PBC, N.D. Cal. 23 June 2025).
**Cover AI-generated code:** State how the target uses AI-generated code, and that it has checked such code for matches to licensed code (good practice).
**Cover bank data:** State that no bank data or confidential information was used to train or improve a model, with a look-back period that matches the deal (good practice).
evidence: AI and data representations with disclosure schedule
Training data list and rights statement

items.title: Review IP claims, letters and settlements
detail: **Collect every claim:** Collect demand letters, lawsuits, petitions for inter partes review and settlements, with dates and status, since a settled claim can still limit the target's use of code (35 U.S.C. § 311; good practice).
**Check the settlements:** Read each settlement for licences, covenants not to sue and change-of-control terms that would pass to the buyer (good practice).
**Test any takedown history:** Check each takedown notice the target sent or received, since a knowing material misrepresentation in a notice creates liability (17 U.S.C. § 512(f)).
evidence: Claims register with status and dates
Settlement terms and any licence granted

items.title: Protect continuity if the vendor becomes insolvent
detail: **Disclaimer:** In a winding up, a liquidator may, with leave of the court and within 12 months of the winding up starting, disclaim unprofitable contracts and other property that is not readily saleable because of onerous obligations (Cap. 32 s.268(1)).
**No IP rule:** Hong Kong has no equivalent of US 11 U.S.C. § 365(n), which protects licensees of IP when a licensor goes bankrupt (reported; check).
**Protection:** Negotiate escrow, step-in and transition terms, so the bank can keep running the code if the vendor fails (good practice).
evidence: Escrow, step-in and transition clauses in the vendor contract
Vendor financial health review at signing

sources.label: Companies (Winding Up and Miscellaneous Provisions) Ordinance (Cap. 32)

items.title: List closing deliverables: assignments, source, credentials
detail: **Get the copyright assignments:** Obtain signed assignments from the seller, its founders and its contractors, since a transfer of copyright ownership is not valid unless it is in a signed writing (17 U.S.C. § 204(a)).

**Get the patent assignments:** Obtain signed patent assignments in writing, and consider a certificate of acknowledgment, which the statute treats as prima facie evidence of execution rather than a condition of recording (35 U.S.C. § 261).
**Hand over the code:** Deliver the repositories, build credentials, signing keys and escrow access, and check each against the asset map before payment (good practice).
evidence: Signed assignment set with recordal forms
Source and credential handover receipt

sources.label: Deal practice
sources.note: Drafting inference; not a source of law.

items.title: Record assignments at the USPTO and Copyright Office
detail: **Record patents within three months:** Record each patent assignment at the USPTO within three months of its date, or before any later purchase or mortgage, since an unrecorded assignment is void against a later purchaser or mortgagee for value without notice (35 U.S.C. § 261).

**Record copyright transfers:** Identify each work and register it, since recordal in the Copyright Office gives constructive notice only then, and priority between conflicting transfers turns on timing (17 U.S.C. § 205(c)-(d)).
**Keep the proof:** Keep the filing receipts and recordal certificates with the closing file, with the date of each filing (good practice).
evidence: USPTO recordal notice for each patent
Copyright Office recordation certificate

sources.label: Deal practice
sources.note: Drafting inference; not a source of law.

items.title: Obtain third-party consents
detail: **List the consents:** List each licence and contract that needs consent for the transfer or change of control, with its consent deadline (good practice).

**Get them in writing:** Obtain each consent in writing before closing, since a non-exclusive patent licence cannot pass without the licensor's consent unless its terms allow it (In re CFLC, Inc., 89 F.3d 673 (9th Cir. 1996)).
**Plan for refusal:** Where a consent is refused, price the loss into the deal or agree a workaround before signing, since the licence does not follow the asset (good practice).
evidence: Consent tracker with status and deadline
Signed consent letters

sources.note: Drafting inference; not a source of law.

items.title: Bring the target under the bank's open source policy
detail: **Set the baseline:** Record each open source component the target ships or runs, and bring it under the bank's approval process, since copyleft in shipped code can require source offers (OpenChain, ISO/IEC 5230; good practice).
**Fix the gaps first:** Schedule remediation for diligence findings, such as copyleft components in distributed code or unknown licences, before that code is released or combined (good practice).
**Set owners and dates:** Name an owner for each product and a review date for each component, and track both in the integration plan (good practice).

Open source inventory after integration

items.title: Keep the diligence file and track remediation
detail: **Keep the full file:** Keep the request list, responses, scans, findings, decisions and signed documents in one file, with dates and reviewers, since the file shows what the bank knew when it signed (good practice).
**Track each fix:** Log each remediation item with an owner, a due date and proof of closure, and report open items to the business owner (good practice).
**Set retention:** Keep the file for as long as claims under the deal can be brought, and longer where a claim or regulator inquiry is open (good practice).
evidence: Diligence file index with reviewer and dates
Remediation log with proof of closure

items.title: Register patent and trade mark transactions within 6 months
detail: **Patents:** A new owner or exclusive licensee who does not apply to register within 6 months cannot recover damages or an account of profits for the gap (Cap. 514 s.87(a)-(b)). An earlier unregistered transaction can also lose out to a later one (s.52(1)).

**Trade marks:** A new owner or licensee who does not apply to register the transaction within 6 months loses damages and profits for the gap, and the transaction is ineffective against a conflicting interest acquired in ignorance of it (Cap. 559 s.29(3)-(4)).

**Past infringement:** An assignment of a patent, or an exclusive patent licence, can carry the right to sue for earlier infringement (Cap. 514 s.50(7)). Decide and state expressly whether that right passes.
evidence: Registration filing dated within 6 months of each transaction
Clause stating whether the right to sue for past infringement passes

title: AI-generated code and models
oneLiner: AI output needs a human author, only people can be inventors, and training and licence questions are still being decided case by case.
keyPoints: Copyright protects human-authored work. The D.C. Circuit held in Thaler v. Perlmutter, 130 F.4th 1039 (D.C. Cir. 2025), that the Copyright Act (17 U.S.C. § 102(a)) requires human authorship for registration, so the bank must document its own contribution.

**Inventorship:** Under the Patent Act (35 U.S.C. § 100(f)), inventors are individuals, and the Federal Circuit held in Thaler v. Vidal, 43 F.4th 1207 (Fed. Cir. 2022), that an AI system cannot be one. Name the people who conceived each claim.

**Training:** Early decisions point in different directions on whether training is [[fair use]]. Training on lawfully acquired books was held fair use in Bartz, but building a library from pirated copies was not (17 U.S.C. § 107).

**Output:** AI tools can reproduce licensed code word for word. The copy keeps its licence, so distributing it brings the licence conditions with it, and stripping notices can engage [[copyright management information]] rules (17 U.S.C. § 1202(b)).

**Model licences:** A released model comes under its own licence, which can limit use, set user thresholds and restrict outputs. Read it as a contract and do not assume it is open source (good practice).
**Bank overlay:** Model risk, third-party and NYDFS guidance all reach the AI tools and models the bank uses, and prompts can expose trade secrets and customer data (good practice).

deepDive.heading: Human authorship
deepDive.lede: Copyright needs a human author, and AI output adds a documentation duty.

visual.caption: The Copyright Office's disclosure approach for works with AI material.

items.label: Identify AI material
items.note: Find output that is more than de minimis

items.label: Check the human contribution
items.note: Expression, selection, arrangement or modification

items.label: Disclose and exclude
items.note: Disclose the AI material and leave it out of the claim

items.label: Describe the human author's role
items.note: Set out what the person contributed in the application

points: **Statutory base:** The Copyright Act (17 U.S.C.) protects original works of authorship (§ 102(a)) and vests copyright initially in the author or authors (§ 201(a)).

**Registration:** The D.C. Circuit held in Thaler v. Perlmutter, 130 F.4th 1039 (D.C. Cir. 2025), that the Act requires human authorship for registration. Certiorari was reported denied on 2 March 2026 (reported; check).
**Prompts alone:** The Copyright Office says prompts alone do not give the user enough control to become an author (Copyright Office, Part 2, 29 January 2025).

**Human expression:** Human expression perceptible in the output, and human selection, arrangement or modification of AI material, can be protected. The Office decides case by case (Copyright Office, Part 2, 29 January 2025).

**Disclosure:** The Office's policy statement says applicants must disclose AI-generated material that is more than de minimis, exclude it from the claim and describe the human contribution (88 Fed. Reg. 16190).
deepDive.takeaway: Keep dated records of who wrote, selected and edited each part of the code. A later registration or dispute will turn on them.

deepDive.heading: Inventorship and patents
deepDive.lede: Patent rights attach to people, not tools.
points: **Definition:** The Patent Act defines an inventor as the individual, or the individuals jointly, who invented the claimed subject matter (35 U.S.C. § 100(f)).
**Natural persons:** In Thaler v. Vidal, 43 F.4th 1207 (Fed. Cir. 2022), the court held that only natural persons can be inventors, so an AI system cannot be named.

**USPTO practice:** The USPTO's February 2024 guidance on AI-assisted inventions was reported to have been rescinded in November 2025. Its replacement treats AI as a tool and looks for conception by a natural person (reported; check).
**Declarations:** The Patent Act requires each individual inventor to sign an oath or declaration for the application, unless a substitute statement is permitted (35 U.S.C. § 115(a), (d)).
**Inventor record:** Record which staff member conceived each claimed step, and which steps an AI tool suggested, so the inventor list can be defended (good practice).

deepDive.heading: Training and fair use
deepDive.lede: Whether training is fair use depends on where the copies came from and what the output does to the market.

visual.caption: How the courts have treated training so far. Decisions are fact-specific.

items.label: Lawfully acquired books
items.note: Training was held fair use (N.D. Cal. 2025)

items.label: Pirated central library
items.note: Building it was held not fair use

items.label: Non-generative competitor
items.note: Copying headnotes was held not fair use (D. Del. 2025)

items.label: Market dilution
items.note: Could defeat fair use in other cases

points: **Bartz:** In Bartz v. Anthropic PBC (N.D. Cal. 23 June 2025), the court held that training on lawfully acquired books was fair use, but that building a central library from pirated copies was not.
**Settlement:** A USD 1.5 billion class settlement in Bartz was reported to have received final approval in July 2026 (reported; check).

**Kadrey:** In Kadrey v. Meta Platforms, Inc. (N.D. Cal. 25 June 2025), summary judgment went to Meta on fair use on the record presented. The court stressed that market dilution could defeat fair use in other cases.

**Ross:** In Thomson Reuters Enterprise Centre GmbH v. Ross Intelligence Inc. (D. Del. February 2025), the court held that copying Westlaw headnotes to train a non-generative legal research tool was not fair use. The Third Circuit was reported to have affirmed on interlocutory appeal on 29 September 2026 (reported; check).

**Copyright Office:** Its pre-publication Part 3 report (9 May 2025) says training is not automatically fair use and can weigh against it where outputs compete with or dilute the market. It is guidance, not law. A final version is not confirmed (reported; check).

**Open cases:** The New York Times case, now part of In re OpenAI Copyright Infringement Litigation (S.D.N.Y.), largely survived the motions to dismiss in March 2025. Fair use summary judgment motions were reported pending as at November 2026 (reported; check).

deepDive.heading: Code tools, output and licence compliance
deepDive.lede: AI tools can reproduce licensed code verbatim, and the licence conditions apply to the copy when it is distributed or conveyed.

visual.caption: Risk layers, from the copy in the codebase to the claim against the bank.

items.label: Verbatim licensed code
items.note: The copy carries the licence it came under

items.label: Licence conditions
items.note: Source offers on distribution, licence copy and notices

items.label: Copyright management information
items.note: Stripping licence headers can engage the statute

items.label: Vendor indemnity
items.note: A defence, often conditional on using the vendor's filters

points: **Doe v. GitHub:** In Doe v. GitHub, Inc. (GitHub Copilot), most claims were dismissed in the district court. The Ninth Circuit was reported on 16 September 2026 to have affirmed dismissal of the § 1202(b) claim (reported; check).

**Identicality:** The Ninth Circuit was reported to have rejected a strict identicality rule, but to have found that the outputs alleged were not copies with copyright management information removed (reported; check).

**CMI:** Copyright management information includes the terms and conditions for use of a work (17 U.S.C. § 1202(c)(6)). Removing it without authority breaches § 1202(b) only where done intentionally and with knowledge that it will induce, enable, facilitate or conceal infringement; reasonable grounds to know suffice only for civil remedies.

**Licence duties:** Distributing GPL-licensed code in object form requires the Corresponding Source, offered by one of the routes the licence allows (GPL-3.0 s.6). Apache-2.0 requires anyone who distributes the work to give recipients a copy of the licence and to mark modified files with notices (Apache-2.0 s.4).

**Vendor cover:** Microsoft's Copilot Copyright Commitment, announced in September 2023 and renamed the Customer Copyright Commitment, defends customers against IP claims over output if they use the built-in content filters and guardrails (reported; check).
**Limit of cover:** A vendor defence does not cure a licence breach in the bank's own code, so treat it as a backstop for claims and not as clearance (good practice).

deepDive.heading: Model licences
deepDive.lede: A model licence is a contract that sets use limits. Open weights are not automatically open source.
points: **Community licences:** Meta's Llama 4 Community License (5 April 2025) requires licensees whose products had over 700 million monthly active users to take a separate licence from Meta, and Meta's Acceptable Use Policy applies (reported; check).
**Patent terms:** A model released under Apache-2.0 carries the licence's patent grant, which ends for a licensee who sues over patent infringement by the work (Apache-2.0 s.3).
**Open source AI:** The [[Open Source AI Definition]] 1.0, published by the OSI on 28 October 2024, sets out the OSI's view of open source AI. It is a view, not law (reported; check).
**Review before use:** Check the use field, user thresholds, acceptable use rules and any patent terms before the bank deploys a model (good practice).

deepDive.heading: A policy for AI coding tools
deepDive.lede: Set the rules before engineers adopt the tools, not after.

visual.caption: A minimum policy path for AI-assisted code. Each step is good practice rather than a legal requirement.

items.label: Approve tools and models
items.note: Name them, and the data each may see

items.label: Lock down settings
items.note: No training on bank code or prompts, settings logged

items.label: Review every change
items.note: A named engineer approves AI-written code before merge

items.label: Record provenance and scan
items.note: Tag AI-assisted commits and run licence and similarity scans

points: **Approved list:** Name the AI coding tools and models staff may use, and the data each may see (good practice).
**Settings:** Lock down any setting that lets a vendor use bank code or prompts for training, and keep a record of the configuration (good practice).
**Human review:** A named engineer reviews AI-generated code before merge, which also builds the human-authorship record (good practice).
**Provenance:** Tag AI-assisted changes in version control and keep records of the tool and model used, so questions about who wrote what can be answered later (good practice).
**Exceptions:** The policy owner decides exceptions in writing and reviews the approved list at least once a year (good practice).

provisions.title: Subject matter of copyright: In general
provisions.summary: Copyright protects original works of authorship fixed in a tangible medium, including literary works such as computer programs (§ 102(a)). It does not extend to any idea, procedure, process, system or method of operation, however it is embodied (§ 102(b)).
provisions.counselNote: Copyright in AI-assisted code depends on whether a person's original expression is in it, so the bank's evidence of human expression matters.

provisions.title: Limitations on exclusive rights: Fair use
provisions.summary: The fair use of a work is not an infringement. Courts weigh the purpose and character of the use, the nature of the work, the amount used and the effect of the use on the market for the work.
provisions.counselNote: Training disputes are fought on these four factors, so keep the source and acquisition record for any training data the bank uses or commissions.

provisions.title: Ownership of copyright
provisions.summary: Copyright vests first in the author or authors of a work (§ 201(a)). For a work made for hire, the employer or commissioning party is treated as the author and owns the rights unless the parties agree otherwise in a signed writing (§ 201(b)).
provisions.counselNote: Whether the bank owns staff or vendor output depends on authorship and the contract, so write AI-assisted deliverables into employment and vendor terms.

provisions.title: Integrity of copyright management information
provisions.summary: It bans knowingly giving false copyright management information (CMI) with intent to induce, enable, facilitate or conceal infringement. It also bars intentionally removing or altering CMI without authority, where the person knows that this will induce, enable, facilitate or conceal infringement (for civil claims, reasonable grounds to know is enough) (§ 1202(a), (b)). CMI includes the terms and conditions for use of a work (§ 1202(c)(6)).
provisions.counselNote: Licence headers and notices in code may count as CMI (reported; courts have accepted this in some cases), so an AI rewrite or refactor that strips them can create exposure beyond the licence itself.

provisions.title: Definitions
provisions.summary: An inventor is the individual, or the individuals collectively in a joint invention, who invented or discovered the subject matter of the invention (§ 100(f)).
provisions.counselNote: Read with Thaler v. Vidal, the definition leaves no room to name an AI system as an inventor. The inventor list must name the people who conceived each claim.

provisions.title: Inventor's oath or declaration
provisions.summary: Each individual who is an inventor or joint inventor of a claimed invention must execute an oath or declaration for the application, subject to limited substitute statements (§ 115(a), (d)).
provisions.counselNote: A declaration is a signed statement by a person, so each inventor should have a record of their own contribution before signing.

provisions.title: Conveying Non-Source Forms
provisions.summary: Object code may be conveyed only if the machine-readable Corresponding Source is also provided, by one of the routes the licence lists, such as, for object code in a physical product, a written offer valid for at least three years and for as long as spare parts or customer support are offered.
provisions.counselNote: A verbatim AI copy of GPL code in a shipped product brings these duties with it, which is why scanning AI output before release matters.

provisions.title: Grant of Patent License
provisions.summary: Each contributor grants a royalty-free patent licence to the work, limited to claims the contribution necessarily infringes. The licence ends for a licensee who starts patent litigation alleging that the work infringes.
provisions.counselNote: Code or a model released under Apache-2.0 carries this patent grant, so check it when the bank adopts or publishes such material.

provisions.title: Copyright registration requires human authorship
provisions.summary: The D.C. Circuit held on 18 March 2025 that the Copyright Act requires human authorship for registration. Certiorari was reported denied on 2 March 2026 (reported; check).
provisions.counselNote: A registration claim over output without human authorship will fail, so the bank's registration strategy must rest on documented human contribution.

provisions.title: Only natural persons can be inventors
provisions.summary: The Federal Circuit held that only natural persons can be inventors under the Patent Act, so an AI system cannot be named as an inventor.
provisions.counselNote: Filings that name an AI tool, or that leave out the staff who conceived a claimed step, are exposed to inventorship challenges (good practice).

provisions.instrument: Thomson Reuters Enterprise Centre GmbH v. Ross Intelligence Inc.
provisions.title: Copying to train a non-generative legal research tool was not fair use
provisions.summary: The court held that copying Westlaw headnotes to train a non-generative legal research tool was not fair use. The Third Circuit was reported to have affirmed on interlocutory appeal on 29 September 2026 (reported; check).
provisions.counselNote: A bank that trains a model on third-party material for a competing product faces this reasoning, but the ruling turns on its facts, and the Third Circuit's affirmance does not decide training for generative AI (reported; check).

provisions.title: Copyright and Artificial Intelligence, Part 2: Copyrightability
provisions.summary: The Office says prompts alone do not give the user enough control to become an author. Human expression perceptible in the output, and human selection, arrangement or modification of AI material, can be protected, case by case.
provisions.counselNote: This is the Office's practical test for AI-assisted code, so the record of human edits is the evidence the bank will need.

provisions.title: Cybersecurity Risks Arising from Artificial Intelligence and Strategies to Combat Related Risks
provisions.summary: The letter is guidance, not a new rule. It covers AI-enabled threats and covered entities' own use of AI, including diligence on AI vendors.
provisions.counselNote: New York-regulated banks should fold AI vendor diligence into their third-party programme and cybersecurity policy (good practice).

checklist: **Confirm the human-authorship record:** Keep dated evidence of who wrote, selected and edited each AI-assisted part of released or registered code.
**Approve AI coding tools by name:** Publish the list of tools and models, the data each may see and the settings that must be applied.
**Block training on bank code and prompts:** Get written confirmation from each vendor that bank code, prompts and outputs are not used to train models, and check the settings.
**Require human review:** Make a named engineer approve AI-written changes before merge, and record that approval.
**Scan AI-assisted code before release:** Run licence, snippet and vulnerability scans, and act on copyleft or unknown-origin matches.
**Keep licence headers:** Forbid stripping or rewriting copyright notices and licence headers when code is generated or refactored.
**Check model licences before use:** Review use restrictions, user thresholds, patent terms and acceptable use rules, and record the decision.
**Name inventors on the facts:** Record who conceived each claimed step before filing, and keep AI systems off the inventor list.
**Assess AI vendors:** Run them through the third-party risk process, covering indemnity conditions, data use, audit rights and exit terms.
**Refresh the model inventory:** Add AI tools and models that inform decisions or customers to the bank's model inventory and risk tiering.
itAngle: **Tag AI-assisted commits:** Use commit trailers or a repository label for AI-assisted changes, so the review and provenance record can be pulled from history (good practice).
**Scan for verbatim copies:** Snippet and similarity scanners catch code that came from public repositories. Run them in CI on AI-assisted pull requests, not only at release (good practice).
**Put models in the bill of materials:** Record model names, versions and licences alongside library components, using SPDX or CycloneDX fields where they fit (good practice).
**Keep prompts under retention rules:** Prompts and tool logs can hold customer data or code. Apply the same retention and access rules as for other development logs (good practice).
**Pin model versions:** A model update can change output and licence terms, so pin the version in use and record it as a dependency (good practice).
virtualBankNotes: **Model risk:** The model risk guidance (SR 11-7 and OCC Bulletin 2011-12) was replaced on 17 April 2026 by SR 26-2 and OCC Bulletin 2026-13. Test whether an AI model that informs decisions is in scope under the bank's own model policy.

**Third-party guidance:** The interagency third-party guidance (88 Fed. Reg. 37920) is technology-neutral. It covers AI vendors across the life of the relationship, not as a separate AI rule (drafting inference).

**NYDFS:** Covered entities must have written procedures for secure development (23 NYCRR 500.8) and a third-party service provider policy (23 NYCRR 500.11). AI tools that touch code or data fall within those controls (drafting inference).

**Customer data and secrecy:** Prompts that carry customer data or confidential code can weaken the secrecy the bank needs to keep trade secret status, which depends on reasonable measures (18 U.S.C. § 1839(3)).
**Examiner readiness:** Keep the AI policy, the approved list and the review evidence ready for supervisors at all times (good practice).
productNotes: **Keep a record of human input:** Ask engineers and designers to keep dated notes of what they wrote, selected and edited in AI-assisted code and content, because the Copyright Office's guidance is that prompts alone do not make the user an author (17 U.S.C. § 102(a); Copyright Office, Part 2, 29 January 2025). Tell counsel which AI coding tools engineers use and what data they may see (good practice).

**Name people as inventors:** Tell counsel who conceived each claimed step of a product invention before filing, and keep the AI tool off the inventor list, since only natural persons can be inventors (35 U.S.C. § 100(f); Thaler v. Vidal, 43 F.4th 1207 (Fed. Cir. 2022)).

**Tell counsel where training data came from:** Describe the data a model will train on and how the bank acquired it before the feature is built, because one district court, in Bartz, held that training on lawfully acquired books was fair use while building a library from pirated copies was not; that ruling does not bind other courts and the answer is still unsettled (17 U.S.C. § 107; Bartz v. Anthropic PBC (N.D. Cal. 23 June 2025)).

**Read the model licence before launch:** A model licence can set user thresholds and use limits, such as the Llama 4 separate-licence test at 700 million monthly active users, so bring the licence to counsel before a launch (Llama 4 Community License s.2). Do not call open weights open source in marketing, since they come under their own terms (good practice).
pitfalls: **Assuming ownership:** Treating prompt-only output as owned, registrable code without evidence of human authorship.
**Naming the tool:** Listing an AI system as an inventor, or leaving off the staff who conceived a claimed step.
**Trusting the cover:** Relying on a vendor's indemnity without checking its conditions, such as the use of the vendor's content filters.
**Stripping notices:** Letting an AI rewrite or refactor remove licence headers or copyright notices from reused code.
**Open weights as open source:** Treating a model as open source because its weights are public, without reading the licence's use limits (good practice).
**Confidential prompts:** Pasting confidential code or customer data into a tool the bank has not approved and assessed.

points: **Training summary duty:** providers of general-purpose AI models must have a copyright policy and publish a training-content summary, from 2 August 2025 (AI Act, Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, Art. 53(1)(c)-(d)).
**Open models keep copyright duties:** open-source models are exempt only from the documentation duties in Art. 53(1)(a)-(b), not from the copyright duties (Art. 53(2)).

**Text and data mining:** Art. 4 of the DSM Directive allows text and data mining, subject to a machine-readable opt-out for online content (Directive (EU) 2019/790, Art. 4); Kneschke v LAION (Hamburg Regional Court, 27 September 2024) (reported; check).
**Computer-generated works:** the author is the person who made the arrangements necessary for creation, with a 50-year term (CDPA 1988 s.9(3), s.12(7)), unlike the US position on authorship.
**Training claims:** Getty Images v Stability AI [2025] EWHC 2863 (Ch) held a trained model was not an infringing copy, with permission to appeal granted (reported; check).
**Unsettled:** the Copyright Act does not deal with AI authorship or training expressly, and no Canadian appellate court has decided either question (drafting inference; check).
**Moral rights in AI-assisted work:** moral rights can be waived but not assigned (Copyright Act s.14.1), which matters for any human contributions to AI-assisted code.

hongKong.summary: Hong Kong gives a computer-generated work an author: the person who undertook the arrangements needed to create it, with a 50-year term. Unlike the US position on authorship, that protection exists, but the bigger risk sits at the input stage, because the Ordinance has no text and data mining exception. Patent rights belong to the inventor, and whether an AI system can be named as inventor is untested in Hong Kong (reported; check).
keyPoints: **Computer-generated works:** Where no human author exists, the author is the person who undertook the arrangements needed to create the work (Cap. 528 s.11(3); s.198(1)). Copyright then lasts 50 years from the end of the calendar year in which the work was made (Cap. 528 s.17(6)).

**Training copies:** Storing a work in any electronic form is copying (Cap. 528 s.23(2)). Loading a work into a training set therefore needs the owner's licence or another permitted act, even if no output is ever published.

**No text and data mining exception:** The Ordinance has no such exception, and fair dealing for research or private study is narrow (Cap. 528 s.38(1), (3)). Reports say a proposed amendment has stalled and that guidelines may come first (reported; check).

**Personal data in training:** Data must be collected for a lawful purpose directly related to the bank's function, and it must not be used for a new purpose without the data subject's prescribed consent (Cap. 486 Sch. 1, DPP 1(1), DPP 3(1)).
**Inventorship:** The right to a patent belongs to the inventor or the inventor's successor in title (Cap. 514 s.9E(1)). The inventor has a right to be mentioned as such (Cap. 514 s.9F(1)).

sections.heading: Authorship and ownership of AI output
sections.lede: AI output can be protected in Hong Kong, but ownership depends on who set up the generation and on the contract with any vendor.
points: **Arrangement maker is author:** For a computer-generated literary, dramatic, musical or artistic work, the author is the person who undertook the arrangements necessary for its creation (Cap. 528 s.11(3)).
**Term:** Copyright in a computer-generated work expires 50 years from the end of the calendar year in which the work was made (Cap. 528 s.17(6)).
**No right to be identified:** The right to be identified as author does not apply to a computer program or to a computer-generated work (Cap. 528 s.91(2)(a), (c)).
**Bank as likely author:** Where the bank's own staff set up the generation, the bank is the likely author under this rule (drafting inference). Keep a record of who set up each run (good practice).
**Employee contributions:** A work made by an employee in the course of employment belongs to the employer unless agreed otherwise (Cap. 528 s.14(1)).
sections.takeaway: Before the first generation run, decide who sets up the arrangements, check what the vendor contract says about output, and record that choice (good practice).

sections.heading: Training data and copying
sections.lede: Training copies the work at least once, so the input stage carries most of the copyright risk in Hong Kong.
points: **Storage is copying:** Storing a work in any electronic form is copying (Cap. 528 s.23(2)), so a training store needs a licence or a permitted act.

**Transient copies:** Copies that are transient or incidental to another use are still copies and are restricted (Cap. 528 s.23(6)); only narrow exemptions apply, and only on their conditions: s.65 for a transient and incidental copy technically required to view or listen to a work communicated to the public, and s.65A for temporary copies made by service providers. A training copy kept in a dataset is unlikely to be transient (drafting inference).

**Narrow research fair dealing:** Fair dealing for research or private study is judged by the purpose and nature of the dealing, the amount taken, and its effect on the market for the work (Cap. 528 s.38(1), (3)).

**Shared datasets:** Fair dealing does not protect copying for another person if the copier knows or has reason to believe the copies will go to more than one person at the same time for the same purpose (Cap. 528 s.38(2)(b)).
**No mining exception:** Because the Ordinance has no text and data mining exception, each training source needs its own licence or permitted act (drafting inference).
sections.takeaway: Obtain a licence or confirm a permitted act for each training source before the data is loaded, and keep that record with the dataset (good practice).

sections.heading: Personal data in AI training and use
sections.lede: The privacy rules apply to training data as they do to any other use of customer data, so the purpose has to be set before collection.
points: **Collection purpose:** Personal data must be collected for a lawful purpose directly related to the bank's function or activity, and must be adequate but not excessive for that purpose (Cap. 486 Sch. 1, DPP 1(1)).
**Notice at collection:** The data subject must be told the purpose and the classes of persons to whom the data may be transferred, on or before collection (Cap. 486 Sch. 1, DPP 1(3)(b)(i)).
**New purpose:** Using personal data for a new purpose needs the data subject's prescribed consent (Cap. 486 Sch. 1, DPP 3(1)).
**Processor retention:** A bank that gives model hosting or processing to a data processor must stop the processor keeping the data longer than needed (Cap. 486 Sch. 1, DPP 2(3)).
sections.takeaway: Before collecting or reusing customer data for training, record the purpose, give the required notice, and obtain prescribed consent for any new purpose (good practice).

provisions.title: Author of a computer-generated work
provisions.summary: For a computer-generated literary, dramatic, musical or artistic work, the author is the person who undertook the arrangements necessary for its creation.
provisions.counselNote: The bank's own staff may be the author of AI output, so the team that sets up generation needs to know it. Record who did the set-up.

provisions.title: Computer-generated work defined
provisions.summary: A computer-generated work is one generated by a computer in circumstances where there is no human author of the work.
provisions.counselNote: This definition decides whether the arrangement-maker rule applies. Where a human author can be identified, the ordinary authorship rules apply instead.

provisions.title: Duration for computer-generated works
provisions.summary: For a computer-generated work, copyright expires 50 years from the end of the calendar year in which the work was made.
provisions.counselNote: Model outputs can stay protected for a long time, so the licence terms for outputs need to cover that period.

provisions.title: Copying includes electronic storage
provisions.summary: Copying means reproducing a work in any material form, and storing a work in any medium by electronic means is copying. Transient or incidental copies are also restricted.
provisions.counselNote: Loading a work into a training store is copying even if nothing is published. Any training pipeline needs a licence or a permitted act at the input stage.

provisions.title: Fair dealing for research or private study
provisions.summary: Fair dealing for research or private study does not infringe copyright. The court considers the purpose and nature of the dealing, the nature of the work, the amount taken, and the effect on the market. Copying for others who will receive the same material at the same time is excluded.
provisions.counselNote: Bank teams that share a dataset are the typical case that falls outside this defence. Do not rely on it for a shared training corpus.

provisions.title: No right to be identified for programs and computer-generated works
provisions.summary: The right to be identified as author does not apply to a computer program or to a computer-generated work.
provisions.counselNote: Model documentation and output licences cannot rely on an attribution right, so the contract must set out any attribution terms.

provisions.title: Right to a patent belongs to the inventor
provisions.summary: The right to a patent belongs to the inventor or the inventor's successor in title. Where an employee is the inventor, the law of the place of employment decides, and where two or more people invent the same thing independently, the earlier or earliest material date decides.
provisions.counselNote: Patent rights attach to people, so the bank's AI invention filings must name the people who made the inventive contribution. Whether a system can be named is untested.

provisions.title: Collection of personal data
provisions.summary: Personal data may be collected only for a lawful purpose directly related to a function or activity of the data user, and only in an amount that is adequate but not excessive. The data subject must be told the purpose and the classes of transferees on or before collection.
provisions.counselNote: Bulk scraping of customer or public data for training may fail this principle. Each collection needs a documented purpose and notice.

provisions.title: Use of personal data for a new purpose
provisions.summary: Personal data must not be used for a new purpose without the data subject's prescribed consent. A new purpose is any purpose other than the one for which the data was to be used at collection, or a purpose directly related to it.
provisions.counselNote: Reusing customer data to train a model is usually a new purpose. Get consent or fix the purpose before the data is used.

provisions.instrument: HKMA circular: Consumer Protection in respect of Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence
provisions.title: GenAI in customer-facing applications
provisions.summary: Applies four consumer-protection principles to customer-facing generative AI: governance and accountability, fairness, transparency and disclosure, and data privacy and protection. It adds GenAI-specific expectations.
provisions.counselNote: Before a chatbot, robo-advice or AI marketing goes live, check board accountability, fairness testing and customer disclosure. The circular is guidance, not law.

bankNotes: **Customer-facing AI:** The HKMA's circular of 19 August 2024 applies its consumer protection principles (governance and accountability, fairness, transparency and disclosure, data privacy) to customer-facing generative AI, so chatbots, robo-advice and AI marketing need board and senior management accountability, fairness testing and disclosure before go-live. It is guidance, not law.
**Sandbox:** The HKMA-Cyberport GenA.I. Sandbox gives supervisory feedback but no legal exemption, so a sandbox pilot does not change the bank's legal position.
**Personal data framework:** The PCPD has issued a Model Personal Data Protection Framework for AI. It is guidance, not law (reported; check).

**Vendor models:** Where a model provider processes customer data for the bank, the bank must use contractual or other means to stop it keeping the data longer than needed (Cap. 486 Sch. 1, DPP 2(3)). The HKMA's outsourcing expectations apply as well (SA-2, para 1.3.2).

glossary.definition: The requirement that copyright protection and registration rest on a human author's original expression. The D.C. Circuit held in Thaler v. Perlmutter that the Copyright Act requires it for registration (130 F.4th 1039).
A limit on copyright under 17 U.S.C. § 107, assessed on four factors: purpose and character, nature of the work, amount used and effect on the market. Courts decide it case by case.

Information that identifies a work, its author or owner, or its terms of use, conveyed with copies of the work (17 U.S.C. § 1202(c)). Removing it without authority can breach § 1202(b) where the knowledge or intent test is met.
The individual, or the individuals jointly, who invented or discovered the claimed subject matter (35 U.S.C. § 100(f)). Under Thaler v. Vidal, only a natural person can be one.

Microsoft's commitment, announced in September 2023 under its earlier name, to defend customers against IP claims over output if they use the built-in content filters and guardrails (reported; check).
The OSI's Open Source AI Definition 1.0, published on 28 October 2024, which sets out what the OSI treats as open source AI. It is a view, not law (reported; check).
A set of use rules that a model licence incorporates, such as the policy that applies under Meta's Llama 4 Community License (reported; check).

The bank's framework for identifying, validating and governing models that inform decisions, shaped by supervisory model risk guidance. The guidance was reported replaced in April 2026 (reported; check).
Latin for 'too trivial to matter'. The Copyright Office's statement of policy asks applicants to disclose AI-generated material only where it is more than de minimis (88 Fed. Reg. 16190).
The source form that GPL-3.0 requires a distributor to provide with, or offer for, object code it conveys (GPL-3.0 s.6).
A work generated by a computer in circumstances where there is no human author (Cap. 528 s.198(1)). The arrangement maker is the author (Cap. 528 s.11(3)).
A person who processes personal data on another's behalf and not for its own purposes (Cap. 486 Sch. 1, DPP 2(4)).

title: Disputes and enforcement
oneLiner: Each right brings its own remedies, deadlines and forums, and timing, notice and cure often decide the outcome.
keyPoints: Start with the right, not the forum. Copyright, patent, trade secret, licence and computer-access claims each carry different remedies, deadlines and courts.

**Copyright:** Owners can seek injunctions, actual damages and profits, or statutory damages, but suit on a US work needs registration and statutory damages depend on timing (17 U.S.C. §§ 411(a), 412, 502, 504).

**Patents:** Damages are at least a reasonable royalty and can reach three times the award. Marking and notice limit early damages, and the PTAB and the ITC run as separate routes (35 U.S.C. §§ 284, 287; 19 U.S.C. § 1337).

**Trade secrets:** The Defend Trade Secrets Act (DTSA) allows injunctions, damages and exemplary damages up to twice the award, but an injunction cannot bar a person from a job merely for what they know (18 U.S.C. § 1836(b)(3)).

**Open source:** GPL-2.0 ends the licensee's rights on any attempt to copy, modify, sublicense or distribute the program outside the licence, while GPL-3.0 allows reinstatement after a timely cure, so a fast, documented response matters (GPL-2.0 s.4; GPL-3.0 s.8).
**Counsel's role:** Preserve evidence, check the facts before replying, and put every demand, response and insurer notice in writing (good practice).

deepDive.heading: Remedies by right
deepDive.lede: Each right gives different relief, so the bank's exposure depends on which right is claimed.
points: **Injunctions:** Under the Copyright Act (17 U.S.C.), a court may grant temporary and final injunctions, and they operate throughout the United States (§ 502(a)-(b)).
**Profits:** The owner recovers actual damages and the infringer's profits. It proves only gross revenue, and the infringer must prove its deductible costs (§ 504(b)).
**Choice of award:** The owner may elect instead [[statutory damages]] of $750 to $30,000 per work, up to $150,000 for wilful infringement and down to $200 for innocent infringement (§ 504(c)).
**Fees:** The court may award costs and a reasonable attorney's fee to the prevailing party, at its discretion (§ 505).
**Licence conditions:** Where a licence condition limits the licence itself, breaking it is infringement and not only a contract breach (Jacobsen v. Katzer, 535 F.3d 1373 (Fed. Cir. 2008)).

visual.caption: Relief by right, as the statute or licence states it. Each row is a separate claim with its own forum.

items.label: Computer access

deepDive.heading: Registration and timing
deepDive.lede: Registration and dates often decide the money more than the merits.
points: **Registration first:** A suit on a US work cannot start until registration has been made, not just applied for (17 U.S.C. § 411(a); Fourth Estate Public Benefit Corp. v. Wall-Street.com, LLC, 586 U.S. 296 (2019)).

**Late registration:** Statutory damages and fees are lost for infringement that began before registration took effect, unless a published work was registered within three months of first publication (§ 412).

**Time limit:** A civil claim must be brought within three years after it accrued (§ 507(b)). Warner Chappell Music, Inc. v. Nealy, 601 U.S. 366 (2024), held that a claim timely under the discovery rule is not capped at three years of damages, though the Court assumed the rule applies.
**Criminal cases:** Criminal copyright proceedings must start within five years (§ 507(a)).

visual.caption: The timing rules that set copyright exposure on a US work.

items.label: Infringement begins
items.note: The point from which the § 412 test and the claim period run

items.label: Registration
items.note: Must be made, not just applied for (§ 411(a))

items.label: Statutory damages
items.note: Lost where infringement began before a late registration took effect

items.label: Limitation period
items.note: From accrual of the claim (§ 507(b))

deepDive.heading: Patent forums and remedies
deepDive.lede: A patent dispute can run in three places, and each produces a different outcome.
points: **Damages:** The court awards damages adequate to compensate, never less than a reasonable royalty, and may raise them up to three times (35 U.S.C. § 284). Halo Electronics, Inc. v. Pulse Electronics, Inc., 579 U.S. 93 (2016), limited enhancement to egregious cases, typified by wilful misconduct.

**Fees:** The court may award fees to the prevailing party in an exceptional case (§ 285). Octane Fitness, LLC v. ICON Health & Fitness, Inc., 572 U.S. 545 (2014), judges that on the totality of the circumstances.

**Time and notice:** Damages reach back no more than six years before the complaint (§ 286). A patentee that fails to mark can recover damages only after actual notice of infringement, and filing suit counts as notice (§ 287(a)).

**PTAB:** Inter partes review tests only novelty and obviousness, on patents or printed publications. Post-grant review can raise any invalidity ground, if filed within nine months of grant (35 U.S.C. §§ 311(b), 321). Both decide validity, not damages.

**Current practice:** The PTAB's institution practice changed sharply in 2025, and a proposed rule would narrow review where parallel litigation is likely (reported; check the current practice before relying on it).
**ITC:** A violation finding leads to an [[exclusion order]] that bars infringing imports, unless the public interest weighs against it (19 U.S.C. § 1337(d)).

visual.caption: Each forum decides different questions and gives different relief.

items.label: District court
items.note: Damages and fees; venue where the defendant resides (for a corporation, its state of incorporation), or where it has committed acts of infringement and has a regular and established place of business

items.label: PTAB (IPR or PGR)
items.note: Cancels or upholds claims; no damages

items.label: ITC
items.note: Exclusion order against infringing imports

deepDive.heading: Trade secret remedies
deepDive.lede: The DTSA gives fast interim relief, but it limits what a court may order against staff.
points: **Seizure:** A court may seize property ex parte only in extraordinary circumstances, on specific findings, including that the applicant has not publicised the request (18 U.S.C. § 1836(b)(2)(A)).
**Staff limit:** An injunction may not stop a person entering a job, and conditions on a job must rest on evidence of threatened misappropriation, not on what the person knows (§ 1836(b)(3)(A)(i)).
**Money:** Damages cover actual loss and unjust enrichment, or, in place of those measures, a reasonable royalty (§ 1836(b)(3)(B)).

**Enhancement:** Exemplary damages go up to twice the award for wilful and malicious misappropriation, and fees can go to the prevailing party where a claim is made in bad faith, a motion to terminate an injunction is made or opposed in bad faith, or the misappropriation was wilful and malicious (§ 1836(b)(3)(C)-(D)).

**Limits and reach:** Suit must start within three years of the date the misappropriation was, or with reasonable diligence should have been, discovered (§ 1836(d)). The DTSA can reach misappropriation abroad where an act in furtherance occurred in the US (Motorola Solutions, Inc. v. Hytera Communications Corp., 108 F.4th 458 (7th Cir. 2024)).

items.label: Injunction

items.label: Damages
items.note: Actual loss and unjust enrichment, or a reasonable royalty

items.label: Exemplary damages and fees
