deepDive.heading: Open source enforcement
deepDive.lede: Most licence disputes start with a compliance letter, and the licence text sets the clock.
points: **Termination:** Under GPL-2.0 s.4, any attempt to copy, modify, sublicense or distribute outside the licence is void and automatically ends the licensee's rights. Recipients who stay in full compliance keep theirs.

**Cure:** GPL-3.0 s.8 reinstates rights provisionally once the violation stops. It reinstates them permanently if the holder gives no notice within 60 days after the violation stops, or if the licensee cures within 30 days of receiving a first notice.

**Court outcomes:** In Jacobsen, the licence conditions were enforced through copyright. In Artifex Software, Inc. v. Hancom, Inc. (N.D. Cal. 2017), the court refused to dismiss a claim that the GPL was an enforceable contract, and the case then settled.
**Kernel statement:** The Linux Kernel Enforcement Statement (2017) has signatory developers apply GPLv3-style cure terms to the kernel, and some companies made similar commitments (reported; check).

**Pending case:** Software Freedom Conservancy v. Vizio, Inc. (Cal. Super. Ct., Orange County) tests whether a buyer can enforce the GPL as a third-party beneficiary. Pre-trial rulings are reported to hold that the GPL requires source sharing, leaving scope for a jury; no final judgment is confirmed as at November 2026 (reported; check).

visual.caption: A typical path from a GPL compliance letter to closure. GPL-2.0 has no cure window in its text, so the first steps matter more.

items.label: Check the claim
items.note: Confirm the code, version and distribution before replying (good practice)

items.label: Stop the violation
items.note: Halt the non-compliant copying, modification or distribution at once

items.label: Cure after first notice
items.note: Permanent reinstatement if cured within 30 days of the first notice (GPL-3.0 s.8)

items.label: No notice from holder
items.note: Provisional rights become permanent if no notice comes within 60 days of stopping the violation (GPL-3.0 s.8)

items.label: Document the close
items.note: Keep the cure, source offers and correspondence on file (good practice)

deepDive.heading: Takedowns and computer access
deepDive.lede: Two US statutes shape how the bank can act against copied code and scraped data, and both punish overreach.
points: **Notices:** A takedown notice under the Digital Millennium Copyright Act (DMCA) (17 U.S.C. § 512(c)(3)) needs a good-faith statement and a statement under penalty of perjury that the sender is authorised to act (§ 512(c)(3)(A)(v)-(vi)).
**Misrepresentation:** A person who knowingly and materially misrepresents that material is infringing is liable for damages and fees to anyone harmed when a host relies on that claim (§ 512(f)).

**[[counter-notice|counter-notification]]:** The poster may counter-notify under penalty of perjury. The host must restore the material 10 to 14 business days later, unless the claimant has sued (§ 512(g)(2)(C), (g)(3)).
**Takedown history:** GitHub disabled youtube-dl in October 2020 after a notice invoking § 1201, and restored it in November 2020 (reported; check).

**Computer access:** The Computer Fraud and Abuse Act (CFAA) (18 U.S.C. § 1030(a)(2)) covers intentional access without authorisation, or beyond it, to obtain listed categories of information. Van Buren v. United States, 593 U.S. 374 (2021), held that this reaches off-limits areas, not misuse of data one may access (§ 1030(e)(6)).

**Scraping:** hiQ Labs, Inc. v. LinkedIn Corp., 31 F.4th 1180 (9th Cir. 2022), held that scraping publicly available profiles was likely not access without authorisation. A civil CFAA claim must start within two years (§ 1030(g)).

deepDive.heading: Running the dispute
deepDive.lede: Process decides much of the cost, so preserve, verify and route the claim before anyone replies.
points: **Litigation hold:** Once a claim is reasonably anticipated, issue a [[litigation hold]] covering repositories, commit history, build records, SBOMs and messages, and suspend routine deletion (good practice).
**Source code protocol:** Produce code only under a protective order, in a review room with logged access and no copies, since the other side's experts will read it closely (good practice).
**Insurers:** Give notice within each policy's deadline. R&W insurance usually excludes matters known from diligence, so known open source issues need special indemnities (reported; market practice).
**Vendor indemnities:** Tender an IP claim to the vendor at once, and check its conditions, such as the use of content filters. Terms differ by vendor (reported; check each contract).

**Dispute terms:** Most open source licences, such as the GPL, Apache-2.0 and MIT, do not choose a forum or governing law, though some do (MPL-2.0 s.8; EUPL-1.2 ss.14-15), so the bank can usually set those only in its own contracts (drafting inference).

**Regulators:** The interagency third-party guidance (88 Fed. Reg. 37920) treats vendor disputes as risks to manage across the relationship. A material dispute is worth logging and reporting internally, because examiners may ask about it (good practice).

provisions.title: Remedies for infringement: Injunctions
provisions.summary: Lets a court with jurisdiction grant temporary and final injunctions on reasonable terms to prevent or restrain copyright infringement. Subsection (b) makes an injunction operative and enforceable throughout the United States.
provisions.counselNote: An injunction is often the fastest threat against a supplier or former employee. The bank should expect one as well as a damages claim.

provisions.title: Remedies for infringement: Damages and profits
provisions.summary: The owner may recover actual damages and profits, or elect statutory damages of $750 to $30,000 per work. Wilful infringement can raise that to $150,000, and innocent infringement can reduce it to $200. The owner proves only gross revenue, and the infringer proves its deductible costs.
provisions.counselNote: Statutory damages run per work, so how the bank counts works in a codebase matters. Timely registration decides whether they are available at all.

provisions.title: Limitations on actions
provisions.summary: A civil action must start within three years after the claim accrued (§ 507(b)). A criminal proceeding must start within five years (§ 507(a)).
provisions.counselNote: Check the discovery date as well as the infringement date when testing an old claim, because a timely discovery-rule claim can recover older damages.

provisions.title: Limitations on liability relating to material online
provisions.summary: Sets notice-and-takedown rules for hosts, which can keep their liability limited if they act on valid notices. A takedown notice needs a good-faith statement and a statement under penalty of perjury. A knowing misrepresentation carries liability for damages and fees (§ 512(f)). A subscriber can counter-notify to restore material (§ 512(g)).
provisions.counselNote: The bank is both a sender and a recipient. It can use takedowns against copied code, and it must answer accurately any notice about its own repositories or hosted sites.

provisions.title: Civil proceedings
provisions.summary: Gives an owner a civil action for misappropriation of a trade secret related to a product or service in interstate or foreign commerce. Remedies include injunctions that cannot stop a person taking a job, damages for actual loss and unjust enrichment or a reasonable royalty, and exemplary damages up to twice the award. Suit must start within three years of the date the misappropriation was, or with reasonable diligence should have been, discovered (§ 1836(d)).
provisions.counselNote: The employment limit means the bank cannot stop a departing engineer joining a competitor only because of what they know. It must show threatened misappropriation.

provisions.title: Damages
provisions.summary: Requires damages adequate to compensate for infringement, in no event less than a reasonable royalty, with interest and costs. The court may increase the damages up to three times the amount found.
provisions.counselNote: The reasonable royalty is the floor, so counsel should model a licence fee as the baseline exposure in any patent demand against the bank.

provisions.title: Attorney fees
provisions.summary: The court in exceptional cases may award reasonable attorney fees to the prevailing party. The Supreme Court judges exceptional cases on the totality of the circumstances (Octane Fitness).
provisions.counselNote: Fee shifting runs both ways. A weak claim that the sender takes to court can expose it to the bank's fees in an exceptional case, so the bank should assess its own position early.

provisions.title: Unfair practices in import trade
provisions.summary: Makes certain unfair import practices unlawful, including importing articles that infringe a valid and enforceable US patent, where a domestic industry relating to the patented articles exists or is being established (§ 1337(a)(1)(B), (a)(2)). When the ITC finds a violation, it directs that the articles be excluded from entry, unless the public interest weighs against that. All legal and equitable defences may be presented (19 U.S.C. § 1337(c)).
provisions.counselNote: An exclusion order works at the border and can disrupt hardware the bank buys from abroad, so check supplier indemnities before a dispute starts.

provisions.instrument: Computer Fraud and Abuse Act (18 U.S.C.)
provisions.title: Fraud and related activity in connection with computers
provisions.summary: Prohibits intentionally accessing a computer without authorisation, or beyond authorised access, to obtain information in the categories listed in (a)(2). Exceeds authorised access means using permitted access to obtain or alter information one is not entitled to obtain or alter (§ 1030(e)(6)). A civil action needs a listed harm factor and must start within two years (§ 1030(g)).
provisions.counselNote: Employee misuse of data the employee can already reach is usually a contract, policy or trade secret matter. A CFAA claim needs the access boundary to be clear.

provisions.title: Termination
provisions.summary: Rights end automatically for anyone who propagates or modifies outside the licence. They return provisionally once the violation stops, and permanently if the copyright holder gives no notice within 60 days after the violation stops. They also return permanently if the licensee cures within 30 days of a first notice from that holder.
provisions.counselNote: Calendar the 30-day window from receipt of the first notice and the 60-day window from the day the violation stopped. A documented cure inside the window keeps the bank's licence intact.

provisions.title: Termination
provisions.summary: Any attempt to copy, modify, sublicense or distribute the program other than as the licence allows is void and automatically terminates the licensee's rights. Parties who received copies, or rights, from the licensee keep their licences so long as those parties stay in full compliance.
provisions.counselNote: The text has no cure period, so a GPL-2.0 breach by the bank can end its rights at once. Review older GPL-2.0 components with that in mind.

provisions.instrument: Warner Chappell Music, Inc. v. Nealy
provisions.title: Damages and the discovery rule
provisions.summary: The Court held that a claim timely under the discovery rule is not subject to a separate three-year cap on damages. It assumed, without deciding, that the discovery rule applies.
provisions.counselNote: Dating a claim from the infringement date alone can understate exposure, so the discovery date matters in both directions.

provisions.title: Exceeds authorized access under the CFAA
provisions.summary: The Court held that exceeding authorised access covers obtaining information from areas of a computer that are off limits. It does not cover misusing information the user may access.
provisions.counselNote: Access controls and terms of use should define the boundaries the CFAA protects. Without them, a misuse dispute becomes a weaker CFAA claim.

provisions.title: Licence conditions enforced as copyright
provisions.summary: The court held that the Artistic License's attribution and change-notice terms were conditions limiting the scope of the licence. A user who broke them could be sued for copyright infringement, not only for breach of contract.
provisions.counselNote: Treat open source licence conditions as enforceable through copyright remedies when the bank uses or ships the code, not only as contract terms.

checklist: **Identify the right first:** Map each threatened claim to copyright, patent, trade secret, licence or computer-access law, with its remedies, deadlines and forum.
**Check registration and timing:** Confirm which works are registered, when infringement began and when the claim accrued, before valuing any copyright exposure.
**Adopt a compliance letter procedure:** Verify the facts, cure within the GPL-3.0 windows where the licence applies, and log every step with dates.
**Review every takedown:** Require legal sign-off on each § 512 notice, check its good-faith basis and penalty-of-perjury statement, and log the outcome.
**Issue a litigation hold early:** Cover repositories, commit history, build records, SBOMs and messages once a claim is reasonably anticipated.
**Set a source code review protocol:** Produce code only under a protective order, in a controlled review environment with logged access and no copies.
**Diarise insurer and vendor deadlines:** Record notice periods in the bank's IP, cyber and technology policies and in each vendor's indemnity clause.
**Agree dispute terms in bank contracts:** Set governing law, forum, escalation and injunctive relief in every bank-facing licence and services contract.
**Plan the public line:** Agree who speaks, and what is said, before an open source or IP dispute becomes public.
itAngle: **Commit history as evidence:** Repository history, tags and build records show who wrote what and when. Keep them under the hold, not under the normal clean-up job.

**Scan reports for the disputed release:** SBOMs and licence scan reports show which versions shipped where. Run them against the release in dispute, so the bank can say exactly which version is affected.
**Takedown readiness:** Hosting platforms process DMCA notices, and a single notice can disable a whole repository. Keep a current list of the bank's public repositories, owners and contacts.
**Access records:** A CFAA dispute turns on what a credential could reach. Keep role mappings and access logs that show the authorisation boundaries.
**A source archive for each shipped build:** Keep corresponding source for every distributed build, so the bank can supply it quickly if a GPL cure requires it.
virtualBankNotes: **Third-party guidance:** The interagency guidance (88 Fed. Reg. 37920) expects banks to manage vendor risk across the life of the relationship. A dispute with a vendor or open source supplier is a risk event to log and report.

**Cybersecurity rules:** Where NYDFS Part 500 applies, the regulation requires written procedures for secure development (23 NYCRR 500.8) and a third-party service provider security policy (500.11). Link dispute outcomes to those procedures.

**Examiner access:** Examiners may ask for dispute files, vendor correspondence and remediation records. Keep them organised, mark privileged material, and keep them apart from ordinary business records.

**Customer data in disputes:** Code reviews and seized materials can contain customer data. Redact it and limit access, as the bank would for any third-party disclosure. A DTSA civil seizure order requires the court to take seized material into its custody and limit access to it (18 U.S.C. § 1836(b)(2)(D)), and seizure is available only in extraordinary circumstances.
**Public attention:** An open source dispute involving a bank can reach the press and the community quickly. Regulators and customers may hear of it from others first (good practice).
productNotes: **Route every letter to counsel the day it arrives:** Send any infringement, takedown or compliance letter to counsel at once, do not reply on your own, and keep the repositories, commit history and messages as they are, since a litigation hold may apply (good practice).

**Start the GPL clock on the first notice:** Under GPL-3.0 s.8 a licensee that cures within 30 days of a first notice keeps its licence, so the product team should stop any non-compliant copying straight away and log the date (GPL-3.0 s.8). GPL-2.0 has no cure window in its text, so the first step matters more (GPL-2.0 s.4).

**Do not send a takedown on a hunch:** A takedown notice needs a good-faith statement and a statement under penalty of perjury, and a knowing misrepresentation carries liability for damages and fees (17 U.S.C. § 512(c)(3), (f)).

**Do not call a colleague's access a hack:** Misuse of data an employee can already reach is usually a contract or trade secret matter, since the CFAA reaches only areas that are off limits (18 U.S.C. § 1030(e)(6); Van Buren v. United States, 593 U.S. 374 (2021)).
pitfalls: **Suing on unregistered code:** Assuming the bank can sue on a US work before registration has been made, and learning late that the suit cannot be filed.
**Missing the GPL-3.0 window:** Answering a compliance letter slowly and passing the 30-day cure period in s.8.
**Overreaching takedowns:** Sending DMCA notices without a good-faith check, which can expose the bank to liability under § 512(f).
**Treating misuse as hacking:** Filing a CFAA claim over data the employee was allowed to reach, a claim Van Buren makes weak.
**Assuming a GPL-2.0 cure:** Planning around a cure route that the GPL-2.0 text does not contain (GPL-2.0 s.4).
**Late insurer notice:** Letting a policy's notice deadline pass because the claim seemed weak at the start (good practice).

points: **Trade secret claims:** the Trade Secrets Directive (EU) 2016/943 is the EU basis for trade secret claims, which member states apply through national law.
**Patent forum:** the Unified Patent Court opened on 1 June 2023, so infringement actions over European patents may be brought there rather than in national courts.
**Trade secret enforcement:** the Trade Secrets (Enforcement, etc.) Regulations 2018 (SI 2018/597) sit alongside the law of confidence.
**Outside the UPC:** UK patent disputes are not heard in the Unified Patent Court, so UK actions follow UK forums.

**No trade secret statute:** there is no federal civil trade secret statute, so claims rest on common law and Quebec civil law; Criminal Code s.391 covers trade secret offences from 1 July 2020 (reported; check).
**Enforcement as contract or copyright:** Canada has no general open source statute, so licence claims are brought as contract or copyright claims (Copyright Act, C-42).

hongKong.summary: Hong Kong enforcement starts with the right and then the forum. Copyright owners can get damages, injunctions and accounts, with additional damages for flagrancy and benefit (Cap. 528 s.107(2), s.108(2)), but there is no general copyright groundless-threats remedy. Hong Kong has no trade secrets statute, so confidential information is pursued through the law of confidence and contract (reported; check).
keyPoints: **Start with the right:** Each right brings its own remedies, clock and forum, so frame the claim before anyone replies (good practice).

**Copyright remedies:** The owner may sue for damages, injunctions and accounts (Cap. 528 s.107(2)). The court may add damages for flagrancy, benefit to the defendant, conduct and wide circulation (Cap. 528 s.108(2)), and an innocent defendant escapes damages but not other remedies (Cap. 528 s.108(1)). Copyright damages follow general principles rather than a US-style statutory damages scheme (drafting inference).

**No general copyright threats remedy:** Section 187 covers only threats over parallel-imported copies (Cap. 528 s.187(1), (3)). Groundless-threats relief exists for patents, registered trade marks and registered designs (Cap. 514 s.89; Cap. 559 s.26; Cap. 522 s.57).

**Short prosecution clocks:** A copyright prosecution must start within 3 years of the offence (Cap. 528 s.120A), and a telecommunications computer-access prosecution must start within 3 years or 6 months after discovery, whichever ends first (Cap. 106 s.27A(4)).
**No trade secrets statute:** Confidential information is protected by the equitable action for breach of confidence and by contract, so a claim should be framed in those terms (reported; check).

sections.heading: Remedies and forums by right
sections.lede: Each right decides what the bank can ask for and which court or tribunal hears the claim.
points: **Delivery up:** The copyright owner may apply for an order that an infringing copy be delivered up where the holder has it in its possession, custody or control for the purpose of or in the course of a trade or business, or that an article specifically designed or adapted for copying a particular work be delivered up where the holder knows or has reason to believe it is used to make infringing copies (Cap. 528 s.109(1)(a)-(b)).

**Delivery-up time limit:** The application may not be made more than 6 years after the copy or article was made, subject to exceptions for disability and fraud or concealment (Cap. 528 s.110(1)-(2)).

**District Court:** The District Court can hear delivery-up applications where the value of the articles is within its tort limit, and the Court of First Instance keeps its jurisdiction (Cap. 528 s.134(1)-(2)).

**Arbitration:** IP disputes over ownership, validity, infringement and transactions in an IP right can be arbitrated between the parties (Cap. 609 s.103D(1)), and an award binds those who claim through them (Cap. 609 s.73(1)).

**Third-party licensees:** A licensee does not become a person claiming through a party merely because it holds a licence, although its contract and operation-of-law rights are preserved (Cap. 609 s.103E(2)-(3)).
sections.takeaway: Decide the right and the forum together, because a delivery-up order and a damages claim may need different courts (good practice).

sections.heading: Time limits and notice rules
sections.lede: Clocks and notice periods often settle a dispute before the merits are reached.
points: **Contract and tort:** A claim must be brought within 6 years of accrual (Cap. 347 s.4(1)). That limit does not apply to injunctions or other equitable relief, although the court may apply it by analogy (Cap. 347 s.4(7)).

**Concealment:** Fraud or deliberate concealment postpones the start of the limitation period until the claimant discovers it or could with reasonable diligence have discovered it (Cap. 347 s.26(1)(a)-(b)).

**Patent threats:** A person threatened over a patent can seek a declaration that the threats are unjustifiable, an injunction and damages, but a notice that a patent exists is not a threat, and no relief lies for a threat over making a product for putting on the market or using a process (Cap. 514 s.89(1)-(5)).

**Short-term patent defence:** Where no certificate of substantive examination has issued, the defendant must prove infringement and validity, and must have provided the patent information, without charge, within 14 days of a written access request (Cap. 514 s.89A(2)-(3)).
**Trade mark threats:** Relief is lost if the registered owner, or a licensee with power to sue, begins an action within 28 days of the threat and pursues it with due diligence (Cap. 559 s.26(6)).
sections.takeaway: Diary the 28-day trade mark window and any 14-day patent information request on the day a threat letter arrives (good practice).

sections.heading: Computer access, takedowns and platforms
sections.lede: Criminal computer-access rules and the platform regime shape how the bank can act against copied code, scraped data and infringing content.
points: **Dishonest access:** Accessing a computer with intent to commit an offence, to deceive, for dishonest gain or to cause loss is an offence with up to 5 years' imprisonment, and the intended offence, gain or loss may fall on a later occasion (Cap. 200 s.161(1)).

**Unauthorised access:** Knowingly causing a computer, by telecommunications, to obtain unauthorised access to a program or data is an offence with a level 4 fine (Cap. 106 s.27A(1)). Access is unauthorised where the person is not entitled to control access of that kind, has not been authorised by someone who is, and does not believe they were or would have been authorised (Cap. 106 s.27A(2)(b)).

**Data as property:** A program or data held in a computer counts as property for the criminal damage offences, and altering or erasing it can be damage, and the s.60(1) offence needs property belonging to another person (Cap. 200 ss.59, 60(1)-(2)).

**Platform safe harbour:** A service provider is not liable for copyright damages merely for providing online services if it takes reasonable steps once it is notified or aware, gets no direct financial benefit, does not interfere with standard technical measures and has a designated agent (Cap. 528 s.88B(1)-(2)).
**Presumption of compliance:** Where a provider shows that it complied with a condition, the court must presume compliance unless there is evidence to the contrary (Cap. 528 s.88I).

**Own devices:** Section 161(1)(c) does not extend to a person's use of their own computer (Secretary for Justice v Cheng Ka Yee [2019] HKCFA 9), so a leak through a staff member's own phone is usually pursued through confidence and contract rather than this offence (drafting inference).

**Identifying infringers:** The court can order an internet service provider to disclose the identity of subscribers alleged to have infringed copyright (Norwich Pharmacal relief), as in Cinepoly Records Co Ltd v Hong Kong Broadband Network Ltd [2006] HKCFI 84 (reported; check).
sections.takeaway: Write down when the bank first learned of copied code or scraped data, because the platform safe harbour turns on how quickly the provider acts after a notice (good practice).

provisions.title: Additional damages and innocent infringers
provisions.summary: The court considers all the circumstances when it awards additional damages, including flagrancy, benefit to the defendant, conduct and wide circulation. Damages are barred only where the defendant did not know and had no reason to believe that copyright subsisted, and other remedies stay available.
provisions.counselNote: Additional damages are the main lever on a copyright claim against a vendor or contractor, so evidence of flagrancy and benefit matters. The innocence bar is narrow in effect, so an injunction or accounts can still follow even where damages are barred.

provisions.title: Delivery up of infringing copies
provisions.summary: The copyright owner may apply to court for an order that infringing copies, or articles made for copying a work, be delivered up. The application may not be made more than 6 years after the copy or article was made, subject to the exceptions in s.110.
provisions.counselNote: Delivery up is the practical remedy when unlicensed copies sit on a bank's servers or in a vendor's hands, so the copies should be preserved rather than destroyed before the order is decided (good practice).

provisions.title: Three-year limit for prosecutions
provisions.summary: No prosecution for an offence under the Ordinance may be commenced more than 3 years after the offence was committed.
provisions.counselNote: The clock runs from commission, not discovery, so historic unlicensed use may fall outside prosecution while a civil claim remains open (drafting inference).

provisions.title: Narrow copyright threats relief
provisions.summary: Relief against threats of copyright proceedings applies only to threats over parallel-imported copies that are infringing only because of the importation rule. A notice of copyright is not a threat.
provisions.counselNote: A vendor or rights holder letter about software generally is outside this section, so the bank cannot rely on it for those letters.

provisions.title: Patent groundless threats
provisions.summary: A person aggrieved by threats of patent infringement proceedings may seek a declaration that the threats are unjustifiable, an injunction and damages. A notice that a patent exists is not itself a threat.
provisions.counselNote: A letter from a patent holder to a product team can trigger this route, so it should go to counsel before any reply. The defences for standard patents turn on proof of infringement and invalidity (s.89A).

provisions.title: Trade mark groundless threats
provisions.summary: A person threatened over use of a registered trade mark, other than applying it to goods or packaging or supplying services under it, may seek a declaration, an injunction and damages. A notice that a mark is registered is not a threat, and relief is lost where the owner sues within 28 days with due diligence.
provisions.counselNote: Disputes with competitors often start with a letter threatening proceedings, so the 28-day window works both ways and should be diarised from the date of the threat.

provisions.title: Access to a computer with dishonest intent
provisions.summary: Obtaining access to a computer with intent to commit an offence, with dishonest intent to deceive, with a view to dishonest gain, or with dishonest intent to cause loss is an offence, whether the intended offence, gain or loss falls on the same occasion or a future one. It is triable on indictment and carries up to 5 years' imprisonment.
provisions.counselNote: This is relevant to insider misuse of bank systems and to a former employee who keeps access after leaving. The intent must exist when the access is obtained, but the intended offence, gain or loss may come later (Cap. 200 s.161(1); drafting inference).

provisions.title: Unauthorised access by telecommunications
provisions.summary: Knowingly causing a computer, by telecommunications, to obtain unauthorised access to a program or data is an offence with a level 4 fine. A prosecution must start within 3 years of the offence or within 6 months after the prosecutor discovers it, whichever expires first.
provisions.counselNote: Scraping through an interface the bank has not authorised may fall within this offence, so the bank's access terms should say clearly what is authorised.

provisions.title: Service provider safe harbour
provisions.summary: A service provider is not liable for damages or other pecuniary remedies for infringement on its platform merely because it provides online services, if it meets the conditions: reasonable steps after notice or awareness, no direct financial benefit, no interference with standard technical measures, and a designated agent.
provisions.counselNote: The bank's own platforms, such as a community forum or a third-party app store listing, need a notice route and a designated agent to rely on this protection.

provisions.title: Arbitration of IP disputes
provisions.summary: IP disputes over ownership, validity, infringement and transactions in an IP right can be referred to arbitration between the parties, and an award is final and binding on the parties and on those who claim through them.
provisions.counselNote: A vendor or licence clause can send IP ownership and patent validity disputes to arbitration, so the clause should say which disputes it covers (good practice).

provisions.instrument: Secretary for Justice v Cheng Ka Yee
provisions.title: Using one's own computer is not 'obtaining access'
provisions.summary: The Court of Final Appeal held that s.161(1)(c) of the Crimes Ordinance, obtaining access to a computer with a view to dishonest gain, does not apply to a person's use of their own computer. Teachers who used their own phones and a computer to send out interview questions were therefore outside the offence.
provisions.counselNote: Staff who copy confidential material on their own devices may fall outside s.161, so the bank's protection rests more on confidence, contract and access controls on its own systems (drafting inference).

bankNotes: **Incident notice:** If the bank is designated as a critical infrastructure operator, an incident that disrupts or is likely to disrupt its core function must be notified to the Commissioner within 12 hours of becoming aware, and other incidents within 48 hours, with a written report within 14 days (Cap. 653 s.28; Sch. 6).

**Vendor disputes:** The HKMA's outsourcing guideline (SA-2) says outsourcing needs written agreements, monitoring, contingency planning and HKMA access. A dispute with a vendor should not leave a critical service without a way to keep it running (good practice). The guideline is guidance, not law.

**Personal data in disputes:** Customer data produced in a dispute must still be protected by all practicable steps against unauthorised access, and a data processor must be bound by contract (Cap. 486 Sch. 1, DPP 4(1)-(2); drafting inference).

glossary.definition: An award an owner may elect instead of actual damages and profits: $750 to $30,000 per work, up to $150,000 for wilful infringement and down to $200 for innocent infringement (17 U.S.C. § 504(c)).
Damages of up to twice the award for wilful and malicious trade secret misappropriation under the Defend Trade Secrets Act (18 U.S.C. § 1836(b)(3)(C)).
The limit on a host's liability for user-posted copyright material, available only if it meets the conditions of 17 U.S.C. § 512, including acting on valid takedown notices.

A written reply from the subscriber whose material was removed, under penalty of perjury, that the removal was a mistake. Material may be restored 10 to 14 business days later unless the claimant has sued (17 U.S.C. § 512(g)(3)).
An order of the International Trade Commission that bars infringing imports from entering the United States, subject to a public interest review (19 U.S.C. § 1337(d)).
A Patent Trial and Appeal Board proceeding in which a third party challenges patent claims on novelty or obviousness grounds, using patents or printed publications (35 U.S.C. § 311(b)).
A patent case that stands out, judged on the totality of the circumstances, which can lead to fee shifting under 35 U.S.C. § 285.
The time a GPL licensee has to stop a violation and keep or regain its licence. Under GPL-3.0 s.8 it is 30 days after a first notice from the copyright holder. The GPL-2.0 text has no equivalent.
A written instruction to preserve documents, data and code that may be relevant to a claim, suspending routine deletion until the hold is lifted (good practice).

A tribunal created by the Copyright Alternative in Small-Claims Enforcement (CASE) Act of 2020, which hears copyright claims with capped damages. A respondent can opt out (reported; check the current caps).
A court order requiring infringing copies or articles to be handed over so that they can be dealt with under the court's direction.
A threat of infringement proceedings, made by letter or otherwise, that the person threatened can challenge in court under the Patents, Trade Marks or Registered Designs Ordinance.

title: Product counsel: IP from idea to launch
oneLiner: Product counsel at a bank spots IP questions while a feature is still an idea, settles the simple ones quickly, and brings in specialists for the rest.
keyPoints: Product counsel is the lawyer embedded with a bank's product managers, designers and engineers. This stage shows how to find IP questions from the first idea for a feature, through naming, design and build, to launch and after.

**Triage early:** Run a short IP triage on each feature before design is fixed, covering the name, assets, code and services, data, AI, inventions, partners and claims (good practice). Send the hard points to specialists.

**Clear the name first:** Search for conflicting marks before any announcement, and file an intent-to-use application if the launch date is set (15 U.S.C. § 1051(b)). Once the mark registers, the filing date gives nationwide priority (15 U.S.C. § 1057(c)).

**Mark the product accurately:** Use ® only for a registered mark, and only in the form the statute allows (15 U.S.C. § 1111). Refer to a wallet, card scheme or partner's brand only as nominative fair use, and follow the partner's brand rules (New Kids on the Block v. News America Publishing, 971 F.2d 302 (9th Cir. 1992)).

**Protect the look, not the idea:** Copyright never reaches the idea, procedure or method of operation behind an interface (17 U.S.C. § 102(b)). Product-design trade dress needs secondary meaning and cannot be functional (Wal-Mart Stores v. Samara Brothers, 529 U.S. 205 (2000); TrafFix Devices v. Marketing Displays, 532 U.S. 23 (2001)) (reported; check).

**Fonts, images and AI output:** Check the licence scope of each typeface, icon set and stock image before it ships, because the SIL Open Font License bars selling the font software by itself (OFL-1.1 condition 1) and bars a Reserved Font Name in a modified version without permission (OFL-1.1 condition 3).

conceptMap.caption: Where product counsel checks IP as a feature moves from idea to launch and after

items.label: Idea and naming
items.note: Search for conflicting marks and decide on the filing before any public announcement (good practice).

items.label: Design
items.note: Screens get copyright only for their original expression. Trade dress and design rights need their own analysis.

items.label: Build
items.note: Open source goes to the stage 11 review. SDK, API and map terms set how the product may use and store data.

items.label: Launch
items.note: Marks, notices and customer terms must be accurate on the day the product goes live.

items.label: After launch
items.note: A new SDK, a licence change upstream, a new market or a new AI model reopens the review.

deepDive.heading: The product counsel's seat
deepDive.lede: Product counsel works inside the product team, not at the end of it. The job is to spot IP problems early, settle the easy ones fast and bring in specialists for the rest.
points: **Get in early:** Join the feature brief before the design is fixed, because a name, a font or an SDK chosen late is costly to change (good practice).
**Run the triage:** Ask the same eight questions for every feature: the name, assets, code and services, data, AI, inventions, partners and claims (good practice).

**Know who to call:** Patent counsel handles inventions and freedom to operate, the open source office handles licences, privacy handles personal data, and regulatory counsel handles the bank's approvals (good practice).

**Use the bank's approval gate:** The OCC's risk management principles for new bank products and services expect a bank to assess a new product's risks before it launches (OCC Bulletin 2017-43, 20 October 2017; check current status). An IP sign-off belongs in that gate (drafting inference).
**Escalate by risk:** Settle a point at the desk when the answer is a standard licence or a clear name search, and send anything that could block the launch to counsel (good practice).
deepDive.takeaway: The seat works when product counsel is in the room before the decisions are made, not when it reviews a finished launch.

deepDive.heading: Names, brands and partner marks
deepDive.lede: A name is cheap to choose and costly to change after launch, so the name check comes first.
points: **Clear the name before it is announced:** Search for conflicting marks and act on the result before a logo, domain or press release goes out (good practice).

**File on intent:** A person with a bona fide intention to use a mark in commerce can file an intent-to-use application (15 U.S.C. § 1051(b)(1)). No registration issues until a verified statement of use is accepted (15 U.S.C. § 1051(d)).

**Use the filing date:** Filing an application to register is constructive use, contingent on registration, and gives nationwide priority from the filing date. Earlier users and earlier filers keep their position (15 U.S.C. § 1057(c)).

**Use the ® only when it is earned:** Using ® on a mark that is not registered is improper (USPTO TMEP § 906.02) (reported; check). Notice is optional, but a registrant that omits it cannot recover profits or damages unless the defendant knew of the registration (15 U.S.C. § 1111).

**Use a partner's mark with care:** A partner's name can be used to refer to that partner's product where the product cannot be identified without it, only as much of the mark as is needed is used, and nothing suggests sponsorship (New Kids on the Block v. News America Publishing, 971 F.2d 302 (9th Cir. 1992); Toyota Motor Sales v. Tabari, 610 F.3d 1171 (9th Cir. 2010)). Follow the partner's brand rules as well (good practice).

**Make comparative claims provable:** Advertising that misrepresents the nature, characteristics or qualities of goods or services can be sued on by anyone who is or is likely to be damaged (15 U.S.C. § 1125(a)(1)(B)). Lexmark International v. Static Control Components, 572 U.S. 118 (2014), requires a plaintiff to fall within the statute's zone of interests and to show proximate cause. Keep evidence for every comparison (good practice).

visual.caption: Four name and mark rules a product team will meet

items.label: Intent to use
items.note: File before the mark is in use. Nothing registers until a verified statement of use is accepted.

items.label: Filing priority
items.note: Nationwide priority from the filing date, if the mark registers, subject to earlier users.

items.label: Registration notice
items.note: Optional. Without it, no profits or damages unless the defendant knew of the registration.

items.label: Partner names
items.note: Names a partner's product only as needed, with no suggestion of sponsorship.

deepDive.takeaway: Clear the name, file on intent, use ® only once a mark is registered, and treat a partner's brand as the partner's property.

deepDive.heading: Screens, icons, fonts and images
deepDive.lede: Most of what a team builds on screen is protected in some way, but not by one right. Each right covers a different part of the work.
points: **Copyright covers expression, not method:** Copyright protects original works of authorship but never an idea, procedure, process, system or method of operation (17 U.S.C. § 102(a), (b)). Lotus v. Borland treated a menu command hierarchy as an uncopyrightable method of operation, and Apple v. Microsoft filtered out unprotectable and licensed interface elements, leaving thin protection against near-verbatim copying (Lotus Development Corp. v. Borland International, 49 F.3d 807 (1st Cir. 1995); Apple Computer v. Microsoft, 35 F.3d 1435 (9th Cir. 1994)) (reported; check).

**Trade dress needs meaning and non-function:** Product-design trade dress is protected without registration only on proof of secondary meaning, and functional features cannot be trade dress (Wal-Mart Stores v. Samara Brothers, 529 U.S. 205 (2000); TrafFix Devices v. Marketing Displays, 532 U.S. 23 (2001)) (reported; check). The claimant must prove the trade dress is not functional (15 U.S.C. § 1125(a)(3)).

**Design patents cover the look of an icon:** A design patent can protect the ornamental design of a computer-generated icon or interface shown on a display screen (35 U.S.C. § 171; MPEP § 1504.01(a)) (reported; check). The term runs for 15 years from grant (35 U.S.C. § 173) (reported; check). Ask patent counsel before the design is shown outside the team, because a public showing can start a bar period (drafting inference).

**Typefaces and font software differ:** A typeface as such is not subject to US copyright (37 C.F.R. § 202.1(e)) (reported; check), but original font software can be registered as a literary work (reported; check). Under the SIL Open Font License, fonts may be used, embedded and bundled, but the font software may not be sold alone and a Reserved Font Name may not be used in a modified version without permission (OFL-1.1 conditions 1 and 3).

**Read the stock and AI licences:** A stock image licence sets the permitted use, the territory, the term and the number of users, and the bank's marketing use must fit inside them (good practice). The Copyright Office guidance says applicants must disclose AI-generated content that is more than de minimis and exclude it from the claim (88 Fed. Reg. 16190, 16 March 2023) (reported; check).

visual.caption: Which right covers which part of an interface

items.label: Copyright
items.note: Covers original expression, not the idea or the method of operation.

items.label: Trade dress
items.note: Needs secondary meaning and non-function, and the claimant proves non-function.

items.label: Design patent
items.note: Covers the ornamental look of an icon or screen shown on a display.

items.label: Font licence
items.note: Free to use and bundle, but the font software cannot be sold by itself.

deepDive.takeaway: Protect each design element by the right that fits it, and record the licence scope of every typeface, icon and image in the asset register (good practice).

deepDive.heading: Third-party code, SDKs, APIs and data
deepDive.lede: Open source, SDKs, APIs, scraped data and map data all arrive with terms attached. Product teams often pick them up during a sprint, so counsel needs to see each one before it reaches a build.
points: **Open source goes to the stage 11 review:** Any third-party code, including a sample app or a snippet copied from a forum, goes through the open source approval before it reaches a build. A permissive licence still carries notice duties, and copyleft or network copyleft code needs counsel's view before the design is fixed (good practice).

**SDK and API terms are contracts:** An SDK or API comes with terms that limit use, caching and the data it returns. Google Maps Platform, for example, bars caching of map content except as its service-specific terms allow (Google Maps Platform Terms of Service) (reported; check). Product should read the terms before the SDK ships, because the provider can change or end them (good practice).

**Online terms bind only with notice and assent:** A website's or API's terms bind a user only if the notice is reasonably conspicuous and the user takes an action that shows assent. Terms behind a link were not enforced in Nguyen v. Barnes & Noble, 763 F.3d 1171 (9th Cir. 2014); a clear sign-up screen was enforced in Meyer v. Uber Technologies, 868 F.3d 66 (2d Cir. 2017); and Berman v. Freedom Financial Network, 30 F.4th 849 (9th Cir. 2022), refused terms where the notice was small and the button did not signal agreement (reported; check). Product should design sign-up flows with that test in mind (good practice).

**Scraping and the CFAA:** Scraping public pages is not automatically lawful. Under the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act, exceeding authorised access means getting into areas that are off limits, not misusing data one is entitled to reach (Van Buren v. United States, 593 U.S. 374 (2021)) (reported; check). In hiQ Labs v. LinkedIn, 31 F.4th 1180 (9th Cir. 2022), the Ninth Circuit held that scraping public profiles was likely not access “without authorization”, but the district court later found that hiQ had breached LinkedIn's User Agreement, and the parties settled with a consent judgment and a permanent injunction; the settlement terms are not judicial findings (reported; check). Product should not plan a feature that collects a third party's data without counsel's review (good practice).

**Map and database licences:** A public derivative database must be offered under the ODbL or a compatible licence, while a produced work such as a rendered map needs an attribution notice (ODbL-1.0 s.4.3). Publicly using a produced work made from a derivative database also makes that database publicly used, so it must then be offered under the ODbL or a compatible licence (ODbL-1.0 s.4.4(c)). Product should decide early whether the feature keeps a derivative database or only renders map images, because each choice brings a different duty (drafting inference).

**App store rules:** Apple's App Review Guideline 5.2 says an app should include only content the developer created or is licensed to use, and guideline 5.2.1 says not to use third-party trademarks, copyrighted works or patented ideas without permission (Apple App Review Guidelines, s.5.2 and 5.2.1). The Free Software Foundation's view that App Store terms conflict with the GPL is a view, not a court ruling (reported; check), so GPL code goes into an app store only after counsel's review (good practice).
deepDive.takeaway: Counsel should see the terms before the code or data is in the build, not after the launch date is set.

deepDive.heading: Inventions found in product work
deepDive.lede: Product work often turns up a patentable idea: a better flow, a model technique or a data method. The first public showing can start a clock, so product should bring the idea to counsel before it shows the idea to anyone outside the bank.
points: **Disclose to counsel before any demo, beta or talk:** An invention disclosure lets counsel decide whether to file before the idea is shown outside the bank. Internal design reviews are a safe place to raise the idea first (good practice).

**The US grace period is one year:** A disclosure by the inventor, or by someone who got the subject matter from the inventor, is not prior art if it was made one year or less before the effective filing date (35 U.S.C. § 102(b)(1)(A)). A second exception covers a later disclosure by others of subject matter the inventor had already publicly disclosed (§ 102(b)(1)(B)), but the one-year clock still runs, so the grace period is not a reason to wait (drafting inference).

**Other markets give little or no grace:** The European Patent Convention applies absolute novelty, and Art. 55(1) disregards a disclosure made within six months only for evident abuse or an official exhibition (European Patent Convention Art. 54 and 55(1)) (reported; check). The UK has similar but not identical narrow exceptions within six months (Patents Act 1977 s.2(4)) (reported; check). Hong Kong's exceptions are also narrow and run for six months (Cap. 514 s.37B and s.109).

**Provisional applications give an early date:** A provisional application needs no claims (35 U.S.C. § 111(b)(2)), and it is regarded as abandoned 12 months after filing unless it is converted (§ 111(b)(5)). A later application that claims its benefit under § 119(e)(1) can take the provisional's filing date for an invention disclosed as § 112(a) requires, if it is filed within 12 months (reported; check). Product should ask for a provisional filing when a feature may launch within a year (good practice).

**Freedom to operate and willfulness:** A feature that may use a competitor's patent needs a freedom-to-operate review before launch. In Halo Electronics v. Pulse Electronics, 579 U.S. 93 (2016), the Supreme Court let courts increase damages up to three times in egregious cases of culpable willful infringement (35 U.S.C. § 284) (reported; check). Under 35 U.S.C. § 298, failing to get or present advice of counsel cannot be used to prove willful infringement, but relying on an opinion can still waive privilege. Product should route the review through counsel so that the privilege question is managed (good practice).

**Marking and false marking:** A patentee that does not mark its patented article cannot recover damages for infringement before the infringer was notified of it, and filing suit counts as notice (35 U.S.C. § 287(a)). Marking a product with a patent word or number to deceive the public is false marking, and only the United States may sue for the fine, while a person with a competitive injury may sue for damages (35 U.S.C. § 292(a), (b)). Product should check every patent marking and virtual marking page before it goes live (good practice).

deepDive.heading: Launch: notices, claims and terms
deepDive.lede: Launch puts the bank's notices, marks and terms in front of customers. Product, design and marketing write much of that text, and counsel reviews the words before release because they decide what the bank can enforce.
points: **Open source notices screen:** Shipped open source needs the notices its licence requires, which often means the copyright lines and the licence text in the app or the product documentation. The notices screen is built from the open source review in stage 11 (good practice).

**Copyright notice:** A copyright notice is optional, but if a proper notice appears on the published copies, an infringer cannot rely on innocent infringement to reduce actual or statutory damages (17 U.S.C. § 401(d)). The notice takes the form of the symbol, the year of first publication and the name of the owner (17 U.S.C. § 401(b)). Product should put it in the footer of the app or on the legal page (good practice).

**Patent pending and marks:** Use “patent pending” only while an application is pending: marking it when no application is pending, to deceive the public, is false marking (35 U.S.C. § 292(a)). For an intent-to-use application, a mark is registered only once a statement of use is accepted (15 U.S.C. § 1051(d)), so the ® symbol waits until registration. The notice of registration is optional, but a registrant that does not give it recovers no profits or damages unless the defendant had actual notice (15 U.S.C. § 1111).

**Customer terms by clickwrap:** Customer terms bind when the notice is conspicuous and the customer's click shows assent (Meyer v. Uber Technologies, 868 F.3d 66 (2d Cir. 2017)) (reported; check). Product should place the terms link beside the button the customer presses, and label that button so it means agreement (good practice).

**User content, the DMCA agent and Section 230:** A platform that stores user uploads keeps the storage safe harbour only if it has designated an agent with the Copyright Office to receive infringement notices (17 U.S.C. § 512(c)(2); 37 C.F.R. § 201.38). The designation expires after three years unless it is renewed, and a lapsed designation loses the safe harbour (reported; check). Section 230 gives no shield against federal IP claims, because 47 U.S.C. § 230(e)(2) leaves intellectual property law alone, but the circuits differ on state-law IP claims (reported; check). Product should put the renewal date in the team calendar and build a takedown route (good practice).

**Feedback clauses:** Under California law, a person who discloses an idea that the recipient accepts, knowing that payment is expected, can recover if the idea is used, even where the idea is not copyrightable (Desny v. Wilder, 46 Cal. 2d 715 (1956)) (reported; check). A feedback clause that licenses suggestions to the bank manages that risk (good practice). Product should not run idea contests, beta suggestion forms or pitch forms without that clause in the terms (good practice).
deepDive.takeaway: Notices, marks and terms are cheap to fix before release and expensive to fix after customers have seen them (drafting inference).

deepDive.heading: After launch: changes, feedback and claims
deepDive.lede: Launch starts a new phase of IP work. Changes reopen the review, letters arrive, and AI features bring model licences and vendor promises that can change over time.
points: **What reopens the review:** A new SDK, an upstream licence change, a new market, a new data source or an AI model swap each reopens the review (good practice). Product should tell counsel before the change ships, not at the next audit (good practice).

**Infringement and takedown letters:** Letters that claim infringement go to counsel at once, and no one on the product team replies to them (good practice). Some letters start a clock: for hosting services in the EU, Article 16 of the Digital Services Act requires a notice-and-action mechanism and a timely decision on each notice (Regulation (EU) 2022/2065, Art. 16) (reported; check).

**Llama 4 licence terms:** A licensee that had more than 700 million monthly active users in the preceding calendar month, measured at the Llama 4 release date of 5 April 2025, must request a separate licence from Meta, and may not exercise the licence rights until Meta grants it (Llama 4 Community License, s.2). “Built with Llama” must be prominently displayed where Llama materials or derivatives are made available (Llama 4 Community License, s.1.b.i). Product should check these terms before a model is chosen, not after (good practice).

**Vendor AI indemnities:** Microsoft's Copilot Copyright Commitment (September 2023), Google's generative AI indemnity (12 October 2023) and OpenAI's Copyright Shield (6 November 2023) extend defence to customers for named or paid services, but each has conditions, such as using the built-in guardrails and not deliberately generating infringing material (reported; check). Product should record those conditions in the feature plan, because a missed guardrail can take away the cover (drafting inference).

**EU AI Act output marking:** Article 50(2) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 requires providers of AI systems that generate synthetic audio, image, video or text to mark the outputs in a machine-readable way, and it applies from 2 August 2026 to new systems. The reported 2026 Digital Omnibus gives generative systems already on the market before 2 August 2026 until 2 December 2026 (Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, as reported; check the timing). Product should confirm which dates apply to the feature before it launches (good practice).

**Keep a record of the model:** Record the model name and version, its licence, its vendor indemnity and the conditions attached to it in the feature record, so counsel can see what changed when the model is swapped (good practice).
deepDive.takeaway: Launch closes the first review, not the IP work: each change, letter and model swap needs its own check.

provisions.title: Intent-to-use application and statement of use
provisions.summary: A person with a bona fide intention to use a mark in commerce may apply to register it. No registration issues until the applicant files a verified statement of use, which is due within six months after the notice of allowance and can be extended (15 U.S.C. § 1051(b)(1), (d)(1), (d)(2)).
provisions.counselNote: A name can be filed before the launch, which secures the filing date for priority. Nothing is registered until the statement of use is accepted, so launch copy cannot say 'registered' (drafting inference). Ask trademark counsel to clear the name before any announcement (good practice).

provisions.title: Constructive use from the filing date
provisions.summary: Filing an application to register is constructive use, which gives nationwide priority from the filing date if the mark registers. The priority does not run against a person who used the mark, or had a pending or registered application for it, before that filing (15 U.S.C. § 1057(c)(1) to (c)(3)).
provisions.counselNote: An early filing protects the priority date against later adopters of the name. It does not beat a party that used the mark before the filing date, so a clearance search still comes first (drafting inference).

provisions.title: Notice of registration
provisions.summary: A registrant may display 'Registered in U.S. Patent and Trademark Office', 'Reg. U.S. Pat. & Tm. Off.' or the letter R in a circle with the mark. The notice is optional, but a registrant that sues without it cannot recover profits or damages unless the defendant had actual notice of the registration (15 U.S.C. § 1111).
provisions.counselNote: A symbol on an unregistered mark is improper (TMEP § 906.02, reported; check), so the product team uses ® only on registered marks (good practice). Marketing copy that calls a pending mark 'registered' creates the same problem (drafting inference).

provisions.title: False designations of origin and false advertising
provisions.summary: A person who uses a word, name, symbol or false or misleading representation of fact in commerce is liable where it is likely to confuse as to origin or sponsorship, or where, in commercial advertising or promotion, it misrepresents the nature, characteristics or qualities of goods or services (15 U.S.C. § 1125(a)(1)(A), (B)).
provisions.counselNote: A comparison claim in a launch advertisement needs evidence before it goes out, because a rival named in the comparison can sue under this section (drafting inference). Fair use of a famous mark in comparative advertising, other than as a designation of source for the bank's own goods or services, is not actionable as dilution (15 U.S.C. § 1125(c)(3)(A)).

provisions.title: Subject matter of copyright: in general
provisions.summary: Copyright protects original works of authorship fixed in a tangible medium, including pictorial and graphic works. It does not extend to any idea, procedure, process, system, method of operation or concept, whatever form it takes (17 U.S.C. § 102(a), (b)).
provisions.counselNote: Copyright in a screen covers the artwork and the code, not the workflow or the layout idea. A court treated a menu command hierarchy as an uncopyrightable method of operation (Lotus Development Corp. v. Borland International, 49 F.3d 807 (1st Cir. 1995), reported; check). Copying a rival's screen closely is where the risk sits, not a similar workflow (drafting inference).

provisions.title: Notice of copyright on published copies
provisions.summary: A notice of copyright may be placed on publicly distributed copies. If a proper notice appears on the copies, no weight is given to a defence of innocent infringement in mitigation of actual or statutory damages, if the notice is in the form and position the section specifies (17 U.S.C. § 401(a), (b), (d)).
provisions.counselNote: The notice is optional, but a proper notice on the app, the documentation and the site means an innocent-infringement defence is given no weight in reducing damages (17 U.S.C. § 401(d)). Product counsel adds the notice at launch, with the year of first publication (good practice).

provisions.title: Storage safe harbour for user content
provisions.summary: A service provider can use the storage safe harbour for material that users post only if it has designated an agent with the Copyright Office to receive infringement notices. A designation has to be renewed, and a lapsed designation loses the safe harbour (37 C.F.R. § 201.38, reported; check). Section 512(c)(2) requires the designated agent, not the renewal.
provisions.counselNote: A feature that lets customers upload images, reviews or comments needs the designated agent in place before launch. Someone must diarise the renewal date, because a lapse removes the protection (good practice).

provisions.title: Conditions for patentability: novelty and the inventor's grace period
provisions.summary: A disclosure made one year or less before the effective filing date is not prior art if the inventor made it, or someone who got the subject matter directly or indirectly from the inventor made it. A second exception covers a later disclosure by others of subject matter the inventor had already publicly disclosed (35 U.S.C. § 102(a)(1), (b)(1)(A), (B)).
provisions.counselNote: A demo, beta or conference talk counts as the inventor's own disclosure only if the person giving it is the inventor or got the subject matter from the inventor, so the one-year clock starts on that date for those disclosures (drafting inference). Outside the US the same demo can count against novelty, because the EPC applies absolute novelty with narrow exceptions (reported; check).

provisions.title: Provisional application
provisions.summary: A provisional application does not need the claims that section 112(b) to (e) would otherwise require (35 U.S.C. § 111(b)(2)), and it is treated as abandoned 12 months after filing unless it is converted into a non-provisional application (35 U.S.C. § 111(b)).
provisions.counselNote: A provisional is a fast, low-cost early filing date for a feature the team is about to show publicly (good practice). It does not become a patent by itself, so the full application must be filed within 12 months to claim its date (reported; check).

provisions.title: Patents for designs
provisions.summary: Whoever invents a new, original and ornamental design for an article of manufacture may obtain a design patent, subject to the conditions and requirements of the patent statute (35 U.S.C. § 171(a), (b)).
provisions.counselNote: A screen icon or an interface layout can be protected by a design patent when it is shown on a display screen (MPEP § 1504.01(a), reported; check). A public showing before filing can use up the one-year grace period (35 U.S.C. § 102(b)(1)(A)), so the design team tells counsel before the first demo (good practice).

provisions.title: Marking and notice
provisions.summary: A patentee may give notice by marking the article with 'patent' or 'pat.' and the patent number, or with an internet address of a free public posting that links the article to the number. Without marking, damages run only from when the infringer is notified of the infringement, and filing suit counts as notice (35 U.S.C. § 287(a)).
provisions.counselNote: Virtual marking lets a product page show the patent number instead of the device or package. The marking rule covers articles claimed in the patent, not method claims alone (drafting inference), so ask patent counsel which claims issued before the team writes the marking text (good practice).

provisions.title: False marking
provisions.summary: Only the United States may sue for the fine of up to $500 per offence for false marking. A person who suffers a competitive injury may sue for damages. Marking a product with an expired patent is not a violation (35 U.S.C. § 292(a) to (c)).
provisions.counselNote: Marking a product as 'patented' when no patent covers it is the risk the product team must avoid (drafting inference). Marking text should come from patent counsel, not from marketing (good practice).

provisions.title: Advice of counsel
provisions.summary: An infringer's failure to obtain advice of counsel, or to present it to the court or jury, may not be used to prove willful infringement or intent to induce infringement (35 U.S.C. § 298).
provisions.counselNote: The team cannot be penalised for skipping an opinion, but relying on one can waive privilege over the advice (drafting inference). Product counsel should decide with patent counsel when an opinion is worth the cost, before a feature is built around a third party's claims (good practice).

provisions.title: Font software in products
provisions.summary: Fonts may be used, studied, modified, embedded and bundled with software, but the font software cannot be sold by itself (OFL-1.1 condition 1). A modified version may not use a Reserved Font Name without written permission (OFL-1.1 condition 3), and font software must stay under the licence (OFL-1.1 condition 5). Documents made with the fonts are not covered.
provisions.counselNote: A brand team that wants a custom build of an open font cannot keep a Reserved Font Name without permission, and cannot sell the font alone (drafting inference). Documents such as statements and marketing PDFs are outside the licence, so the brand team needs no font licence for them (drafting inference).

provisions.instrument: Open Data Commons Open Database License v1.0
provisions.title: Share-alike for public derivative databases
provisions.summary: A derivative database that is publicly used must be offered under the ODbL or a compatible licence. A produced work, such as a rendered map image, needs only an attribution notice, but publicly using a produced work made from a derivative database can also trigger the share-alike duty (ODbL-1.0 full text, reported; check).
provisions.counselNote: A feature that builds a map or a dataset from OpenStreetMap data can oblige the bank to share the derivative database if it is publicly used (drafting inference). The product team should ask counsel before the data is merged with the bank's own records (good practice).

provisions.instrument: Lexmark International, Inc. v. Static Control Components, Inc.
provisions.title: Zone of interests and proximate cause for false advertising
provisions.summary: A false advertising plaintiff under § 1125(a)(1)(B) must fall within the statute's zone of interests, which means an injury to a commercial interest in reputation or sales, and must show proximate cause.
provisions.counselNote: Only a party with a commercial injury can sue, so the likely plaintiff in a comparison dispute is a rival whose product is named (drafting inference). Keep the evidence behind each comparison ready to produce (good practice).

provisions.title: Intellectual property in apps
provisions.summary: Apps should include only content the developer created or has a licence to use. Third-party material such as trademarks, copyrighted works or patented ideas must not be used without permission, and an app should be submitted by the entity that owns or licenses the IP.
provisions.counselNote: A partner logo or a licensed image in a bank app needs written permission before the build is submitted, because a rejection delays the launch (good practice). The submitting entity must be the one that holds the rights (drafting inference).

checklist: **Name and marks:** Clear the feature name before any announcement. If the bank has a bona fide intention to use the mark in commerce, file an intent-to-use application before launch (15 U.S.C. § 1051(b)(1)). Constructive use then dates from the filing date, if the mark registers (15 U.S.C. § 1057(c)).

**Partner marks:** Ask whether the feature shows a wallet, card scheme or partner mark, and get the partner's brand rules in writing before the first screen is drawn. Naming another owner's product with its mark can be nominative fair use only where the product cannot readily be identified without it and nothing suggests sponsorship (New Kids on the Block v. News America Publishing, 971 F.2d 302 (9th Cir. 1992)).

**Comparative claims:** Every launch claim that compares the bank's product with a rival, or states a quality or performance level, needs supporting evidence before it goes live (15 U.S.C. § 1125(a)(1)(B); Lexmark International v. Static Control Components, 572 U.S. 118 (2014)).

**Screens and icons:** Ask early what in the design is worth protecting. Copyright covers the expression in an interface, not the method of operation (17 U.S.C. § 102(b); reported; check). Product-design trade dress needs secondary meaning and cannot be functional (Wal-Mart Stores v. Samara Brothers, 529 U.S. 205 (2000); TrafFix Devices v. Marketing Displays, 532 U.S. 23 (2001); reported; check). A design patent can cover an icon shown on a display screen (35 U.S.C. § 171; reported; check).

**Fonts and images:** Confirm that each typeface, font file, icon set and stock image is licensed for the bank's use, including app bundles, web delivery and print. Font software cannot be sold by itself, and a modified font may not use a reserved font name without permission (OFL-1.1 conditions 1 and 3). Stock licences often limit the number or type of uses (good practice).

**Code, SDKs and APIs:** Send each open source component to the open source review (stage 11). Read each SDK and API term before the SDK ships, because those terms often limit caching and data use (Google Maps Platform terms on caching; reported; check).

**Data sources:** Confirm that the bank holds a licence or contract for each data source, including public data gathered by scraping. Website terms bind a user only where notice is clear and assent is shown (Nguyen v. Barnes & Noble, 763 F.3d 1171 (9th Cir. 2014); reported; check). Scraping can also raise a CFAA question, which turns on access to areas that are off limits rather than on misuse of data the user can reach (Van Buren v. United States, 593 U.S. 374 (2021); reported; check).

**Inventions:** Ask whether the feature uses a new method, model or system. If it does, the invention disclosure should be filed before any demo, beta, pilot or conference talk (35 U.S.C. § 102(b)(1)(A); good practice).

**Notices:** Match every marking to the real position. Marking an article falsely can expose the bank to a fine that only the United States may sue for (35 U.S.C. § 292(a)). A registrant that omits the registration notice loses profits and damages in an infringement suit unless the defendant had actual notice (15 U.S.C. § 1111). A proper copyright notice means an infringer's plea of innocent infringement is given no weight in reducing damages (17 U.S.C. § 401(d)).

**Customer terms:** Show the terms at the point of assent, with a button that signals agreement to them. Clear notice on a sign-up screen was enforced in Meyer v. Uber Technologies, 868 F.3d 66 (2d Cir. 2017), while a small notice and a button that did not signal agreement were not enforced in Berman v. Freedom Financial Network, 30 F.4th 849 (9th Cir. 2022) (reported; check).
itAngle: **Feature flags:** Launch new features behind a flag, so that a name, asset or licence problem can be switched off without a new app store build (good practice).

**Asset register:** Record the source, licence, version and owner of each font, icon, image, SDK and model in the build manifest, so the notices screen and any takedown can be answered from one list (good practice).

**Generated notices:** Generate the open source notices and the copyright text from the software bill of materials at build time, and test that they appear in each app bundle and web build (good practice).

**Web delivery of fonts:** A font loaded from a third-party host or content delivery network is still font software delivered to users, so check that the licence covers that delivery method (OFL-1.1 condition 1; good practice).
**Scraping controls:** Route data collection through licensed feeds or APIs, with logged access and rate limits, so the bank can show what it took and under which terms (good practice).
virtualBankNotes: **Product approval:** Put the IP triage into the bank's new product approval record. The OCC expects new products and services to be risk-assessed before launch, as Bulletin 2017-43 sets out (check current status).

**Third-party risk:** The interagency guidance (88 Fed. Reg. 37920) covers the whole life cycle of third-party relationships, including contracting, and the agencies say it adds no new requirements (reported; check). SDK, API and AI model providers belong in the vendor inventory (drafting inference).

**Model risk for AI features:** SR 11-7 and OCC Bulletin 2011-12 were rescinded on 17 April 2026 and replaced by OCC Bulletin 2026-13 and SR 26-2. Whether the replacement applies from that date or from 2027 is unsettled, and commentary reports that it does not cover generative or agentic AI. Ask the model risk team which policy governs an AI feature (drafting inference).

**Customer terms:** Terms accepted by clickwrap need clear notice and an action that shows assent (Meyer v. Uber Technologies, 868 F.3d 66 (2d Cir. 2017); reported; check). Product should not change a sign-up flow without counsel's review of the terms (good practice).

**Vendor AI indemnities:** Vendor IP indemnities for AI output are conditional. Microsoft's Copilot Copyright Commitment, for example, depends on the customer using the built-in guardrails and not deliberately generating infringing material (reported; check). Product should know those conditions, because the bank loses the protection if it steps outside them (good practice).
productNotes: **Name and claims:** Ask what customers will call the feature, whether a partner's name or card scheme mark appears in it, and what the launch copy will say about rivals or performance. Those answers set the clearance and evidence work before any announcement (good practice; 15 U.S.C. § 1125(a)(1)(B)).

**Design assets:** Ask who made each icon, illustration, font and image, under what licence or contract, and whether any new screen or icon is meant to be distinctive enough to protect. Ask before the design is handed to engineering (good practice).

**Code, SDKs, data and models:** Ask which libraries, SDKs, APIs, datasets and AI models the feature uses, and which of them the bank does not yet hold a licence for. Send open source to the stage 11 review, and SDK terms to counsel, before the build starts (good practice).

**Inventions and disclosure:** Ask whether the feature has a new method or model, and when the team plans any demo, beta, pilot, conference talk or press release. A public disclosure can bar a patent abroad, where the US one-year grace period does not apply (35 U.S.C. § 102(b)(1)(A); EPC Art. 54; reported; check).
pitfalls: **Launch before clearance:** A public launch under a name nobody has cleared can force a rename after the marketing spend is committed. An intent-to-use filing before launch is the low-cost step (15 U.S.C. § 1051(b)(1); good practice).

**Demo before filing:** A beta, a conference talk or an app store listing can be a public disclosure. The US gives the inventor a one-year grace period, but Europe, the UK and Hong Kong give only narrow exceptions (35 U.S.C. § 102(b)(1)(A); EPC Art. 54; reported; check).

**Stock and font licences:** A stock licence bought for a website may not cover app screens, print or resale. A font licence may not allow the font to be sold alone or bundled in the way the product team plans (OFL-1.1 condition 1; good practice).

**Registration statements:** Writing 'registered' beside an unregistered mark is a false statement. In Hong Kong it is an offence where the person knows or has reason to believe the claim is false (Cap. 559 s.94(1)), and in the UK it is an offence on a similar test under the Trade Marks Act 1994 s.95(1)(a) (reported; check).

**App store content:** An app that uses third-party material without permission can be rejected, and apps should be submitted by the entity that owns or licenses the IP (Apple App Review Guidelines 5.2 and 5.2.1).

**Model swaps:** Changing the AI model can change licence terms, indemnities and output marking. Llama 4's community licence requires a separate licence from Meta for a licensee above the 700 million monthly active user test, and it requires a 'Built with Llama' notice where the licence applies (Llama 4 Community License, s.2 and s.1.b.i).

points: **Design law covers screens:** Regulation (EU) 2024/2822 defines product to include non-physical manifestations such as graphical user interfaces, but computer programs stay outside the definition (reported; check).

**No general grace period:** Europe applies absolute novelty. A disclosure before filing is disregarded only in narrow cases, such as an evident abuse or an official exhibition (EPC Art. 54 and 55; reported; check).

**Database right:** A database that needed substantial investment has a sui generis right against extraction or re-use of a substantial part of its contents (Directive 96/9/EC, Art. 7; reported; check).

**False registration:** Falsely representing a mark as registered is an offence, and the use of 'registered' or a similar word can count as a representation of registration (Trade Marks Act 1994 s.95(1)(a), (2); reported; check).

**Narrow six-month window:** The UK disregards a disclosure made within six months before filing only where the matter was obtained unlawfully or in breach of confidence, or was shown at a qualifying exhibition (Patents Act 1977 s.2(4); reported; check).
