**Computer-generated works:** The government's report of 18 March 2026 recommends removing copyright protection for computer-generated works under CDPA 1988 s.9(3). Nothing has been legislated, and the report is not binding (reported; check).

**Registration without use:** Since 17 June 2019 a Canadian trademark can be registered on use or on an intention to use in Canada, without a declaration of first use. Prior use still decides priority in a dispute (Trademarks Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. T-13; reported; check).
**Generous grace period:** The applicant's own disclosures in the year before filing are not prior art (Patent Act s.28.2(1)(a)).

**Notice and notice:** An internet intermediary must forward a copyright owner's notice of claimed infringement to the user and tell the claimant, without a duty to remove the content (Copyright Act ss.41.25 to 41.27; reported; check).

hongKong.summary: Product counsel in Hong Kong works with registration-based brand rights, a short list of marking offences and narrow patent grace periods. Brands are protected by registration, with passing off for unregistered names (Cap. 559 s.10(1), (3)). The consumer offences in the Trade Descriptions Ordinance do not reach banking services whose supply is itself regulated under the Banking Ordinance (Cap. 362 s.2, Sch. 4), so for those products the HKMA's conduct expectations do that work. The biggest differences from the US are the six-month patent grace period limited to abuse or exhibitions (Cap. 514 ss.11A, 37B, 109) and the rule that software cannot be registered as a design (Cap. 522 s.8(1)).
keyPoints: **Names and brands:** A registered trade mark is a property right (Cap. 559 s.10(1)), and an unregistered name is protected only by passing off, because the Ordinance gives no infringement action for an unregistered mark (Cap. 559 s.10(3)).

**False registration claim:** Falsely representing that a sign is a registered trade mark, knowing or having reason to believe it is false, is an offence with a level 3 fine, and the word 'registered', or a symbol importing registration, used in Hong Kong is treated as a representation of registration in Hong Kong unless it is shown to refer to a registration elsewhere that in fact covers the goods or services (Cap. 559 s.94(1)-(2)).

**Patent applied for:** Representing that a patent has been applied for on an article sold for value, when no application exists or it was refused, withdrawn or deemed withdrawn, is an offence unless a defence applies (Cap. 514 s.143(1), (4)).

**Software and designs:** Computer programs are not registrable as designs (Cap. 522 s.8(1)), so a screen or icon must be claimed as a feature applied to an article, and whether a screen is an article is an open point (reported; check).

**Grace period:** A disclosure made no earlier than 6 months before filing is disregarded only where it was an evident abuse or a display at an official or officially recognised international exhibition (for a standard patent (R), a prescribed exhibition or meeting), and the filing must state the display (Cap. 514 ss.11A, 37B, 109).

sections.heading: Names, brands and partner marks
sections.lede: A name is cheap to choose and costly to change, so registration rules and offences should shape the name check.
points: **Filing and registration:** An application is filed with the Registrar (Cap. 559 s.38). Once accepted and not successfully opposed, the mark is registered as of the filing date (Cap. 559 ss.47-48).
**Term:** Registration lasts 10 years and can be renewed for further 10-year periods (Cap. 559 s.49(1)-(2)).

**Confusion refusal:** A mark identical to an earlier mark for identical goods or services is refused outright, and a mark identical or similar to an earlier mark for identical or similar goods or services is refused where confusion is likely (Cap. 559 s.12(1)-(3)).

**Prior use:** A person who has used an unregistered sign in trade in Hong Kong, continuously from before the earlier of the registrant's first use in Hong Kong and its registration date, is not infringed by the registered mark (Cap. 559 s.19(4)).

**Transactions:** An assignment of a registered mark must be in writing and signed (Cap. 559 s.27(4)), and a transaction for which no application to register is made within 6 months cannot found a claim for damages or profits for the gap (Cap. 559 s.29(4)).
sections.takeaway: Run a clearance search and file before any public use of a new name, because the registration date is the filing date and prior use is a narrow defence (good practice).

sections.heading: Screens, icons and the rest of the interface
sections.lede: Most interface work is covered by copyright and design rights, and each right covers a different part of the work.
points: **Copyright first:** A computer program is a literary work, and preparatory design material for a program is also a literary work (Cap. 528 s.4(1)(b)-(c)).
**No registration for copyright:** Copyright needs no application or registration, and protection begins once the work is recorded in writing or otherwise (Cap. 528 s.2(1)(a), s.4(2)-(3)).

**Design registration:** A registered design protects features of shape, configuration, pattern or ornament applied to an article and judged by the eye (Cap. 522 s.2(1)). The appearance must be material to buyers or users (Cap. 522 s.6).
**Term:** A registered design lasts 5 years from filing, extendable in 5-year periods to 25 years in total (Cap. 522 s.28(1)-(2)).
**Private use:** A registered design does not extend to private non-commercial acts, or to acts done for evaluation, research or teaching (Cap. 522 s.31(3)).
sections.takeaway: Keep dated design files and source code from the first sprint, because copyright arises on recording and a design filing must claim a feature applied to an article (good practice).

sections.heading: Marketing claims and customer terms
sections.lede: Hong Kong's consumer offences do not reach most regulated banking services, but trade mark, contract and exemption clause rules still shape what the product says and what customers accept.
points: **Comparative claims:** Using a competitor's registered mark to identify its goods or services does not infringe if the use is in accordance with honest practices in industrial or commercial matters, and the court may weigh unfair advantage, detriment to the mark's distinctive character or repute, and deception (Cap. 559 s.21(1)-(2)). This is the rule comparative advertising meets (drafting inference); how the courts apply it to comparative advertising is reported only (reported; check).

**Trade descriptions:** The false trade description offence for services and the unfair trade practice offences (misleading omissions, aggressive practices, bait advertising, bait and switch, wrongly accepting payment) apply to a "product", which excludes goods or services a bank authorised under the Banking Ordinance supplies where that supply is itself regulated under that Ordinance (Cap. 362 s.2, s.7A, ss.13E-13I, Sch. 4).

**What stays in scope:** Goods and services outside that regulated supply, such as merchandise, a rewards item or a non-bank partner's offer shown in the app, can still fall within those offences (Cap. 362 Sch. 4; drafting inference).

**Online acceptance:** An offer and its acceptance may be expressed by electronic records, and section 17 keeps the common-law rule that the offeror, usually the bank, may prescribe how acceptance is given, such as a specific click or confirmation step (Cap. 553 s.17(1)-(3)).

**Exclusion clauses:** The bank's customer terms cannot exclude liability for death or personal injury caused by negligence, and other exclusions of negligence liability, or of contract liability against a consumer or on the bank's written standard terms, must be reasonable, which the bank must prove (Cap. 71 s.3(6), s.7, s.8). In a consumer contract the court may also refuse to enforce an unconscionable term, and the customer must prove the unconscionability (Cap. 458 s.5).
sections.takeaway: Review each launch claim and each change to customer terms against these rules, and treat the HKMA's conduct expectations as the main control on regulated banking products (good practice).

provisions.title: Falsely representing a registered trade mark
provisions.summary: It is an offence to falsely represent that a sign is a registered trade mark, or to misdescribe the goods or services covered by a registration, if the person knows or has reason to believe the representation is false. Using 'registered' or a similar word or symbol in Hong Kong counts as a representation of registration here, unless it is shown to refer to a registration elsewhere that in fact covers the goods or services.
provisions.counselNote: Marketing teams often add a registered symbol to a brand that is only applied for or unregistered, so the marks on product pages and packaging should be reviewed before launch.

provisions.title: Use of another's mark to identify its goods or services
provisions.summary: Using a registered trade mark to identify goods or services as those of the owner or a licensee does not infringe, but use that is not in accordance with honest practices in industrial or commercial matters is treated as infringing. The court may consider unfair advantage, detriment to distinctive character or repute, and deception.
provisions.counselNote: This is the test a comparison with a competitor's product meets, so marketing copy that names a rival should be fair, accurate and free of disparagement.

provisions.title: Claiming a patent applied for
provisions.summary: A person who represents that a patent has been applied for on an article disposed of for value commits an offence where no application exists, or where it was refused, withdrawn or deemed withdrawn. Due diligence is a defence, and marking the article with those words counts as a representation.
provisions.counselNote: 'Patent pending' on a consumer device is a common launch-time marking, and it is an offence if the application does not exist or has lapsed.

provisions.title: Non-prejudicial disclosure for standard patents (R)
provisions.summary: A disclosure is disregarded for novelty only if it was made no earlier than 6 months before filing and was due to an evident abuse or a display at an official or officially recognised international exhibition (for a standard patent (R), a prescribed exhibition or meeting). The filing must state the display and include the required evidence. The same structure applies to standard patents (O) under s.37B and to short-term patents under s.109.
provisions.counselNote: A public launch, a beta programme or a conference demo before filing can destroy novelty for the feature, and the grace period will not cover it unless one of the narrow limbs applies.

provisions.title: Computer programs not registrable
provisions.summary: Computer programs and protected layout-designs are not registrable as designs. The rules may also exclude designs for articles of a primarily literary or artistic character.
provisions.counselNote: A design filing for a user interface must claim a feature applied to a physical article, which is a drafting question for the design team and counsel together (drafting inference).

provisions.title: Excluded products: regulated financial services
provisions.summary: Goods or services supplied by a person regulated under the Insurance, Banking, Mandatory Provident Fund Schemes or Securities and Futures Ordinances are excluded where their supply by that person is itself regulated under one of those Ordinances. The definition of "product" in s.2 leaves them out.
provisions.counselNote: Most of the bank's regulated products sit outside the trade description and unfair practice offences, but rewards items, merchandise and partner offers may not.

provisions.title: Misleading omissions
provisions.summary: A trader commits an offence if, in relation to a consumer, it engages in a commercial practice that omits or hides material information, or gives it in an unclear, unintelligible, ambiguous or untimely way, so that the average consumer is likely to take a transactional decision they would not otherwise take.
provisions.counselNote: Apply it to anything in the app that is not a regulated banking service, such as a partner's offer or a rewards catalogue.

provisions.title: Online formation of contracts
provisions.summary: An offer and its acceptance may be expressed by electronic records, and a contract is not invalid only because electronic records were used. The offeror may prescribe the method by which acceptance is communicated.
provisions.counselNote: Click-through terms can form a contract, and the bank can require a specific click or confirmation step. Acceptance by conduct alone is a common-law question, not covered by this section (drafting inference).

provisions.title: Negligence and contract liability
provisions.summary: Liability for death or personal injury caused by negligence cannot be excluded. Other negligence liability, and contract liability where the other party deals as consumer or on written standard terms, can be excluded or restricted only so far as the term is reasonable.
provisions.counselNote: The bank's app terms and any partner terms it offers need these limits built in, and the bank carries the burden of proving reasonableness (s.3(6)).

provisions.title: Unconscionable consumer contracts
provisions.summary: Where one party deals as consumer in a contract for the sale of goods or supply of services, the court may refuse to enforce the contract or part of it, enforce the rest, or revise the unconscionable part, judged at the time the contract was made.
provisions.counselNote: Consumer terms in a retail product can be challenged on this ground, but a business-to-business software licence would generally fall outside it (drafting inference).

bankNotes: **Generative AI features:** The HKMA's circular of 19 August 2024 applies its consumer-protection principles to customer-facing generative AI, covering governance and accountability, fairness, transparency and disclosure, and data privacy. The circular is guidance, not law, and its points are a sensible set of launch checks (good practice).
**Sandbox:** The HKMA-Cyberport GenA.I. Sandbox gives supervisory feedback but no legal exemption, so a sandbox test does not change the position under the Ordinances (drafting inference).

**Material changes:** For a designated critical infrastructure operator, a material change to the design, configuration, security or operation of a critical computer system must be notified to the regulator within 1 month (Cap. 653 s.22(1), (2)(a), (3)).

glossary.definition: A trademark application filed by a person who has a bona fide intention to use the mark in commerce but is not yet using it. Registration waits until a verified statement of use is accepted (15 U.S.C. § 1051(b)).

Using another company's mark to name that company's product, where the product cannot readily be identified without the mark. Only as much of the mark as needed is used, and nothing suggests sponsorship. Partners and integrators rely on it when they name a wallet or card scheme (good practice) (New Kids on the Block v. News America Publishing, 971 F.2d 302 (9th Cir. 1992)).

The overall look of a product or its packaging, which the law can protect as a sign of origin. Unregistered product design needs proof of secondary meaning, and a functional feature cannot be trade dress (Wal-Mart Stores v. Samara Brothers, 529 U.S. 205 (2000), reported; check).

A patent for the new, original and ornamental design of an article of manufacture, such as a display screen showing an icon or interface (35 U.S.C. § 171). The term is 15 years from grant for applications filed on or after 13 May 2015 (reported; check).

The program files that make a font work on screen or in print. A typeface as such is not protected by US copyright, but font software can be, where it has enough original authorship (reported; check). The Open Font License sets the terms for using and bundling it.

Online terms that a user accepts by clicking a button after the terms are shown with clear notice. A court enforces them where the notice is clear and the click signals assent. Terms that sit behind a link without any prompt are much weaker (Meyer v. Uber Technologies, 868 F.3d 66 (2d Cir. 2017), reported; check).

A work such as a rendered map image or a report, made by using a substantial part of a database through a search or query. Under the ODbL it needs an attribution notice, and publicly using it can trigger the share-alike duty for the database behind it (reported; check).

An internal record of a new idea that may be patentable, sent to patent counsel before any demo, beta, talk, paper or sale. The US grace period for the inventor's own disclosures is one year, but it is narrow or absent in most other markets (35 U.S.C. § 102(b)(1)(A)). Sending the record before any showing is good practice.

An assessment of whether a product or feature is likely to infringe a third party's valid patent claims, usually by a search of patents and a claim-by-claim review (good practice). Advice can matter to a willfulness claim, but relying on it can waive privilege (35 U.S.C. § 298).

Marking a product with the word 'patent' and an internet address of a free public web page that links the product to its patent number. It counts as marking under 35 U.S.C. § 287(a), so the number can sit on a product page rather than on the device or package.

The person a service provider names with the Copyright Office to receive infringement notices, so that it can use the storage safe harbour for user content. The designation must be renewed, and a lapsed one loses the safe harbour (17 U.S.C. § 512(c)(2); renewal under 37 C.F.R. § 201.38, reported; check).

A term in the customer or developer terms that licenses to the company any suggestions or ideas the user sends. It is a common way to manage the risk of a claim that an idea was used for payment (Desny v. Wilder, 46 Cal. 2d 715 (1956), reported; check).
A Hong Kong patent granted after formality examination only, lasting up to 8 years from filing if renewed after the 4th year.

A Hong Kong patent registered from a patent granted by a designated patent office outside Hong Kong (the Mainland's China National Intellectual Property Administration, the UK Intellectual Property Office, or the European Patent Office for a patent designating the UK), rather than examined in Hong Kong.

intro: **What this is:** product counsel's checklist for one new feature or product, from the first brief to the weeks after launch: its name, its screens and assets, the code, services and data it is built from, any invention in it, and what ships with it. Each step says what to check, why, who owns it and what goes on the file, with the legal force of each source on its pill.

**Start with the profile:** say what the feature involves. The list then shows only the steps that apply (a step shows when any option it depends on is picked; steps for every feature always show). Ticks, open issues and notes stay in this browser and go into the downloads.

**Where it fits:** the open source review on stage 11 covers one component in depth, the release checklist on stage 12 covers publishing code, and the diligence checklist on stage 13 covers buying software or a company. This list is the product-level pass that sends work to them.
**Model wording:** some steps carry wording to adapt (feedback terms, notices, contract clauses). It is a template to fit to the facts.

options.label: A new product or feature name
options.hint: Or a new logo, tagline or app store listing

options.label: New screens, icons, illustrations or fonts
A third-party SDK, API or online service
Data from outside the bank
options.hint: Licensed data, map data, scraped or public web data

options.label: An AI model, or AI-generated code, text or images
Content or feedback from customers or partners
A new technical method
options.hint: A new way to detect fraud, route payments or authenticate

options.label: A demo, beta, talk or paper before launch
A vendor or contractor builds part of it
A partner's brand appears in it
options.hint: Co-branding, a wallet or card scheme logo

options.label: On a website or customer portal
Customers or launches outside the US
Customers or launch in Hong Kong

phases.title: Idea and naming
phases.lede: Catch the IP questions while the feature is still a brief: what it will be called, what is new in it, and who will build it.

phases.title: Design and assets
phases.lede: Screens, icons, fonts and images come with their own rights and licences, and a competitor's look is not free to borrow.

phases.title: Code, services, data and AI
phases.lede: Most of a feature is built from other people's code, services and data, each on terms that limit what the bank may do.

phases.title: Launch
phases.lede: What ships with the feature: notices, marks, claims and the terms customers accept.

phases.title: After launch
phases.lede: Features change, feedback arrives and letters come in. Some of these reopen the review.

items.title: Triage the feature before any build starts
detail: **Eight questions:** Ask what the feature is called, what assets it uses, which code and services it runs on, what data it reads, whether it uses AI, whether it has a new method, which partners appear in it and what it claims (good practice).
**Early flags:** Mark each answer that touches IP in the feature brief, so product counsel sees it before the design is fixed (good practice).
**Approval:** The OCC expects a bank to assess the risks of a new product before launch, through its own approval process (OCC Bulletin 2017-43) (check current status).
evidence: Feature brief with IP flags
Names of the people who reviewed it, and the date

sources.label: OCC Bulletin 2017-43, New, Modified, or Expanded Bank Products and Services
sources.note: Check current status before relying on it.

items.title: Clear the name before it is announced
detail: **Search first:** Run a clearance search on the name, the logo and close variants before any announcement, app store listing or press release (good practice).
**Use decides rights:** Trademark rights arise from use in commerce, and an unregistered mark is protected under the Lanham Act (15 U.S.C. § 1125(a)).
**Record:** Keep the search results, the decision and its date on the file (good practice).
evidence: Name clearance note: searches run, results and decision
Date of the announcement decision

items.title: File an intent-to-use application before the name is public
detail: **Who may file:** A bank with a bona fide intention to use a mark in commerce may file an intent-to-use application (15 U.S.C. § 1051(b)(1)).

**Priority:** A filing to register gives nationwide priority from its date, but only if the mark registers, and it does not run against anyone who used or applied for the mark first (15 U.S.C. § 1057(c)).
**No ® yet:** No mark is registered until a verified statement of use is accepted (15 U.S.C. § 1051(d)), so the ® symbol waits for registration (USPTO TMEP § 906.02) (reported; check).
evidence: Intent-to-use filing receipt and date
Calendar entry for the statement of use deadline

sources.label: Lanham Act, application based on intent to use

items.title: Use a partner's mark only within its brand rules
detail: **Brand rules first:** Get the partner's logo rules and approval steps in writing before any mock-up goes out (good practice).

**Nominative fair use:** Naming a partner's card or wallet is nominative fair use only where the product cannot be identified without the mark, only as much of the mark as needed is used, and nothing suggests sponsorship (New Kids on the Block v. News America Publishing, 971 F.2d 302 (9th Cir. 1992)) (Toyota Motor Sales v. Tabari, 610 F.3d 1171 (9th Cir. 2010)).
**Logo lockups:** A combined logo suggests affiliation, so get written consent for it rather than relying on a reference (drafting inference).
evidence: Partner brand guide and approval record
Written consent for any logo lockup

sources.label: New Kids on the Block v. News America Publishing

items.title: Check every comparison with a competitor before it is drafted
detail: **False advertising:** A rival that is or is likely to be damaged may sue over a misstatement of a product's nature, qualities or characteristics in advertising (15 U.S.C. § 1125(a)(1)(B)). The rival must fall within the statute's zone of interests, an injury to a commercial interest in reputation or sales (Lexmark International v. Static Control Components, 572 U.S. 118 (2014)).

**Naming a rival:** Naming a rival's product in a comparison needs the same care as a partner mark: only the name needed, and no suggestion of sponsorship (New Kids on the Block v. News America Publishing, 971 F.2d 302 (9th Cir. 1992)) (drafting inference).
**Proof:** Keep the test data, the source of each figure and the date it was measured, so the claim can be defended (good practice).
evidence: Substantiation file for each claim
Approval record for the comparison

sources.label: Lexmark International v. Static Control Components

items.title: Disclose an invention to patent counsel before any demo, beta or talk
detail: **Before the demo:** Record each new method and send an invention disclosure to patent counsel before any demo, beta, talk or paper (good practice).

**US grace period:** A disclosure by the inventor, or by someone who got the subject matter from the inventor, is not prior art if it was made one year or less before filing (35 U.S.C. § 102(b)(1)(A)). A later disclosure by others of subject matter the inventor had already publicly disclosed is also excluded (§ 102(b)(1)(B)).
**Who is the inventor:** Name the people who conceived each claim. An AI system cannot be an inventor (35 U.S.C. § 100(f); Thaler v. Vidal, 43 F.4th 1207 (Fed. Cir. 2022)).
evidence: Invention disclosure with dates and contributors
Date of the first public demo, beta or talk

sources.label: Patent Act, prior art and inventor's disclosures

items.title: Consider a provisional application to fix the filing date
detail: **Low bar:** A provisional application needs no claims (35 U.S.C. § 111(b)(2)).

**Deadline:** The application is regarded as abandoned 12 months after filing unless it is converted, and a later application that claims its benefit gets its date, if filed within 12 months (35 U.S.C. § 111(b)(5); § 119(e)(1)) (reported; check).
**Timing:** The filing date is only as good as the disclosures before it: a public demo starts the one-year grace clock (35 U.S.C. § 102(b)(1)(A)) (drafting inference).
evidence: Provisional filing receipt and date
Conversion deadline entered on the docket

items.title: Check the grace period in each market before a disclosure
detail: **EU and UK:** A six-month window applies in both, but only for narrow cases: evident abuse or an official exhibition under the European Patent Convention (Art. 55(1)), and in the UK, matter obtained unlawfully or in breach of confidence as well (Patents Act 1977 s.2(4)) (reported; check).

**Hong Kong:** A disclosure within six months is disregarded only for evident abuse or an official exhibition, for standard (O) and short-term applications (Cap. 514 s.37B and s.109); for a standard patent (R) the exhibition limb covers a prescribed exhibition or meeting (s.11A).
**Canada:** A disclosure by the applicant in the year before filing is not prior art, so the bank's own early demo does not count against it (Patent Act s.28.2(1)(a)).
evidence: Market list for each launch and demo date
Patent counsel's grace period note for each market

items.title: Agree who owns vendor-built work before the work starts
detail: **Signed writing:** A transfer of copyright needs a signed writing, so code a vendor writes without one may still belong to the vendor (17 U.S.C. § 204(a)).
**Scope:** Name the deliverables, the vendor's pre-existing code and any open source it brings in, and require a list of both (good practice).
**Inventions:** Patent assignments need their own written instrument (35 U.S.C. § 261) (drafting inference).
evidence: Signed assignment or licence clause
Schedule of deliverables, pre-existing code and open source
wording: The vendor assigns to the bank all rights in the deliverables it creates for the bank under this agreement, with effect from creation, and will sign any document the bank needs to record that assignment. The vendor lists any pre-existing code and open source it includes in the deliverables.

items.title: Clear and file the product name in Hong Kong
detail: **Registration:** A registered trade mark is a property right (Cap. 559 s.10(1)). An unregistered name is protected only by passing off (s.10(3)), which is a weaker position to rely on (drafting inference), so file the name in Hong Kong before launch.
**Clashes:** An earlier registration over a similar mark for similar goods or services is the main clearance risk, so search the register for the name and close variants (good practice).
**Partner marks:** Where a partner's mark appears in the product, record the licence or consent for that use (good practice).
evidence: Name search and register result, dated
Filing decision, with the filing date or the reason for not filing

items.title: Disclose inventions only after filing
detail: **Disclosure:** A demo, pitch or release that makes the invention available to the public before filing puts it in the state of the art (Cap. 514 s.9B(2)). The six-month relief covers only an evident abuse against the applicant or a display at an official or officially recognised international exhibition (for a standard patent (R), a prescribed exhibition or meeting) (ss.11A, 37B, 109).

**Earlier filings:** An earlier application published after the new application's material date can also defeat novelty (s.9B(3)), so competitor filings should be checked before the product is shown (drafting inference).
**Order:** File before any demo to an outside party, or agree confidentiality first (good practice).
evidence: Invention disclosure record, with the date of each demo
Filing receipt, or a dated decision not to file

items.title: Know what copyright protects in a screen
detail: **Expression only:** Copyright covers the creative expression in a screen, not the idea, method or function it serves (17 U.S.C. § 102(b)).

**Menus and command structures:** The First Circuit held that the Lotus 1-2-3 menu command hierarchy is an uncopyrightable method of operation (Lotus Development Corp. v. Borland International, 49 F.3d 807 (1st Cir. 1995)) (reported; check).

**Filtering:** Courts filter out unprotectable and licensed interface elements before comparing what remains, which gives the rest only thin protection against near-verbatim copying (Apple Computer v. Microsoft, 35 F.3d 1435 (9th Cir. 1994)) (reported; check).
evidence: Design files with the author and date of each screen element
Reference list of competitor screens reviewed, with the reason

sources.label: Lotus Development Corp. v. Borland International

items.title: Do not copy a competitor's look
detail: **Secondary meaning:** Product design is protected as unregistered trade dress only on proof of secondary meaning (Wal-Mart Stores v. Samara Brothers, 529 U.S. 205 (2000)) (reported; check).

**Function:** A functional feature cannot be trade dress (TrafFix Devices v. Marketing Displays, 532 U.S. 23 (2001)), and for unregistered dress the claimant must prove the dress is not functional (15 U.S.C. § 1125(a)(3)) (reported; check).
**Independent work:** A rival's distinctive look is a risk even when the bank designs independently, so compare the design with the rival's screens before design review (good practice).
evidence: Comparison of the design with named competitor screens
Record of who approved the final look

sources.label: Lanham Act, trade dress and functionality

items.title: Consider a design patent for a distinctive screen icon
detail: **What it covers:** A design patent can protect the ornamental design of a computer-generated icon or interface shown on a display screen (35 U.S.C. § 171) (reported; check).
**Term:** The term is 15 years from grant for applications filed on or after 13 May 2015 (35 U.S.C. § 173) (reported; check).

**Drawings:** USPTO supplemental guidance from 13 March 2026 no longer requires the display screen to be drawn in solid or broken lines where the title and claim name the article (Federal Register doc. 2026-04987) (reported; check). Check the drawing rules before filing.
evidence: Drawings of the icon as shown on the screen
Filing decision, and the date the icon first appeared in public

items.title: Check the font licence before the font ships
detail: **Typeface and software:** A typeface as such is not copyright subject matter in the US (37 C.F.R. § 202.1(e)) (reported; check), but original font software can be registered as a literary work (Compendium (Third) § 723) (reported; check).

**Open Font License:** The bank may use, embed and bundle the font, but the font software cannot be sold alone, a modified version may not use a Reserved Font Name without permission, and redistributed font software must stay under the licence (OFL-1.1 conditions 1, 3 and 5).

**Output:** Documents created using the font are not subject to the licence, but an app or website that ships the font file distributes the font software, which stays under the licence (OFL-1.1, Permission and Conditions).
evidence: Font register: name, licence, version and source
Licence text kept with the design system

items.title: Check the scope of each stock image licence
detail: **Scope:** Check that the licence covers each use the bank needs: the app, the website, print, advertising and any template or resale use (good practice).
**People and marks:** Recognisable people and logos in a picture need their own releases and clearance, even when the picture is licensed (good practice).
**Record:** Keep the licence, the asset ID and the campaign it was used in, so a renewal or takedown can be answered quickly (good practice).
evidence: Licence register: asset, licensor, scope and term
Usage record for each campaign

sources.label: Stock image licence terms
sources.note: Terms vary by provider; read the licence for each asset.

items.title: Record the human contribution in AI-generated images
detail: **Registration:** Copyright Office guidance of 16 March 2023 asks applicants to disclose AI-generated material that is more than de minimis, explain the human contribution and exclude the AI material from the claim (88 Fed. Reg. 16190) (reported; check).
**Output terms:** Read the image tool's terms on who owns the output and what the vendor will defend, and note any conditions (good practice).
**Likeness and marks:** A generated image can reproduce a real person, a logo or a stock picture, so screen it like any other asset (drafting inference).
evidence: Record of the tool, version and prompts used
Note of the human changes made to each image
wording: The bank created this image with [tool]. A person chose the concept, wrote the prompts, selected the output and changed it by [describe changes]. The claim covers the human contributions only and excludes the AI-generated material.

sources.label: Copyright Registration Guidance: Works Containing AI-Generated Material

items.title: Send open source through the stage 11 review before it is built in
detail: **Route it:** Send each open source component to the open source office before any build uses it (good practice).
**Trigger:** Most open source licence duties attach on distribution or conveying, so an internal-only feature may carry fewer duties than a shipped one (GPL-3.0 s.0).

**Online use:** A network copyleft licence such as AGPL-3.0 can reach a modified service that users interact with over a network (AGPL-3.0 s.13), but GPL-3.0 s.0 says that mere interaction through a computer network is not conveying, so flag AGPL or other network copyleft code in any online feature (drafting inference).
evidence: Intake record for each component, with its licence
Routing decision from the open source office

sources.label: OpenChain (ISO/IEC 5230)
sources.note: Licence compliance programme standard; good practice.

items.title: Read SDK and API terms before the code ships
detail: **Use limits:** SDK and API terms usually restrict use, caching and data handling, and the provider can change or end them (good practice).
**Example:** Google Maps Platform terms bar caching of map content except as the service-specific terms allow (Google Maps Platform Terms of Service) (reported; check).
**Third-party risk:** The guidance covers the whole life cycle of third-party relationships, including contracting (88 Fed. Reg. 37920) (reported; check).
evidence: Terms version and date reviewed
Record of the caching and data uses in the design

sources.label: Google Maps Platform Terms of Service
sources.note: A provider's contract terms: they bind the bank as a licensee.

items.title: Accept online terms only through a process that shows assent
detail: **Assent:** Online terms bind only where the notice is reasonably conspicuous and the user takes an action that shows assent. Terms behind a link, with no sign-up step, were not enforced (Nguyen v. Barnes & Noble, 763 F.3d 1171 (9th Cir. 2014)) (reported; check).

**Clickwrap:** A sign-up screen with clear notice was enforced (Meyer v. Uber Technologies, 868 F.3d 66 (2d Cir. 2017)), while a small notice and a button that does not signal agreement failed (Berman v. Freedom Financial Network, 30 F.4th 849 (9th Cir. 2022)) (reported; check).
**Who clicks:** Route vendor sign-ups through procurement, so that the person accepting the terms has authority for the bank (good practice).
evidence: Copy of the terms accepted, with the date and the account that accepted them

sources.label: Nguyen v. Barnes & Noble; Meyer v. Uber Technologies

items.title: Do not scrape a site without its terms and the CFAA in view
detail: **CFAA:** Exceeding authorised access means obtaining information from areas of a computer that are off limits, not misusing data one is entitled to reach (Van Buren v. United States, 593 U.S. 374 (2021)) (reported; check).

**No safe harbour:** Scraping public pages was held likely not to be access without authorisation (hiQ Labs v. LinkedIn, 31 F.4th 1180 (9th Cir. 2022)), but the case then ended in a contract finding and a settlement with a permanent injunction (reported; check).
**Decision:** Use an approved data supplier or a licence where one exists, and get counsel's sign-off before any scraper goes live (good practice).
evidence: Source list with the terms reviewed and the date
Counsel sign-off for each scraper

items.title: Check the licence on map and database data
detail: **Share-alike:** A public derivative database must be offered under the ODbL or a compatible licence (ODbL-1.0 s.4.4) (reported; check).

**Produced works:** A rendered map or text made from the database needs only an attribution notice (ODbL-1.0 s.4.3), but publicly using a produced work made from a derivative database makes that database publicly used, so the share-alike then applies (ODbL-1.0 s.4.4(c)).
**Contract limits:** Where no database right or copyright applies, a contract can still limit use (Ryanair v PR Aviation, Case C-30/14 (CJEU 2015)) (reported; check).
evidence: Data licence register: source, licence, attribution text and share-alike check

sources.label: Open Data Commons Open Database License 1.0

items.title: Read the model licence as a contract
detail: **User threshold:** Meta's Llama 4 Community License needs a separate licence from Meta if, on the Llama 4 release date, the licensee had more than 700 million monthly active users in the preceding calendar month, and the licensee may not use the rights until Meta grants it (Llama 4 Community License Agreement, s.2).

**Branding:** Where Llama materials or derivatives are distributed or made available, 'Built with Llama' must be prominently displayed on a related website, user interface or product documentation (Llama 4 Community License Agreement, s.1.b.i).
**Output and use limits:** A model licence can set user thresholds and restrict outputs, so check the terms for each use before launch (good practice).
evidence: Model licence, version and date reviewed
Threshold and branding check, with the result

items.title: Keep a record of human authorship in AI-assisted code
detail: **Authorship:** The D.C. Circuit held that registration requires human authorship (Thaler v. Perlmutter, 130 F.4th 1039 (D.C. Cir. 2025); 17 U.S.C. § 102(a)). The bank should therefore document its own contribution (drafting inference).

**Copies:** An AI tool can reproduce licensed code word for word. The copy keeps its licence, so shipping it brings that licence's conditions with it, and removing notices can engage 17 U.S.C. § 1202(b) (drafting inference).

**Training data:** Early decisions point in different directions on whether training is fair use, and building a library from pirated copies is treated differently from training on lawfully acquired works (17 U.S.C. § 107).
evidence: Record of which code an AI tool wrote or changed
Licence scan of AI-suggested snippets

items.title: Run a freedom-to-operate check before a feature that may use third-party patents ships
detail: **Scope:** Check whether the new method may infringe a patent held by others by reading the claims, not only by confirming that the bank invented the method (good practice).

**Enhanced damages:** Courts may award enhanced damages, up to three times, in egregious cases of culpable, typically subjective, wilful infringement (35 U.S.C. § 284; Halo Electronics v. Pulse Electronics, 579 U.S. 93 (2016)) (reported; check).

**Opinions:** Failing to obtain or present advice of counsel cannot be used to prove wilful infringement or intent to induce infringement (35 U.S.C. § 298), but relying on an opinion can still waive privilege, and courts differ on whether the omission may be weighed in setting the amount of any enhanced damages (drafting inference).
evidence: Freedom-to-operate note with the claims checked and the date
Decision on any opinion of counsel and who holds it

items.title: Make customer terms enforceable and fair
detail: **Acceptance:** An offer and its acceptance may be expressed by electronic records (Cap. 553 s.17(1)-(2)), and s.17(3) keeps the common-law rule that the offeror, usually the bank, may prescribe how acceptance is given. Acceptance by conduct alone is a common-law question, not covered by section 17 (drafting inference).

**Exclusions:** Liability for death or personal injury from negligence cannot be excluded (Cap. 71 s.7(1)). Other exclusions must be reasonable, the bank must prove that they are (s.3(6)), and section 8 applies to consumers and written standard terms (s.8(1)-(2)).
**Unconscionability:** Relief for an unconscionable term is available only in consumer contracts for goods or services (Cap. 458 s.5(1)), so consumer terms should be fair when they are made.
evidence: Acceptance record for each user, with the version of the terms and the time of acceptance
Exclusion clause review with a note on reasonableness

items.title: Clear the name and any partner mark before the announcement
detail: **Clear the name first:** Run a search before the name is announced (good practice). A bona fide intention to use a mark in commerce is enough to file an intent-to-use application (15 U.S.C. § 1051(b)(1)). Filing gives nationwide priority from the filing date, unless someone used the mark or applied for it first (15 U.S.C. § 1057(c)).

**Use the registration notice correctly:** Use ® only once the mark is registered. A registrant that omits the notice cannot recover profits or damages unless the defendant had actual notice (15 U.S.C. § 1111). Using ® on a mark that is not registered is improper (USPTO TMEP § 906.02; reported; check).

**Use a partner's mark with care:** A wallet, card scheme or partner logo may name the partner's product, but only as much of the mark as is needed, and nothing may suggest sponsorship (New Kids on the Block v. News America Publishing, 971 F.2d 302 (9th Cir. 1992)). Follow the partner's brand rules too (good practice).
evidence: Search results and the filing decision, with dates
Partner's written approval of its logo and brand use

sources.label: New Kids on the Block v. News America Publishing
USPTO Trademark Manual of Examining Procedure

items.title: Support every comparison and performance claim before it is published
detail: **Keep the evidence:** Keep the test method, the data and the date behind each claim on file before the marketing copy is final (good practice).

**Comparisons:** A false or misleading statement about a product in commercial advertising can be challenged by a person who is or is likely to be damaged (15 U.S.C. § 1125(a)(1)(B)). The claimant must show an injury to a commercial interest in reputation or sales, and that the statement caused it (Lexmark International v. Static Control Components, 572 U.S. 118 (2014)).

**Competitor names:** Fair use of a famous mark in comparative advertising, other than as a designation of source, is not actionable as dilution (15 U.S.C. § 1125(c)(3)(A)), but a competitor's name should appear only as far as needed to identify the competitor, and never in a way that suggests the competitor backs the bank's product (good practice).
evidence: Substantiation file for each claim, dated
Approved claims list with the approver named

sources.label: Lexmark International v. Static Control Components

items.title: Ship the notices: the open source screen and the copyright line
detail: **Open source notices:** Ship each licence notice and copyright line that the open source review set for the release, in the app or its documentation. The MIT licence, for example, requires the copyright notice and the permission notice in all copies or substantial portions of the software (MIT full text).

**Copyright line:** A copyright notice is optional for works published since 1 March 1989, but a proper notice on published copies stops an infringer from relying on innocent infringement to reduce damages (17 U.S.C. § 401(d)). The notice takes three elements: the symbol, the year of first publication and the owner's name (17 U.S.C. § 401(b)).

**Keep third-party notices:** Removing a licence header or copyright line can engage 17 U.S.C. § 1202(b) where the bank knows, or has reasonable grounds to know, that infringement will follow (drafting inference).
evidence: Notices screen text and the licence list for this release
Copyright line approved by legal
wording: © [year of first publication] [bank's legal name]. All rights reserved.

items.title: Mark only what a patent covers, and never with a false patent claim
detail: **Marking:** Mark an article with a patent number only once an issued patent covers it, either on the article or through a public web address that links the article to the number (35 U.S.C. § 287(a)). Marking an unpatented article with the word 'patent' to deceive the public is prohibited (35 U.S.C. § 292(a)).

**Wording while pending:** Say 'patent pending' only while an application is pending: marking it when none is pending, to deceive the public, is false marking (35 U.S.C. § 292(a)). Add a number only once the patent issues (good practice).

**Damages and false marking:** A patentee that does not mark loses damages for the period before notice, and filing an infringement action counts as notice (35 U.S.C. § 287(a)). Only the United States may sue for the fine, but a person with a competitive injury may sue for damages (35 U.S.C. § 292(a), (b)). Marking with an expired patent is not a violation (35 U.S.C. § 292(c)).
evidence: Marking list for each product, with patent numbers and expiry dates
Web page for virtual marking, if used

items.title: File the invention disclosure before any demo, beta or talk
detail: **Disclose first:** Send an invention disclosure to patent counsel before any demo, beta, talk or paper, because a public showing can start the clock on filing (good practice). If a filing is needed quickly, a provisional application needs no claims, but it is regarded as abandoned 12 months after filing unless it is converted (35 U.S.C. § 111(b)(2), (b)(5)).

**US grace period:** A disclosure made by the inventor one year or less before the effective filing date is not prior art (35 U.S.C. § 102(b)(1)(A)). A second exception covers a later disclosure by others of subject matter the inventor had already publicly disclosed (§ 102(b)(1)(B)).

**Elsewhere the grace is narrow:** Under the European Patent Convention, a disclosure is disregarded only in narrow cases, such as evident abuse or an official exhibition (EPC Art. 54 and 55; reported; check). Hong Kong gives six months only for abuse or official exhibitions (Cap. 514 s.37B and s.109). Canada gives one year for the applicant's own disclosures (Patent Act s.28.2(1)(a)).
evidence: Invention disclosure form, with the date it was received
Filing decision, including any provisional application

items.title: Make customers accept the terms through a clear clickwrap step
detail: **Clear notice and assent:** Online terms bind a user only where the notice is reasonably conspicuous and the user takes an action that clearly shows assent. A sign-up step with a visible link and a button that says the user agrees is the usual approach (Meyer v. Uber Technologies, 868 F.3d 66 (2d Cir. 2017)) (reported; check).

**Browsewrap risk:** Terms reached only by a link at the foot of a page were not enforced in Nguyen v. Barnes & Noble, 763 F.3d 1171 (9th Cir. 2014) (reported; check). Berman v. Freedom Financial Network, 30 F.4th 849 (9th Cir. 2022), refused to enforce terms where the notice was small and the button did not signal agreement (reported; check).

**Keep the proof and review changes:** Log the terms version, the date and the screen each customer accepted, and have counsel review any redesign of the sign-up step, since the layout decides whether assent is clear (good practice).
evidence: Screen capture of the acceptance step, dated
Acceptance log showing the terms version
wording: By tapping Agree, you accept the [bank] Terms of Use and Privacy Notice.

items.title: Set up a takedown agent and a feedback clause for customer content
detail: **Designate an agent:** A hosting service qualifies for the storage safe harbour only if it has designated an agent to receive infringement notices with the Copyright Office (17 U.S.C. § 512(c)(2)). An electronic designation expires three years after registration unless it is renewed, and a lapsed designation loses the safe harbour (37 C.F.R. § 201.38; reported; check).

**Feedback clause:** Ask customers and partners to accept terms that license their suggestions to the bank. A feedback clause is a common way to manage the risk of a claim for payment for an idea, because California law can enforce such a claim where the recipient knew payment was expected (Desny v. Wilder, 46 Cal. 2d 715 (1956)) (reported; check).
**Content licence:** Take a licence to host and display customer content, and publish a route for rights holders to give notice (good practice).
evidence: Copyright Office agent designation, with its renewal date
Feedback and content clause as accepted by users
wording: By sending feedback, you give the bank a worldwide, royalty-free right to use it for any purpose, without payment or credit to you.

items.title: Check the app store rules before the app is submitted
detail: **Own or licence all content:** Apple's App Review Guidelines say an app should include only content the developer created or has a licence to use, and should not use third-party trademarks, copyrighted works or patented ideas without permission (App Review Guidelines 5.2 and 5.2.1).

**Right entity submits:** The app should be submitted by the entity that owns or licenses the intellectual property (App Review Guidelines 5.2.1). Name that entity on the listing and in the licence record (good practice).

**Open source in a store:** The Free Software Foundation holds that store terms conflict with the GPL, because they restrict redistribution that the GPL permits. That is a view, not a court ruling, and VLC was removed from the App Store in January 2011 after a complaint by a VLC contributor under the GPL, though sources disagree on whether VideoLAN itself asked for removal (reported; check).
evidence: Submission record with the owning entity named
Licence check for each open source component in the app, from the open source review

sources.label: Free Software Foundation view on the GPL in app stores
sources.note: A view, not a ruling. Reported; check.

items.title: Check marks, notices and filings in each market before a foreign launch
detail: **Registration claims:** Falsely representing a mark as registered is an offence in Hong Kong where the person knows, or has reason to believe, the claim is false (Trade Marks Ordinance (Cap. 559) s.94). In the UK, falsely representing a trade mark as registered is an offence (Trade Marks Act 1994 s.95(1)(a); reported; check). Use ® only where the mark is registered in that place (good practice); both laws excuse a reference to a registration elsewhere only if that is shown and the mark is in fact registered there for the goods or services (Cap. 559 s.94(2); Trade Marks Act 1994 s.95(2); reported; check).

**Notice and action:** EU hosting services must run notice and action mechanisms for illegal content, including IP-infringing content, and must tell the notifier whether they acted (Regulation (EU) 2022/2065 Art. 16; reported; check). Hong Kong has a notice-based safe harbour for online service providers (Copyright Ordinance (Cap. 528) ss.88A to 88J).

**Marks in Canada:** Canada has registered trademarks without prior use since 17 June 2019, so a name cleared only in the US may be taken there first (reported; check; drafting inference). Passing off is prohibited by Trademarks Act s.7(b).
evidence: Clearance note for each market
Local notice and marking list signed off by counsel

items.title: Mark AI-generated output and keep a record of AI material
detail: **Machine-readable marking:** Providers of AI systems that generate synthetic audio, image, video or text must mark the outputs in a machine-readable way (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 Art. 50(2)). The duty applies from 2 August 2026 to new systems, and generative systems already on the market have until 2 December 2026 under the 2026 Digital Omnibus (reported; check the timing).

**Copyright claims:** The Copyright Office's guidance expects applicants to disclose AI-generated content that is more than de minimis, to explain the human author's contribution, and to exclude that content from the claim (88 Fed. Reg. 16190 (16 March 2023); reported; check).
**Keep a record of AI material:** Log which screens, icons and images were AI-generated, with the tool used and the person who made the human contribution (good practice).
evidence: Marking method and its test result, for each output type
Register of AI-generated assets in the feature

items.title: Mark the product only with rights that exist in Hong Kong
detail: **Registered symbol:** Use the registered symbol only where the mark is registered in Hong Kong (good practice). Using the word 'registered' or a symbol importing registration here is treated as a representation of registration in Hong Kong, unless it is shown to refer to a registration elsewhere that in fact covers the goods or services (Cap. 559 s.94(2)).

**Patent pending:** Use 'patent pending' only where an application is on file. Otherwise it is an offence, with a level 3 fine, to represent that an application has been made (Cap. 514 s.143(1), (3)). Due diligence is a defence (s.143(4)).

**Patent marking:** Marking an item sold for value as patented when it is not is an offence, with a due diligence defence (s.142(1)-(2), (4)), so the marking review should cover packaging, the website and the app store listing (good practice).
evidence: Marking review of the packaging, website and app store listing
Application number for any 'patent pending' wording

items.title: Check comparative and service claims against Hong Kong rules
detail: **Rival products:** Naming a rival in advertising needs honest practices (Cap. 559 s.21(1)). Use of a mark outside honest practices is treated as infringing.

**Banking services:** The Trade Descriptions Ordinance offences do not reach banking services whose supply is itself regulated under the Banking Ordinance (Cap. 362 s.2, Sch. 4). For those products the HKMA's conduct expectations do that work (drafting inference).

**Other products:** Non-regulated services, and services that partners not regulated under those Ordinances supply, stay within the offences, so each claim must be checked against the product it describes (good practice).
evidence: Claims review with the source for each comparison
Note of which products are Banking Ordinance services and which are not

items.title: Reopen the review when a dependency, licence, market or model changes
detail: **Triggers:** Reopen the feature review when a new SDK, API or open source component is added, when an upstream licence changes, when the feature goes to a new market, or when the AI model is swapped (good practice).
**Route new components:** Send any new open source component through the open source review on stage 11 before it ships, and keep the approval with the release record (good practice).
**Keep a dated log:** Record each change and the outcome of its review, so the bank can show later who approved what and when (good practice).
evidence: Change log for the feature, with dates
Re-review record and outcome for each trigger

sources.label: OpenChain (ISO/IEC 5230)
sources.note: Licence compliance programme standard; good practice.

items.title: Send infringement and takedown letters to counsel the same day
detail: **Same-day routing:** Send any infringement or takedown letter to counsel on arrival, including a takedown notice for user content, so that counsel can decide the response before any deadline in the letter runs (good practice).

**Section 230 is no shield:** Section 230 does not limit any law pertaining to intellectual property (47 U.S.C. § 230(e)(2)), so it gives no general shield against IP claims over user content. Circuits differ on state-law IP claims: the Ninth Circuit reads the carve-out as federal IP only (Perfect 10, Inc. v. CCBill LLC, 488 F.3d 1102 (9th Cir. 2007)), while the Third Circuit held that a state publicity claim is not immunised (Hepp v. Facebook, 3d Cir. 2021) (reported; check).

**Outside the US:** EU hosts must run notice and action mechanisms and tell the notifier whether they acted (Regulation (EU) 2022/2065 Art. 16; reported; check). Canada's notice-and-notice regime requires an intermediary to forward a claimant's notice to the user, without a duty to remove the content (Copyright Act ss. 41.25 to 41.27; reported; check).
evidence: Letter log with the date received and the owner
Response and decision recorded for each notice

items.title: Check model licence terms and vendor indemnities at each model change
detail: **Model licence limits:** Meta's Llama 4 Community License requires a licensee that, on the Llama 4 release date, had more than 700 million monthly active users in the preceding calendar month to request a separate licence from Meta, and until Meta grants it the licensee may not exercise the licence rights (Llama 4 Community License s.2). Where Llama materials or derivatives are made available, 'Built with Llama' must be displayed prominently (s.1.b.i).

**Vendor indemnities:** Vendor AI indemnities, such as Microsoft's Copilot Copyright Commitment, Google's generative AI indemnity and OpenAI's Copyright Shield, apply only on conditions, such as use of built-in guardrails or certain paid tiers (reported; check). Read the conditions before relying on one.
**A new model is a new review:** A model swap can change the licence, the indemnity and the output marking, so counsel reviews it before the switch (good practice).
evidence: Licence and indemnity terms for each model version
List of indemnity conditions and whether the bank meets each one

items.title: Check data and map licences after launch and before any public database
detail: **Share-alike on public databases:** Under the ODbL 1.0, a derivative database that is publicly used must be offered under the ODbL or a compatible licence (ODbL-1.0 s.4.4). A produced work, such as a rendered map image, needs only the attribution notice (ODbL-1.0 s.4.3).

**Scraped and public web data:** Under the CFAA, a person exceeds authorized access by getting into areas that are off limits to them, not by misusing information they are entitled to reach (Van Buren v. United States, 593 U.S. 374 (2021); reported; check). Scraping terms bind only where notice and assent exist (drafting inference).

**Map caching limits:** Map terms can limit caching and data use, and the provider can change them. Google Maps Platform terms, for example, bar caching except as their service-specific terms allow (reported; check).
evidence: Data licence register with caching and share-alike limits
Share-alike check for any public database or export

items.title: Run a takedown process for user content
detail: **Safe harbour:** A service provider is not liable for damages for copyright infringement on its platform merely because it provides online services, if it meets the conditions in s.88B, such as taking reasonable steps once it is aware or notified (Cap. 528 s.88B(1)-(2)).
**Notices:** Notices and counter-notices must meet ss.88C and 88E, and a provider that shows evidence of compliance is presumed to comply, unless there is evidence to the contrary (s.88I).
**Record:** Keep a log of each takedown notice, action and counter-notice, with dates, so that compliance can be shown (good practice).
evidence: Takedown log showing each notice, the action taken and its date
